Don Joaquín Velázquez de León, Advocate of Causes in the Royal Audiencia of Mexico, formerly Public Professor of Mathematics in the Illustrious University, and Literary Member of the Royal Cantabrian Society of the Friends of the Country, gave this opinion.

> EXCELLENTISSIME DOMINE.

M O S T E XC E L L E N T L O R D.

The volumes which were brought to me by Your command, bearing this title, Elements of the Newer Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri — when I had turned through them, I wondered at the Author’s labor, diligence, alacrity, brevity. For it is scarcely credible to say how much he himself, how learnedly, how vigorously he has labored to instruct Youth in Philosophy (in a philosophy that truly deserves to be called by the name of philosophy)! So far, indeed, are these School Institutions themselves from thrusting upon us anything adverse or hostile either to morals, which ought to be kept uncorrupted, or to the most holy laws, that in my judgment (if I may be permitted to discern anything,

> VOlumina, quae jussu Vestro ad me adlata sunt, hunc inscripta titulum RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE ELEMENTA á P. Doct. D. Johanne Benedicto Diaz de Gamarra & Davalos Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Presbytero Seculari quum evolverim, miratus sum Auctoris laborem, diligentiam, alacritatem, brevitatem. Vix enim credibile dictu est, quàm multa ipse, quàm eruditè, quàm ad Juventutem in Philosophia (quae verè philosophiae nomine adpellanda sit) erudiendam, strenuè operam navarit! Tantum verò abest, ut Scholares Institutiones ipsae hae aliquid, aut moribus quos incorruptos esse decet, aut sanctissimis legibus adversum atque inimicum obtrudant; ut me judice, (si quid cernere mi [PDF 10] hi licet, non admodum mediocriter versato) via haec, & ratio tradendae Philosophiae, cum vera germanaque, saepè â praeclarissimis Viris cooptatâ, & qualem hac tempestate apud nostrates, jussu Regio, Hispanae Academiae jam pridem sectatae sunt, plurimum consentiat. Quae quum ita sint, Princeps Excellentissime, nihil causae subest, quamobrem horum Elementorum per typos evulgatiò prohibeatur. Ita equidem censeo. Dat. Mexici postrid. Non. Septemb. anno D. 1774.

¶ [PDF 10] being not altogether indifferently versed in these matters) this way and method of teaching Philosophy agrees very closely with the true and genuine one, often adopted by most distinguished Men, and such as the Spanish Universities among our countrymen have long since followed in these times by Royal command. This being so, Most Excellent Prince, there is no reason why the publication of these Elements in print should be forbidden. Such, at least, is my opinion. Given at Mexico, on the day after the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord 1774.

> Joachimus Velasquez de Leon.

> EXCMÔ. SR.

Having seen the Books which, by superior command of Your Excellency, were sent to me with this Title: Rudiments of the Modern Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, I admired the labor of the Author, his diligence, his comprehensiveness, and at the same time the concision with which he writes. Indeed, it can scarcely be believed what a variety of things the Father Doctor has taken up, with how much erudition, and how earnestly he has undertaken this labor in order to instruct Youth in a Philosophy that well deserves this name! And these School Institutions are so far from including anything opposed either to the Laws of the Kingdom or to the integrity and purity of morals, that, on the contrary, in my opinion (if I may give one in these subjects, in which I am not without some experience) this method of teaching Philosophy agrees closely with the true one, which has always been desired by the Authors of better doctrine

> HAviendo visto los Libros, que por Superior mandato de V. Exciá. se me remitieron con este Titulo: RUDIMENTOS DE LA MODERNA FILOSOFIA, por el P. Dr. D. Juan Benito Diaz de Gamarra y Davalos Presbytero Secular de la Congregacion del Oratorio de San Felipe Neri: admiré el trabajo del Autor, su diligencia, la generalidad, y al mismo tiempo la concision con que escribe. En efecto, apenas puede creerse, quanta variedad de cosas el P. Dr. con quanta erudicion, y quan seriamente se haya tomado este trabajo para instruir á la Juventud en una Filosofia, que merece bien este nombre! Y están tan lexos estas Instituciones Escolares de incluir algo, que se oponga, ô â las Leyes del Reyno, ô â la integridad, y pureza de las costumbres; que antes bien en mi dictamen (si puedo darlo en estos asuntos, en que no dejo de estár algo versado) este metodo de enseñar Filosofia conviene mucho con el verdadero, que han deseado siempre los Autores de mejor doctri [PDF 12] na y gusto, y que en este tiempo se ha comenzado yá â poner en practica en las Universidades de nuestra España de orden del Rey Nuestro Señor. Por lo qual, nada hallo, Señor Excelentissimo, que impida la impresion, y publicacion de esta Obra. Asì lo juzgo. Mexico, y Septiembre 6. de 1774.

> JUssu Congregationis Michaelopolitanae, summâ ope nisus sum, ut volumina haec duo, quibus titulo est Elementa Recentioris Philosophiae, quantâ maximè potui adtentione perlegerem. Verebar autem, ne praejudicio magis, & Clariss. Auctoris (quo cum conjunctissimè vivere jam pridem coeperam) existimatione, quàm jure meritò de hoc opere sentirem. At ingenuè fateor, me in eo totum fuisse, ut superciliosi censoris, non putidi efrontisque laudatoris personam agerem. Itaque postquam diu multumque cogitavi, quid tandem mihi eamobrem scribendum esset, & ad Conscriptos Familiae nostrae Patres deferendum: en pauca haec animo ocurrebant, quae censurae loco erunt. Theology, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri of San Miguel el Grande.

At the bidding of the Congregation of San

Miguel I have striven with all my might to read through, with the greatest attention I could, these two volumes whose title is Elements of the Newer Philosophy. I feared, however, lest I should judge of this work more from prejudice and from my esteem for its most distinguished Author (with whom I had long since begun to live in the closest intimacy) than by right and deservedly. But I frankly confess that I gave myself wholly to playing the part of a supercilious censor, not of a fulsome and shameless praiser. And so, after I had long and much considered what in the end I ought to write on this account and lay before the Conscript Fathers of our Family, behold, these few things came to mind, which will serve in place of a censure. First, indeed, that our countryman, Father Doctor Don Juan Benito, has hit the nail on the head, in that under the name of Philosophy he has brought together for the benefit of the young not an empty fallacy, by deceiving, but a doctrine of the first utility, by teaching. For these Elements

> [PDF 16]

[PDF 16] of the Newer Philosophy seem to me to embrace, with wonderful brevity and clarity, and likewise in wonderful order, whatever the English, the French, the Dutch, the Italians and the Spaniards, earnestly intent upon philosophical matters through long decades of years, have searched out. The young beginner will certainly find here a great many things duly treated which he would seek elsewhere in vain; unless, having grown older, he devotes himself strenuously for the rest of his life (which happens to very few indeed) to Philosophy and to books, of which we have no great supply. But if anyone should compare those little questions so often debated, On Prescissions, On the Being of Reason, On the Appetite of Matter, On the Categorematic Infinite, or others far emptier still, which the Author knowingly and prudently passed over, with the disquisitions he has briefly written out On God, One and Existing, On the Immortality of Souls, On Virtue, On Duties, and on many others of that kind: he will, by Hercules, perceive which of them are better able to pave and smooth the way both to the right instruction of boys and to Sacred Theology. And truly, so the matter stands. For neither the right Instruction of boys, nor the duties of civil life, nor the science of corporeal nature, nor the best arts (nay, not even the cobbler’s,

> haec Recentioris Philosophiae mira brevitate, perspicuitate, miro item ordine complecti mihi videntur, quidquid Angli, Galli, Hollandi, Itali, Hispani, per longas annorum decadas seriò in rem philosophicam intenti, perquisivêre. Comperiet utique tyro Juvenis quamplurima hìc, ritè tractata, quae frustrà alibi requirat; nisi adolescentior factus, in reliqua vita [quod paucis admodùm contingit] strenuam Philosophiae, ac libris, quorum non multa nobis copia fit, operam dabit. Quod si quaestiunculas illas, toties agitari solitas, De Praescissionibus, De Ente rationis. De Materiae appetitu, De Infinito cathegorematico, aliasve multò vaniores, quas Auctor sciens prudensque praetermisit, cum disceptationibus à se breviter exaratis De Deo Uno existente, De Animorum immortalitate; De Virtute, De Officiis, deque multis id genus aliis, quisquam compararit: is mehercule sentiet, utrae magis ad rectam puerorum institutionem, tùm ad Sacram Theologiam viam sternere, ac complanare queant. Profectò verò res ita se habet. Non enim recta puerorum Institutio, non vitae civilis officia, non scientia rerum naturae corporeae, non artes optimae (imò ne sutoria

> [PDF 17]

[PDF 17] although it is commonly held the most illiberal of all), nor finally Sacred Theology, can be helped or increased by those very trifles which we have mentioned above. Let men, then, otherwise most grave, cease to weep whole days and nights over the burial of the Summulae and the Categories, and over the felled Porphyrian Tree, as though it were all over with the commonwealth, with themselves too and their children, with altars and hearths. This is most ridiculous, and is to be met not with much bile but rather with phlegm, that is, with laughter. Wherefore my opinion is this: that the Fathers of our Congregation ought in no way to hinder these volumes from being committed to the press, since the Author has most diligently excerpted from every side, compiled and explained a doctrine both sound and useful; and that it will be of advantage and profit to the young men who will apply themselves to Philosophy among us, I for my part in no way doubt. Given at San Miguel el Grande, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the Year mdcclxxiv.

> quidem, quum illiberalissima omnium haberi soleat), non denique Sacra Theologia, ipsis iis nugis, quas supra commemoravimus, juvari augerive possunt. Desinant ergo Viri, alioquin gravissimi, totos dies noctesque consepultis Summulis, Cathegorijs, atque praecisae Arbori Porphyrianae illachrymari, quasi actum porrhò esset de republica, de se quoque liberisque suis, de aris atque focis. Quod perridiculum est, nec multâ tamen bile, sed pituitâ magis, hoc est, risu excipiendum. Quare ita censeo: nihil morari Patres Congregationis nostrae debere, ut volumina haec typis mandari sinant, quum & sanam, & utilem doctrinam Auctor diligentissimè undique excerptam, congesserit, explanárit: quod Juvenibus, qui apud nos Philosophiae operam dabunt, commodo atque emolumento fore, nullus equidem dubito. Dabam Michaelopoli X. Kal. Majas Ann. MDCCLXXIV.

Whereas the Elements of the Newer Philosophy, prepared for the use of the Salesian College by Father Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Deputy Priest of our Congregation and Rector of the same College, have been examined by our order, and nothing is found in them out of harmony with right morals, or contrary to the Faith, to Religion and to the Royal Ordinances, but rather they are judged most apt for governing morals, for defending the Faith and Religion, and finally for instructing Youth in a wholesome and useful Philosophy, we grant permission that they be committed to the press, if it shall so seem good to those to whom the rest pertains. In witness whereof we have ordered these present letters, signed by our hand and fortified with the Seal of our Congregation, to be dispatched at San Miguel el Grande from the House of the Congregation, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the Year of Restored Salvation mdcclxxiv.

¶ N. B. The names of the most learned Doctors and Fathers have been written down in precisely that order which the Illustrious University of Mexico has hitherto observed, so that (saving the precedence of the Faculties and Sciences) he who is prior in time is also prior in right and in place. As for the Sacred Families of the Orders, exactly the same custom has been retained as is publicly observed in Academic Disputations. We acknowledge, meanwhile, that some most distinguished Men, on account of their dignity and their ornaments of honor, some more eminent than others, ought perhaps to have been listed otherwise: which was not ours to do, nor indeed a thing to be done rashly.

## To the Youth of America

> JUVENTUTI AMERICANAE

Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra sends greetings and his lucubrations.

> Jo. Bened. Diaz Gamarra S. vigiliasque.

Your cause, all of you, is at stake, young men of most excellent talent, fitted beyond other nations for the Sciences. It is your cause that is now at stake. For I did not wish these pages to be written for, or dedicated to, learned Men who think they have attained Philosophy, such as it is, by the labor of two years (and not very strenuous labor at that); nor to those who all day long pronounce from the School’s lectern, as from a tripod, on matters exceedingly difficult and not equally well known to themselves (*). But to you, young men, who are now for the first time approaching these sacred rites, and who are about to enter, when at length it may be allowed, the citadel of human Philosophy, than which nothing can be more delightful.

> VEstra omnium res agitur, Juvenes ingenio praestantissimi, & praeter ceteras gentes ad Scientias comparati. Vestra nunc res agitur. Neque enim doctis ego Viris, qui se Philosophiam, qualem illam cunque biennii labore ( nec admodùm improbo ) adsequutos esse arbitrantur; neque verò iis haec conscripta volui, & nuncupata, qui totos dies ê suggestu Scholari tanquam ex trípode, de rebus multò difficillimis, non item multò sibi compertissimis (*), pronunciant. Sed vobis, Juvenes, qui sacra haec primùm adoriemini, humanae Philosophiae, quî nihil jucundius esse potest, arcem, ubi aliquando tandem liceat, ingressuri.

To you, great hope of our Country, I submit these Institutions of the Newer Philosophy, excerpted, very briefly indeed, from here and there; and I would give you far other things, and a good many of them, were the course of the Schools not so short, which by custom you must run through. But come, and since it was for your

> Vobis, magna Patriae spes, Recentioris Philosophiae Institutiones, brevissimè quidem hinc inde excerptas subjicio, longè alia daturus, benè multa, nisi adeò breve curriculum Scholae esset, quod de more vobis est percurrendum. Age verò, & quoniam

sake

> (*) Cl. Melch. Cano Lib. VIII. de Loc. Theolog. [PDF 25] vestri gratiâ hoc muneris ac laboris susceptum est, quid scribendo praestiterim, aut saltem conatus fuerim, paucis accipite.

(*) The renowned Melchor Cano, bk. VIII of De locis theologicis. [PDF 25] sake that this task and labor were undertaken, hear in a few words what I have accomplished in writing, or at least have attempted.

> Principio enim, Philosophiae quam adgredimini, *Historiam*, breviusculè exaratam in ipso Institutionum limine, etiam atque etiam vobis commendo. Ipsam perlegite, volvite, meditamini, ac reputate cum animis vestris, quanti momenti futura sit ad Philosophiam ipsam rectè atque ordine perdiscendam. Nam ubi nescias, quid Philosophia sit, sub quibus Auctoribus nata, quousque apud majores nostros, & quo tandem in pretio habita, quae fata, qui progressus, quae via ratioque docendi; omninò fieri non potest quin passim turpiter erres. Cujus erroris genus non aliud magis, meâ quidem sententiâ, cavendum vitandumque est; quàm eorum, quibus hoc unum ad veram philosophiam refertur, quod pueri imberbesque ipsi didicerint; cetera pro nihilo ducunt, quasi vana fingentis aegri somnia essent. Quocirca meritò ridentur.

First of all, then, I commend to you again and again the History of the Philosophy you are entering upon, set down rather briefly at the very threshold of the Institutions. Read it through, turn it over, meditate on it, and weigh in your minds how important it will be for learning Philosophy itself thoroughly, correctly and in due order. For if you do not know what Philosophy is, under what Authors it was born, how far and in what esteem it was held among our forebears, what its fortunes were, what its progress, what its way and method of teaching, it cannot possibly be that you will not err shamefully at every turn. And no kind of error, in my opinion at least, is more to be guarded against and avoided than that of those for whom this alone counts as true philosophy, what they themselves learned as beardless boys; everything else they hold as nothing, as though it were the empty dreams of a sick man’s fancy. For which reason they are deservedly laughed at.

Others, however, and indeed very many in these times, are so delighted both by Aristotle and, above all, by what, under the name of so great

> Alios autem, & quidem plurimos hac tempestate, cùm Aristoteles, tùm vero quae [PDF 26] tanti Viri nomine ( nam ultro fatemur, summum utique virum fuisse ) vulgò in Scholis venditantur, adeò delectant, ut seriò adfirment, non aliud aptius commodiusve ad exacuenda puerorum ingeniola, & ad Sacram Theologiam dissertè atque eruditè tradendam inveniri unquam posse, quàm exercitamenta illa sempiterna, concertationes, logomachias *De Universalibus*, *De Ente rationis*, *De Formis substantialibus*; *De Unione*, *& toto Composito*, & sexcentis id genus aliis, quibus ingenia torquentur quidem, adteruntur; at timeo nè nihilo acutiora fiant ad sapientiae studium, & optimas disciplinas, quò nostra omnis vis ac cogitatio, tanquam ad scopum, collimare debet. ¿Ecquid autem, amabo, vanissima illa Mahumedanorum *Avicennae*, *Averrois*, *Alpharabii*, & reliquae Arabum turbae interpretamenta, ad veram religionem, ad Christi Ecclesiam, ad Sacram denique Theologiam emolumenti adferre poterunt? Scilicet venerandi Ecclesiae Patres, majores nostri, nunc apud Caelites Conscripti, *Dionysius Areopagita*, *Ephremus*, *Irenaeus*, *Cyprianus*, *Athanasius*, *Epiphanius*, *uterque Gregorius*,

¶¶¶ [PDF 26] a Man (for we freely admit that he was certainly a very great man), is commonly peddled in the Schools, that they seriously affirm that nothing fitter or more convenient could ever be found for sharpening the little wits of boys, and for teaching Sacred Theology eloquently and learnedly, than those everlasting exercises, the disputes and logomachies On Universals, On the Being of Reason, On Substantial Forms, On the Union and the Whole Composite, and six hundred others of that kind, by which minds are indeed tortured and worn down; but I fear they grow no sharper for the pursuit of wisdom and for the best disciplines, at which all our strength and thought ought to aim, as at a target. And what profit, pray, will those utterly empty interpretations of the Mahometans Avicenna, Averroes, Alfarabi, and the rest of the Arab throng be able to bring to the true religion, to the Church of Christ, and finally to Sacred Theology? No doubt the venerable Fathers of the Church, our forebears, now Fathers Conscript among the dwellers in heaven, Dionysius the Areopagite, Ephrem, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Athanasius, Epiphanius, both Gregories, Chrysostom,

[PDF 27]

Basil, Leo, Hilary, Prosper, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, did not themselves also either defend the Church, or discourse on Theological matters, or rout the profane innovators, the Heretics. On the contrary, they did so above all: for their golden volumes bear witness to it. And yet one would look for Aristotle there in vain. Not that these very great men were ignorant of dialectic and syllogisms, or ordered them banished altogether when matters of the very gravest weight were to be treated or debated: a thing which, had it been done, would have been done quite rashly and heedlessly (yet it was not done by them), and which we would by no means imitate, since the subtleties of syllogisms do not so greatly displease us. But, as I judge, admonished by the saying of Paul, where he says: Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit, these most Holy Men resolved, in holiness, to treat all those things which pertain, by God’s revelation, to holiness of life and to everlasting beatitude: from which, assuredly, the whole Philosophy of the Heathen is all but alien. Let them cease, therefore, to deafen our ears, and even to tear us and ours to pieces with abuse, who think they cannot approach Sacred Theology

> *Chrysostomus*, *Basilius*, *Leo*, *Hilarius*, *Prosper*, *Ambrosius*, *Hieronymus*, *Augustinus*, non ipsi quoque aut Ecclesiam tutati sunt, aut de rebus Theologicis disseruere, aut prophanos novatores Haereticos profligârunt. Imo verò maximè: id enim aurea volumina testantur. Atqui frustra quisquam ibi Aristotelem requirat. Non quòd summi viri dialecticen & syllogismos ignorârint, aut penitus exulare jusserint, dum esset de rebus multò gravissimis agendum, disceptandumvè: id quod omninò temerè atque oscitanter factum ( nec tamen ab iis factum ) nos haudquaquam imitaremur, quippè quibus syllogismorum acumina non adeò displicent. Sed, ut ego arbitror, Pauli effato commonefacti, dum ait: *Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam, & inanem fallaciam*, Sanctissimi Viri sanctè sibi tractanda omnia voluerunt, quae ad vitae sanctimoniam, & sempiternam beatitudinem, Deo revelante, pertinerent: à quibus profectò parum abest, quin tota Ethnicorum Philosophia abhorreat. Desinant ergo nobis aures obtundere, maledictis etiam nos nostraque lacerare, qui se non antè Sacram Theologiam [PDF 28] adgredi posse putant, quàm integras quaestiuncularum centurias in discrimen vocaverint. Nisi fortean ii ( quod vehementer equidem suspicor, doleoque ) non Sacram denique Theologiam, quae divina prorsus scientia est; sed Theologiae fumum atque umbram consectantur, nubem pro Junone amplexati, quod est in proverbio.

¶¶¶2 [PDF 28] until they have called whole hundreds of petty questions into contest. Unless perhaps these men (as I strongly suspect, and grieve) are pursuing not, after all, Sacred Theology, which is an altogether divine science, but the smoke and shadow of Theology, having embraced a cloud for Juno, as the proverb has it.

> At enimvero, inquies, Divum Albertum cognomento Magnum, Divum THOMAM AQUINATEM, ( ut nihil interim de Div. Johanne Damasceno ) Divum quoque Bonamventuram, ceterosque recentioris aevi Theologos, Sapientissimos Viros, consilio, maturitate, moribus spectabiles, Petrum Lombardum, Scotum, Halesium, multos in disceptando fuisse, non operosas quaestiones, non syllogismos, non Aristotelem dedignatos: cui Philosopho auctoritatem plurimam quòd saepè tribuerint, non ideò tamen quasi inferioris subsellii Philosophos, ac minimè dissertos Theologos, tantos Viros jure quisquam reprehendat. ¿Nonnè compertissima haec sunt, & posita ante omnium oculos, meridie ipso clariora? Ajo. Sed quoniam ejus rei men-

But surely, you will say, St. Albert, surnamed the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas (to say nothing for the moment of St. John Damascene), St. Bonaventure too, and the other Theologians of the more recent age, Most Wise Men, admirable for counsel, maturity and character, Peter Lombard, Scotus, Alexander of Hales, were much given to disputation, and did not disdain laborious questions, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle: and because they often attributed very great authority to this Philosopher, no one could rightly reproach such great Men on that account, as though they were Philosophers of a lower bench and Theologians of little eloquence. Are not these things most certain, and set before the eyes of all, clearer than noonday itself ? I grant it. But since mention of this matter

> [PDF 29]

[PDF 29] has come up, and it calls for circumspect and well-considered speech, let us, if you please, pursue the matter in order.

> tio incidit, circunspecto autem maturèque dicto opus est: rem, si placet, ordine persequamur.

As for St. Thomas (for of all the others I must speak afterwards), no mortal ever embraced more, none more skillfully, more learnedly, more temperately, none more briefly, all the things that seemed to bear upon Sacred Theology, or could in any way be referred to it. Immortal God! what genius the Man had! what abundance in disputation! how constant, how great his diligence in unrolling the volumes of the Sacred Page! how he revered the Holy Fathers of the Church! how incredible and almost divine that acumen of his altogether Angelic mind in discerning the most difficult things! what candor in writing, what method in teaching, what severity in judging! You might truly say (as Cicero had said before, in a matter not very unlike) that the books of St. Thomas Aquinas, and especially that Theological Summa, though all should roar against it, far and greatly surpass the libraries of all the Theologians, both in the abundance of the greatest matters and in the strength of authority. For St. Thomas

> Ad Divum THOMAM quod adtinet, ( nam de ceteris omnibus posteà dicendum ) nemo unquam mortalium plura, nemo solertiùs, eruditiùs, temperatiùs, nemo breviùs omnia complexus est, quae ad Sacram Theologiam spectare, aut quoquo pacto referri posse viderentur. ¡Deus immortalis! quale Viro ingenium! quanta disceptandi copia! quàm adsidua, quàm multa in evolvendis Sacrae Paginae voluminibus diligentia! quàm fuit ille veritus Sanctos Ecclesiae Patres! quàm incredibile ac penè divinum ejus, cernendo difficillima, acumen illud mentis prorsùs Angelicae! quis in scribendo candor, quae docendo méthodus, severitas in judicando! Verè utique dixeris ( id quod in re satis absimili Cicero prior dixerat ) Divi THOMAE AQUINATIS libros, ac praesertim SUMMAM illam THEOLOGICAM, omnium Theologorum bibliothecas, fremant omnes licet, & maximarum rerum ubertate, & auctoritatis róbore longè multumque superare. Plura enim Div.

> [PDF 30]

[PDF 30] brought into Theology, with his immortal and more than Sallustian brevity, more things, exceedingly learned and most worth knowing, than most others even desired. And this outstanding praise of St. Thomas as a Theologian remains, and will remain as long as learning is held in honor. But if at times (for I return to the point from which I had digressed) he is wont in disputing to attribute authority to Aristotle, he did so unwillingly indeed, where Sacred Doctrine was in question. Unless you would have it that so great a Man was so dull of wit, so inept too and heedless, that what he had deliberately laid down in the preceding pages, namely in Art. VIII of Quest. I, about diminishing the authority of all save that of divine revelation, made to the Apostles and Prophets who wrote the Canonical Books, he himself afterwards weakened on purpose by his own example. But if the question concerns St. Thomas not as Theologian but plainly as Philosopher, remember that it is not now that Thomas Aquinas, the light and ornament of the Church, but a Heathen Philosopher (lately made pious from impious), Aristotle by name, who is making trouble for you, a trouble which will amount to next to nothing.

> THOMAS immortali suâ & plusquàm Sallustianâ brevitate in rem Theologicam invexit, adprimè erudita, ac scitu dignissima, quàm plerique ceteri concupiverunt. Haec autem Divum THOMAM *Theologum* egregia laus manet, manebitque quandiù scientiae honos erit. Quòd si interdum ( nam eò, unde discesseram, redeo ) Aristoteli auctoritatem tribuere disceptando solet, invitus quidem fecit, ubi de Sacra Doctrina ageretur. Nisi velis, summum Virum adeò hebetem ingenio, adeò etiam ineptum atque oscitantem fuisse, ut quae consultò in superioribus, *Art.* nimirum *VIII. Quaest.* I. statuerat, de minuenda omnium auctoritate praeterquam divinae revelationis, Apostolis & Prophetis factae, qui Canonicos Libros scripserunt; eadem postèa exemplo suo ipsemet, datâ operâ infirmaret. Sin verò de Divo THOMA, non Theologo, sed planè *Philosopho*, quaeritur, mementote, non jam THOMAM illum AQUINATEM Ecclesiae lumen atque ornamentum; sed Ethnicum ( ex impio pium recens factum ) Philosophum, nomine *Aristotelem*, negotium vobis facéssere, quod propemodùm

[PDF 31]

> nullum erit. ¿Nam quotusquisque nescit, Angelicum Doctorem repurgâsse quidem Peripateticam Philosophiam, sexcentis passim erroribus commaculatam, ceterùm quod reliquum erat, non idcircò firmum, ratum, sanctum denique fore voluisse, nisi quod invicta ratio suadéret? ¿Ubinam ergo sunt, qui nos de oppugnato laesove Divo THOMA toties postulârunt? praepósteri homines, quibus satiùs multò fuisset strenuam operam in legendo Divum THOMAM navâsse, quod minimè isti faciunt; quàm sedentibus otiosisque, per summam ignaviam, quae nè adtigére quidem, aut certe non adsequuntur, ludibrio, joco esse. Sed haec hactenus.

For how few do not know that the Angelic Doctor did indeed purge the Peripatetic Philosophy, stained everywhere with six hundred errors, but that he did not on that account wish what remained to be firm, ratified, and in a word sacrosanct, except what unconquered reason urged? Where, then, are those who have so often arraigned us for attacking or injuring St. Thomas? Perverse men, for whom it would have been far better to have spent strenuous effort in reading St. Thomas, which is the last thing they do, than, sitting idle, out of utter sloth, to make a mockery and a jest of things they do not even touch, or at least do not grasp. But enough of this.

> Venio nunc ad reliqua: nimirùm Divi *Jo. Damascenus*, *Antoninus*, *Albertus*, *Bonaventura*: Doctores post hominum memoriam praeclarissimi, *Scotus*, *Halesius*, ( nam Episcopo Parisiensi alia mens fuerat ) neque quaestiones, hoc est, ancipites illas controversias multùm in Scholis agitari sólitas, neque syllogismos, neque Aristotelem aspernantur. ¿An verò nos aspernamur, aut disceptationibus Scholae bellum indicimus? I come now to the rest: namely Sts. John Damascene, Antoninus, Albert, Bonaventure, Doctors most illustrious within the memory of man, Scotus, Hales (for the Bishop of Paris had been of another mind), do not spurn questions, that is, those doubtful controversies much agitated in the Schools, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle. And do we, then, spurn them, or declare war on the disputations of the School? Assuredly

> [PDF 32]

[PDF 32] the thing speaks for itself: we too have humored our age, and our Masters, who are held in great esteem among our countrymen, embracing questions, syllogisms, and finally Aristotle himself, where he seemed to judge rightly; but all of it, as far as our strength and our want of skill allowed, soberly, prudently, temperately. For the very pursuit of brevity, which ought to have been our whole care and concern, would have compelled us to restrain the pen, even had it otherwise been worth the trouble to write much more, lest we overwhelm our young recruits.

And since we have set forth enough so far, by way of our defense, lest anyone (as usually happens) should take our silence for a bad conscience, it remains for us to add briefly something about the plan of our work. And first, we present to you a philosophy that is not the common one, set down in a style a little more polished than that in which it is commonly taught, and that both as concisely as could be done and also as plainly as possible, and complete in every respect: so that I would be persuaded that I had done something like a marvel, had not nearly everything come from all the best

Philosophers of the newer age, culled with great labor and likewise with the utmost fidelity. This alone I rightly claim for myself, judging that no ordinary diligence was needed even for that very task: and therefore that you, young men, will one day render me no small thanks, if not while I live, then at least when I am dead. For what? I turned over more than a hundred volumes, and not carelessly either, before I set my hand to writing these Elements. I surveyed everything with my own eyes; I resolved to grow pale over papers day and night, so as to provide for our Youth. What more? My leisure [if God, Best and Greatest, leaves any to those who labor without rest for Christ Jesus], my home in my sweet Country; money, a sum large enough, which I have spent; and, what mortals are wont to hold dearer, my reputation and the good opinion of my name (since I am arraigned before the ignorant crowd as guilty of overthrowing Philosophy and the ancestral religion of our forefathers): all these I have valued, to be sure, but only so far as to judge that your instruction and training were to be held of greater worth, or rather by far the greatest.

But in truth, it is a newer philosophy that I myself

> Vos igitur, Juvenes, moneo obtestorque, ne quis vestrûm ab incoepto harum Institutionum & recentioris Philosophiae cur-

Beggars, actresses, buffoons, all that breed, while they indulge their own wit too freely, while they strive to overturn the Church of Christ from its foundations, as though about some other business, these very men, together with the Peripatetic School, corrupt, ruin and go about to destroy the orthodox faith, the Christian religion, and the morals held most holy for so many centuries now.

Is it so indeed? O splendid, watchful, excellent guardians of the Church! Of course Aristotle, whom you worship as the god of philosophy, was orthodox after all, he was outstanding in piety and religion. But what is the point of saying more about these things now? Each man, as a rule, defends his own philosophy, received from his forebears, as if it were some household gods, and would grieve most bitterly to see them attacked, conquered, plundered.

I warn and adjure you, therefore, young men, that none of you, from the course once begun of these Institutions and of the newer Philosophy,

(*) A most distinguished Doctor, a countryman of ours, three years ago brought to light a Book to which he had given the title La Lógica de D. Andrés Piquer, in which he is so prolix in censuring (harshly enough, not to say jejunely and ineptly) whatever Moderns he has ever read, that you would almost say he raves rather than reasons. Bacon, Arnauld, Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Locke, Heineccius, Wolff, Genovesi, Verney he holds of no account, as if they had not advanced Logic themselves but only treated it perfunctorily. Aristotle alone is esteemed great and famous, after whom Piquer alone handed down the precepts of Logic; the rest have all too often inculcated mere trifles, and things not at all to the point. So great indeed was the most distinguished man’s philautia (let him tell us himself, in his usual way, what the force of that word is in Latin, Greek and Spanish), and his preconceived opinion in favor of antiquity, that he has roused that venerable Old Man, the ornament of our now aging century and of our Spain, lately gone to his fate, Fr. Benito Jerónimo Feijóo, whom he holds up to ridicule on the ground that he had praised some of the Moderns named above without discrimination. [PDF 36] where truer things will not be at hand. Detractors of this stamp, querulous, difficult, more frivolous even than anyone could imagine men of mature mind to be, whom riding on a reed, and nuts, and odd-and-even no longer delight: these, I say, do not listen to. For they are tiresome and empty.

§. I.

The origin and progress of Philosophy from the creation of the world to the coming of Christ our Lord.

hilosophy means the same as Study, or Love of Wisdom. “Wisdom, 1

P        moreover, is (as Tully says, following the opinion of the ancients (a)) the

knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these things are held together.” For in Philosophy, things pertaining both to God and to other things placed outside God are examined, namely with the help of natural reason, and their causes are derived, by a well-ordered consequence complete according to its own laws, from principles either altogether certain or highly probable. Those who seek it are named Philosophers, a name retained all the more carefully ever since the modest answer of Pythagoras, as we shall say later.

2 Adam, the first parent of mankind, is said to have received from Almighty

God, without any labor, a Philosophy complete in every respect. But when, as

Purchot says (b), for violating the law of God he

(a) Bk. 2 of On Duties.

the works of Brucker, Stanley, Klausius and others. [p. 2] had been expelled from the garden of delights in which he had been placed, then, given over to the darkness of ignorance among the other penalties of sin to which he became subject, he dragged all his posterity with him into that darkness. Hence almost no traces of that excellent and heavenly gift remained in men’s minds, when some, shaking off the sloth of the rest, moved by admiration of the most beautiful things and taught by frequent observation of particular effects, which is called experience, set about restoring it from its foundations with every effort and zeal.

> §. I.

3 It is agreed among nearly all, moreover, that the study of natural science and of the liberal arts flourished above all in Greece; but what Diogenes Laertius says in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, that Philosophy was born in Greece just as men themselves were, is altogether foreign to the truth. For, to pass over what Josephus says (c), that the grandsons of Seth observed the order of the Heavens and the courses of the stars, “and, lest their discoveries should slip out of men’s knowledge, since Adam had foretold a general destruction of the World, the one by fire, the other by flood, set up two columns, one of brick, the other of stone, and carved their discoveries on both, so that if the brick one should perish in the flood, the stone one would survive and give men the means of learning”: to pass over these things, I say, which are commonly known (although they were for the most part unknown to the Heathen), no one will indeed deny that the Patriarchs and leaders of the Hebrews, such as Abraham, Moses and others, were instructed in the science of natural things, just like Solomon, King of the Jews, who, as the Sacred Scriptures testify (d), “treated about trees from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.” This moreover is certain from the testimony of the Heathen themselves, that the Assyrians and Chaldeans were laudably versed in Astronomy, invited, namely, by the flat and open region they inhabited, from which they could freely observe the courses of the stars. Hence Tully (e) records that the Chaldeans excelled in the knowledge of the stars and in the shrewdness of their minds.

> *Philosophiae origo & progressus á mundo condito usque ad Christi D. adventum.*

4 From the Assyrians and Chaldeans, moreover, as Josephus witnesses (f), Arithmetic was carried by Abraham to the Egyptians, who, compelled by necessity, likewise studied Geometry: since, as Proclus reports, the boundaries of their fields were so confounded by the annual flooding of the Nile that they could not afterwards be distinguished without Geometry.

6 Therefore we must not credit Philosophy to the Greeks alone: but just as among them there arose men excelling in ingenuity and in the knowledge of natural things, who were first called Wise Men, afterwards Philosophers, so the other nations too had their own interpreters and teachers of truth: among the Hebrews, indeed, the Rabbis; of Babylon and Assyria, the Chaldeans; among the Persians, the Magi; among the Indians, the Brahmans, or Gymnosophists; nay, even on the shores of the farthest East, among the Chinese, there were cultivators of the human disciplines and of the liberal Arts, among whom Confucius is most celebrated, who is therefore called the Chinese Philosopher. Likewise among the Egyptians the Hierophants flourished, and among the Gauls the Druids.

A     sect, moreover, is a certain multitude of men which, in some way cut off and di‐

vided from others, follows a certain kind of doctrine under some Leader. Hence it was named secta either from secando [cutting] or from sectando [following].

9 Further, the first Philosophers of the Greeks are divided into two sects, namely the Dogmatic and the Academic.

10 The Dogmatic sect comprises those Philosophers who contend that they have attained the truth, at least in most things; and it is in turn twofold, the Ionic and the Italic.

11 The leader of the Ionic sect was Thales, called the Milesian, either because he had as his native city Miletus, which is the capital City of Ionia, or because, although he was of Phoenician origin, he was enrolled, as some relate, among the

Citizens of Miletus. Apollodorus, in Diogenes Laertius’s life of him, records that he was born in the first year of the 35th Olympiad, and died in the seventieth year of his age. That first year of the 35th Olympiad, moreover, is the year 639 before the common era of the Christians, and 3365 from the founding of the world. (*) Thales was followed by Anaximander,

> trajecto mari, delata est Geometria; quam videlicet in AEgypto didicit Thales Milesius, & in Graeciam intulit, ut narrat ipse Diogenes Laertius in ejus vita.

Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Democritus, and others, all of whom made the Philosophy of their master illustrious, and carried it down as far as Socrates and Plato.

> 6 Itaque non Graecis solis acceptam referre debemus Philosophiam; sed quemadmodum apud eos extitére viri ingenio, & rerum naturalium cognitione praecellentes qui *Sapientes* primùm, postea *Philosophi* sunt adpellati: ita ceteris quoque nationibus sui fuerunt veritatis interpretes, ac doctores; Hebraeis quidem *Rabbini*, Babylonis, & Assyriis *Chaldaei*; Persis *Magi*; Indis *Brachmanes*, seu *Gymnosophistae*; imò & in extremis Orientis oris apud *Sinas* fuere disciplinarum humanarum, & liberalium Artium cultores, in quibus maximè celebratur *Confucius*, qui ideò *Sinensis Philosophus* adpellatur. Item apud AEgyptios *Hierophantae*, apud Gallos *Druidae* floruerunt.

12 The chief of the Italic sect was Pythagoras of Samos, who, having been a disciple of Pherecydes the Syrian, and having traveled through Egypt and Babylonia for the sake of acquiring learning, at length betook himself to Italy, in the time of Servius Tullius, King of the Romans; and at Croton, not far from Tarentum, he devoted himself to Philosophy for about twenty years; and having afterwards gone from there to Metapontum, as Justin testifies (g), he died there in the 4th year of the 70th Olympiad. By him the name of Philosopher was first used. For when, passing through the Peloponnese, he was asked by Leon, Tyrant of the Sicyonians, or of the Phliasians (Sicyon and Phlius, moreover, were cities of the Peloponnese), what he professed himself to be, he answered that he was a Philosopher, that is, one devoted to Wisdom; using, namely, a more modest appellation, says Diogenes Laertius in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, in order to beat down the arrogance and pride of the Greeks, who proclaimed themselves Wise Men: because God alone can truly be called Wise, whereas men are rather to be named lovers of Wisdom than Wise.

> 7 Praecipua autem Philosophiae gloria Graecis ideo tribuitur, quòd ii diligentiùs incubuerint in singulas illius partes, eamque in quoddam veluti corpus digestam Scriptis suis ad posteros transmiserint. Quamobrem illustriores Philosophorum sectae, de quibus mentio fit in Scholis, á Graecis sunt repetendae.

13 Among others, the doctrines of Pythagoras were embraced by Timaeus of Locri, Archytas of Tarentum, Philolaus of Croton, Parmenides and Zeno, both of Elea, the latter of whom is called the author of Dialectic by Diogenes Laertius, and Melissus of Samos: all of whom gave their chief attention to Physics, or natural science, right up to the institution of the old Academy, whose Chief was Socrates; at which time the Philosophers, following the example of Socrates, turned their minds from Physical things to the science of morals.

> §. II.

14 The Academic sect took its name from the Academy, that is, from a wooded place situated in a suburb of Athens, which a noble hero, Academus by name, had consecrated to the exercises of the Philosophers. The Philosophers of this sect withheld all assent; they affirmed nothing whatever: and the sect itself was in turn divided into the old, the middle, and the new Academy.

> *Illustriores Philosophorum Sectae.*

15 The Chiefs of the old Academy were Socrates and his disciple Plato. Hence the old Academics were called by the same token Platonists, and also Sceptics, or Inquirers: because, although they judged truth to be unknown, they nevertheless did not despair of finding it, and therefore devoted themselves constantly to the inquiry after it. They were also called Pyrrhonists, from Pyrrho, an Academic.

> 8 SEcta autem est quaedam hominum multitudo quae ab aliis quodammodò *secta* & divisa certum doctrinae genus sub aliquo Duce *sectatur*. Hinc vel à *secando*, vel à *sectando* nominata est *secta*.

16 Socrates was born in Attica in the 4th year of the 77th Olympiad, according to Diogenes Laertius in his life; that is, in the year of the world 3536 according to Ussher’s calculation. He died, however, in the 1st year of the 95th Olympiad, in the seventieth year of his age. “It was he who first, from things hidden (as Tully says (h)) and wrapped up by nature herself, in which, before him, all

> 9 Porrhò primi Graecorum Philosophi in duas sectas dividuntur, scilicet in *Dogmaticam*, & *Academicam*.

the

> 10 Secta Dogmatica eos comprehendit Philosophos, qui veritatem adsecutos esse se, saltem in pluribus, contendunt: quae iterum duplex est, *Jonica*, & *Italica*.

(g) Bk. XX of the Histories, ch. 4.

> 11 Ionicae sectae dux fuit Thales, dictus Milesius, sive quia Miletum, quae Urbs est Ioniae caput, patriam habuit; sive quia quum ex Phaenicia oriundus esset, inter Cives Milesios, ut quidam tradunt, fuit adscriptus. Ipsum anno primo Olympiadis 35. natum esse memorat Apollodorus apud Diogenem Laertium in ejus vita, mortuum verò anno aetatis septuagesimo. Annus autem ille primus Olympiadis 35. est 639. ante aeram vulgarem Christianorum, & à mundo condito 3365. (*) Thaletem sectati sunt Anaximander,

> (*) Olympias spatium est quatuor annorum. Olympias prima celebrata est anno mundi 3250. [p. 5] Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Democritus, & alii, qui omnes praeceptoris sui Philosophiam illustrarunt; & ad Socratem usque, ac Platonem perduxerunt.

(h) Academic Questions, bk. 1. [p. 5] the Philosophers had been occupied, called Philosophy away and brought it to common life, so that it should inquire about virtues and vices, and in general about good and evil things; and he held that heavenly things were either far removed from our knowledge, or, even if they were known as fully as possible, still contributed nothing to living well. In nearly all the discourses which were written down, variously and copiously, by those who heard him, he disputed in such a way that he affirmed nothing himself, refuted others, and said that he knew nothing, except that very thing.”

> 12 Italicae princeps fuit Pythagoras Samius, qui quum Pherecydis Syri fuisset discipulus, ac AEgyptum & Babyloniam doctrinae comparandae gratia perlustrasset, tandem recepit se in Italiam, tempore Servii Tullii Romanorum Regis; & Crotone non longe à Tarento Philosophiae per annos circiter viginti operam navavit; indeque postea Metapontum profectus, testante Justino (g), diem ibi supremum obit anno 4 Olympiadis 70. Ab eo primùm Philosophi nomen usurpatum est. Quippe quum per Peloponnesum transiens interrogatus esset à Leonte Sicyoniorum, vel Phliasiorum Tyranno (erant autem Sicyon, & Phlius urbes Peloponnesi) quem se profiteretur: respondit se PHILOSOPHUM esse, hoc est, Sapientiae studiosum; modestiore scilicet, adpellatione usus, inquit Diogenes Laertius in Proemio ad vitas Philosophorum, ut retunderet fastum ac superbiam Graecorum, qui se Sapientes praedicabant: quià solus Deus vere Sapiens dici potest; homines verò potius Sapientiae amatores sunt nominandi, quàm Sapientes.

17 Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclid and others were followers of Socrates. But among them all Plato the Athenian was eminent, who also succeeded Socrates in the Academy and, keeping to his method, affirmed nothing, but, as the same Tully says (i), “in his books many things are argued on both sides, everything is inquired into, nothing certain is said.” Plato, moreover, had among his other disciples Aristotle, afterwards the Chief of the Peripatetic sect, and his own adversary.

> 13 Pythagorae dogmata inter ceteros amplexi sunt Timaeus Locrensis, Archytas Tarentinus, Philolaus Crotoniata, Parmenides, & Zeno ambo Eleatae, quorum hic Dialecticae auctor dicitur á Diogene Laertio, ac Melissus Samius: qui omnes Physicae seu naturali scientiae praecipuam dederunt operam ad institutionem usque veteris Academiae, cujus Princeps fuit Socrates: quo tempore Philosophi animum á rebus Physicis ad morum scientiam Socratis exemplo converterunt.

18 After the death of Plato and of Speusippus, the other successors of Socrates in the Academy cast off that timid method of philosophizing; and, having passed over to the party of the Dogmatics, they established a threefold Sect, that of the Peripatetics, of the Stoics, and of the Epicureans.

> 14 Secta Academica nomen suum desumpsit ab Academia hoc est a loco nemoroso in suburbio Athenarum sito, quem heros nobilis, Academus nomine, Philosophorum exercitationibus consecrarat. Hujus sectae Philosophi adsensum omnem cohibebant: nihil omnino adfirmabant: ipsaque rursus in veterem, mediam, & novam Academiam fuit divisa.

19 The Peripatetics glory in Aristotle as their master. He was born at Stagira, a town of Macedonia, about the year of the world 3621, namely in the first year of the 99th Olympiad, his father being Nicomachus and his mother Phaestis, and in his seventeenth year he heard Plato. When he had been trained in the Philosophical disciplines for full twenty years and his master had been taken from among the living, Aristotle betook himself to Hermias, tyrant of the Atarneans in Mysia; and having stayed with him for three years, he set out for Macedonia to instruct Alexander, and, after spending eight years with him, returned to Athens. Here, since he found Xenocrates, the successor of Speusippus, in the Academy, he chose for himself the Lyceum (a place in the suburb, which had been built by Pericles so that he himself might train newly levied soldiers in it in the arts of war); and since in that station he discoursed on philosophical matters while walking about, it came about that the School was called Peripatetic, from its custom of walking about.

> 15 Veteris Academiae Principes fuere Socrates, & ejus discipulus Plato. Unde veteres Academici, iidem Platonici dicti sunt, ut & Sceptici seu Inquisitores: quod licet ignotam esse veritatem arbitrarentur, de ea tamen invenienda non desperarent; ideoque ejus inquisitioni constanter vacarent. Pyrrhonici quoque vocati sunt, à Pyrrhone Academico.

20 Strabo is our authority (k), and the Writers of the History of Philosophy agree wonderfully with him on this, that Aristotle handed over his writings and his Library to his disciple Theophrastus, to whom he also left his School; and that Theophrastus likewise bequeathed by will both his own books and Aristotle’s to Neleus of Scepsis, who had been a hearer of him and of Aristotle, as Diogenes Laertius testifies (l). Neleus, therefore, carried that Library over to the town of Scepsis, and at his death left it to his heirs, unlearned men. But they, when they learned of the zeal of the Attalid Kings, to whom Scepsis

[p. 6] ,, Philosophi occupati fuerant, avocavit Philosophiam, & ad vitam communem adduxit, ut de virtutibus, & vitiis, omninoque de bonis rebus, & malis quaereret: caelestia autem vel procul esse á nostra cognitione censeret, vel si maximè cognita essent, nihil tamen ad benè vivendum conferre. Hic in omnibus ferè sermonibus, qui ab iis, qui illum audierunt, perscripti varie, & copiosè sunt, ita disputabat, ut nihil adfirmaret ipse, refelleret alios, nihil se scire diceret, nisi id ipsum.

(l) In the life of Theophrastus. [p. 6] was subject, in seeking out books from every quarter to furnish the Library of Pergamum, buried their own in the ground lest they be carried off; and there they lay a long time, abandoned and, as it were, entombed. At length, dug up by the successors of those men, damaged and gnawed by damp and by moths, they were sold for a great sum of money to Apellicon of Teos, a man more devoted to books than to learning. Apellicon, for his part, after an unskilled restoration of the eaten-away parts, transcribed the books into new copies, which nevertheless still teemed with very many faults, and with very many gaps also left unfilled.

> 17 Operam Socrati dedere Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclides, &c. Sed inter eos omnes eminebat Plato Atheniensis, qui & Socrati in Academia successit, ejusque methodo insistens nihil adfirmabat, sed, ut ait idem Tullius (i) ,, multa in ejus libris in utramque partem disseruntur, de omnibus quaeritur, nihil certi dicitur ,,. Plato autem discipulum inter ceteros habuit Aristotelem Peripateticae sectae postea Principem, & sibi adversarium.

21 But immediately after the death of Apellicon his library, which was at Piraeus, was carried off by L. Sulla, as Plutarch records in his life, and taken to Rome, where a certain Grammarian, Tyrannio, asked to be allowed the use of the Aristotelian books; and, having obtained this permission, he himself corrupted a great many things in them, and shared copies with a certain Andronicus of Rhodes, by whom, after they had been likewise interpolated, they were at length brought out into the light. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the books of Aristotle were wretchedly defiled and full of gaps in many places, so that no one can affirm for certain which are the words of Aristotle himself, and what Apellicon supplied, what Tyrannio and Andronicus. Whoever wishes to know more of this, let him read Stanley (m). We pass on to the rest.

> 18 Post mortem Platonis, & Speusippi, ceteri Socratis successores in Academia timidam illam Philosophandi methodum abjecere; & in Dogmaticorum partes translati triplicem constituere Sectam, Peripateticorum, Stoicorum, & Epicureorum.

22 The Leader of the Stoics was Zeno of Citium, that is, a native of Citium, a town of Cyprus, who at Athens, in the Portico, taught the doctrines of a severer Philosophy, with great celebrity of name, about the 130th Olympiad.

> 19 Peripatetici praeceptore gloriantur Aristotele. Hic natus Stagyrae opido Macedoniae circa annum mundi 3621 scilicet anno primo Olympiadis 99, patre Nicomacho, matre Phaestide, septimum decimum annum agens Platonem audivit. Philosophicis disciplinis ipsos viginti annos excultus, magistro é vivis sublato, ad Hermiam Aternensium in Mysia tyrannum se contulit Aristoteles, apud quem triennio ubi versatus fuisset, in Macedoniam ad erudiendum Alexandrum profectus, exactis cum eo annis octo, Athenas rediit: hic Xenocratem Speusippi successorem in Acedemia quum reperisset, Lyceum (in suburbio locus fuerat à Pericle conditus, ut lectum recens militem ipse in eo bellicis artibus instrueret) sibi delegit: qua in statione, quoniam de rebus philosophicis inambulando disseruit, factum iccircò, ut Schola ab inambulandi consuetudine PERIPATETICA vocaretur.

23 The Epicureans were so called from Epicurus, the Patron of this sect, who in the gardens where he held his gatherings expounded the tenets of Democritus, which he had made his own. He died in the second year of the 127th Olympiad, in the year 3735 after the founding of the world, having lived 72 years. Lucretius, twelve years younger than Cicero, wrote out the Philosophy of Epicurus in Latin verses divided into six books. Epicurus is censured by Tully (n) for having despised Logic, but far most of all because “he tore Religion up by the roots from the minds of men, abolishing it, together with the immortal Gods, in reality, while leaving the Gods in words.” We add this one thing: that the School of Epicurus lasted, in a continuous succession and with a rare agreement, down to the age of Augustus, fourteen Masters filling a space of 237 years.

> 20 Auctor est Strabo (k) & in eo mirè consentiunt Historiae Philosophiae Scriptores, Aristotelem scripta sua & Bibliothecam discipulo suo Theophrasto tradidisse, cui & Scholam reliquit. Theophrastum pariter & suos, & Aristotelis libros testamento legasse Neleo Scepsio, qui fuerat illius, & Aristotelis Auditor, ut testatur Diogenes Laertius (l). Igitur Neleus Bibliothecam illam in oppidum Scepsin transtulit, eamque haeredibus ineruditis hominibus moriens reliquit. Illi autem ubi Attalicorum Regum, quibus Scepsis

24 Meanwhile, however, the method of Socrates had been revived by Arcesilaus about the 120th Olympiad, whence he himself is named the Chief of the second, or middle, Academy. He, moreover, added this to the opinion of Socrates: that he not only affirmed with Socrates that nothing is known, but contended that nothing whatever can even be known. Hence the new Academics were also called Acataleptics, as if you were to say, men who professed that they could comprehend nothing at all.

## §. III

On the Eclectic Philosophy, and on Philosophy after the Birth of

Christ.

26

This Philosophy is called Eclectic by the Greeks, Elective by the Latins. This manner of philosophizing is explained by Clement of Alexandria when, after discoursing at length in praise of Philosophy, he adds that he had declared all this not of the Stoic Philosophy, nor of the Platonic, nor of the Epicurean or the Aristotelian; but whatever things have been rightly said by these sects, which teach justice together with pious knowledge, this whole selection, he says, he calls Philosophy (o). As if

(as Stanley adds (p)) “he judged the study of those who do not hesitate superstitiously to swear by the words of a single master not worthy even of the name of Philosophy.”

The Eclectics, namely, imitate the bees, which (these are Seneca’s words (q)) “wander about and pluck the flowers fit for making honey, then arrange whatever they have brought in, and distribute it through the combs, and, as Virgil says:

……………………the liquid honey

They pack, and swell the cells with sweet nectar.”

27 The Chief of this Philosophy was Potamon of Alexandria, and this manner of philosophizing (for this method of philosophizing cannot come under the name of a

Sect) had hearers who had won illustrious fame. Men renowned for Holiness also strove to defend the Eclectic philosophy with especial zeal, foremost among them

Clement of Alexandria and Gregory Thaumaturgus, having professed it, namely, for no other reason “than that they might draw from many sects the truth which could not be found in one”; which Lactantius intimates, affirming at the same time that “all those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their forefathers, and, like cattle, by others are

(o) Stromata, bk. 1.

(p) Hist. of Philos., vol. 2, On the Eclectics, ch. 2.

> [p. 8]

(q) Letter 85. [p. 8] are led; nor do they think it possible either that they themselves should be wiser, because they are called the younger, or that those others should have been foolish, because they are named the elders (r).”

> 25 Arcesilae suffragati sunt Lacydes, novae, seu tertiae Academiae Auctor, Evander, & praecipuè Carneades, qui Romae magna cum eloquentia novorum Academicorum doctrinam explicuit, ibique discipulos habuit Clitomachum, Philonem, & Antiochum, à quibus eruditus est M. T. Cicero, qui & ipse Academicus fuit, ac Platonicae methodi strenuus adsertor.

28 In the following ages after the coming of Christ, the doctrine of Plato always held first place until about the eighth century of the Church, and very many of the Holy Fathers consecrated their study and their vigils to it. Among the Latin Fathers it was most diligently cultivated by St. Augustine, who, being of a most penetrating wit, illustrated it in many parts and happily employed it to refute the errors of the Heathen and to assert the truth of the Christian Religion.

> De Eclectica Philosophia, deque Philosophia post Christum natum.

29 As for the Aristotelian Philosophy, it is certain that in the first ages of the Church it never held any dominion; nay rather, the Holy Fathers derided it with countless reproaches. These may be read in the celebrated Petavius (s). Their file is led by St. Justin Martyr (or whatever other Christian Doctor wrote the book entitled The Overthrow of Certain Aristotelian Doctrines). Clement of Alexandria follows, writing thus (t): “But it will not be irksome to recall also the Peripatetics, the father of whose sect, understanding nothing about that Father who is Supreme, teaches very many errors.” Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons (u), refutes two things received from Aristotle, namely hair-splitting talk and subtlety, by which the simplicity and candor of the Christian Faith are corrupted. This very thing is censured in Aristotle by Origen (x), Lactantius Firmianus (y), Eusebius of Caesarea (z), Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria (a), Basil (b), Gregory of Nyssa (c), Ambrose (d), John Chrysostom (e), Augustine (f), and Jerome (g), who testifies that the Arian heresy borrows the streams of its argumentations from the fountains of Aristotle; which St. Ambrose (h) also confirms, saying: “For thus we know that the Arians rushed headlong into perfidy: they abandon the Apostle,

> 26 Quae Philosophia Graecis Eclectica, Latinis Electiva dicitur. [p. 9] they follow Aristotle.” Gregory Nazianzen too (i) laments that the captious arguments of the sophists and the depraved artifice of the Aristotelian art had crept into the Church like certain Egyptian plagues. St. Augustine addresses the Pelagians thus (k): “Your heresy has been brought to this, that your followers groan that no Dialectician Judges from the Schools of the Peripatetics are to be found in the Church by whom you might be acquitted.” St. Vincent Ferrer exclaims querulously (l) that Aristotle and Averroes were vials of the wrath of God poured out upon the waters of Christian wisdom, whence they were made bitter as wormwood. Whoever wishes more, let him read the celebrated Guido Grandi. Let us follow our History.

> 28 Sequentibus temporibus post Christi adventum doctrina Platonis ad octavum circiter Ecclesiae seculum primas semper obtinuit, eique plurimi SS. Patres studium, & vigilias suas consecrarunt. Eandem inter Latinos Patres diligentissimè excoluit S. Augustinus, qui ut erat acerrimo ingenio, multis eam partibus illustravit, & ad refellendos Ethnicorum errores, adserendamque Religionis Christianae veritatem feliciter adhibuit.

30 The Western Provinces, meanwhile, presented a far different face of things. For the Arabs, toward the end of the eighth century and the beginning of the ninth, having previously subdued very extensive regions and obtained dominion far and wide through Africa and Spain, revived the doctrine of Aristotle, rendered from Greek into Arabic and from Arabic into Latin and illustrated with commentaries, and brought it into the public schools; and this system indeed held them for nearly five hundred years, the understanding of the Greek and Latin languages being almost buried along with it. This method of philosophizing, brought by the Arabs into Spain, migrated to the English and the French and was spread far and wide; then the eloquent and richer style of Plato’s discourse began to be neglected and dialectical acumen to flourish, the interpreters of Aristotle zealously pursuing a subtle, minute, contentious, excessively talkative manner of discoursing: among whom are reckoned as chief Avicenna, Alfarabi, Alkindi, but easily the prince of all Averroes of Córdoba, called by the singular title of the Commentator. Hence was born the disputatious and contentious Philosophy, which brought barbarism of speech with it into the Schools, and was called Scholastic, because it has been in use in the Schools down to our own times; although it has met with varied fortune at different times, and if I had a mind to draw out my discourse on it at greater length, whole volumes of Brucker and others would have to be copied out by me; we shall, however, touch on some chief points.

> 29 Quod verò Philosophiam Aristotelicam adtinet, certum est, illam primis Ecclesiae seculis nullum unquam obtinuisse dominatum, quinimo SS. Patres innumeris conviciis eam derisere. Illos legere est apud Cl. Petavium (s) Eorum agmen ducit S. Justinus Martyr (sive quis alius Christianus Doctor, qui librum inscripsit: Quorundam Aristotelicarum dogmatum eversio) Clemens Alexandr. sequitur ita scribens. (t) ,, Sed nec molestum fuerit meminisse etiam Peripateticorum, cujus quidem sectae qui pater est, nihil de eo Patre qui est Supremus intelligens errores plurimos docet ,,. Iraeneus Lugdunensis Episcopus (u) duo ab Aristotele refutat accepta nimirùm minutiloquium, & subtilitatem, quibus Christianae Fidei simplicitas, & candor corrumpitur. Hoc ipsum in Aristotele reprehendunt Origenes (x), Lactantius Firmianus (y), Eusebius Caesariensis (z), Athanasius Alexandr. Episcopus (a) Basilius (b), Gregorius Nicenus (c), Ambrosius (d), Johann. Chrisostomus (e), Augustinus (f), Hieronymus (g) qui testatur quod Ariana haeresis argumentationum rivos de fontibus Aristotelis mutuatur, quod & confirmat S. Ambrosius (h) inquiens: ,, Sic enim Arianos in perfidiam ruisse cognovimus, relinquunt Apostolum,

31 In the year 1209, by Decree of the Council of Paris, the principal books of Aristotle were burned and the reading of them forbidden. In the year 1591 Francesco Patrizi urges Gregory XIV to remove the Philosophy of Aristotle from the Schools of Christians. Afterwards Peter Ramus defended Theses at Paris against the doctrine of Aristotle. Then John Pico della Mirandola attempted to restore the Pythagorean Philosophy, Bessarion and Marsilio Ficino the Platonic, Caspar Scioppius the Stoic, Bernardino Telesio that which is called the Parmenidean.

Augustinus ita Pelagianos compellat (k) ,, Ad hoc redacta est haeresis vestra, ut gemant Sectatores vestri non inveniri Dialecticos Judices in Ecclesia de Scholis Peripateticorum à quibus possitis absolvi ,,. Peter Abelard and his disciple Peter Lombard. It is divided into three ages, of which the first, in the opinion of some, began about the middle of the eleventh century and was carried down to the middle of the twelfth. At that time there flourished Abelard; Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences because he expounded the sentences collected from the ancient Fathers; Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Comestor, and John of Salisbury. The second period runs to about the year 1330; it was made illustrious by the geniuses of Albert the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas, and St. Bonaventure. The third lasted until letters and the arts were restored; in which age Durandus, Ockham, and Cardinal Pierre d’Ailly were renowned.

> 30 Occidentales interea Provincias haud paulò alia rerum facies habuit. Arabes namque sub finem octavi seculi, & noni principium subactis antea amplissimis regionibus per Africam latè & Hispaniam dominationem adepti, Aristotelis doctrinam ex Graeco Arabicè, & ex Arabico Latinè redditam, commentariisque illustratam exsuscitarunt, atque in scholas publicas invexére; quae quidem ratio ipsos penè quingentos annos tenuit, linguarum Graecae ac Latinae intelligentia ferè consepultâ. Haec philosophandi methodus per Arabes in Hispaniam invecta ad Anglos & Gallos transmigravit, latèque diffussa est, Platonis tùm facundus & uberior in sermone stylus negligi, acumen dialecticum vigére coepit, Aristotelis interpretibus subtile, minutum, contentiosum, nimiùm loquax disserendi genus studiosè consectantibus: quos inter praecipui numerantur Avicenna, Alpharabius, Alchindus, omnium autem facile princeps Averroes, Cordubensis, nuncupatione singulari Commentator adpellatus. Hinc nata Philosophia disputatrix, & contentiosa, quae sermonis barbariem secum in Scholas invexit, & Scholastica vocata est, eo quod in Scholis ad nostra usque tempora sit usurpata: quamvis tamen variam diversis temporibus fortunam experta sit, de qua si longiùs orationem protrahere mens foret exscribenda mihi essent integra volumina Bruckerii, aliorumque: aliqua tamen capita delibabimus.

33 Among the Scholastics, or new Peripatetics, three more illustrious sects are reckoned: namely those of the Thomists, the Scotists, and the Nominalists. The first follow as their leader St. Thomas, born in the year 1224 in the Castle of Aquino, who afterwards professed the Rule of the Order of Preachers, and on account of the purity of his morals and the excellence of his doctrine was justly and deservedly distinguished with the title of the Angelic Doctor. Among the Thomists are celebrated Dominic of Flanders, Francisco de Vitoria, the Most Illustrious Melchor Cano, Domingo de Soto, Medina and very many others, whom it would take long to recount.

> 31 Anno 1209. Parisiensis Concilii Decreto praecipui Aristotelis libri combusti sunt, & eorum lectio interdicta. Anno 1591 Franciscus Patricius Gregorio XIV. suadet ut é Scholis Christianorum Aristotelis Philosophia tollatur. Postea vero Petrus Ramus Parisiis defendit Theses contra Aristotelis doctrinam Dein Johann. Picus Mirandulanus Philosophiam Pythagoricam restituere conatus est. Besarion & Marcilius Ficinus Platonicam, Gaspar Scioppius Stoicam, Bernardinus Telesius illam quae Parmenidis adpellatur.

34 The second School acknowledges as its chief John Duns, who, whether he was a Scot by country (a surname that is still given to him even now and is carried over to the sect founded by him), or was born at Dunstan in Northumberland, or in the village of Duns in Ulster (for the Writers are not agreed about this), entered the Order of Minors and flourished chiefly at the beginning of the fourteenth century. His subtle wit, and the Wisdom answering to it, brought forth the title of Subtle Doctor; and both together brought it about that, while he held the Theological Chair at Oxford, thirty thousand Scholars and more flocked together to hear him. Among the followers of Scotus there excelled Francis of Meyronnes, who had received the doctrine while his Master was still living, John Punch, Bartholomew Mastrius, Martin Meurisse, and Claude Frassen, a celebrated Scotist, who was taken from among the living in the eleventh year of this century (m).

> 32 Scholasticae Philosophiae Principem alii Lanfrancum Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem statuunt. Nonnulli, inter quos Naudaeus à D. Johann. Damasceno primam originem repetunt, á quo ad La-

35 The third sect is that of the Nominalists, who contended that names and words are the object of Logic, and whose Doctor was William of Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, and a disciple of Scotus. The Scholastics are also divided into Realists and Nominalists. The matter of this disagreement, moreover, was furnished by the treatment of universals, since the former contended that universal natures exist, as it were, in reality, while the latter affirmed that they are constituted only in words.

Tres in aetates dividitur, quarum prima initium sumpsit quorundam ex sententia sub medium seculi undecimi ad medium duodecimi perducta; Effloruere id temporis Abaelardus, Lombardus dictus Magister Sententiarum propterea quod sententias ex antiquis Patribus collectas exposuerit. Gilbertus Porretanus, Petrus Comestor, & Johann. Sarisberiensis. Secunda periodus ad ann. circitèr 1330 excurrit, hanc illustrarunt ingenia Alberti Magni, D. THOMAE AQUINATIS, & D. Bonaventurae. > 33 Inter Scholasticos verò seu novos Peripateticos tres numerantur illustriores sectae: Thomistarum nempè, Scotistarum, & Nominalium. Primi ducem sequuntur D. THOMAM natum ann. 1224 in Castro Aquino, Regulam Ordinis Praedicatorum subinde professum, atque ob morum nitorem, doctrinaeque praestantiam Doctoris Angelici nuncupatione jure merito insignitum. Celebrantur Thomistas inter Dominicus de Flandria, Franciscus Victoria, Illustrissim. Melchior Cano, Dominicus Soto, Medina aliique plurimi, quos longum esset recensere.

Innovators in Philosophy who Revived the Ancient Doctrine.

> 34 Altera Schola principem agnoscit Johannem Duns, qui seu patriâ Scotus fuerit, quod cognomentum & ipsi tribuitur etiamnum, & in sectam ab eo constitutam derivatur, seu Dunstonae in Nortumbria, aut é vico Duns in Ultonia (neque enim de eo inter Scriptores convenit) ortus, Ordinem Minorum ingressus sub exordia quartidecimi seculi potissimum claruit. Ingenium subtile, & respondens ei Sapientia Doctoris Subtilis peperit nomenclationem: utrumque effecit, ut dum Cathedram Theologicam moderaretur Oxonii, ejus audiendi gratiâ, triginta & amplius Scholarium millia confluxerint. Scoti adseclae eminuerunt Franciscus Mayronius, qui adhuc dum superstitis Magistri doctrinam exceperat, Johann. Ponzius, Barthol. Mastrius, Martinus Meurisse, & Claud. Frassen, celeber Scotista anno seculi hujus undecimo, è vivis sublatus (m).

36

> 35 Tertia secta est Nominalium, qui nomina & voces objectum esse Logicae contendebant, quorum Doctor fuit Guillelmus Ochamus, natione Anglus, Ordin. Fratrum Minor., & Scoti discipulus. Dispecuntur etiam Scholastici in Reales & Nominales. Argumentum porrhò hujus discrepantiae, universalium tractatio praebuit, quum primi, naturas universales reapse velut existere contederent, postremi non nisi in vocibus eas constitutas adfirmarent.

About the middle of the seventeenth century Galileo, the excellent

> (m) Wadingus in Bibliotheca Minorum.

Mathematician of the Grand Duke of Tuscany (n), shook off the yoke of the custom grown inveterate in the Schools and tried new paths. Following in his footsteps, very many Men outstanding in learning restored the Mechanical philosophy.

37 Pierre Gassendi, Royal Professor of Mathematics in the Academy of Paris, was born in the year 1562. He put together a system of the Epicurean Philosophy, rejecting those things which could not well be reconciled with Religion. And indeed the tenets of Epicurus as emended by him so commended themselves to the Learned that from this eminent restorer the Gassendist sect arose.

38 Certain men devised a new kind of Philosophy, called the Philosophy of the Christians. Of their number is Thomas Burnet in the Sacred Theory of the Earth, where he busies himself with interpreting Moses, but most wretchedly distorts the Mosaic narrative. To him must be joined the Theory of Whiston; both of these, however, were refuted by learned Men. To the same class belong Edmund

Dickinson in his Physica vetus et nova, and John Comenius in his Physica ad lumen divinum reformata. His hypotheses were for the most part retained by Johann

Bayer in the Work entitled Ostium et atrium naturae.

39 At this point mention must now be made of the restored Philosophy of the Chemists, and of those who as it were dug it out of the ashes, cultivated it, and rendered this discipline Experimental, by laboriously scrutinizing nature, subjecting bodily things to trials, and putting useful experience in place of the sterile speculations of others. That the origin of metallurgical Chemistry is most ancient is shown, among others, by the celebrated Boerhaave (o). Paracelsus is said to have revived the Chemical art, chiefly among the Germans, whence he is also called the Father of the Chemists. That part of this discipline which comprises metallurgy was cultivated, after Georg Agricola, by Lazarus Ercker, Joachim Becher and Johann Kunckel. Chemistry was made useful to Medicine and Physics by

Boyle, Slare, Homberg, Geoffroy, Lémery the Younger, Hoffmann, and the celebrated Hermann Boerhaave, who brings forward these and others.
