## The Division of Ideas. 24

> omnes à cérebro, vel à cerebéllo & spinali medúlla ducantur, facillimè eumdem motum in cérebro éxcitant, ex quo mens percipit contactum, id est, adquirit ideam tactus, ut optimè explicat Hallerius, Faye, & Verdier, (i)

An idea, as we have already said, is the genuine image of any object whatever, which the mind contemplates immediately, or any thought whatever about any thing. Sometimes we perceive a thing in such a way that, when it presents itself again, we easily distinguish it from others; this is called a clear idea: if I cannot so distinguish a thing from another, the idea is confused. Thus, e.g., everyone, even among the common people, has a clear idea of the Moon, but not likewise of Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, stars which a man of the people will easily confuse with the fixed stars.

> 21 Hinc manifestum fit organorum munus esse excipere impressionem corporum, eamque ad cérebrum transmíttere: idque mediis nervis, qui hisce peragendis sunt quàm aptissimi: mentem verò esse quae rerum ideas pro varietate sensuum élicit. Dicimus autem oculum videre, aurem audire, &c. quod secùs est. Nam oculus tantùm excipit cum imagine motum quendam, ut ita dicam, quem cùm cérebro commúnicat; mens verò per talem motum occasionalitèr admonita sibi eformat ideam rei visae. Sed quum motum illum organi, sequatur mentis perceptio, idcircò utrumque confúndimus; & existimamus oculum videre, &c.: quamvis nos lateat omninò quo pacto sensuum adfectiones ad cérebrum perveniant, easque motitationes, quae in cerebro imprimuntur mens nostra percipiat. Itaque in omnibus penè sensationibus, ut optimè notat Mallebranche, (j) quatuor licet diversa confunduntur, quia scilicet simul, & velut uno temporis puncto aguntur.

25 But even if I easily distinguish some thing from others, it sometimes happens that I am able to enumerate one by one all the marks that separate the thing from the rest, and sometimes not; in the first case the clear idea is distinct, in the second indistinct. E.g., when I know that a triangle can be distinguished from other figures by the number of the lines by which it is enclosed, I am said to have not only a clear but also a distinct idea of it. On the other hand, if, seeing that a magnet draws iron to itself, I separate the magnet from other stones by this mark, but cannot enumerate one by one all the other marks that set the magnet apart from other stones, I have a clear but confused idea of the magnet.

> 22 Primum quod confunditur est actio corporis externi, hoc est, in calore ex. gr. impulsio, & motus particularum ligni in fibras manus. Secundum est passio organi sensus, hoc est, agitatio fibrarum manus orta ex impulsione particularum ignis, quae agitatio ad cérebrum usque pervenit. Tertium est sensatio aut perceptio mentis, hoc est, id quod quilibet sentit quum ad ignem accedit. Quartum est judicium, quo mens judicat, id quod sentit esse in manu sua & in igne.

A distinct idea therefore expresses more than a clear one, and a clear idea is rightly divided into distinct and confused.

> 23 Haec quatuor, ut videre est, longè diversa sunt, nec tamen vulgò distinguuntur; nemo tamen est, qui ad rem adtendens non videat ex hisce quatuor, quae in nobis aguntur, quum aliquo externo corpore adficimur, duo priora ad corpus, duo posteriora ad mentem duntaxat pertinére. His obiter dictis, quo pacto animus noster claras, distinctas, atque adaequatas ideas sibi formet, paulò adcuratiùs erit considerandum.

26 But if I not only have the thing and its marks enumerated, but also have a distinct idea of those very marks which enter into that distinct notion, this idea will be adequate; where it is otherwise, the idea will indeed be distinct, but inadequate. Thus, e.g., the marks by which I discern fire from other materials are light, heat, the power of setting on fire, etc. If anyone has a distinct idea of all these things, he will have an adequate notion of fire; if not, an inadequate one.

> (i) Haller ad Boerhaav. Praelect. tom. 3. §. 418. Faye Princípes de Chirurgie. Verdier Abregé d' Anatomie. Volum 2. c. 4. art. 6. & seqq.

An adequate idea therefore expresses more than a distinct one; nor can we acquire adequate ideas of all things, for we do not have a distinct idea of all the adjuncts of which each thing consists; indeed, very few adequate ideas can be obtained in this life, as Wolff rightly warns on this point.

> (j) Recherche de la Veritè lib. 1. c. 2.

Moreover

[p. 13]

> CAPUT IV.

27 Further, ideas are either of Substances, or of Modes, or of Relations. For all the things we know either can exist apart from each single mode, and this we call substance; or they are modes of some thing, and these we call accidents, or modes; and among modes, again, there is something that is conceived as referred to another, and this we call relation. This division is adequate; for it is plainly impossible that there be any perception which is neither a perception of substance, nor a perception of a mode, nor a perception of some relation.

> Divisio Idearum.

28 The whole is made clear by an example: a square piece of wood is a thing that can exist apart from the square figure, for it can be made round; and this we call substance. On the other hand, you will nowhere find squareness and roundness separately in natural bodies, and this we call an accident, or mode of substance; and if I conceive squareness as a mode proper to a body, it necessarily leads me to the knowledge of the body, and this we call relation.

> 24. IDEA, ut jam diximus, est objecti cujusvis genuina imago, quam mens immediatè contemplatur, vel est quaelibet de re quavis cogitatio. Aliquando rem ita percipimus, ut eam quum iterùm se offert ab aliis facilè secernamus; haec vocatur idea clara: si non possum sic distinguere rem ab alia, haec idea est confusa; íta ex. gr. Lunae claram ideam unusquisque etiam ex plebe habet, non item Jovis, Martis, Saturni, quas stellas plebejus facilè cum stellis fixis confundet.

29 From what has been said it becomes manifest that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but a very obscure one. For the ideas we have of particular substances are acquired by sense; but the senses reach only the modes that adorn the substance, not likewise the nature of the substance: hence substance cannot be clearly separated from other things. E.g., iron offers us the idea of a heavy, hard body, which is melted only by a great fire, which is consumed by rust, and which is altogether suited to cutting bodies, etc.; and however much we try to know the nature of iron thoroughly, we shall achieve nothing. For this idea represents nothing other than the modes of iron. Who indeed would dare to say that he finds anything else in iron besides these? Therefore the idea of iron that we have is composed of the ideas of all its modes. Since, however, we know for certain that those adjuncts can be changed, e.g. the square figure into a round one, etc., and that iron can become harder and better suited to splitting wood, without the very nature of iron being changed, we conclude that there is something in iron besides its adjuncts and properties, which we call substance and subject. But what that is, and in what it is distinguished from other things, we do not know.

> 25 Verùm etiam si rem aliquam ab aliis facilè distinguam, evenit aliquandò, ut notas omnes, quae rem à ceteris secernunt, singilatim enumerare valeam, aliquandò non item; primo casu idea clara, est distincta, secundo indistincta: ex. gr. quum sciam triangulum ab aliis figuris numero linearum, quibus inclusum est distingui posse, ejus non modò claram, sed & distinctam habere ideam dicor. Contrà si videns magnetem ferrum ad se trahere, ex hac nota secerno magnétem ab aliis lapidibus, sed nequeo singilatìm numerare ceteras notas omnes quae magnétem ab aliis lapidibus sejungunt; habeo ideam claram, sed confusam magnétis. Igitur plus éxprimit idea distincta, quam clara, & rectè idea clara dividitur in distinctam, & confusam.

30 Thus the notion of substance, as Locke rightly warns, is the idea of a thing altogether unknown to us, or the idea of a most obscure thing, which we feign to be the subject of accidents. But the idea of particular substances, as of iron and of wood, is an idea composed of the ideas of all their properties. Those, therefore, philosophize badly who hold that the nature of a thing is fully known from the properties we know. For even if we know some properties, we cannot affirm with certainty that no properties remain which are not known to us. Wherefore from the properties which we know

> 26 Quòd si non modò rem ejusque notas in numero habeo, sed & harum ipsarum notarum, quae illam distinctam notionem ingrediuntur, ideam distinctam habeo, idea haec erit adaequata, quod ubi secùs se habet, idea distincta quidem, sed inadaequata erit. Sic ex. gr. notae quibus ignem ab aliis materiis discerno, sunt lux, calor, potentia incendendi, &c. Harum rerum omnium, si quis habet ideam distinctam, notionem ignis adaequatam habebit, sin minus inadaequatam. Igitur plus éxprimit idea adaequata quàm distincta; nec póssumus acquirere ideas adaequatas omnium rerum, non enim habemus ideam distinctam adjunctorum omnium, quibus unaquaeque res constat, imò paucissimae ideae adequatae comparari possunt in hac vita, ut rectè hoc loco monet Wolffius.

> [p. 14]

[p. 14] we can separate things from one another, and the more properties we discern, the more nearly we approach the knowledge of the nature; yet this is far removed from a clear and distinct perception of the essence, or nature, and much farther still from an adequate one.

> 27 Praeterea ideae vel sunt Substantiarum, vel Modorum, vel Relationum. Nam omnia quae cognoscimus, vel à singulis modis seorsùm esse possunt, & id vocamus substantiam, vel sunt modi alicujus rei, & haec vocamus accidentia, seu modos: ex modis autem, vel est aliquid, quod ad aliud fingitur referri, & id vocamus relationem. Haec divisio adaequata est; etenim planè impossibile est dari aliquam perceptionem, quae nec sit perceptio substantiae, nec perceptio modi, nec perceptio alicujus relationis.

31 Relations, as we have said, are ideas of which one refers to the other in such a way that one cannot be understood without the other, or that the consideration of the one involves the consideration of the other. From this we infer that those err not a little who affirm or deny something absolutely of a relative idea, and do not duly weigh the foundation of the relation. How useful this observation is for avoiding logomachies, and indeed for calming the sadder passions, cannot be told. Thus many grieve that they are poor, though they lack nothing necessary. And why so, unless because they take very rich men as the foundation of the relation, compared with whom they seem to themselves very poor? Elegantly says Seneca, (k)

> 28 Totum claret exemplo: lignum quadratum est res, quae seorsùm à figura quadrata potest existere: nam fieri potest rotundum, & id vocamus substantiam. Contrà quadraturam, & rotunditatem nusquàm in corporibus naturalibus invenies separatim, id autem vocamus accidens, seu modum substantiae, quòd si quadraturam concipio ut modum proprium corporis, necessariò id me ducit in cognitionem corporis, & hoc vocamus relationem.

To bear the lot that all men suffer

> 29 Ex dictis fit manifestum non habere nos ideam claram & distinctam substantiae, sed valdè obscuram. Nam ideae, quas habemus singularum substantiarum sensu acquiruntur; at sensus adtingunt tantùm modos, qui substantiam ornànt, substantiae verò naturam non itèm: propterea substantia ab aliis rebus nequit clarè sejungi. Ex. gr. ferrum offert nobis ideam corporis gravis, duri, quod non nisi magno igne liquefít, quodque rubígine consúmitur, & omninò est adcommodatum ad corpora secanda, &c. & quamvis conemur ferri naturam penitùs cognoscere, nihil efficiemus. Verùm haec idea nihil aliud repraesentat, nisi modos ferri. ¿Quis ením audeat dicere, aliud se praeter ista in ferro reperire? Ergò idea ferri, quam habemus est composita ex ideis omnium modorum. Quia tamen certò scimus, adjuncta illa posse mutari ex. gr. figuram quadratam in rotundam, &c. fieri duriùs, & dividendis lignis accommodatiùs, quin ipsa natura ferri mutetur, colligimus praeter adjuncta, & proprietates, aliud in ferro esse, quod nos vocamus substantiam, & subjectum. Quid verò illud sit, & in quo ab aliis secernatur nescímus.

No one refuses.

No one believes himself wretched, though he be.

Take away the fortunate, take far away

The rich in gold, take away those who

Cleave rich fields with a hundred oxen;

The poor man’s downcast spirits will rise.

No one is wretched, except by Comparison.

C H A P T E R V.

On singular, particular and universal ideas, where also of the five predicables. 32

Some ideas represent to us the thing itself in the individual, e.g. Alexander; others what the thing has in common with certain others, e.g. his royal dignity; others what the thing has in common with all things of the same nature, e.g. humanity. Ideas of the first kind are called singular, of the second particular

> 30 Itaque notio substantiae, ut rectè monet Lockius, est idea rei nobis prorsùs incognitae, seu idea rei obscurissimae, quam nos fingimus esse subjectum accidentium. Idea verò singularum substantiarum, ut ferri, & ligni est idea composita ex ideis proprietatum omnium. Malè itaque philosophantur, qui censent ex iis, quas cognoscimus proprietatibus, naturam rei planè cognosci. Nam & si nonnullas proprietates noscamus, certò adfirmare non póssumus, nullas superesse proprietates, quae nobis cognitae non sint. Quare ex proprietatibus, quas [p. 15] novimus, res alias ab aliis sejúngere possumus, & quò plures proprietates internoscimus, eò magis ad cognítionem naturae accedimus, id tamen longè distat à clarâ, & distinctâ, & multò magis ab adaequata essentiae, seu naturae perceptione.

(k) In Troad. V. 1016. [p. 15] particular, of the third universal. Universals, therefore, are not outside the mind,

> 31 Relationes, ut diximus sunt ideae, quarum una ad alteram se refert, ut una sine altera intelligi nequeat, vel ut unius consideratio considerationem alterius involvat. Ex quo inferimus haud parùm errare, qui de idea relativa aliquid absolutè adfirmant, vel negant, nec fundamentum relationis ritè expendunt. Quae observatio quantae utilitatis sit ad evitandas logomachias, quin & adfectus tristiores sedandos, dici non potest. Sic multi se pauperes esse dolent, quum nulla re necessaria indigeant. Et ¿curverò nisi quòd fundamentum relationis ponunt homines admodùm divites, quibuscum comparati sibi pauperrimi videntur? Eleganter Seneca, (k)

or, as the Scholastics put it, a parte rei [on the side of the thing]. Universal man is nothing but an idea; for the men who exist are singular.

33 The Peripatetics, following Porphyry, made five classes of universals:

> CAPUT V.

Genus, Species, Specific Difference, Property and Accident. Genus is defined by

> De ideis singularibus, particularibus, universalibus, ubi de quinque praedicabilibus.

Porphyry as a universal notion which is predicated of many things differing in species, when it is asked what a thing is: e.g. animal is the genus of man and of horse, because it designates the notion common to both, and it is what is usually offered by one who answers someone asking what a man, what a horse is. Species is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as their whole essence, as man, which is predicated of Peter, and Paul, and the other individuals of human nature. An Individual, moreover, is that which cannot be divided into several things such as it is itself: e.g. Peter. Specific Difference is a universal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as a metaphysical form, determining the genus to such a species, e.g. rationality.

34 Property is said in four ways: first, what belongs to one species alone, but not to the whole of it, as to be a Physician. Second, conversely, what belongs to the whole species, but not to it alone, as to be two-footed. Third, what belongs to one species alone and to the whole of it, but not always, as in man to be conversing. Fourth, what belongs to the whole species, and always: such in man is the faculty of discourse, or of conversing; for, as Cicero excellently says: for in this one thing above all we excel the beasts, that we converse with one another, and that we can express our thoughts by speaking. Accident is a universal notion which can be present to or absent from many things while their nature remains intact, or, as the Scholastics put it: that which can be present or absent without the corruption of the subject; such in Peter is whiteness. It will be enough to have indicated these things for the present.

> 32 IDEAE aliae nobis rem ipsam repraesentant in individuo, ex. gr. Alexandrum, aliae quod res cum aliis quibusdam commune habet, ex. gr. regiam ejus dignitatem: aliae quod res cum omnibus ejusdem naturae commune habet, ex. gr. humanitatem. Primi generis ideae singulares, secun-

On the Antepredicaments and the Categories of the

Peripatetics. 35

> (k) In Troad. V. 1016. [p. 16] cundi particulares; tertii universales adpelantur. Universalia igitur non sunt extra mentem, seu ut Scholastici loquuntur aparte rei. Homo universalis non est nisi idéa, homines enim qui existunt, singulares sunt.

The Peripatetics call the categories, or Predicaments, a philosophical Dogma, which cannot be called into doubt in Philosophy. Nonsense! For the predicaments are nothing other [p. 16] than a nomenclature, which shows by what name Aristotle named certain beings: in actual fact it is an inept division, as we shall show below; but first we shall explain a few things about the antepredicaments.

> 33 Peripatetici secundum Porphyrium quinque universalium classes fecére, Genus, Speciem, Differentiam Specificam, Proprium, & Accidens. Genus à Porphyrio dicitur: notio universalis, quae de pluribus praedicatur specie differentibus, cum quid sit quaeritur: ex. g. animal, hominis & equi genus est, quia notionem utríque communem designat, & adferri solet ab eo, qui respondet interroganti, quid homo, quid equus sit. Species est universalis notio, quae de pluribus dicitur numero differentibus, tamquam tota essentia, ut homo, qui enuntiatur de Petro, & Paulo, & aliis naturae humanae individuis. Individuum autem est id, quod in plura talia quale ipsum est, dividi nequit: ex. gr. Petrus. Differentia specifica, est notio universalis, quae de pluribus dicitur numero differentibus tamquam forma metaphysica, determinans genus ad talem speciem ex. gr. rationalitas.

36 Aristotle counted four Antepredicaments: Univocals, Equivocals, Analogues and Denominatives. Univocals are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether the same in all. Those words altogether the same signify not identity, but likeness. Equivocals are those whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether different. A common example is Dog, which is taken for the domestic animal and for a star. Analogues are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is partly the same, partly different, or belongs properly to one, improperly to another; thus laughter is analogous with respect to a man and to a meadow. Denominatives are those which are derived from some name, as brave from bravery, etc. And these are the antepredicaments. But if we consider the things themselves, we shall understand without effort that all ideas can be reduced to three classes, as it were: Substance, Adjuncts, Relations, as we also said above.

> 34 Proprium quatuor dicitur modis: primo, quod soli speciei accidit, sed non toti, ut esse Medicum. Secundo è converso, quod toti speciei accidit, sed non soli, ut esse bipedem. Tertio, quod soli, & toti speciei accidit, sed non semper, ut in homine sermocinari. Quarto quod toti speciei, & semper accidit, talis est in homine facultas sermocinandi, seu colloquendi, nam ut egregiè ait Cicero: hoc enim uno praestamus, vel maxime feris, quod colloquimur inter nos, & quod exprimere dicendo sensa possumus. Accidens est notio universalis, quae pluribus adesse potest, vel abesse incolumi eorum natura, seu ut loquuntur Scholastici: quod potest adesse, vel abesse absque subjecti corruptione, talis est in Petro albedo. Haec in praesentia indicare satis fuerit.

37 Aristotle, however, refers all things that exist to ten classes, which he calls categories, and others Predicaments. One is that of substance, or of a thing that can exist by itself; the others are those of accidents, or of those things that cannot exist by themselves. In the first class he counts two substances. The second is Quantity, either discrete, as numbers, or continuous; and this either permanent, as a body, or successive, as motion. The third is Quality, either of the mind, as virtues and sciences, or of the body, as heat, etc. The fourth is Relation, by which one thing leads to the knowledge of another. The fifth is Action, either that which is in the agent, as love, or that which is received in another, as heating. The sixth is Passion, the contrary of action, as being heated. The seventh is Where, or place, as to be at Rome, to be at home, to be in the country, etc. The eighth is Time, as when, to words signifying time, we answer tomorrow, etc. The ninth is Position, which is expressed by these words: stands, lies, etc. The tenth is Habit, that is, the things that clothe the body, as a cloak, etc. Behold the predicaments. Behold the Philosophical dogma which the Peripatetics judge it rash to call into doubt.

> CAPUT VI.

> 39. Et re vera talis distributio inepta prorsus videtur, quum plurima certe contineat, quae non vera entium genera, sed solae denominationes extrinsecae dici debent, ut Relatio, Ubi, Tempus; quòd si denominationes omnes, & modi extrinseci admitti deberent, jam non decem, sed infinita penè entium genera admitterentur. Desunt etiam multa, ex. gr. plures species accidentium, tum corporis, ut quies, tùm spirituum, ut cognitio, &c. In hoc ulterius reprehenditur, quod hominem sub corpore tamquàm sub genere collocet, quum similiter contineri possit sub mente, nec minori jure dicatur Mens, quàm Corpus. Falsa & pugnantia habet: nam refert longitudinem, latitudinem, & pondus ad quantitatem, deinde objecta sensuum ad qualitates, quum tamen extensio, & motus incurrant etiam in visum, pondus, & motus in tactum; adeoque Quantitas sit simul Qualitas. Ut alia hujus generis flagitia omittam.

39 And in fact such a distribution seems altogether inept, since it certainly contains a great many things that ought to be called not true genera of beings but only extrinsic denominations, as Relation, Where, Time; for if all denominations and extrinsic modes were to be admitted, then not ten but almost infinite genera of beings would have to be admitted. Many things are also missing, e.g. several species of accidents, both of body, as rest, and of spirits, as cognition, etc. It is further faulted in this, that it places man under body as under a genus, although he could equally be contained under mind, and could with no less right be called Mind than Body. It contains things false and conflicting: for it refers length, breadth and weight to quantity, and then the objects of the senses to qualities, although extension and motion also fall under sight, and weight and motion under touch; and so Quantity would be at the same time Quality. To pass over other enormities of this kind.

> 40 Adcuratius itaque Recentiores Philosophi septem entium genera, vel cathegorias numerant, ut sub communi, supremoque entis genere, duplex substantiae species, corpus nimirum, & spiritus, sive mens, atque insuper etiam quinque modorum species, nitida, perfectaque serie contineantur. Hinc in illorum sententia,

40 More accurately, therefore, the Modern Philosophers count seven genera, or categories, of beings, so that under the common and supreme genus of being there are contained, in a neat and perfect series, two species of substance, namely body and spirit, or mind, and in addition five species of modes. Hence, in their view,

> Mens, Mensura, Quies, Motus, Positura, Figura
> Sunt cum Materia cunctarum exordia rerum.

Mind, Measure, Rest, Motion, Position, Figure

> 41 Persuassum namque est hujus Philosophiae sectatoribus his septem rebus omnem naturam exhauriri. Nomine Mentis intelligitur substantia spiritualis, ut Deus, Angeli, & Anima rationalis. Mensura quantitatem significat. Quies permanentiam corporis in loco in quo reperitur. Motus est translatio sive migratio corporis ex uno in alium locum. Positura significat partium dispositionem, illam praesertim, quae intima est, quaeque variari non potest, quin eadem substantia varietur. Figura est illa partium dispositio quae exterius adparet, quaeque salva rei substantia variari potest. Materia denique corpus, aut corpoream substantiam significat, quidquid demum corporis, sive materiae nomine intelligatur. Haec verò septem entium genera cunctarum exordia rerum dicuntur, quia nihil concipi potest, quod in ejusmodi rerum generibus non includatur, aut nulla denique singularis substantia reperiatur, in qua plures, aut omnes etiam ex modis ipsis distingui sive reperiri non possint. Verùm ut omnia inlustrius adpareant sequentem tabulam vobis offero, ut ab aliquibus Recentioribus depicta est.

Are, with Matter, the beginnings of all things.

41 For the followers of this Philosophy are persuaded that the whole of nature is exhausted by these seven things. By the name of Mind is understood spiritual substance, as God, the Angels and the rational Soul. Measure signifies quantity. Rest, the permanence of a body in the place in which it is found. Motion is the translation or migration of a body from one place to another. Position signifies the disposition of the parts, above all that which is innermost and which cannot be varied without the substance itself being varied. Figure is that disposition of the parts which appears outwardly, and which can be varied while the substance of the thing remains intact. Matter, finally, signifies body or corporeal substance, whatever in the end may be understood by the name of body or matter. And these seven genera of beings are called the beginnings of all things because nothing can be conceived that is not included in these genera of things; or, finally, no singular substance is found in which several, or even all, of these modes cannot be distinguished or found. But so that everything may appear more clearly, I offer you the following table, as it has been drawn by some of the Moderns.

> CAPUT VII.

On Definitions and Divisions.

> De Definitionibus, & Divisionibus.

hoever has acquired for himself distinct and adequate ideas of 42

Quibus sanè instrumentis carére non potest, qui véritatis investigandae studio tenetur. Si enim distinctam habemus ideam, rem definire possumus, si adaequatam nihil facilius erit, quàm eam dividere.

W                 things will now find it easy not only to describe things, but also

> 43 Definitio ergò est oratio rem ita determinans ut ab aliis omnibus semper distingui possit. Descriptio à definitione ita differt, quod licet utraque vera sit, illa tamen rei non nisi certis sub circunstantiis; haec semper cómpetat. Ex. gr. si dico: horologium est machínula hoc vel illo modo facta, quae vel stilo, vel percussione ostendit quota sit hora diei: haec est definitio horologii: si dico est theca rotunda, quae pendet ex caténa propè lectum, haec propositio tametsi clara, est descriptio horologii.

to define and divide them. And indeed one who is bound to the study of investigating the truth cannot do without these instruments. For if we have a distinct idea, we can define the thing; if an adequate one, nothing will be easier than to divide it.

> 44 Quum ergò definitio semper competere debeat rei, consequens est, ut primo id quo cum aliis ejusdem naturae rebus convenit, ac deinde ideam quae ad essentiam rei primario pertinet, & qua à reliquis omnibus distinguitur, comprehendere debeat, adeoque constare ex genere, & differentia specìfica. Ex. gr. triangulum est figura tribus lineis circunscripta. Quod si differentiam illam specìficam desumo à nota aliqua, qua rem mihi obviam ab aliis omnibus semper discernere possim, definitio illa dicetur nominalis: ex. gr. circulus est figura, cujus peripheria à centro ubique aequaliter distat. Si differentiam in eo ponam, ut ostendam modum, quomodo illa res oriatur, vel quomodo possibilis sit, definitio realis emerget, ex. gr. circulus ést figura, quae radio circa punctum circumacto describitur.

43 Definition, then, is a statement so determining a thing that it can always be distinguished from all others. Description differs from definition in this, that although both are true, the former applies to the thing only under certain circumstances, the latter always. E.g. if I say: a clock is a little machine made in this or that way, which, either by a hand or by striking, shows what hour of the day it is, this is the definition of a clock; if I say: it is a round case that hangs from a chain near the bed, this proposition, though clear, is a description of a clock.

44 Since, then, a definition must always apply to the thing, it follows that it must comprehend first that in which the thing agrees with other things of the same nature, and then the idea which belongs primarily to the essence of the thing and by which it is distinguished from all the rest; and so it must consist of genus and specific difference. E.g. a triangle is a figure bounded by three lines. But if I take that specific difference from some mark by which I can always tell the thing I meet apart from all others, that definition will be called nominal: e.g. a circle is a figure whose periphery is everywhere equally distant from the center. If I place the difference in showing the manner in which the thing arises, or how it is possible, a real definition will result; e.g. a circle is a figure described by a radius turned about a point.

45 If, however, the definition of the name is altogether accurate, so that it distinguishes the very thing signified by the name from any other thing whatever, it makes no difference whether such definitions are called definitions of the thing or of the name, as the celebrated Jacquier very well observes. From this it readily appears, first, that a definition ought not to be negative, since in that way a thing is not distinguished from a thing by what belongs to its essence.

> 45 Si tamen definitio nominis adcurata omninò sit, ita ut rem ipsam nomine significatam ab alia qualibet re distinguat, nihil interest tales definitiones vel rei vel nominis adpelari, ut optime advertit Cl. Jacquier. Ex quibus facile patet primò definitionem non debére esse negativam, quià ita res à re non distinguitur, per id quod ad essentiam pertinet. Secundò cum definito reciprocari debere, sive, ut Scholae loquuntur, quod mu- [p. 19] tuo convertantur definitum & definitio. Tertió eamdem constare debére verbis propriis, perspicuis, aut certè jam antea definitis. Quartò quod definitum non ingrediatur definitionem, seu quod non explicetur idem per idem, ex. gr. circulus est circulus. Quinto definitionem convenire debere omni & soli definitio, unde vitiosa est illa definitio hominis: animal bipes sine plumis. Ex quibus regulis fluunt quatuor in Scholis recepta axiomata: cui convenit definitio, convenit & definitum, & è contrario: item cui repugnat definitio, repugnat & definitum, & è converso.

Second, that it ought to be reciprocal with the thing defined, or, as the Schools say, that the thing defined and the definition be mutually [p. 19] convertible. Third, that it ought to consist of proper and perspicuous words, or at least of words already defined beforehand. Fourth, that the thing defined should not enter into the definition, that is, that the same should not be explained by the same, e.g. a circle is a circle. Fifth, that the definition ought to apply to all of the thing defined and to it alone; hence that definition of man is faulty: a two-footed animal without feathers. From these rules flow four axioms received in the Schools: to whatever the definition belongs, the thing defined belongs also, and conversely; likewise: to whatever the definition is repugnant, the thing defined is repugnant also, and vice versa.

> 46 Duo tamen hic curemus oportet. Primum, ut obscura nomina, quae in controversiam veniunt, adcurate definiamus, ne ex ambiguo disputemus. Peccant in hanc legem nonnulli Philosophi, qui quòd vocabula non definiant, ad convicia, atque pugnos usque altercantur inter se, & si eadem ambo disputantes dicant aliis & aliis verbis. Secundum: ne quum nomina definimus, putemus nos rem ipsam definire. In hanc regulam etiam peccant illi ipsi Philosophi: quum enim certa vocabula arbitratu suo definiant persuadent sibi, se naturas rerum significatarum penitus cognoscere, & definire: ex. gr. interroges eos, ¿quid sit arbor? Ajunt esse vivens insensitivum. ¿Quit sit fulmen? Reponunt, esse exhalationem in nube accensam, quae tendit deorsum. Verum hae explicationes tantum declarant; quae res iis nominibus significentur, at rerum naturas non aperiunt, nisi prius distincte cognoscam, quid sit vivens insentivum, exhalatio, nubes, accensio, cetera. Sed jam de divisione pauca dicamus.

46 Two things, however, we must take care of here. First, that we define accurately the obscure names that come into controversy, lest we dispute from an ambiguity. Some Philosophers sin against this law, who, because they do not define their terms, wrangle with one another even to abuse and fisticuffs, even if both disputants are saying the same things in different words. Second: that when we define names, we should not think that we are defining the thing itself. Against this rule those very Philosophers also sin: for when they define certain words at their own discretion, they persuade themselves that they thoroughly know and define the natures of the things signified: e.g. ask them, what is a tree? They say it is a living insensitive thing. What is lightning? They answer that it is an exhalation kindled in a cloud, which tends downward. But these explanations declare only what things are signified by those names; they do not lay open the natures of the things, unless I first know distinctly what a living insensitive thing, an exhalation, a cloud, kindling and the rest are. But now let us say a few things about division.

> 47 Divisio est propositio, quae resolvit totum in partes, quo facilius quid contineat intelligatur, aut meliùs: ideae universalis in plures particulares solutio. Id quod resolvitur, dicitur divisum, partes in quas dividitur, membra dividentia. Alia est divisio Physica, ut quum dividimus lignum in partes, alia Logica, ut quum mente divido substantiam in corpus, & spiritum. Hae partes vocantur inferiora.

47 Division is a statement that resolves a whole into its parts, so that what it contains may be more easily understood; or better: the resolution of a universal idea into several particular ones. That which is resolved is called the thing divided; the parts into which it is divided, the dividing members. One division is Physical, as when we divide wood into parts; another Logical, as when I divide substance in my mind into body and spirit. These parts are called inferiors.

48 The first law of division is that the dividing members be equal to the whole divided. Faultily, therefore, do the Aristotelians divide being into ten categories, since more can be established. The second, that one member not be contained in another; hence number is not rightly divided into even, odd and binary: for the binary is contained in the even. Let the Logician, therefore, in his wisdom so divide a thing that a clearer knowledge of the thing may be had from it, so that he may define it the more easily and accurately. And let him carefully beware of what we warned above concerning definition, lest, when he divides the signification of a name, he think he is dividing the thing itself: an enormity which Aristotle

> 48 Lex prima divisionis est, quod membra dividentia adaequent totum divisum. Vitiose igitur dividunt Aristotelici ens in decem cathegórias, quia plures constitui possunt. Secunda, quod unum membrum non contineatur in alio, quare numerus non rectè dividitur in parem, & imparem, & binarium: nam binarius continetur in pari. Logicus itaque pro sua sapientia rem ita dividat, ut clarior inde rei cognitio habeatur, quo facilius, & adcuratius eam definiat. Atque illud caveat studiosè, quod supra de definitione monuimus, ne quum dividit significationem nominis, existimet se rem ipsam dividere: quod flagitium Aris- [p. 20]

C2 [p. 20] himself and some of the Ancients imprudently committed. What we have warned concerning division must be understood of subdivisions as well, although care must be taken that subdivisions are not multiplied beyond necessity. For the more a great rock is ground into dust, the less do we grasp its size with the mind.

## CHAPTER VIII

> toteles ipse, & Veteres nonnulli imprudentes admiserunt. Quae de divisione monuimus, eadem & de subdivisionibus intelligenda, quamvis danda sit opera, ne subdivisiones praeter necessitatem multiplicentur. Quò magis enim magnum saxum in pulverem conteritur, eò minus ejus magnitudinem animo comprehendimus.

On Judgments and Propositions, and on the matter, form, quantity and quality of a proposition: on the opposition, equipollence and conversion of propositions.

> CAPUT VIII.

hen the mind compares two ideas, accurately perceived, with 49

> De Judiciis, & propositionibus, de que propositionis materia, forma, quantitate, qualitate: de oppositione, aequipollentia, & conversione propositionum.

W              each other, and either connects them or pulls them apart, there

> 49 QUando mens binas ideas adcuratè perceptas interse comparat, easque vel nectit, vel divellit nascitur inde judicium quod est: perceptio convenientiae, aut disconvenientiae, quae reperitur inter duas ideas. Judicium autem verbis expressum Propositio, vel enunciatio adpelatur. Propositio autem est: oratio adfirmans, vel negans aliquid de aliquo. Respondet enim judicio, quod vel duas ideas connectit, vel disjungit.

arises from this judgment, which is: the perception of the agreement or disagreement that is found between two ideas. Judgment expressed in words is called a Proposition, or enunciation. A proposition, moreover, is: a statement affirming or denying something of something. For it corresponds to judgment, which either connects or disjoins two ideas.

50 Every proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, or attribute, terms which the copula is joins together; although this, just like the subject, often lies hidden in the predicate, and so the whole proposition consists of one or two words, e.g. Peter loves, I die, in which these are understood: Peter is loving, I am dying. The subject is that of which something is said. The predicate, what is said of the subject. The copula is the link, or union of subject and predicate. By the copula, or by the verb is, or is not, the force of judging is signified, that is, it is shown that the predicate is included, or not included, in the subject. For this proposition, God is just, means this: in the idea of God the idea of justice is included. This other, a man is not a horse, means: in the idea of man the idea of horse is not included.

> 50 Omnis propositio constat subjecto, & praedicato, seu adtributo, quos terminos inter se jungit copula est, quamvis haec aequè ac subjectum saepè in praedicato latitet, adeoque tota propositio uno, vel binis vocabulis constet. ex. gr. Petrus amat, morior, in quibus subaudiuntur hae: Petrus est amans, ego sum moriens. Subjectum est id de quo aliquid dicitur. Praedicatum, quod dicitur de subjecto. Copula est nexus, sivè unio subjecti & praedicati. Per copulam, seu per verbum est, vel non est vis judicandi significatur, idest, ostenditur praedicatum in subjecto includi, vel non includi. Haec enim propositio: Deus est justus, hoc dicere vult, in idea Dei inclusa est idea justitiae. Haec altera, homo non est equus, hoc vult dicere, in idea hominis non inclusa est idea equi. Nulla enim propositio adfirmans est vera, nisi quia totum praedicatum in subjecto includitur, nulla ne- [p. 21] gans verò nisi quia totum non includitur, ex. gr. quum dico ego sum vivens pronomine ego designo ideam complexam mei individui, & volo dicere meum individuum est vivens; quod valet, in idea cómplexa mei individui includitur idea viventis.

For no affirmative proposition is true except because the whole predicate is included in the subject; no negative [p. 21] one, except because the whole is not included. E.g. when I say I am living, by the pronoun I I designate the complex idea of my individual self, and I mean my individual self is living; which amounts to: in the complex idea of my individual self the idea of living is included.

> 51 Materia propositionis sunt illae voces quibus eadem propositio veluti partibus componitur. Rationae materiae propositio dicitur necessaria, quando praedícatum necessario convenit subjecto, ut homo est animal; contingens quando contingenter convenit, ut Joannes est albus; impossibilis, quando ei repugnat, ut Sempronius est lapis. Sed haec item ad necessariam refertur: nam illa dicitur necessario vera: haec necessario falsa.

51 The Matter of a proposition is those words of which the same proposition is composed, as it were of parts. By reason of its matter a proposition is called necessary when the predicate agrees necessarily with the subject, as man is an animal; contingent when it agrees contingently, as John is white; impossible when it is repugnant to it, as Sempronius is a stone. But this too is referred to the necessary: for the former is called necessarily true, the latter necessarily false.

> 52 Forma propositionis est ipsa copula, quae conjungit praedicatum cum subjecto. Ratione formae dividitur propositio in adfirmativam, quae adtribuit unum alteri, & in negativam, quae negat unum de alio: Ubi obiter nota, propositionem negativam esse, quando particula non, cadit supra verbum. Dividitur etiam in Cathegorematicam, quae sine conditione adfirmat vel negat, & in hypotheticam, que adfirmat sub conditione, ut si Sol lucet, dies est. Propositio complexa, est quae pluribus propositionibus constat, ut Magister docet, & discipulus capit.

52 The Form of a proposition is the copula itself, which joins the predicate with the subject. By reason of its form a proposition is divided into affirmative, which attributes one thing to another, and negative, which denies one thing of another. Note here in passing that a proposition is negative when the particle not falls upon the verb. It is divided also into Categorematic, which affirms or denies without condition, and hypothetical, which affirms under a condition, as if the Sun shines, it is day. A complex proposition is one that consists of several propositions, as the Master teaches, and the disciple learns.

> 53 Quantitas propositionis est extensio subjecti formalis ad significanda plura, vel pauciora. Inde propositio est universalis, si subjectum sit universale, ut omnis homo est animal, particularis si subjectum est particulare, ut aliquis homo currit, singularis, si subjectum singulare sit, ut Petrus currit. His accedit propositio indefinita, cujus subjectum est commune & non coarctatur, ut homo legit, non enim dicitur omnis, aut aliquis, aut hic, sed indefinitè homo legit.

53 The Quantity of a proposition is the extension of the formal subject to signify more or fewer things. Hence a proposition is universal if the subject is universal, as every man is an animal; particular if the subject is particular, as some man runs; singular if the subject is singular, as Peter runs. To these is added the indefinite proposition, whose subject is common and is not restricted, as man reads; for one does not say every, or some, or this, but indefinitely man reads.

> 54 Qualitas propositionis dicitur veritas vel falsitas, quia propositió in communi praescindit ab eo quod sit vera vel falsa, sed si reduplicative sumatur ut vera vel falsa, tunc veritas, vel falsitas, utpotè forma denominans propositionem illi convénit essentiáliter: ast propositioni specificative sumptae solum convenít contingenter. Propositiones modales dicuntur illae in quibus explicatur modus, quo praedicatum adfirmatur, vel negatur de subjecto, ut quum dicitur: necesse est hominem esse animal.

54 The Quality of a proposition is said to be its truth or falsity, because a proposition in general abstracts from being true or false; but if it is taken reduplicatively as true or false, then truth or falsity, being a form that denominates the proposition, belongs to it essentially; whereas to a proposition taken specificatively it belongs only contingently. Those propositions are called modal in which the mode is expressed in which the predicate is affirmed or denied of the subject, as when one says: it is necessary that man be an animal.

> 55 Hinc omnes propositiones ad quatuor classes referuntur. Id exprimunt Scholastici quatuor literis A. E. I. O. A. universalis adfirmans, ut omnis homo est justus E universalis negans, ut nullus vitiosus est beatus. I particularis adfirmans, ut aliquis vitiosus est dives. O particularis negans, ut aliquis vitiosus non est dives; sed ut facilius memoriae haec inhaereant his versiculis comprehensa sunt.

55 Hence all propositions are referred to four classes, which the Scholastics express by four letters, A. E. I. O. A, the universal affirmative, as every man is just; E, the universal negative, as no vicious man is happy; I, the particular affirmative, as some vicious man is rich; O, the particular negative, as some vicious man is not rich; but so that these may stick more easily in the memory, they have been comprised in these little verses.

A

[p. 22]

> Asserit A, negat E. verum generaliter ambae.
> Asserit I, negat O, sed particulariter ambae.

A affirms, E denies, but both universally.

> 56 Oppositio est repugnantia duarum propositionum, quae eodem subjecto, & praedicato constant. Quadruplex vulgò statui solet oppositio propositionum: contradictoria, contraria, subcontraria, & subalterna. Oppositio contradictoria est inter duas propositiones, quarum una est universalis, altera particularis, una adfirmans, altera negans ex. gr. omnis homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus. Contradictoriae quoque dicuntur propositiones singulares, quarum una negat, quod adfirmat altera: ex. gr. Aristoteles est Philosophorum princeps, Aristoteles non est Philosophorum princeps. Contradictio enim est adfirmatio & negatio ejusdem praedicati de eodem subjecto, & secundum idem tempus.

I affirms, O denies, but both particularly.

> 57 Propositionum contradictoriarum, una semper est vera, altera falsa. Oppositio contraria est inter duas propositiones universales, quarum una est adfirmans, altera negans, ut omnis homo est albus, nullus homo est albus. Oppositio subcontraria est inter duas propositiones particulares, quarum una est adfirmans, altera negans, ut aliquis homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus. Oppositio subalterna (quae rigorosa oppositio non est) versatur inter duas propositiones, quarum una est universalis, altera particularis, sed utraque vel est adfirmans, vel negans, ut omnis homo est albus, aliquis homo est albus, nullus homo est albus, aliquis homo non est albus, quae ut clarius intelligatis in subjectum paradigma oculos conjicite.

56 Opposition is the incompatibility of two propositions that consist of the same subject and predicate. Opposition of propositions is commonly held to be fourfold: contradictory, contrary, subcontrary and subalternate. Contradictory opposition is between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, one affirmative, the other negative, e.g. every man is white, some man is not white. Singular propositions are also called contradictory when one denies what the other affirms: e.g. Aristotle is the prince of Philosophers, Aristotle is not the prince of Philosophers. For contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same predicate of the same subject, and at the same time.

> A Omnis homo est albus. CONTRARIAE. E Nullus homo est albus.

57 Of contradictory propositions, one is always true, the other false. Contrary opposition is between two universal propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as every man is white, no man is white. Subcontrary opposition is between two particular propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as some man is white, some man is not white. Subalternate opposition (which is not opposition in the strict sense) is found between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, but both either affirmative or negative, as every man is white, some man is white; no man is white, some man is not white; and to understand these more clearly, cast your eyes on the diagram below.

> SUBALTERNAE. CONTRADICTORIAE. SUBALTERNAE.

A: Every man is white. — E: No man is white. — I: Some man is white. — O: Some man is not white. Above: Contraries. Below: Subcontraries. At the sides: Subalterns. Across: Contradictories.

> I Aliquis homo est albus. SUBCONTRARIAE O Aliquis homo non est albus.

[p. 23]

## 58 Take, finally, these most certain rules for recognizing opposition: those

> 58 Accipite demum certissimas regulas ad oppositionem dignoscendam: quae nec simul verae, nec simul falsae esse possunt, contradictoriae sunt, quae non simul verae, sed tamen possunt esse simul falsae, contrariae sunt, quae non possunt esse simul falsae, & possunt esse simul verae, subcontrariae. Propositionum subalternarum, aliquando una est vera, & altera falsa, aliquando utraque falsa, aliquando utraque vera: ex. gr. omnis homo est animal, aliquis homo est animal.

which can be neither true together nor false together are contradictories; those which cannot be true together, but can nevertheless be false together, are contraries; those which cannot be false together, and can be true together, are subcontraries. Of subalternate propositions, sometimes one is true and the other false, sometimes both are false, sometimes both true: e.g. every man is an animal, some man is an animal.

> 59 Aequipollentia, seu aequivalentia propositionum est reductio oppositarum propositionum ad eumdem sensum ope particulae non, quae in contradictoriis praeponitur subjecto, in contrariis post ponitur, in subalternis verò praeponitur simul atque postponitur, ut hoc versiculo demonstratur.

59 Equipollence, or equivalence, of propositions is the reduction of opposite propositions to the same sense by means of the particle not, which in contradictories is placed before the subject, in contraries is placed after it, and in subalterns is placed both before and after, as is shown by this little verse:

> Prae contradic: post contra, prae postque subalter.

Before for contradic., after for contra., before and after for subalter.

> 60 Conversio propositionum est reciproca mutatio subjecti in praedicatum, & praedicati in subjectum, quando nimirum praedicatum ponitur loco subjecti, & subjectum ipsum loco praedicati, remante tamen propositionis illius veritate, quamvis aliquando propositionis extensio, sive quantitas varietur. Conversio autem propositionum ex Grammatica potius, quam ex Logica est colligenda. En mysteria Veterum Logicorum adcuratius quàm illi faciunt explicata. Noluimus tamen ea omittere, ne ereptam juventuti rem utilem, aut fructuosam fortassè Veteres suspicentur.

60 Conversion of propositions is the reciprocal change of the subject into the predicate and of the predicate into the subject, namely when the predicate is put in the place of the subject, and the subject itself in the place of the predicate, the truth of that proposition nevertheless remaining, although sometimes the extension, or quantity, of the proposition is varied. The conversion of propositions, however, is to be gathered from Grammar rather than from Logic.

Here are the mysteries of the old Logicians, explained more accurately than they themselves explain them. We did not wish, however, to omit them, lest the Ancients should perhaps suspect that something useful or fruitful had been snatched away from the youth.

## CHAPTER IX

> CAPUT IX.

On Reasoning, or the Syllogism, and the various kinds of argumentation.

> De Ratiocinatione, vel syllogismo, & variis argumentationum generibus.

easoning, or Syllogism, is the operation of the intellect by which, having set 61

> 61 Ratiocinatio, vel Syllogismus est operatio intellectus, qua ille constituta duarum idearum comparatione cum tertia, jungendae ne istae sint, an separandae cognoscit, vel ut Scholastici loquuntur. Ratiocinatio est cognitio, quae ex una, vel duabus propositionibus aliam infert. Si ex una tantum propositione aliam inferat, ex. gr. cogito: ergo existo, vocatur Enthymema, si autem ex duabus propositionibus inferatur alia, ex. gr. omne quod cogitat existit, sed ego cogito: ergo existo dicitur Syllogismus.

R          up a comparison of two ideas with a third, it learns whether they are to be

joined or to be separated; or, as the Scholastics put it, Reasoning is the cognition that infers another proposition from one or from two propositions. If it infers another from one proposition only, e.g. I think: therefore I exist, it is called an

Enthymeme; but if another is inferred from two propositions, e.g. everything that thinks exists; but I think: therefore I exist, it is called a Syllogism.

Since

[p. 24]

> 62 Quum ergo, ut diximus tres sint ideae in Syllogismo comparandae; consequens est, ut simul ac quatuor ideas in unum Syllogismum compingimus, vitiosa emergat ratiocinatio, quod plerumque fit, ubi vocabulum aliquod, aequivocatione laborat. Hinc male quis ratiocinaretur: Spiritus est substantia cogitans; sed spiritus vini est spiritus: ergo spiritus vini est substantia cogitans, nam quatuor ideae in unum Syllogismum compinguntur. Tres illae ideae, si verbis exprimuntur, termini vocantur, & is quidem de quo aliquid quaeritur terminus minor, quod de eo quaeritur major; & is quocum hi duo termini comparantur medius adpelari solet. Si eg. scire vellim, an aer sit gravis, & hinc has ideas comparem cum pressione corporum: aër erit terminus minor, quia de eo aliquid quaeritur, gravis terminus major, quia hoc ipsum est quod de aëre quaeritur, pressio corporum erit terminus medius, quia cum hac idea duae reliquae comparantur.

62 Since, then, as we have said, there are three ideas to be compared in a Syllogism, it follows that as soon as we cram four ideas into one Syllogism, a faulty reasoning results; which mostly happens when some word suffers from equivocation. Hence one would reason badly thus: Spirit is a thinking substance; but spirit of wine is spirit: therefore spirit of wine is a thinking substance; for four ideas are crammed into one Syllogism. Those three ideas, if they are expressed in words, are called terms; and the one about which something is asked is usually called the minor term, that which is asked about it the major, and that with which these two terms are compared the middle. E.g. if I wished to know whether air is heavy, and therefore compared these ideas with the pressure of bodies: air will be the minor term, because something is asked about it; heavy the major term, because this is the very thing that is asked about air; the pressure of bodies will be the middle term, because the other two are compared with this idea.

> 63 Tribus propositionibus Syllogismus constat, quarum prima, quae ex majori & medio termino componitur dicitur major, secunda, quae ex minore & medio, minor, tertia demum, quae ex minore, & majore, conclusio adpelatur. Sic si Syllogismum construam ex terminis paulò ante propositis: quod premit corpora inferiora est grave; aer premit corpora inferiora: ergo aer est gravis; prima propositio erit major, secunda minor, postrema conclusio seu consequentia adpelatur. In Enthymemate, prima dicitur antecedens, secunda consequentia.

63 A Syllogism consists of three propositions, of which the first, which is composed of the major and the middle term, is called the major; the second, composed of the minor and the middle, the minor; the third, finally, composed of the minor and the major, is called the conclusion. Thus if I construct a Syllogism from the terms proposed a little earlier: what presses on lower bodies is heavy; air presses on lower bodies: therefore air is heavy, the first proposition will be the major, the second the minor, and the last is called the conclusion or consequent. In an Enthymeme the first is called the antecedent, the second the consequent.

> 64 Dilemma est argumentatio ex duabus interrogationibus in quarum qualibet capitur respondens, ex. gr. vel qui peccat recordatur inferni vel non? Si concedis: ergo est stultus; si negas: ergo etiam est stultus, quia tantae poenae non recordatur.

64 A Dilemma is an argumentation from two questions, by either of which the respondent is caught, e.g. does he who sins remember hell, or not? If you grant it: then he is a fool; if you deny it: then he is a fool too, because he does not remember so great a punishment.

> 65 Inductio est argumentatio à singularibus sufficienter enumeratis ad universale, ut si dicas: aurum liquari potest, stannum, plumbum, & ferrum liquari possunt: ergo omne metallum liquari potest. Haec argumentatio erit mala & roboris expers, si vel unam partem ex numerandis non examinet. Exemplum seu paritas est argumentatio ab uno ad aliud simile in eadem linea. Demonstratio est argumentatio, quae constat praemissis evidentibus. Hinc per demonstrationem res manifeste nobis vera adparet. Illud quippe verè evidenterque cognoscitur, quod ex claris, perspicuisque principiis eruitur. Ceterum, aut effectum ex sua causa demonstramus, aut causam ex suo effectu. Prior demonstratio à priore, posterior à posteriore dicitur.

65 Induction is argumentation from singulars sufficiently enumerated to the universal, as if you say: gold can be melted; tin, lead and iron can be melted: therefore every metal can be melted. This argumentation will be bad and devoid of strength if it fails to examine even one part of those that are to be enumerated. Example, or parity, is argumentation from one thing to another similar thing in the same line. Demonstration is argumentation that consists of evident premises. Hence through demonstration a thing manifestly appears true to us. For that is truly and evidently known which is drawn out from clear and perspicuous principles. For the rest, we demonstrate either the effect from its cause, or the cause from its effect. The former demonstration is called a priori, the latter a posteriori.

> 66 Sic ex. g. si rotunditatem telluris demonstro ex umbra ejus in Eclipsibus Lunaribus, demonstro causam ex effectu, adeo

66 Thus, e.g., if I demonstrate the roundness of the earth from its shadow in Lunar Eclipses, I demonstrate the cause from the effect, so

> [p. 25]

[p. 25] that this demonstration will be a posteriori. On the other hand, when I demonstrate the immortality of the mind from its spirituality, and this from thought, the demonstration will be a priori. The cognition that is acquired by means of demonstration is called science. Science, moreover, is defined: certain and evident cognition of a necessary thing, proceeding from demonstration.

> que ea demonstratio erit à posteriore. Contra ubi mentis immortalitatem ex ejus spiritualitate, hanc ex cogitatione demonstro, demonstratio erit à priore. Cognitio, quae demonstrationis ope adquiritur scientia vocatur. Definitur autem scientia: cognitio certa & evidens rei necessariae ex demonstratione proveniens.

67 It is called certain cognition, that is, firm and stable and altogether unshaken, and by this science differs from opinion, which is nothing but probable cognition of a thing. It is called evident cognition, namely clear and plainly perspicuous, and hence it is distinguished from faith, which is wholly concerned with obscure things. It is said to be of a necessary thing, so that it may thence be plain that, properly speaking, no science can be had of those things which can be otherwise than as they are known. It is said, lastly, to be proceeding from demonstration, so that it may be distinguished from understanding, namely from the cognition of first principles. For the notion of these does not depend on demonstration, since they are most evident from their own terms, e.g. the whole is greater than its part, etc. Just as one demonstration is a priori and another a posteriori, so a twofold science is distinguished: namely most perfect and less perfect.

> 67 Dicitur cognitio certa, hoc est firma & stabilis, penitùsque inconcusa, & per hoc scientia differt ab opinione, quae non est nisi probabilis rei cognitio. Dicitur cognitio evidens, clara scilicèt & planè perspicua, atque hinc discernitur à fide, quae tota in obscuris versatur. Dicitur rei necessariae, ut inde pateat nullam de iis rebus dari posse scientiam, propriè loquendo, quae aliter esse possunt, ac cognoscuntur. Dicitur postremò ex demonstratione proveniens, ut discernatur ab intelligentia, nempè à cognitione primorum principiorum, Horum enim notio à demonstratione non dependet, quum ex suis terminis sint evidentissima, ex. gr. totum est majus sua parte, &c. Sicut demonstratio, alia est à priore, alia à posteriore, ita duplex scientia distinguitur: perfectissima, scilicèt, & minus perfecta. Illa per demonstrationem à priore adquiritur, haec verò per demonstrationem à posteriore.

The former is acquired through demonstration a priori, the latter through demonstration a posteriori.

70 Here the Peripatetics would have it observed that all the words consist of three syllables, if you except Baralipton and Frisesomorum, to which, for the sake of the meter, as they themselves say, one or two syllables are added that do not pertain to the figure. Recall to memory that A denotes the universal affirmative, etc. Hence a syllogism in Barbara, e.g., consists of three universal affirmative propositions; in Celarem, of a negative major, an affirmative minor and a negative consequent, all universal. The first nine modes, contained in the first two verses, belong to the first figure, the next four to the second, and the rest to the third. Now we ought to treat of the reduction of the syllogism; but we, following the more circumspect Peripatetics, deliberately leave aside a treatment of this kind: for generally, as St. Augustine says, a man of wit sees sooner that a conclusion is not right than he grasps its precepts; a slow man does not see it, and much less what is prescribed concerning it.

his is that celebrated rule devised by the most illustrious Author of 71

T           the Art of Thinking: namely that, for the conclusion to be rightly in‐

ferred, it must be contained in one of the premises, and this very thing must be shown, or indicated, by the other, which is called the applicative, or indicative, just as the first is called the containing one.

[p. 27]

> tinens. In syllogismis adfirmativis nihil planè interest, an majorem, an minorem dicamus esse continentem, vel adplicatam, quia útraque aliquomodo conclusionem cóntinet, útraque etiam mutuò ostendit illam in altera continéri. Nam ex. gr. si dúbito, ¿an homo impius sit miser?, sic argumentabor. Quicumque servit cupiditatibus, est miser, sed impius servit cupiditatibus: ergo impius est miser. Quamcumque praemissarum designáveris, poterit dici conclusionem continére, idque ab altera ostendi. Nam conclusio continetur in majori, quia serviens cupiditatibus, impium sub se continet, & à minori ósténditur, quia serviens cupiditatibus, in sua idea comprehendit ideam miseri.

In affirmative syllogisms it makes no difference at all whether we call the major or the minor the containing or the applicative, since each in some way contains the conclusion, and each also mutually shows it to be contained in the other. For e.g. if I doubt whether an impious man is wretched, I shall argue thus: Whoever is a slave to his desires is wretched; but the impious man is a slave to his desires: therefore the impious man is wretched. Whichever of the premises you designate, it can be said to contain the conclusion, and this to be shown by the other. For the conclusion is contained in the major, because one who is a slave to his desires contains the impious man under itself; and it is shown by the minor, because one who is a slave to his desires comprehends in its idea the idea of the wretched.

> 72 Nihilominus in syllogismis adfirmativis, quum major fere semper sit universalior, ut plurimum haberi poterit pro continente, & minor pro adplicante. In syllogismis verò negativis, praemissa negans est semper propositio continens, & adfirmans est propositio adplicans, quia quum consequentia sit negativa, aequius est, ut in praemissa negativa contineatur, quàm in adfirmante, quum negatio solùm in negatione includatur. Sed principium adplicemus.

72 Nevertheless, in affirmative syllogisms, since the major is almost always the more universal, it can for the most part be taken as the containing premise, and the minor as the applicative. In negative syllogisms, however, the negative premise is always the containing proposition, and the affirmative is the applicative proposition, because, since the consequent is negative, it is more reasonable that it be contained in the negative premise than in the affirmative, since a negation is included only in a negation. But let us apply the principle.

> 73 Dubito ex. g. ¿an iste syllogismus rectè concludat? Evangelium salutem spondet Christianis; quidam impii sunt Christiani: ergo Evangelium salutem spondet quibusdam impiis. Considératis ergo praemissis, evidens est, conclusionem in majori propositione minimè contineri, quamvis prima facie, in minori videatur comprehensa. Etenim Evangelium non omnibus christianis salutem promittit, sed iis tantùm, qui Christi D. mandata observant, quod non faciunt impii. Igitur syllogismus est illegítimus. Eadem ratione nullus est, qui sequitur: omnis homo est animal; equus non est homo: ergo equus non est animal. Conclusio namquè in praemissa negante non comprehenditur. At è contrario isti sunt optimi: Miseri sunt, qui cupiditatibus serviunt; avari cupiditatibus serviunt: ergo avari sunt miseri. Nulla substantia carens partibus destrui potest ab agente creato; anima rationalis est substantia carens partibus: ergo anima rationalis à nullo agente creato destrui potest. Utriusque enim conclusio in majori continetur, quemádmodum minor ipsa propositio palám facit.

73 I doubt, e.g., whether this syllogism concludes rightly: The Gospel promises salvation to Christians; some impious men are Christians: therefore the Gospel promises salvation to some impious men. Having considered the premises, then, it is evident that the conclusion is by no means contained in the major proposition, although at first sight it seems to be comprehended in the minor. For the Gospel does not promise salvation to all Christians, but only to those who observe the commandments of Christ the Lord, which the impious do not do. Therefore the syllogism is illegitimate. By the same reasoning this one is null: every man is an animal; a horse is not a man: therefore a horse is not an animal. For the conclusion is not comprehended in the negative premise. On the contrary, these are excellent: They are wretched who are slaves to their desires; the avaricious are slaves to their desires: therefore the avaricious are wretched. No substance lacking parts can be destroyed by a created agent; the rational soul is a substance lacking parts: therefore the rational soul can be destroyed by no created agent. For the conclusion of each is contained in the major, as the minor proposition itself makes plain.

74 By the help of this principle, too, the fallacy of this syllogism can be detected with little trouble: he who says you are an animal says what is true; but he who says you are a goose says you are an animal: therefore he who says you are a goose says what is true. For it suffices to answer that neither of the premises contains the conclusion. For animal in the major is taken particularly, since it is the predicate of this proposition: you are an animal. Hence, too, may be sought the solution of the sophism that St. Augustine reports: you are not what I am; I am a man: therefore you are not a man: for each

> 74 Ope etiam hujus principii facili negotio détegi potest fallacia hujus syllogismi: qui dicit te esse animal, dicit verum; sed qui dicit te esse anserem, dicit te esse animal: ergo qui dicit te esse anserem dicit verum. Respondére namque sufficit, neutram praemissarum continére conclusionem. Animal enim in majori sumitur particulariter, quia est praedicatum hujus propositionis: tu es animal. Hinc etiam peti potest solutio sophísmatis, quod Sanctus Augustinus refert: non es, quod ego sum; ego sum homo: ergo tu non es homo: nam [p. 28] útraque praemissa loquitur de re singulariter mihi propria, itaque non potest continere conclusionem, quae procedit de re tibi propria.

D2 [p. 28] premise speaks of a thing singularly proper to me, and so it cannot contain the conclusion, which proceeds about a thing proper to you.

> 75 Ad hanc normam, facilemque regulam omne ratiocinium exígite, nec operosa, & prorsùs inutili syllogismorum reductione vobis erit opus, si hanc omnibus communem, & penè in conspectu positam argumentandi legem sequemini. Hujus enim principii lumine cujusvis argumentationis bónitas deprehendi fácile potest, ut aliae proindè leges, vel obscuriores, vel minùs universales, vel inutiles etiam censéri possint; imò verò debeant.

75 To this norm and easy rule submit every reasoning, and you will have no need of the laborious and altogether useless reduction of syllogisms, if you follow this law of arguing, which is common to all and placed almost before one’s eyes. For by the light of this principle the goodness of any argumentation whatever can easily be detected, so that the other laws can accordingly be deemed either more obscure, or less universal, or even useless; nay rather, they must be.

On the Fallacies of the Syllogism.

> De fallaciis Syllogismi.

allacy of a Syllogism, which comes from many sources, is a fault both 76

> 76 Fallacia Syllogismi, quae ex multiplici capite venit, vitium est, & cognoscendum, & vitandum. Primò igitur Syllogismus fallit ex aequivocatione alicujus nóminis, ex. gr. Gallus est avis; sed vir Francus est Gallus: ergo vir Francus est avis. Secundò quum fit transitus à genere ad speciem, ut Sempronius est animal, sed asinus est animal: ergo Sempronius est asinus. Tertia fallacia dicitur ignoratio elenchi, quando nimirùm aliud impugnatur, quàm, quod est in quaestione, quia vel adtribuitur adversario, quod ipse non ádferit, vel ignoratur status quaestionis. Hùc pértinet mutatio medii, quando probaturus ex. gr. Deum esse amandum quia Bonus, relicto medio Bonitatis adsumis Sapientiam, aut Omnipotentiam. Quarta est petitio principii, quando supponitur id quod probari debebat. Ad hoc sophisma revocari possunt rationes illae, quibus probatur ignotum per aequè ignotum, incertum per aequè incertum, aut incertius.

F          to be recognized and to be avoided. First, then, a Syllogism deceives

by the equivocation of some name, e.g. a gallus [cock] is a bird; but a

Frenchman is a Gallus [Gaul]: therefore a Frenchman is a bird. Second, when there is a passage from genus to species, as Sempronius is an animal, but an ass is an animal: therefore Sempronius is an ass. The third fallacy is called ignoratio elenchi, namely when something other is attacked than what is in question, because either something is attributed to the adversary which he himself does not assert, or the state of the question is ignored. Here belongs the change of the middle, when, intending to prove, e.g., that God is to be loved because He is

Good, you abandon the middle of Goodness and take up Wisdom or Omnipotence.

The fourth is petitio principii, when that is supposed which ought to have been proved. To this sophism can be brought back those reasons by which the unknown is proved by the equally unknown, the uncertain by the equally uncertain, or by the more uncertain.

77 The sophism of petitio principii extends widely: for whoever, without any proof, sets down as if perspicuous what altogether needs proof asks that some principle be granted him which was to be proved. This happens either proximately or remotely. Proximately, as when one puts forward as a reason the conclusion to be proved, either in the same words or in synonymous ones, or by a circle.

> 77 Latè patet sophisma petitionis principii: quicumque enim ponit sine ulla probatione véluti perspícuum, quod probatione omninò índiget, is quidem petit concedi sibi principium aliquod, quod erat probandum. Id verò vel proximè, vel remotè fit. Proximè, ut si pro ratione ponat conclusionem probandam, vel eisdem, vel sinónimis verbis, vel per círculum. Remotè, ut si rem apertè falsam, vel mera verba, vel aliquid hujúsmodi ád [p. 29] ferat ad probandam thesim: nam etiam tali casu petit sibi concédi principium, quod ei probandum erat, ut propósitum éfficeret. Quum praemissarum altera, vel plane dubia, vel plane falsa, pro ratione adfertur, hoc sophisma vocatur etiam petitio principii. Id plurimis modis fieri potest, ut supra diximus. Aristoteles probat inerrantia sidera scintilláre, quia plurimum distant à nobis, (l) & plurimum distare quia scintillent. (m) En circulus.

Remotely, as when one brings forward a thing openly false, or mere words, or something of this kind [p. 29] to prove the thesis: for in such a case too he asks that the principle be granted him which he had to prove in order to accomplish what was proposed. When one of the premises, either plainly doubtful or plainly false, is adduced as a reason, this sophism too is called petitio principii. This can happen in very many ways, as we said above. Aristotle proves that the fixed stars twinkle because they are very far distant from us (l), and that they are very far distant because they twinkle (m). Behold a circle.

> 78 Quum adsignant pro causa physica mera verba, quae nihil reapsè significant, dari petitionem principii supra diximus. En exemplum. Philosophi nimis multi, dum res ab ipsa natura involútas explicare conantur, quum id firmis, & perspicuis argumentis nequeant efficere, & inscitiam suam nolint profitéri, ad verba inania recúrrunt, & plaudunt sibi, quasi tale mysterium reserassent. Hinc horror vacui, virtus soporifera, & id genus vocábula, sonóra illa quidem, & ampullósa, sed quae nullam sententiam habent, nec nos faciunt doctiores.

78 When they assign as a physical cause mere words that in reality signify nothing, we have said above that there is a petitio principii. Here is an example. Very many Philosophers, while they try to explain things wrapped up by nature herself, since they cannot accomplish this with firm and perspicuous arguments and are unwilling to confess their ignorance, have recourse to empty words and applaud themselves as though they had unlocked some such mystery. Hence horror of the vacuum, soporific virtue, and words of that kind, sonorous indeed and bombastic, but which have no meaning and do not make us more learned.

> 79 Quinta fallacia est non causae ut causa, ex. gr. Petrus in studiis bona dissipavit, & nihil ipsi profuit: ergo tempus in studiis non debet impendi. Ad hoc sophisma revocanda est, vulgaris illa mentis humanae fallacia: post hoc: ergo propter hoc. Sexta est imperfecta partium enumeratio. Sic pessimè ratiocinatur, qui integro Collegio tribuit peccatum aliquorum ex ipso. Septima est fallacia accidentis quando de natura rei judicatur ex eo, quod illi cónvenit per accidens; sic Medicinae omnia mala tribuuntur, quae proveniunt à circulatorum erroribus. Octava est, quando arguitur à secundum quid, ad simpliciter ex. gr. Aethiops est albus secundum dentes: ergo est albus.

79 The fifth fallacy is non-cause as cause, e.g. Peter squandered his fortune on studies, and they did him no good: therefore time ought not to be spent on studies. To this sophism must be brought back that common fallacy of the human mind: after this: therefore because of this. The sixth is imperfect enumeration of the parts. Thus he reasons very badly who attributes to a whole College the sin of some of its members. The seventh is the fallacy of the accident, when one judges of the nature of a thing from what belongs to it by accident; thus all the evils that come from the errors of quacks are attributed to Medicine. The eighth is when one argues from what holds in some respect to what holds simply, e.g. an Ethiopian is white as to his teeth: therefore he is white.

> 80 Nona est paritas inepta: quando nimirùm, ex eo quod duae res in uno, vel áltero praedicato, sunt símiles, collígimus álteram álteri esse simillimam. Ejusdem sophísmatis auctores sunt illi, qui, ut aliquid álteri faciendum persuadeant, vitia astùtè praetereunt, cómmoda verò in caelum extollunt, ex. gr. Scholastici Philósophi, ut nobis persuadeant, Logicam suam ceteris esse praeferendam, cum jactatione ponunt, se ex Aristotelis Dialéctica disputáre, esse eam utilem ad Theologiam Scholasticam addiscendam: tùm demùm neminem sine ea in abstrusioribus disciplinis posse disputare. Illud autem tacent: talem Dialecticam esse artem cavillandi, & sine ullo fine contendendi, non trádere viam indagandi verum, tùm certum, tùm probabile: nihil de ar

80 The ninth is inept parity: namely when, because two things are similar in one or another predicate, we conclude that the one is very like the other. Authors of the same sophism are those who, in order to persuade someone that something is to be done, cunningly pass over its faults and extol its advantages to the skies; e.g. the Scholastic Philosophers, in order to persuade us that their Logic is to be preferred to the others, boastfully state that they dispute out of Aristotle’s Dialectic; that it is useful for learning Scholastic Theology; and finally that no one can dispute in the more abstruse disciplines without it. But they are silent about this: that such Dialectic is the art of caviling and of contending without any end; that it does not hand down the ways of searching out the true, whether the certain or the probable; that it contains nothing on the art

> (l) De Caelo. 2. cap. 8.

of

> (m) Analyt. Prior. 1. cap. 13. [p. 30] te critica continére, tùm denique nihil utilitatis humano generi adferre, ut in céteris disciplinis rectè sermocinetur, quod tacendum non fuit.
