> 81 Decimà fallacia est: quando non alio argumento infirmamus propositionem veram, nisi auctorem irridendo. Peccant in hoc freqüenter Scholastici cum Recentioribus Philosophis disputantes. Verùm haec confutandi ratio infirma est prorsùs. Cogendi ergò sunt ii, ut theses non cachinnis, & dicteriis, sed argumentis firmis & perspicuis confútent. Fádem viâ cum iis agemus, qui querélis, ejulatu, jurejurándo falsum aliquid nobis persuadére conantur, quia ejusdem sophismatis rei sunt. Dicta sufficiant.

ing rightly in the other disciplines: which ought not to have been passed over in silence.

81 The tenth fallacy is: when we weaken a true proposition by no other argument than by ridiculing its author. The Scholastics often sin in this when disputing with the Modern Philosophers. But this way of refuting is altogether weak. They must therefore be compelled to refute theses not with guffaws and witticisms, but with firm and perspicuous arguments. In the same way shall we deal with those who try to persuade us of something false by complaints, wailing and oaths, because they are guilty of the same sophism. Let what has been said suffice.

## BOOK II

> LIBER II.

On Truth.

> De Veritate.

f anyone uses the operations of the intellect rightly, he certainly uses 82

> 82 SI quis intellectus operationibus rectè utitur, benè sanè utitur ratione, cónseqüensque est, ut hoc modo procédens, inveniat veritatem, de qua jam agendum paulò adcuratiùs. Veritas est, vel Metaphysica, vel Moralis, vel Logica. Metaphysicè verum dicitur, quidquid habet essentiam sibi convenientem. Etiam dicitur metaphysicè verum omne ens, vel existens, vel possibile, quum est consentaneum ideae, quam Deus habet de eo. Quare hoc sensu, Petrus, est verus Petrus, quia respondet ideae Dei. Haec veritas metaphysica vocatur etiam realis. Veritas moralis est, convenientia verborum, signorumque externorum cum cogitationibus mentis. Hinc, qui quod sentit, eloquitur, Verum, qui aliud sentit, aliud loquitur, Falsum dícere perhibetur. Nos verò ágimus de veritate Logica, quae est convenientia idearum nostrarum cum objecto. Hinc, si mihi ex. gr. concipio turrim, vel aliquid rotundum, & ea verè talia sunt, veritatem dicor adsequutus. Conveniunt enim ideae cum objecto. Contrà falsum est disconvenientia idearum cum objecto. Alia deinde veritas est certa, alia probabilis. Certa, quum penitùs sum persuassus, rem ita se habére. Probabilis, quum ita sum persuassus, ut timeam ne id ipsum sit falsum.

I       reason well, and it follows that, proceeding in this manner, he will find

the truth, of which we must now treat a little more accurately. Truth is either Metaphysical, or Moral, or Logical. Whatever has the essence befitting it is called metaphysically true. Every being, too, whether existing or possible, is called metaphysically true when it is in conformity with the idea that God has of it. Hence in this sense Peter is a true Peter, because he corresponds to the idea of God. This metaphysical truth is also called real. Moral truth is the agreement of words and of external signs with the thoughts of the mind. Hence one who speaks out what he thinks is said to speak the True; one who thinks one thing and says another, the False. We, however, are dealing with Logical truth, which is the agreement of our ideas with the object. Hence if, e.g., I conceive a tower, or something round, and these things truly are such, I am said to have attained the truth. For the ideas agree with the object. Conversely, the false is the disagreement of ideas with the object. Further, one truth is certain, another probable. Certain, when I am thoroughly persuaded that the thing is so.

Probable, when I am so persuaded that I fear lest it be false.

84 Pierre Daniel Huet holds that the speech of God alone is what makes us certain that we do not err (n). This opinion is false; for if we can determine nothing with certainty by reason, how shall we become certain that God has said this to us? Not all are breathed upon by the Divine Spirit; and then men are very often deceived in judging. Therefore they cannot plainly establish whether they are made certain by God, or otherwise. Now if our reason is itself the reason of God, we shall be ignorant of nothing; for to infinite reason all things are open. Is anyone so mad as to flatter himself in this way, and to persuade himself that there is nothing he does not know? Spinozism (p), therefore, teems with the most inept ravings.

Mitto alia, ne longior sim quàm quod Elementorum limites patiuntur. At illud certè non omittam, quod unio haec substantialis mentis cum Deo nequit intelligi nisi in Spinosistico systémate. Enim verò, si Deus locus est mentium, ut spatium corporum, aut Dei partes erunt, aut modi, aut Deus ipse. Plura de hoc argumento Clariss. Genovesi. (r)

86 Nicolas Malebranche, Priest of the French Congregation of the Oratory, holds that our mind is essentially joined to God, and that we perceive all things in God’s idea and light, or that the light of God is the criterion of the true, because our mind sees all things in God (q). But if these things are true, I do not see what difference there is between the state of the blessed and that of wayfarers, in which the human mind, subject to so many errors, very often strays from the truth. I pass over other things, lest I be longer than the limits of Elements allow. But this I shall certainly not omit, that this substantial union of the mind with God cannot be understood except in the Spinozist system. For indeed, if God is the place of minds, as space is of bodies, they will be either parts of God, or modes, or God himself. More on this subject in the celebrated Genovesi (r).

> (p) Spinosismus error est, non admittentium nisi unicam substantiam infinitis adtributis praéditam, quae inter numerantur infinita cogitatio, atque infinita extensio: eorum unumquodque aeternam, & infinitam essentiam habet, entia verò infinita oriri finguntur ex necessaria modificatione adtributorum istíus substantiae, animas scilicèt ex modificatione infinitae cogitationis, & corpora ex modificatione extensionis infinitae. Spinosa Deum non distinguit à mundo, Deum facit mutabilem, extensum, & tamen intelligentem. Impiae hypotheseos básim, & fundamentum adsúmit Spinosa non posse dari duas substantias ejusdem essentiae, quia si eamdem habeant essentiam, inquit, sunt una, & eadem substantia. Nullus autèm est, qui statim non videat, duas substantias habere non posse eamdem essentiam identitate numerica, (ut ajunt) posse verò identitate vel generica vel specifica. Nullus quoque est homo sensu communi praéditus, qui ex eo, quod Petrus, & Paulus sint homines, ideoque habeant eamdem essentiam, sive similes sint ratione humanitatis, conclúdat, Petrum, & Paulum esse unum, & eumdem hominem numericè, seu esse unicum individuum. Sed de his oportuniùs in Ethica.

(p) Spinozism is the error of those who admit only a single substance endowed with infinite attributes, among which are numbered infinite thought and infinite extension: each of these has an eternal and infinite essence, while finite beings are imagined to arise from the necessary modification of the attributes of this substance, namely souls from the modification of infinite thought, and bodies from the modification of infinite extension. Spinoza does not distinguish God from the world; he makes God mutable, extended, and yet intelligent. As the basis and foundation of his impious hypothesis Spinoza assumes that there cannot be two substances of the same essence, because if they have the same essence, he says, they are one and the same substance. But there is no one who does not see at once that two substances cannot have the same essence by numerical identity (as they say), but can by identity either generic or specific. Nor is there any man endowed with common sense who, from the fact that Peter and Paul are men, and therefore have the same essence, or are alike by reason of humanity, would conclude that Peter and Paul are numerically one and the same man, or are a single individual. But of these things more opportunely in the Ethics.

assume as true for this reason, that the properties and effects of a thing are conveniently explained from it. E.g. if I assume as true that a subterranean inflammable matter, chiefly nitrous and sulphurous, is the cause of earthquakes, this hypothesis, until something more certain appears, cannot be held to be false: for from it all the phenomena can be explained both easily and plausibly. Or else I assume as a hypothesis the signification of the words, their position, and a connection in agreement with the aim of the author, or the authority of some witness. If the first, that probability is called Hermeneutic, or probable interpretation; if the second, Historical, which is specifically named faith.

88 The foundation, therefore, of Hermeneutic probability is of this kind: What agrees with the signification, position and connection of the words, and likewise with the

Author’s aim, is to be held probably as the Author’s meaning. The foundation of Historical probability is of this kind: What a trustworthy man testifies to be true is probably true.

89 What is handed down to us by men is, first, handed down either by those present, or contemporaries, or by those absent and later. 2. The witnesses are either several or one; and likewise 3. they either perceived the thing with their eyes, or heard it narrated by others; nay, and 4. they either give a reason for their knowledge, or not; and 5. they report a thing either possible in itself, or marvelous, or plainly impossible. Further, 6. they are either known or unknown; 7. they follow the zeal either of neither party or of one party only; 8. they are either prudent or foolish, honest or dishonest, and liars. From these divisions are easily understood the rules by which one can judge of the degrees of human faith. I. is: The more certain I am that the author did not wish to deceive me, the greater the faith I am bound to have in him. II. Whether anyone has wished to deceive me must often be judged from the very circumstances of the narration.

> 90 Certissimum itaque est 1. uni testi rem mirabilem narranti, parùm fidei haberi, etiam si aliàs non adeo suspectus sit, maxime ubi res ita comparata est, ut testis facilè décipi imaginatione potuerit. 2. majorem esse probabilitatis gradum si rem, ut ut mirabilem, non tamen impossibilem, pluresque interim testes, licèt non per omnia eodem modo, iisdemque circunstantiis réferant. 3. multò probabílius esse, quod plures fidedigni iisdem circunstantiis réferunt, eamque probabilitatem haud parum augéri, si testes sint oculati, si personae publicae, si jurati. Plurimae aliae hujus probabilitatis regulae videri possunt apud Clariss. Anton. Genovesi. (s)

90 It is therefore most certain, 1. that little faith is to be had in a single witness narrating a marvelous thing, even if he is otherwise not much suspected, especially when the matter is such that the witness could easily have been deceived by his imagination; 2. that the degree of probability is greater if several witnesses report a thing that, however marvelous, is yet not impossible, even if not in every respect in the same manner and with the same circumstances; 3. that what several trustworthy men report with the same circumstances is much more probable, and that this probability is increased not a little if the witnesses are eyewitnesses, if they are public persons, if they are sworn. Very many other rules of this probability can be seen in the celebrated Antonio Genovesi (s).

> 91 Probabilitas moralis tunc habetur, quando ex signis quibusdam, quae homines praeseferunt, aliquid vel ocultum declaramus, vel praedícimus futurum. Haec pro rebus, quas praedicit adpelatur vel Practica vel Politica. Ex. gr. video Titium facie subtristi adspernantem licitas voluptates, déditum lucro, adtrita & sórdida veste, qui perpetuò clamitat se esse páuperem. Hinc probabiliter ínfero, Titium esse avarum. Haec autem divinandi ratio, quae ex signis externis ratiocinando, animi propensiones investígat, vocatur Probabilitas moralis, seu Practica. Aliquando verò ex hominum consiliis futurum aliquem eventum praedícimus, & haec divinatio peculiari vocábulo nominatur. Probabilitas Politica. Sed hae consecutiones, sunt magis, & minus probabiles, non secus ac judicandi vis, & usus rerum in iis, qui conjectant, qui, si multum prospiciunt, multò veriùs, & probabiliùs judicant.

91 Moral probability is had when, from certain signs that men display, we either declare something hidden or predict something future. According to the things it predicts, this is called either Practical or Political. E.g. I see Titius with a sad face spurning lawful pleasures, given over to gain, in a worn and sordid garment, perpetually crying out that he is poor. Hence I probably infer that Titius is avaricious. This way of divining, then, which by reasoning from external signs investigates the propensities of the mind, is called moral Probability, or Practical. Sometimes, however, we foresee some future event from the counsels of men, and this divination is named by a word of its own, Political Probability. But these consequences are more or less probable, just as the force of judging and the experience of things are greater or less in those who conjecture; those who see far ahead judge much more truly and more probably.

> 92 Probabilitas Physica tunc datur, quùm ex observatione phaenomenórum, & sensationum, hypothesim aliquam cogitamus, quae phaenómena omnia dilucidè explicet, & peritè. Quod si hypóthesis, quam pono est talis, ut ex ea nequeam probare, rem ita se habére; non est hypothesis, sed fictio. Ex. gr. quum dicunt Peripatetici horrorem vacui esse causam, cur antlia hauriat aquam, est mera fictio, quia talia verba non explicant, cur aqua 32 pedes adscendat, ultrò non adscendat in antlia mille pedes longa.

92 Physical Probability is given when, from the observation of phenomena and of sensations, we think out some hypothesis that explains all the phenomena lucidly and skillfully. But if the hypothesis that I posit is such that from it I cannot prove that the thing is so, it is not a hypothesis but a fiction. E.g. when the Peripatetics say that the horror of the vacuum is the cause why a pump draws water, it is a mere fiction, because such words do not explain why water rises 32 feet and rises no further in a pump a thousand feet long.

We are led by authority when, in passing judgment on things, we abide by the sayings of others. That authority which moves us to assent is either Divine or

Human. That we should be deceived by Divine authority is utterly impossible, as we shall say. But that we can be deceived by human authority escapes no one. It matters very greatly, therefore, that we instruct ourselves rightly in this respect. Here, then, are the rules that can be of use to us in believing doctrines.

> (t) Trad. Div. doct. Dei est, non scripta, sed à Deo majoribus nostris revelata, & successoribus de aure in aurem communicata. Haec traditio vocari Dominica solet, quòd à Christo D. Apostolis, & ab his per successores usq́ ad nos derivata sit: hujusmodi est traditio de numero Sacramentorum, de perpetua B. MARIAE Virginitate. 94 Rule I. All those things are to be admitted with the firmest assent which rest on Divine authority. For it is more repugnant that God should be deceived, or deceive, than that those things should not be true which reason shows most evidently. In those things, therefore, which belong to Divine Faith it is most just, as the Apostle says, to bring into captivity the understanding unto the obedience of Christ, namely, so that we do not doubt even in the slightest of the truth of those things which are handed down to us to be believed on divine authority. Rule II. Those things are to be admitted with a firm and constant mind which are proposed to us by the Church to be believed with divine faith. For it cannot happen that the Church should be deceived in defining those things which pertain to faith, and lead us into error, since Christ our Lord said openly that it would never come about that the faith of Peter should fail, nor that the gates of hell should prevail against the Church.

95 Rule III. Great care must be taken that we hold that which has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. For that is of such a kind that it was handed down by word of mouth by Christ our Lord himself to the Apostles, and derived through them to us by constant tradition (t).

Rule IV. Not every opinion is to be deemed safe precisely because the Church has by no means proscribed it. For the Church does not openly condemn all errors, but only those that make a stir. These are conveniently referred to three classes, those of the Senses, of the Will, and of the Mind, about which we shall explain a few things in order.

> 98 Principiò sensus nostri saepissimè nos fallunt. Non quod se ipsa fallant, nam semper aliquid quod re vera éxtat, objiciunt, sed quia occasionem praebent cur fallámur, judicando ita re [p. 37] verà objecta se habére, sicuti nobis adpárent. Itaque dùm, lucem, colores, & alias res objectas vidémus, nos ea vidére verum quidem est, licèt phrenési laborarémus. Omnes enim delirantes haud dubie vident id quod vident, ipsorumque error in solis judiciis consistit, quibus id quod vident, re vera extra se exístere júdicent, eo ipso quod illud videant extrínsecùs pósitum. Sed de fallaciis sensuum tractaturi, initium à visu faciamus.

98 In the first place, our senses very often deceive us. Not that they themselves deceive, for they always present something that really exists, but because they furnish the occasion of our being deceived, by judging that the objects really [p. 37] are just as they appear to us. Thus, while we see light, colors and other objects, it is indeed true that we see them, even if we were suffering from frenzy. For all the delirious without doubt see what they see, and their error consists solely in the judgments by which they judge that what they see really exists outside themselves, by the very fact that they see it placed externally. But as we are about to treat of the fallacies of the senses, let us begin with sight.

> 99 Vix unquam certò judicare póssumus nos veram rerum magnitudinem compraehendere. Nam quemadmodum lentes vitreae, si majoris, aut minoris sphaérae segmenta sunt, ac proinde magis aut minùs convexae, tunc objecta majora, vel minora repraesentant: ita oculi nostri, si magis aut minus sint convexi, idem praestabunt. Si igitur duorum hominum oculi invicèm discrepent, (ut re vera discrepant) aut in densitate humorum, aut in eorumdem figura, aut in ipsorum positione, & situ, diversam extensionem corporis, ut vitreae lentes exhibebunt: ideò nec pro certo dícere póssumus, quàm magnum sit objectum, quod contuemur.

99 We can scarcely ever judge with certainty that we grasp the true magnitude of things. For just as glass lenses, if they are segments of a larger or a smaller sphere, and hence more or less convex, then represent objects larger or smaller, so our eyes, if they are more or less convex, will do the same. If, therefore, the eyes of two men differ from each other (as they really do differ) either in the density of the humors, or in their figure, or in their position and situation, they will exhibit a different extension of a body, as glass lenses do: hence we cannot say for certain how large the object is that we behold.

> 100 Confirmat id ipsum experientia: nam perspicilla, itemque tubi optici uno eodemque modo dispósiti non aequè omnium hominum oculis conveniunt. Decípimur etiam aliquando quum constituimus, corpora esse aequalia, aut inaequalia, nam ex. gr. si data linea quapiam recta horizontali, ad ejus extremum alia recta perpendicularis, & illi aequalis erigatur, ambae invicèm aequales oculis adpárent; at si perpendicularis haec, non ad alterius extremum ducatur, sed medium versùs, quo magis ad illius medietatem accédit, eò major altera horizontali adpáret, ut patet in adjecta figura.

100 Experience confirms this very thing: for spectacles, and likewise optical tubes arranged in one and the same way, do not suit the eyes of all men equally. We are also sometimes deceived when we determine bodies to be equal or unequal; for example, if on some given horizontal straight line another straight line, perpendicular and equal to it, is erected at its extremity, both appear equal to each other to the eyes; but if this perpendicular is drawn not at the extremity of the other but toward the middle, the more it approaches its midpoint, the greater it appears than the other, horizontal, line, as is plain in the adjoined figure.

> 101 Figuram etiam corporum magnorum si longo intervállo distant, vix certò constituemus. Nam turris quadrata quae longè aspicitur, sine ángulis videtur. Etiam corpora exilissima, quae rotunda videntur, ut arenae granum, si microscopio adhibito ea contemplamur, plurimas habent superficies, & figuras diversas. Insensilia verò quae nudis oculis non adparent, si ea microscopio exploramus plurima, & multis figuris praédita se offerunt ex. gr. in aqua in acéto infinita propemodùm animalcula conspicimus, quae sine vitro cónspici non possunt, de quo plura exempla suppéditant sagacissimi Naturae scrutatores Levvenoeck, Hartsoeker, Hook, Joblot, aliique.

101 Nor shall we determine with any certainty the figure of large bodies if they are a long distance away. For a square tower that is viewed from afar appears without angles. Also, the very smallest bodies that appear round, like a grain of sand, if we contemplate them with a microscope applied, have a great many surfaces and diverse figures. And insensible things that do not appear to the naked eye, if we explore them with a microscope, present themselves as very many and endowed with many figures: e.g., in water, in vinegar we behold almost infinite animalcules, which cannot be seen without the glass; of which the most sagacious investigators of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, Hartsoeker, Hooke, Joblot and others, supply further examples.

Men

[p. 38]

> 102 Etiam falluntur homines quum putant colores esse in objecto corpore, quod non indoctis modò, sed & Peripateticis usu venit. Nam ut Cartesium praetermittam ejusque asseclas Malebranchium, Arnauldum, Rohaultium, & alios Clariss. Viros, qui in Gallia post medium anteacti seculi philosophabantur; Summus Isaacus Nevvtonus Angliae lumen atque ornamentum rem acu tetigisse videtur dùm compertissimis experimentis evícit colores omnes in ipsa luce contineri, cujus radios constat esse suaptè naturâ hoc vel illo colore praéditos. Itaque neque Cartesianis adsentítur, qui in varia superficiei corporum textura, ac dispositione sitos esse contendunt; nec verò Idealistis, qui totos in órgano visorio, quasi merae illusiones essent, nihil autem extra animum esse statuunt. Nos igitur, quanquam nólumus (nec enim vacat) Nevvtonianam de luce & coloribus sententiam pro dignitate expósitam hùc adferre; non tamen aliam magis verosimilem agnóscimus.

102 Men are also deceived when they think that colors are in the object body, which happens not only to the unlearned but also to the Peripatetics. For, to pass over Descartes and his followers Malebranche, Arnauld, Rohault, and other most illustrious men who philosophized in France after the middle of the past century, the great Isaac Newton, the light and ornament of England, seems to have hit the mark exactly when by the most certain experiments he proved that all colors are contained in light itself, whose rays, it is established, are endowed by their very nature with this or that color. Accordingly, assent is given neither to the Cartesians, who contend that colors are located in the varied texture and disposition of the surface of bodies, nor indeed to the Idealists, who hold that they are wholly in the organ of sight, as though they were mere illusions, and that nothing exists outside the mind. Although, therefore, we do not wish (for there is no time) to bring in here the Newtonian opinion on light and colors, set out as it deserves, we nevertheless acknowledge no other as more probable.

> 103 Neque enim leve argumentum illud est pro Nevvtonianis, mutato lumine mutari colorem: nam si stúpae multo sale conspersae adfundatur spiritus vini, cum paucula aqua, isque accendatur: ipsa facies humana horrenda specie adpáret. Qui in Solis astrum defixit oculos, vel opthalmía laborat, objecta pluribus coloribus, ac veluti iride quadam circumtecta & circúmdata videt; at coloribus illis, utique objecta re ipsa cincta nullatenùs sunt, si enim ita esset, ab omnibus conspicerentur memorati colores, quod falsum omninò est.

103 For no slight argument for the Newtonians is this, that when the light is changed the color is changed: for if spirit of wine with a very little water is poured on tow sprinkled with much salt, and this is set alight, the human face itself appears with a horrible look. He who has fixed his eyes on the orb of the Sun, or suffers from ophthalmia, sees objects covered and surrounded with many colors, and as it were with a kind of rainbow; but the objects are by no means girt with those colors in reality; for if it were so, the said colors would be seen by all, which is altogether false.

> 104 Facili experimento Cl. Nevvtoni (u) id ipsum osténditur. Si in conclávi obscuro radios lucis per foramen in fenestram factum excipis prísmate crystállino, hi dùm crystallum, & concláve pervadunt, colorati non videntur, dùm verò in adversam chartam albam incurrunt, aut in oppositum parietem feruntur, ita refringuntur, & oculos adficiunt, ut éxcitent in nobis sensationes septem horum colorum, nempè violacei, purpurei, caerulei, viridis, flavi, aurantii, ac rubri, quibus hoc ordine dispositis, quo eos numeravimus paries pictus adpáret. Paries autem & charta facultatem non habent producendi colores, nec mutandi naturam radiorum, qui colorati non erant. Ex quo conséquitur, quid de coloribus nobis statuendum esset, si rem pro dignitate, & non quasi aliud agentes adgrederémur.

104 By an easy experiment of the illustrious Newton (u) this very thing is shown. If in a dark room you catch with a crystal prism the rays of light that come through a hole made in the window, these, while they pass through the crystal and the room, are not seen colored; but when they fall on a white paper set opposite, or are carried onto the opposite wall, they are so refracted, and so affect the eyes, that they excite in us sensations of these seven colors, namely violet, purple, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, and the wall appears painted with them, arranged in the order in which we have enumerated them. But the wall and the paper have no faculty of producing colors, nor of changing the nature of rays that were not colored. From this follows what we should determine about colors, if we approached the matter as it deserves, and not as though we were busy with something else.

> 105 Auditus itidèm frequens errorum est causa. Nam primò existimamus, sonum esse rem, quae extra nos est, & à cor

105 Hearing likewise is a frequent cause of errors. For, first, we think that sound is a thing that is outside us and comes from the body

that

> (u) Opt. p. 103. & 153. [p. 39] pore sonóro venit: quod tamen est falsum. Nam nihil aliud facit corpus sonórum, quàm citissimè & certo modo trémere, qui tremor aërem ad tympanum auris impellit, id que ita movet, ut éxcitet in animo sensum soni. Nullus enim sonus óritur, nisi particulae corporum, quae sonóra dicuntur, motum tremulum concipiant, quod uno, & altero experimento comprobari facillimè potest.

(u) Opticks, p. 103 & 153. [p. 39] that sounds; which, however, is false. For the sonorous body does nothing other than tremble very swiftly and in a certain manner, and this tremor drives the air to the tympanum of the ear and so moves it as to excite in the mind the sensation of sound. For no sound arises unless the particles of the bodies that are called sonorous take on a tremulous motion, which can be very easily proved by one or two experiments.

> 106 Si enim intra vas vítreum aqua infundatur, & admoto ad labrum vasis digito, idem circumducatur aliquátenùs os vasis adsiduè premendo, & confricando, excitatur hac ratione in parietibus vasis tremor, & subsultus, qui aquae contentae statim communicatur, & ad oculum tremor ille manifestò adpáret. Statím autem, ac particulae trémere incipiunt, illicò sónitus sensatio exoritur, eoque tremóre extincto, sive per sese, sive ope nostra id contingat, extinguitur illicò sensatio omnis sónitus.

106 For if water is poured into a glass vessel and a finger, brought to the lip of the vessel, is drawn round the mouth of the vessel for some time, continually pressing and rubbing, a tremor and quivering is in this way excited in the walls of the vessel, which is at once communicated to the water it contains, and that tremor plainly appears to the eye. And as soon as the particles begin to tremble, the sensation of sound immediately arises; and when that tremor is extinguished, whether this happens of itself or by our doing, all sensation of sound is immediately extinguished.

> 107 Praeterea, si in machina Pneumatica aëre exhausta tintinabulum pulsetur (quod utique fieri potest) licèt metalli illius particulae malleolo percussae motum trémulum concipiant, attàmen quum trémor ille aëri communicari non possit, neque enim adest ampliùs aër, atque adeò ad aures usque nostras pertingere nequeat, nulla indè sónitus sensatio óritur: restituto autèm machinae aëre, illicò sensus sónitus excitatur. Non existit ergò in corporibus extrinsecis, id quod percípimus, & sónitum nuncupamus, sed tantùm undularis motus particularum, quibus componuntur; quo posito sensationes sónitus in animis nostris excitantur; dummodò tamèn motus ille aëri communicetur, & ad aures usque nostras pertingat.

107 Further, if in the air pump, the air having been exhausted, a little bell is struck (which can certainly be done), although the particles of that metal, struck by the little hammer, take on a tremulous motion, yet since that tremor cannot be communicated to the air (for there is no longer any air present), and so cannot reach all the way to our ears, no sensation of sound arises from it; but when the air is restored to the machine, the sense of sound is immediately excited. What we perceive and call sound, therefore, does not exist in external bodies; there is only the undulatory motion of the particles of which they are composed, and when this is given, sensations of sound are excited in our minds, provided, however, that that motion is communicated to the air and reaches all the way to our ears.

> 108 Odoratus, & Gustus eodem modò nos decipiunt: propterea quod causa sunt, cur imprudentes existimemus, Odorem, & Saporem esse in corpore quod tangimus; quum tamen sint nihil aliud, quàm animi sensus, qui excitantur in nobis á particulis insensibilibus corporum, quae organa haec duo contingunt. Facili negotio id patebit, si considerémus sensationem omnem, jocundam, aut injocundam nullatenùs posse extra animum existere.

108 Smell and Taste deceive us in the same way, because they are the cause of our thinking, imprudently, that Odor and Savor are in the body we touch; whereas they are nothing other than sensations of the mind, which are excited in us by the insensible particles of the bodies that touch these two organs. This will be plain with little trouble if we consider that no sensation, pleasant or unpleasant, can in any way exist outside the mind.

> 109 Praeterea si odóres & sapóres essent res, quae extra nos extárent: idem corpus odórum, & idem cibus singulos homines eodem modò adficeret. Id tamèn secùs est; nam Zíbethum ex. gr. aut odor lilii gratus est aliis, aliis prorsùs intolerabilis. Nec etiam omnes eodem cibo delectantur. In aegrotis mirabiliora phaenómena saepissimè ocurrunt. ¿Quis nesciat mulieres opilatas terram, carbones, calcem, aliaque id genus devorare, quae ipsae illae benè valentes à morbo liberatae, non sine stómacho videre, imò ne nominare quidem possunt?

109 Moreover, if odors and savors were things existing outside us, the same odorous body and the same food would affect each man in the same way. But it is otherwise; for civet, for example, or the scent of the lily, is pleasant to some, to others utterly intolerable. Nor are all delighted by the same food. In the sick, more wonderful phenomena very often occur. Who does not know that women suffering from obstructions devour earth, coals, lime and other things of that kind, which those same women, when they are well and freed from the illness, cannot see without nausea, nay, cannot even name?

Those

[p. 40]

> 110 Febri laborantes amara sentiunt, quae sani dulcia, & suavia habent. Idem in odóribus obtingit. Haec autèm perspicuè docent, non in objectis corporibus esse odores, & sapores, sed occasionem tantùm cur ea sentiamus: quae pro diversa constitutione organorum, vel duorum vel ejusdem hominis, dùm morbo, vel aetate laborat, diverso modo fibras sensuum movent, pungunt; ut nervi diverso modo adfecti aliàs perceptiones excitent in animo, quae ipsae sunt, vel odores, vel sapores.

110 Those who suffer from fever find bitter the things that the healthy hold sweet and agreeable. The same happens with odors. These things, moreover, teach clearly that odors and savors are not in the object bodies, but only the occasion of our sensing them: for these bodies, according to the diverse constitution of the organs, whether of two men or of the same man when he suffers from illness or from age, move and prick the fibers of the senses in diverse ways, so that the nerves, affected in diverse ways, excite other perceptions in the mind, which are themselves either odors or savors.

> 111 Tactus denique uberrimus errorum fons est. Constat id apertissimis experimentis, quorum quaedam tantùm adferemus. Sine ulla dubitatione judicamus, ea in corporibus externis esse, quae tactu distinguimus, quod falsum est, neque enim in igne existit id quod calorem dicimus, neque in glacie id quod frigus adpelamus, quod praeter allatam rationem §. 108 aliis paene innumeris comprobatur. Si enim álteram manum benè calidam, alteram nimis frígidam, in eamdem aquam tépidam mergas, quae frigida erit, calidam sentiet; contra verò quae calida, frigidam. Non ita dicerémus, si aqua se ipsâ esset calida: nam útraque manus moderatum calorem sentiret: non secùs ac útraque manus sentit, eam esse corpus, esse fluidam, &c. quia ita est.

111 Touch, finally, is a most abundant source of errors. This is established by the plainest experiments, of which we shall adduce only a few. We judge without any doubt that the things we distinguish by touch are in external bodies, which is false; for neither does what we call heat exist in fire, nor what we call cold in ice; and this, besides the reason brought forward in §. 108, is proved by almost innumerable others. For if you plunge one hand, well warmed, and the other, very cold, into the same lukewarm water, the one that is cold will feel it hot, and on the contrary the one that is hot will feel it cold. We would not say so if the water were hot of itself: for both hands would feel a moderate heat, just as both hands feel that it is a body, that it is fluid, etc., because it is so.

> 112 Ulteriùs si quis híemali tempore, cubiculum subeat benè clausum, aërem ibi inclusum, cálidum, tépidum ve dicit; qui verò è lecto recens surrexit, in eodem illo cubiculo constitutus aërem illum potius frigidum esse, quàm tépidum, cálidum ve adserit, quum verò idem corpus, cálidum simul & frigidum re ipsa esse nequeat, manifestò sequitur, argui à nobis non posse, in dato corpore re ipsa inhaerere, id quod calorem, & frigus adpelamus, ex eo quod datum illud corpus calorem, aut frigus in nobis éxcitet.

112 Further, if someone in wintertime enters a well-closed room and says that the air enclosed there is hot, or lukewarm, while one who has just risen from bed, placed in that same room, asserts that that air is cold rather than lukewarm or hot: since the same body cannot in reality be at once hot and cold, it manifestly follows that we cannot argue that what we call heat and cold inheres in reality in a given body from the fact that that given body excites heat or cold in us.

> 113 Multis aliis modis tactu decipimur. Nam si ex. gr. dígitum manus medium, supra indicem imponas, & inter utrumque digitum glóbulum exiguum medium teneas, nisi oculos testes adhibeas, duos à te tangi glóbulos jurabis. Ex quibus omnibus consequitur: sensus nostros plurimam occasionem nobis dare cur fallamur. Sed quoniam Deus nobis sensus non dedit ornatus causâ, sed ut iis utamur, eorumque ope cognitiones adquiramus, iccircò Criterium aliquod sit oportet; quo veras & falsas notiones dignoscamus. Criterium autem est tale.

113 We are deceived by touch in many other ways. For if, e.g., you place the middle finger of the hand over the index finger and hold a small globule in the middle between both fingers, unless you employ your eyes as witnesses, you will swear that two globules are being touched by you. From all of which it follows that our senses give us very much occasion for being deceived. But since God gave us the senses not for ornament, but that we might use them and by their help acquire knowledge, there must therefore be some Criterion by which we may distinguish true and false notions. The criterion, then, is this.

> 114 Eae imagenes certissimae haberi debent, quae adjunctis omnibus adcurate expensis semper ab eodem, vel à ceteris sensibus eaedem reperiuntur; id que, ab uno homine, & multo magis à diversis, qui eas diligenter examinarunt. Nam si ne hoc quidem casu verae haberi possent imagines, delúderet nos perpetuò Deus:

114 Those images must be held most certain which, all the circumstances having been accurately weighed, are always found the same by the same sense, or by the other senses; and this by one man, and much more by diverse men who have examined them diligently. For if not even in this case could the images be held true, God would perpetually delude us:

> [p. 41]

[p. 41] which is foreign to so great a Goodness. In this way, indeed, the fiction of the

> quod à tánta Bonitate alienum est. Quo sanè modo Pyrrhoniorum commentum à veris Philosophis confutatur. Hanc doctrinam tribus canonibus claritatis causa comprehendemus. I. Ne pronunciatio ea esse vera, quae sensus repraesentant, aut non esse, quia in sensus non incurrunt; quin prius sedulò id perpendas, & peritorum sententiam adhibeas. II. De rebus quales in se sunt, ope sensuum tuorum cave ne unquam judices III. Experimenta ne facito, ut Veteres aliqui faciebant: sed exactissimis instrumentis quae Recentiores cogitarunt, & poliverunt diligentissime utitor.

Pyrrhonists is refuted by true Philosophers. For clarity’s sake we shall comprise this doctrine in three canons. I. Do not pronounce that the things the senses represent are true, or that things are not, because they do not fall under the senses, without first diligently weighing the matter and applying the opinion of experts. II. Beware of ever judging, by the help of your senses, of things as they are in themselves. III. Do not make experiments as some of the Ancients did, but use most diligently the most exact instruments that the Moderns have devised and perfected.

> CAPUT V.

C H A P T E R V.

> De Adfectibus Voluntatis, qui veri adsecutionem impediunt.

On the Affections of the Will that impede the attainment of truth. 115

> 115 PArùm haberemus (inquit Cl. Verney (u) si sensus tantummodò nos in errores indúcerent: nam quum errores hujusmodi sint conspicui, esset in promptu remedium, nimirùm de iis, quae sensibus percipiuntur, cautè pronuntiare: eaque ad examen etiam atque etiam vocare, antea quam judicium faceremus. Sed est alia causa, quae quò tectior est, eò validiùs hominem à veritate révocat, & ad errorem impellit. Ejusmodi sunt adfectus animi. Nam quum animus percipit res sensibiles, pro ut bonae vel malae sunt, oritur quidam animi motus, cum fluoris nervorum, & sanguinis ingenti commotione conjunctus, qui adfectus nuncupatur: quemque vel voluptas animi, vel dolor sequitur.

We should have little to fear (says the illustrious Verney (u)) if the senses alone led us into errors: for since errors of this kind are conspicuous, the remedy would be at hand, namely, to pronounce cautiously about the things that are perceived by the senses, and to call them to examination again and again before we made a judgment. But there is another cause which, the more hidden it is, the more strongly calls a man back from truth and drives him to error. Of this kind are the affections of the mind. For when the mind perceives sensible things according as they are good or bad, there arises a certain motion of the mind, joined with a great commotion of the nervous fluid and of the blood, which is called an affection; and this is followed either by pleasure of mind or by pain.

> 116 Mirabile dictu est, quàm validè, quàmque celèriter hi adfectus, si sunt vehementes, hominem transversum agant, quod usu exploratum est. Hi primò mentem impediunt; ne adcuratè éxaminet ea, de quibus deliberare debet. Ex quo consequitur, ut ideas obscuras adquirat, & judicando fallatur. Deinde, quaedam ut amemus, efficiunt; quaedam verò refugiamus, quae non debemus. Nam non secùs ac microscopia, & ea, quae placent, & displicent, ampliant, dilatant adeò; ut mens tali fulgore per

116 It is wonderful to say how strongly and how swiftly these affections, if they are vehement, lead a man astray, as has been ascertained by experience.

First, they hinder the mind from examining accurately the things about which it ought to deliberate; from which it follows that it acquires obscure ideas and is deceived in judging. Next, they bring it about that we love some things, and shun others, as we ought not. For just like microscopes, they so enlarge and dilate the things that please and those that displease, that the mind, struck by such brilliance,

F                                        judges

> (u) De Re Logica. [p. 42] culsa judicet ésse bonum, aut malum, quod re verà non est. Id tàm multis argumentis evinci potest, ut copia me inopem faciat. Pauca tamèn addam: in ceteris moneo, ut unusquisque se ipsum cónsulat: si enim suas actiones oderetur, & aéstimet pro merito, exempla nimis multa reperiet.

(u) De Re Logica. [p. 42] judges to be good or bad what in reality is not. This can be proved by so many arguments that plenty makes me poor. I shall add a few, however; as for the rest, I advise each one to consult himself: for if he scrutinizes his own actions and weighs them as they deserve, he will find all too many examples.

> 117 Praecipuus adfectuum fons, ex quo omnes dimanant, est immódicus amor, quo unusquisque se amat, quam Philautiam nominamus: quare Philautia haberi debet parens errorum, qui à Voluntate oriuntur. Amamus vehementèr nos, nostraque omnia, dicta, facta, cogitata. Nec aliquid tàm gloriosum de úllo homine praedicari posse putamus, quod non de nobis potiori jure dici debere arbitremur. Hic adfectus quasi morbus quidam non semidoctos modò, sed etiam doctissimos aliquandò pervásit.

117 The principal source of the affections, from which they all flow, is the immoderate love with which each one loves himself, which we call Philautia [self-love]: wherefore Philautia must be held to be the parent of the errors that arise from the Will. We love vehemently ourselves and everything that is ours, our sayings, deeds and thoughts. Nor do we think that anything so glorious can be declared of any man that we do not judge it ought to be said of ourselves with better right. This affection, like a kind of disease, sometimes pervades not only the half-learned but even the most learned.

> 118 Hinc & illud existit, ut de rebus judicium feramus, non pro ut re sunt, sed pro modo, quo nos adficiunt. Itaque quae nobis convenire putamus, bona, pulchra, justa: quae non convenire, è contrario judicamus. Amicos suos, conjunctos, praeceptores, populares, plurimi ita extollunt, ut nihil sanctiùs, nihil erudítiùs, nihil omni laude cumulatius ne cogitari quidem posse censeant. Si quem verò eorum errata notantem audiunt, ei mala omnia inprecantur: & quasi hominem súperis invísum, reipublicae perniciosum, nova, atque nefaria fácinora mollientem adeò adversantur, ut nihil ultra.

118 Hence arises this too, that we pass judgment on things not as they are in reality, but according to the way in which they affect us. Thus what we think suits us we judge good, beautiful and just; what does not suit us, the contrary. Very many so extol their friends, kinsmen, teachers and countrymen that they think nothing holier, nothing more learned, nothing more heaped with every praise can even be conceived. But if they hear anyone noting their errors, they call down every evil upon him, and oppose him, as a man hateful to the gods above, pernicious to the commonwealth, and plotting new and nefarious crimes, so fiercely that nothing could go further.

> 119 Apertiùs id videtur in iis, qui alicui sectae nomen dederunt. ¿Quis enim ei Philosopho dixerit, doctorem ejus errasse? ¿Quis persuaserit, debere eum praeceptoris sententias ad aliorum doctorum lumen revocare? Vulgatum illud est Aberroësii, qui, quum Aristotelem interpretaretur, hoc dicere non dubitarit: Aristotelis doctrina est summa veritas, quoniam ejus intellectus fuit finis intellectus humani: quare bene dicitur de illo, quod ipse fuit creatus, & datus nobis à Divina providentia, ut non ignoremus possibilia sciri: Et alio loco: Nullus eorum, inquit, qui secuti sunt eum usque ad hoc tempus, quod est mille, & quingentorum annorum, quidquam addidit: nec invenies in ejus verbis errorem alicujus quantitatis.

119 This is seen more openly in those who have given their names to some sect. For who would tell such a Philosopher that his teacher has erred? Who would persuade him that he ought to bring his master’s opinions to the light of other doctors? Well known is that saying of Averroes, who, when he was interpreting Aristotle, did not hesitate to say this: The doctrine of Aristotle is the highest truth, since his intellect was the limit of the human intellect: wherefore it is well said of him that he was created and given to us by Divine providence, so that we might not be ignorant of what can be known. And in another place: None of those, he says, who have followed him up to this time, which is a period of one thousand five hundred years, has added anything; nor will you find in his words an error of any magnitude.

> 120 Hec homini Ethnico, tam rudi aetate scribenti, & qui bonos auctores non legerat, condonari possunt: at in viris Catholicis, & in hac Litterarum luce, ferenda non sunt. Audivi ego Peripateticum dicentem, veteres Episcopos à primo Ecclesiae seculo, Aristotelem quasi normam disputandi, etiam in rebus Fidei, habuisse: nec latum unguem ab ejus sententiis recessisse. Nec adfirmare dubitarim, plurimos etiam nunc in ea

120 These things can be pardoned in a Heathen man, writing in so rude an age, and one who had not read good authors; but in Catholic men, and in this light of Letters, they are not to be borne. I have heard a Peripatetic say that the ancient Bishops, from the first century of the Church, held Aristotle as a kind of norm of disputing, even in matters of Faith, and did not depart a finger’s breadth from his opinions. Nor would I hesitate to affirm that very many even now persist in the same

> [p. 43]

[p. 43] heresy, though more covertly.

> dem haeresi, quamvis occnltiùs permanére.

121 Hence arises this too, that those who are held by such opinions think nothing right except what flows from those sources. These they defend constantly and stubbornly; the rest they reject as false and harmful. They fear, namely, lest they incur the mark of inconstancy or of error, and lose by an ingenuous confession of error the praise they acquired with so much sweat. This philautia prevents men from tracking down the truth; and this happens much more in the old than in the young.

> 121 Hinc, & illud existit, ut qui talibus opinionibus tenentur, nihil rectum putent, nisi quod ex illis fontibus dimanat. Haec constantèr, & pertinacitèr tuentur; respuunt cetera tanquam falsa, & damnosa. Verentur scilicèt, ne inconstantiae, aut erroris notam subeant: & laudem, quam tantis sudoribus compararunt, ingenua erroris confessione perdant. Haec philautia homines prohibet, ne verum pervestígent: quod in senibus multo magis, quam in adolescentibus usu venit.

122 Hence the writings of those who hold the contrary opinion they either do not read at all, or read yawning; and if they examine them a little more attentively, they do so with this design, to refute their opinions. For how few are there, even of those who with great disdain censure the opinions of the Moderns, who, when they have turned over Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Leibniz, Wolff and the other most acute Philosophers, do not rather condemn them on another’s judgment than call them back to their own circumspect examination?

> 122 Hinc eorum, qui in contraria sententia sunt, scripta, aut omnìnò non legunt, aut oscitantèr legunt: quod si paulò adtentiùs examinant, id eo consilio faciunt, ut eorum sententias confútent. ?Quotus enim qúisque est, eorum etiam, qui magno supercilio Recentiorum sententias vituperant, qui Cartesium, qui Gassendum, qui Malebranchium, qui Leibinizium, qui Wolffium, quique ceteros Philosophos acutissimos, quum evolverit, non potius ex alieno judicio comdemnet, quàm suo in circunspectum examen révocet?

123 Hence that zeal for dissenting, and a certain inexplicable desire of wrangling, which so drives some men that nothing is held so firm and so evident that they do not try to weaken and obscure it with their disputations. For these men, as if they had been born for discord, call everything to the balance of disputation; and if perchance arguments fail them on the matter proposed, they immediately ask whether they are making a conjoined or a separated kind of syllogism. There are Philosophers who, when about to hand down to youths the rudiments of some science, first teach them to contend with words and to chatter rather impudently, instead of handing down some precepts that would lead the boys into the very inner recesses of the science. Books are full of examples, which it would be easy to bring forward, were the matter not exceedingly well known.

> 123 Hinc illud dissentiendi studium, & inexplicabilis quaedam rixandi cupiditas, quae homines nonnullos agit, ut nihil tam firmum, tamque perspicuum hábeatur, quod ii non suis disputationibus debilitare, & obscurare conentur. Hi enim, quasi ad discordiam nati essent, omnia ad disputationis trútinam vocant: & si fortè in proposita materia argumenta iis non súppetant, illicò quaerunt, an conjunctum, an separatum genus syllogismi faciant. Sunt Philosophi, qui traditurì adolescentibus alicujus scientiae rudimenta, eos primùm doceant, certare verbis, & inpudentíusculè garrire, quàm aliqua praecepta tradant quae pueros ad ipsa penetralia scientíae perducant. Pleni exemplorum sunt libri, quae facilè foret proferre, nisi res esset oppidò notissima.

124 Hence is born that intolerable pride by which men so arrogate to themselves the first place in letters that they either diminish the learning of others in other studies or, if they spare these, nevertheless prefer themselves to all in the faculty they profess. It is the way of men (says Cicero) that they do not wish the same man to excel in many things. (x) This way, moreover, has come down even to our own age. A jurist, for example, if he hears a Theologian disputing about Law, whether Public or Private, generally laughs at him. Jurisprudence, forsooth, is open only to him who is adorned with the insignia of a Doctor; all others

> 124 Hinc intoleranda illa nascitur superbia, qua homines adeò principatum sibi tribuunt in literis, ut vel aliorum eruditionem in aliis studiis minuant, vel si iis parcunt, in ea tamèn facultate, quam tractant sese omnibus antéferant. Est mos hominum, (inquit Cicero) ut volint eundem pluribus rebus excellere. (x) Hic autem mos ad nostram usque aetatem pervenit. Jurisperitus ex. gr. Si Theologum de Jure, vel Publico, vel Privato disputantem audit, plerumquè derídet. Scilicèt Jurisprudentia ei solum, qui Doctoris insignibus decoratur, est pérvia: ce-

F2                                         it

> (x) Cic. in Brut. cap, 21 [p. 44] teros à se repellit. Theologus verò etiam si Jurisconsultum laudet, tamen nefarium scelus putat, si ille de Sacra Scientia quidquam delíbat. Quasi leges Caésarum non ex Sacris Litteris, & Ethica disciplina illustrentur: aut quasi Sacrorum statuta Cánonum non Príncipum constitutionibus adjuventur. Atque haec nominatim de philautia ad quam, quia reliqui adfectus reducuntur; de iis pauca subjungémus.

(x) Cic., Brutus, ch. 21. [p. 44] it repels from itself. The Theologian, on the other hand, even if he praises the Jurisconsult, nevertheless thinks it a heinous crime if the latter touches on anything of the Sacred Science. As though the laws of the Caesars were not illustrated by the Sacred Letters and by Ethical discipline; or as though the statutes of the Sacred Canons were not aided by the constitutions of Princes. And so much in particular on philautia; and since the remaining affections are reduced to it, we shall append a few things about them.

> 125 Spes & multo magis Desiderium ¡quid non in mortalium pectore turbant! ¡quám distrahunt mentem, ne ea, quae sunt, advertat! Qui cupiunt, & sperant, ipsi sibi somnia fingunt: haec amant, haec adorant, nihil praeterea vident. Hinc facilè putant, ea se habere, quae sperant; palpatoribus aures praebent, iis credunt, & mirè falluntur. Parálysi, vel hydrópe laboranti dicat aliquis circulator, habere se remedium exquisitum, quo eos unius diei curriculo liberet à morbo: ut ut mille homines gravissimi ostendant, fieri id non posse; aegroti verum esse putabnnt.

125 Hope, and much more Desire, what do they not disturb in the breast of mortals! How they distract the mind, so that it does not attend to the things that are! Those who desire and hope feign dreams for themselves: these they love, these they adore, they see nothing besides. Hence they readily think that they have what they hope for; they lend their ears to flatterers, believe them, and are wonderfully deceived. Let some mountebank tell a man suffering from paralysis or dropsy that he has an exquisite remedy by which he would free such men from the disease within the course of a single day: though a thousand most weighty men should show that this cannot be done, the sick will think it true.

> 126 At verò Ambitio ¡quàm véhementer homines torquet! ¡quàm eosdem in indecóra multa, & quae dignitatem hominis inminuunt, sine ullo pudóre praecípites agit! Hic adfectus latiùs pánditur, quàm vulgò putatur: & studiosè curant homines, ut eum aliis, & aliis nominibus obscurent, ne probro, & risui pateant.

126 But Ambition, how vehemently it torments men! How it drives them headlong, without any shame, into many unseemly things that diminish the dignity of man! This affection spreads more widely than is commonly thought; and men take studious care to obscure it under one name or another, lest they be exposed to reproach and laughter.

> 127 Sunt, qui honores se ambíre dicunt, ut consanguineis & necessariis praesidio sint. Hi ambitionem suam titulo pietatis celant. Alii paulò callidiores clámitant perpetuò, non commissuros se, ut ad honores evehantur, quia omninò digni non sunt. Hi nempe sperant, facilè se hac arte ad aliquod fastigium próvehi posse. En ambitio nomine contemptus honorum involúta. Qui in aulis Regum versantur, plerique eam specioso nomine tegunt obsequii. Nimirùm laudant hi perpetuò facta, & dicta eorum, à quibus fortunas sperant: & mémores Terentiani effati, obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit; imperant sibi omnia adsentari, & omnia pro veris habere. Quae consuetudò, judicium corrumpit, & aciem, judicandi obtundit.

127 There are those who say they seek honors so as to be a protection to their kinsmen and connections. These conceal their ambition under the title of piety. Others, a little more cunning, perpetually cry out that they will never allow themselves to be raised to honors, because they are altogether unworthy of them. These, namely, hope that by this art they can easily be advanced to some eminence. Here is ambition wrapped in the name of contempt of honors. Most of those who live in the courts of Kings cover it with the specious name of compliance. They, namely, perpetually praise the deeds and sayings of those from whom they hope for fortune; and, mindful of Terence’s saying, compliance begets friends, truth hatred, they command themselves to assent to everything and to hold everything as true. This habit corrupts judgment and blunts the edge of judging.

> 128 Simillima huic est Avaritia, quae quàm mentem hominum excaecarit, quot bella in omni mundi aetate suscitarit, quot regna solitaria fécerit, & deserta, Historia luculenter ostendit. Sanè qui tali adfectu aguntur, vix, aut ne vix quidem verum audire, ne dùm ratione comprehendere, & adtentè considerare possunt.

128 Most like this is Avarice: how far it has blinded the minds of men, how many wars it has stirred up in every age of the world, how many kingdoms it has made solitary and deserted, History shows clearly. Truly, those who are driven by such an affection can scarcely, or not even scarcely, hear the truth, much less comprehend it by reason and consider it attentively.

> 129 Timor etiam mirabilia phaenómena in hominum animis progénerat. Qui nimio timore corripiuntur, vix unquam res

129 Fear also generates wonderful phenomena in the minds of men. Those who are seized by excessive fear scarcely ever understand things

> [p. 45]

[p. 45] as they are: they think they see what they do not see, and perpetually reason badly. Hence so many prodigies present themselves in the Histories of the Heathen, which flowed from this source, that peoples persuaded themselves that the immortal gods would exact the penalty for crime by a visible punishment. And once their minds had been stirred to religious awe, it was easy for them to think that whatever happened less ordinarily, whether an eclipse of the Moon or of the Sun, or an egg larger than usual, or a serpent in the house, and follies of that kind, that these, I say, were portents by which those Gods of theirs declared their anger and indignation.

> pro ut sunt, intelligunt: putant se vidére, quod non vident, & perpetuò malè ratiocinantur. Hinc tot portenta in Ethnicorum Historiis se offerunt, quae ex hoc fonte fluxere, quod populi, sibi persuasére, deos immortales visibili supplicio poenas de scelere esse sumturos. Et motis semel in religionem animis, facilè fuit, ut existimarent, quaecumque minus ordinaria eveniebant, vel Lunae, aut Solis defectionem, vel ovum sólitò majus, vel serpentem domi, & id genus ineptias; haec, inquam, esse ostenta, quibus Dii illi sui iram, & indignationem declararent.

130 But among our own people too, how many fables are born of fear! Those who fear assert that they themselves see apparitions of the night, specters of tombs, things horrible to tell. Whatever is heard by night is ghosts. If some old and ragged woman comes along, she, forsooth, displays a marvelous power of calling up demons at pleasure, of doing harm to whomever she will, and of killing a man with impunity: and six hundred most trifling things of this kind, which none but those seized with terror, or fools, will ever affirm.

> 130 Sed & apud nostros ¡quàm multae fabéllae ex timore nascuntur! Qui timent, ipsi noctium occursacula, bustorum spectra, horrenda dictu se videre adsevérant. Quaecumque noctu audiuntur, lémures sunt. Si qua femina annosa, & pannosa ocurrit, haec scilicèt praefefert mirificam potestatem daémonas pro lubitu revocandi, malè faciendi cui velit, & impunè hominem occidendi: & sexcenta hujusmodi nugacissima, quae, nisi terrore correpti, aut fatui nunquam adfirmabunt.

131 How headlong Anger drives men, no one fails to perceive. It clouds the mind and blinds the very eyes, so that nothing so absurd can be said or thought that the angry man does not do in his very fury; so much so that, when master of himself, he is sometimes ashamed of having perpetrated such things. Hence the mind is so vehemently shaken that it can scarcely judge rightly of things: it thinks the things that stand in its way greater, and the rest much smaller, than they are; and therefore it always chooses the worse part. Wherefore, if we reckon up the account, we shall find that the greater calamities of mortals have proceeded from anger.

> 131 Ira quàm praecipites agat homines, nullus non sentit. Haec mentem obnúbilat, oculos ipsos occaécat, ut nihil tàm absonum aut dici, aut cogitari possit, quod iracundus homo in ipso furore non faciat: adeò ut sui cómpotem pudeat aliquandò talia patrasse. Hinc animus tàm vehementèr percéllitur, vix ut possit rectè de rebus judicare: sed, quae obstant, majora; cetera multo minora esse existimat: iccircò deteriorem partem eligit semper. Quare si rationem subducimus, inveniemus mortalium calamitates majores ab iracundia profectas esse.

132 These things being briefly surveyed, it becomes manifest that those motions of the mind which disturb reason (for all of them disturb it) must be restrained, and that it is the Philosopher’s business to take care that we are not agitated by any affections, but have a serene mind, if we desire to judge rightly and wisely. For as a ship in mid-sea, driven by vehement and contrary winds, can neither hold its course nor make for port, so our mind, driven about by those affections as by a wind, will scarcely ever attain the truth toward which it tends; therefore commit this Canon to memory: Do not judge while you are occupied by some affection: and if you have judged, call the matter back again to examination; then at last pronounce, freely, and after the matter has been accurately weighed.

> 132 His brevitèr perlustratis, manifestum fit, eos animi motus, qui rationem perturbant (omnes enim perturbant) compéscì oportére: & Philosophi esse curare, ne adfectionibus ullis agitemur, sed serenam mentem habeamus, si rectè, & sapientèr cúpimus judicare. Nam ut navis in medio mari vehementibus, & contrariis acta ventis, neque cursum tenére, neque portum pétere potest; sic animus noster adfectionibus iis, quasi vento circumactus, vix unquam veritatem, quò tendit, adsequétur, iccircò memoriae mandate hunc Cánonem. Ne, dum adfectu aliquo occupati estis, judicetis: quod si judicastis, rem iterum ad examen revocate: tum demum libere, & re accurate perpensa, pronunciate.

Chapter

[p. 46]

## CHAPTER VI

> CAPUT VI.

On the fallacies of the Mind, which prevent us from finding the truth.

> De fallaciis Mentis, quae obstant, ne verum inveniamus.

ut the weakness of our mind too (continues the cited Verney) will 133

> 133 SED etiam mentis nostrae imbecíllitas (prosequitur laud. Verney) in causa saepius erit multorum errorum, in quos frequentissimè delábimur: quique veri adsecutionem mirabilitèr retardant. Hos ut vitemus necesse est causas pernóscere, & alta mente défigere: quò faciliùs eas, quum occurrerint, declinemus. Nos eas ad tres classes non in commodè revocamus, tarditatem nostram, methodum perversam, & praejudicia: quas eodem ordine explicabimus.

B          more often be the cause of many errors, into which we very fre‐

> 134 Prima ac potissima causa, propter quam fállimur judicantes, est, ipsa mentis nostrae natura: quae & intelligendi facultatem angustis límitibus habet definitam; & illa ipsa, quae intelligit, tàm obscurè intelligit, vix ut credi possit. Id, si cognitiones nostras diligentiùs examinamus, planissimè deprehendemus.

quently slip, and which wonderfully retard the attainment of truth.

> 135 Nam mens nostra, etiam si habitat in corpore, tamen ignorat, planè mirabilem fabricationem corporis, cérebri praesertim. Non quòd minimè sit ad cognoscendum idonea; nam si ei alienum cérebrum objicitur; & partes sunt conspicuae perfectè cognoscit: sed hoc nomine tantùm, quia Deus noluit animum res corporeas pernóscere, nisi per sensus.

To avoid them it is necessary to know their causes thoroughly and to fix them deep in the mind, so that we may more easily avoid them when they occur. We refer them, not inconveniently, to three classes, our slowness, perverse method, and prejudices, which we shall explain in the same order.

> 136 Deinde non adsequitur naturam rerum quantumlibet vulgarium: ex. gr. nequit constituere, an corpus partes infinitas habeat, an secus: quae sit natura Solis, Lunae, Stellarum, tùm earum, quae vagae, tùm quae inerrantes dicuntur: postremò, an in astris sint animantia, & ejusmodi sexcenta. Ut mittam in praesentia res, quae fieri possunt à Deo, de quibus nugacissima multa fabulatur Schola, quae omninò intelligi, ne dum definiri, nequeunt.

134 The first and chief cause on account of which we are deceived in judging is the very nature of our mind, which both has its faculty of understanding confined within narrow limits, and understands the very things it understands so obscurely that it can scarcely be believed. We shall perceive this most plainly if we examine our cognitions more diligently.

135 For our mind, even though it dwells in the body, is nevertheless ignorant of the wholly wonderful fabric of the body, of the brain especially. Not that it is not at all suited to knowing it; for if another’s brain is set before it and its parts are visible, it knows them perfectly: but on this account only, because

God did not will that the soul should know corporeal things thoroughly except through the senses.

136 Next, it does not attain the nature of things, however common: for example, it cannot determine whether a body has infinite parts or not; what the nature is of the Sun, of the Moon, of the Stars, both of those that are called wandering and of those that are called fixed; finally, whether there are living creatures in the stars; and six hundred things of that kind. To pass over for the present the things that can be done by God, about which the School tells many most trifling tales, and which can by no means be understood, much less defined.

137 But this slowness and weakness cannot be wholly amended: we can apply one remedy, to beware studiously of defining those things for the investigation of which we are altogether unfit. Of these, moreover, there are two classes:

> 137 Verùm haec tarditas, & imbecillitas prorsus emendari non potest: unum adhibere possumus remedium, studiosè cavére, ne ea definiamus, ad quae investiganda omninò ápti non sumus. Harum autèm duae sunt classes: altera earum rerum quae intelligentiam nostram súperant: ut natura divinarum proprieta- [p. 47] tum: item que res omnes possibiles; quae nec rationibus naturae, nec divina locutione finiri possunt, & explicari. Altera est rerum, quae intelligi eae quidem possunt, veruntamèn caremus necessariis presidiis, quibus ad earum cognitionem perveniamus: ut eae sunt, quas paulò antè nominavimus, tum etiam historiae antiquissimae, & hujusmodi infinita. Et haec de prima causa.

the one, of those things that surpass our intelligence, such as the nature of the divine properties; [p. 47] likewise all possible things, which can be neither determined nor explained by the reasonings of nature or by divine utterance. The other is of things that can indeed be understood, but we lack the necessary aids by which we might arrive at the knowledge of them: such are those we named a little before, and also the most ancient histories, and infinite things of this kind. And so much on the first cause.

> 138 Altera verò causa est, methodus perversa. Haec latissimè patet, & ex ea plurimi errores, & infinita mala nascuntur. Principiò enim sunt, qui in tortuosam & in obscuro positam viam ingressi ad finem sibi propósitum non perveniunt; sed frequentèr labuntur: imò quò plùs in eadem progrediuntur, eò magis à veritate deflectunt. Frequentissimè hunc scopulum viri quidam literati offendunt.

138 The second cause is perverse method. This extends very widely, and from it arise very many errors and infinite evils. For in the first place there are those who, having entered upon a winding road set in darkness, do not arrive at the end they proposed to themselves, but frequently slip: nay, the further they advance along it, the more they swerve from the truth. Certain men of letters very often strike upon this rock.

> 139 Sunt homines, qui etiam si Mathematicas disciplinas non callent, tamen de Philosophorum Recentiorum scriptis judicium ferunt satis confidenter; audentque plurima in Physica lucubrare. Sunt, qui Sacra Biblia interpretantur, quin Graece, & Haebraice sciant: quin ullam historiae Judaicae, & Profanae notitiam habeant: qui planè hospites sunt in Critica arte. Sunt, qui Romanas leges exponunt, qui nulla Romanae historiae notitia tincti sunt, nec Ethices, & Politices rudimenta vel summis labiis degustarunt. Sunt, qui Pontíficium jus, qui Sacram scientiam docent, quin unquàm Patrum scripta pervólverint, & Ecclesiae veterem disciplinam examinarint. Postremò, ut reliquos omittam, sunt Medici, qui infinitam morborum várietatem, quae corpus humanum exercet, se curaturos esse sibi persuadent, quin unquam humani corporis viderint sectionem. Hi omnes, quia, quae necessaria sunt, ignorant, nihil unquám boni adferre poterunt.

139 There are men who, even if they are not versed in the Mathematical disciplines, nevertheless pass judgment quite confidently on the writings of the Modern Philosophers, and dare to work out a great many things in Physics. There are those who interpret the Sacred Bible without knowing Greek and Hebrew, without having any knowledge of Jewish and Profane history, who are plain strangers to the Critical art. There are those who expound the Roman laws who are tinged with no knowledge of Roman history, and have not tasted even with the tips of their lips the rudiments of Ethics and Politics. There are those who teach Pontifical law, who teach Sacred science, without ever having turned over the writings of the Fathers and examined the ancient discipline of the Church. Finally, to omit the rest, there are Physicians who persuade themselves that they will cure the infinite variety of diseases that afflict the human body without ever having seen a dissection of the human body. All these, because they are ignorant of what is necessary, will never be able to bring forth anything good.

> 140 Alii verò, tametsi rectà pergunt, tamen in contrarium vitium incurrunt. Nimirùm quum aveant omnia scire, & preter ceteros laudari, res planè diversas eodem tempore legunt: quumque minimè indocti videri cupiant, indoctissimi prae ceteris sunt. Etenim mens nostra, quae vix aliquam disciplinam perfectè arripit, dum plura simul legit, nihil pénitus ac profundè cognoscit: adeoque non nisi confusas ideas adquirit; & ea de causa in judicando décipitur.

140 Others, again, although they proceed rightly, nevertheless fall into the contrary vice. Namely, since they long to know everything and to be praised above the rest, they read quite different things at the same time; and though they desire to seem anything but unlearned, they are the most unlearned of all. For our mind, which scarcely grasps any one discipline perfectly, knows nothing thoroughly and deeply while it reads many things at once, and so acquires nothing but confused ideas, and for that reason is deceived in judging.

> 141 Tertia errorum causa sunt praejudicia, seu anticípata judicia, quae mens nostra de aliquibus rebus facit: ex quibus fit, ut cetera judicia planè similia formemus, nec liberè, & meritò de re ulla judicemus. Nam quum homines à prima aetate adsueti sint alios audire, qui eorum animis rerum quarumdam

141 The third cause of errors is prejudices, or anticipated judgments that our mind makes about certain things: from which it comes about that we form our other judgments quite similar to them, and do not judge freely and deservedly about anything. For since men from their earliest age are accustomed to listen to others, who imprint on their minds the images of certain things,

> [p. 48]

[p. 48] they easily persuade themselves that what they hear is true, and attach such faith to such things that they can only with difficulty be turned to the contrary side. From this an infinite crop of errors springs up. And so the incredible multitude of prejudices that holds men is reduced to the prejudice of authority, if you take away a few that arise in adult men either from hatred or from love.

> species ímprimunt, facilè sibi persuadent, esse vera, quae audiunt: & eam fidem talibus adjungunt, ut difficultèr in contrariam partem torqueri possint. Ex quo infinita errorum seges progérminat. Itaque incredibilis praejudiciorum multitudo, quae homines tenet, ad praejudicium auctoritatis revocatur: si pauca demas, quae in adultis hominibus, vel odio, vel amore nascuntur.

142 And first, the authority of parents is to children the norm of judging, and the cause of many errors. For parents imbue their children from the earliest age with foolish prejudices, which the nurses unceasingly confirm; and since tender minds are not strong in the use of reason and are not at all practiced in judging, they cannot persuade themselves that they have been deceived by their parents: and therefore they are deceived to a wonderful degree. Hence specters, and goblins, and ghosts, and the virtues of herbs and of medicines, and the miracles of mountebanks, and the other most trifling things that beat upon the ears of unhappy boys: so much so that, when they have become men, and are admonished by most learned men, they can scarcely at any time free themselves from those prejudices.

> 142 Ac primò parentum auctoritas est filiis norma judicandi, & plurium errorum causa. Parentes enim filios à prima aetate ineptis praejudiciis imbuunt, quae nutríces confirmant indesinentèr: quumque tenelli animi usu rationis non valeant, & in judicando minimè sint exercitati, persuadére sibi non possunt, se à parentibus esse deceptos: iccircò mirum in modum falluntur. Hinc spectra, & larvae, & lemures, & virtutes herbarum, ac medicamentorum, & circulatorum miracula, & nugacissima cetera, quae infelicium puerorum aures pulsant: usque adeò ut viri facti, & ab eruditissimis viris admóniti, iis se praejudiciis, vix ullo tempore liberare queant.

143 Next, nearly all parents treat their children softly and let them indulge their inclination, because they persuade themselves that if they did otherwise it would be to the harm and injury of their little ones. Hence boys are very often immersed in bodily pleasures, especially those of food and of venery, which both blunt the edge of the mind and weaken the memory, and so lead a man astray that he can scarcely ever think about and examine anything seriously and with meditation. For hold this for certain, young men: no more deadly plague befalls either body or mind than the pleasures of the body, which not only gradually undermine the fabric of man, but extinguish all the light of the mind. For laden tables carry off more men from our midst, frequent cups more, venery itself more, than plague, than war.

> 143 Deinde plerique omnes parentes filios suos móllitèr tractant, & genio indulgére sinunt: quòd sibi persuadant si secùs fácerent id filiolis damno, & nocumento fore. Hinc pueri in voluptates corporeas saepissimè inmerguntur, praesertim cibi, & veneris quae & mentis acúmen retundunt, & memoriam debilitant, & hominem ita agunt transversum, ut vix unquàm aliquid seriò, & meditatè cogitare, & examinare possit. Sic enim habetóte, Adolescentes, nullam capitaliorem pestem vel corpori, vel animo obtíngere, quam corporis voluptates: quae non solùm fabricationem hominis sensim labefactant, sed, omne animi lumen extinguunt. Plures enim structae mensae, plures frequentes poculi, plures ipsa venus, quàm pestis, quàm bellum de medio, tollit.

144 Parents are succeeded by Teachers, who frequently imbue little boys with marvelous opinions, and by their authority restrain them from learning other disciplines than those in which they themselves are versed.

> 144 Parentibus succedunt Praeceptores, qui mirificis sententiis frequentèr imbuunt puerulos: & auctoritate sua continent, ne alias disciplinas, quàm, quas ipsi callent, ediscant.

145 The Peripatetic Doctor cries out that the disciplines of the Moderns are futile and weak; the Critical Art, Natural History, Geometry, Arithmetic, Mechanics and things like these he thinks to be boys’ trifles; and he hisses off men illustrious in these disciplines just as if they were madmen. On the other hand, he everywhere sounds forth Universals and Signs, and Syllogistics, and Topics, and the huge throng of despicable little questions that he entitles Physics and Metaphysics; and he contends that the limits of philosophical science are wholly defined by these. Nay, at times he strikes, as it were, terror into the minds of the boys,

> 145 Peripateticus Doctor clámitat fútiles, & infirmas esse Recentiorum disciplinas, Artem Criticam, Historiam Naturae, Geometriam, Arithmeticam, Mechanicam, & iis similia nugas puerorum esse putat: hominesque his disciplinis inlustres, non secùs, ac insános exsíbilat. Contra verò Universalia & Signa, & Syllogisticam, & Topica, & ingentem sputatilicarum quaestiuncularum turbam, quam Physicam, & Methaphysicam inscribit, ubique crepat; atque iis Philosophiae scientiae limites omninò definiri contendit. Quinimò interdùm quasi terrorem puerorum

> [p. 49]

[p. 49] lest they learn Mathematics or the Philosophy of the Moderns, or ever call back to a severe examination the things that he himself holds as settled and fixed.

> animis íncutit, ne ii Mathematicam, vel Recentiorum Philosophiam addiscant: ne ve ea, quae rata, & fixa ipse habet ad sevérum examen unquam révocent.

146 The little boy, nourished on these admonitions, reverently kisses the pronouncements of his Teacher, and thinks that nothing more excellent can be conceived; he turns away from the splendid discoveries of others as though they were mere trifles, and shudders at the mere hearing of the name of the Systems of the Moderns: therefore he is ignorant of the sources of the disciplines, and can neither think nor utter anything worthy of learned ears. And so, when he has grown older, he too nourishes others with the same milk, and propagates ignorance with as much labor as would have been needed for him to be held most illustrious in the best disciplines.

> 146 Puellus hisce admonitionibus innutrítus Praeceptoris sui pronunciata venerabundus deosculatur: existimat que nihil praestantiùs posse cogitari; praeclara aliorum inventa quasi merae, nugae essent, aversatus: & vel solo audito nomine Recentiorum Systematum, exhorrescit: iccircò disciplinarum fontes ignorat, nec aliquid eruditis auribus dignum, aut cogitare potest, aut emíttere. Itaque grandior factus, & ipse alios eodem lacte enutrit: & inscitiam tanto labore propágat, quantò opus non esset, ut in optimis disciplinis clarissimus haberetur.

147 This was the reason why the weightier disciplines lay in squalor for so many centuries: namely, because the teachers who were thought most learned strove with all their might to keep the boys from deserting the old Masters, or from thinking anything new that was not in them. For men of this kind grieved to be surpassed in learning by younger men, and ambitiously took care that this new doctrine and new way of teaching should not undermine the glory they themselves had won by so many labors.
