> (b) Recherche de la Verité lib. 1. cap. 2. [p. 66] satis clarè exponi solet, ut optimè advertit Cl. Jacquier. Si enim hoc nomine intelligant ideas menti perpetuò praesentes, nulla potest esse controversia. ¿ Quis enim dixerit aliquam in nobis esse ideam, quam indesinenter contemplemur? Si autem significare voluerint ideas, quae ante omnem experientiam, omnemque ratiocinationem semper praestò sunt; nemo sane hujusmodi ideae meminit, de qua ante omnem experientiam, omnemque ratiocinationem mens cogitaverit.

(b) Recherche de la Verité, bk. 1, ch. 2. [p. 66] usually set out clearly enough, as the celebrated Jacquier excellently observes. For if by this name they understand ideas perpetually present to the mind, there can be no controversy. For who would say that there is some idea in us which we contemplate unceasingly? But if they mean ideas which are always at hand before all experience and all reasoning, no one surely remembers any idea of this kind which the mind thought of before all experience and all reasoning.

> 203 At si per ideas innatas intelligamus notiones illas, quae aliquàndò sine objectorum externorum occasione, & facili atque expedito rationis usu acquiruntur, innatas in hoc tantùm sensu ideas dicimus esse admittendas. Et re vera quidem, nihil aliud significari posse vocabulo idearum innatarum fatebitur is, qui gravissimam hanc quaestionem non ex disputationis aestu, aut definitionis ambiguitate, sed ex proprio conscientiae testimonio expendet. His explicatis sit conclusio contra Peripateticos, & Gassendum, & Lockium.

203 But if by innate ideas we understand those notions which are sometimes acquired without the occasion of external objects, and by an easy and ready use of reason, we say that ideas are to be admitted as innate in this sense only. And in truth nothing else can be signified by the term innate ideas, as he will confess who weighs this most weighty question, not from the heat of disputation or the ambiguity of a definition, but from the proper testimony of his own consciousness. These things explained, let the conclusion be against the Peripatetics, Gassendi, and Locke.

> 204 Plures habemus ideas purè intellectuales, quarum aliquas facili rationis usu acquirimus. Prob.: in iis quae ad animam pertinent, nulla tutior regula adhiberi debet, quam intimum conscientiae testimonium: atqui conscientiae testimonio experimur nos multa percipere per intellectionem puram absque ulla imagine corporea: ergo plures habemus ideas purè intellectuales. Prob. min.: plures menti nostrae obversantur ideae rerum, quae ab omni materia & sensibili qualitate prorsùs secretae sunt, quales sunt ideae assensus & dissensus, justitiae, intelligentiae, Dei, ergo. Prob. antec.: assensus & dissensus justitia, &c. & alia idearum nostrarum objecta nullam habent similitudinem cum rebus sensibilibus, nulla qualitate sensibili praedita sunt, nullaque proindè sensatione aut imaginatione repraesentari possunt.

204 We have many purely intellectual ideas, some of which we acquire by an easy use of reason. Proof: in those things which pertain to the mind, no safer rule ought to be applied than the inmost testimony of consciousness: but by the testimony of consciousness we experience that we perceive many things by pure intellection without any bodily image: therefore we have many purely intellectual ideas. Proof of the minor: many ideas of things present themselves to our mind which are entirely separated from all matter and sensible quality, such as are the ideas of assent and dissent, of justice, of intelligence, of God: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: assent and dissent, justice, etc., and other objects of our ideas have no likeness to sensible things, are endowed with no sensible quality, and accordingly can be represented by no sensation or imagination.

> 205 Confirmatur conclusio; illae ideae sunt purè intellectuales quarum objecta nec colorata sunt, nec sápida, nec sonóra, nec ulla sensibili qualitate adfecta, ut ait Sanctus Augustinus, (c) atqui multae sunt ideae quarum objecta nec colorata sunt, &c., cujusmodi sunt idea entis generatim, idea Dei, &c.: ergo dantur ideae purè intellectuales.

205 The conclusion is confirmed: those ideas are purely intellectual whose objects are neither colored, nor savory, nor sonorous, nor affected by any sensible quality, as St. Augustine says (c): but there are many ideas whose objects are neither colored, etc., such as are the idea of being in general, the idea of God, etc.: therefore purely intellectual ideas are given.

206 Obj. 1: if there is any purely intellectual idea which does not have its origin from the senses, it is above all the idea of being in general, the idea of God,

I deny the minor: because being in general is neither colored, nor savory, nor endowed with any sensible quality. But you will prove the minor: the idea of being in general is formed by abstraction from singular and individual bodies; but singular bodies are perceived by the senses: therefore such an idea takes its origin from the senses. To the proof, I distinguish the major: it is formed by abstraction from corporeal and spiritual things, I grant; from corporeal things only, I deny the major and the consequent.

> &c.: sed istae ideae ortum ducunt à sensibus: ergo. Nego min.: quia ens generatim nec coloratum est, nec sapidum, nec ulla sensibili qualitate praéditum. Sed probabis minorem: idea entis generatim formatur per abstractionem à singularibus, & individuis corporibus; sed singularia corpora sensibus percipiuntur: ergo talis idea ortum ducit à sensibus. Ad probationem dist. maj.: formatur per abstractionem à rebus corporeis & spiritualibus, conc. à rebus corporeis tantùm, nego maj. & conseq.

207 We call being in general that which can exist; and so, even if it were supposed that there are no bodies, we could form this idea of being from the inmost consciousness of the operations of our mind, and without any relation to body. Moreover, if this idea took its origin only from the senses, it would not comprehend in its extension absolutely all the genera of being, but only corporeal beings; which, however, is false. You will insist 1: Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense; therefore all ideas, and accordingly the idea of being in general, depend on the senses. Dist. the antecedent: which was not first in the external or the internal sense, I grant; in the external sense only, I deny the antecedent, and the consequent.

> 207 Ens generatim dicimus id quod potest existere, itaque etsi nulla esse corpora fingeretur, hanc entis ideam formare possémus ex íntima operationum mentis nostrae conscientia, et sine ulla ad corpus relatione. Praeterea si haec idea ortum tantum duceret à sensibus non omnia planè entis genera in sua extensione comprehenderet, sed tantùm entia corporea, quod tamen est falsum. Instabis 1: Nihil est in intellectu quod prius non fuerit in sensu; ergo ideae omnes ac proindè idea entis generatim pendet à sensibus Dist. antec. quod prius non fuerit in sensu externo vel interno, conc. in sensu tantùm externo, nego antec. & conseq.

208 We confess that there is a twofold origin of ideas: the external sense, by which we acquire the ideas of corporeal things, and the internal sense, by which, through the mind’s attention and reflection upon its own operations, we procure the ideas of spiritual things. You will insist 2: but nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the external sense only: therefore the distinction is false. Proof of the subsumption: that was first in the external sense which is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things; but we do not know spiritual things except by comparison with corporeal things: therefore. Proof of the minor: God is a spiritual substance; but we have no idea of God except insofar as we represent Him to ourselves under the image of a Venerable Old Man: therefore.

> 208 Duplicem esse idearum originem, fatémur, sensum externum, quo rerum corporearum ideas acquirimus, & sensum internum, quo per mentis adtentionem, ac reflexionem in proprias operationes rerum spiritualium idéas comparamus. Instabis 2: atqui nihil est in intellectu quod priùs non fuerit in sensu externo tantùm: ergo falsa est distinctio. Prob. subsumpta: illud priùs fuit in sensu externo, quod à nobis non cognoscitur nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis; sed res spirituales non cognoscimus, nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis: ergo. Prob. min.: Deus est substantia spiritualis; sed Dei nullam habemus ideam, nisi quia sub imagine Venerandi Senis illum nobis repraesentamus: ergo.

209 I reply by denying the minor. It is true indeed that our mind cannot, without the utmost care and attention, entirely purge its ideas of every bodily taint, and that for this reason the ruder sort of men perceive nothing except with an image. But those images, e.g. of an Old Man and of a winged youth, are not themselves the ideas of God and of the Angels, but mere phantasms which accompany those ideas. For if we had no other idea of God than the idea of a Venerable Old Man, all the judgments that we form about God would have to appear to us entirely false, as being contrary to this idea; for we believe those judgments to be false which are contrary to the ideas of things that we have in our mind; and therefore we could not judge God to be incorporeal, invisible, since none of these can in any way agree with the idea of a Venerable Old Man.

> 209 Respondeo negando minorem: verùm quidem est, mentem nostram sine summa cura & adtentione, ideas ab omni prorsùs labe corporea expurgare non posse, & hac de causa rudiores homines nihil nisi cum imagine percipiunt. At illae imagines Senis, ex. gr. & juvenis alati non sunt ipsae Dei, & Angelorum ideae, sed mera phantasmata, quae ideas illas comitantur. Nam si nullam aliam Dei ideam haberemus, praeter ideam Venerabilis Senis, omnia quae de Deo formamus judicia, nobis adparére deberent prorsùs falsa, utporè huic ideae contraria: illa enim judicia falsa esse credimus, quae contraria sunt ideis rerum quas in mente habemus; ideòque non possemus judicare, Deum esse incorporeum, invisibilem, siquidem haec omnia cum idea Venerabilis Senis nulla ratione convenire possunt.

> 210 Instabis 3.: Apostolus ad Rom. cap. 1 scribit: invisibilia Dei, per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur: ergo Deus non cognoscitur à nobis nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis. Dist. antec.: quatenùs ex consideratione rerum corporearum, & spiritualium, rectè concludimus, existere supremum omnium Opíficem, conc., quatenùs idea Dei sit phantasma quoddam per comparationem cum rebus corporeis formatum, nego. Cavendum ergo est, ne, ut loquitur ibidem Sanctus Paulus, mutetur gloria incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis.

210 You will insist 3: The Apostle writes in Rom. ch. 1: the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made: therefore God is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: insofar as from the consideration of corporeal and spiritual things we rightly conclude that the supreme Maker of all things exists, I grant; insofar as the idea of God is some phantasm formed by comparison with corporeal things, I deny. We must beware, therefore, lest, as St. Paul says in the same place, the glory of the incorruptible God be changed into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man.

> 211 Instabis 4: idea Dei formatur ex ideis perfectionum omnium creaturarum etiam corporearum: ergo idea Dei formatur per comparationem cum rebus corporeis. Dist. antec.: formatur ex ideis perfectionum creaturarum etiam corporearum eminenter sumptarum, conc.: formaliter sumptarum, nego & conseq. Adtributa corporea in idea Dei non includimus formaliter, id est prout sunt in corporibus, sed tantùm eminenter, hoc est, modo quodam nobiliori ac sublimiori sine ulla imperfectione, removendò à Deo omnes ideas materiae, divisionis, coloris & ceteras, quae formalitèr sumptae includunt necessariò quasdam imperfectiones, & Enti summo convenire non possunt nisi eminenter.

211 You will insist 4: the idea of God is formed from the ideas of the perfections of all creatures, even corporeal ones: therefore the idea of God is formed by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: it is formed from the ideas of the perfections of creatures, even corporeal ones, taken eminently, I grant; taken formally, I deny, and the consequent. We do not include corporeal attributes in the idea of God formally, that is, as they are in bodies, but only eminently, that is, in a certain nobler and more sublime manner, without any imperfection, removing from God all the ideas of matter, of division, of color, and the rest, which, taken formally, necessarily include certain imperfections, and cannot belong to the supreme Being except eminently.

> 212 Opp. 2.: si quis nasceretur omni sensu orbatus, ita ut neque videret, neque audiret, &c. is sanè nullas ideas haberet: ergo non dantur ideae purè intellectuales. Nego antec.: mens quippe in ea hypothesi viveret; vita autem mentis, in cogitatione consistit, hoc est in perceptione intellectus, & inclinatione voluntatis: ergo mens cogitaret. Non cogitaret autèm de rebus à se remotis, sed de eis quae praesentes sibi forent, & à quibus commoveretur. Nihil autem menti magis praesto est, quam ipsa sibi, ut docet Sanctus Augustinus: ergo se ipsam per quamdam conscientiam cognosceret.

212 Obj. 2: if someone were born deprived of every sense, so that he neither saw nor heard, etc., he would surely have no ideas: therefore there are no purely intellectual ideas. I deny the antecedent: for in that hypothesis the mind would live; but the life of the mind consists in thinking, that is, in the perception of the intellect and the inclination of the will: therefore the mind would think. It would not, however, think of things remote from it, but of those which were present to it and by which it was moved. But nothing is more present to the mind than itself, as St. Augustine teaches: therefore it would know itself by a certain consciousness.

> 213 Opp. 3. contra secundam conclusionis partem; si aliquae essent ideae, quae facili rationis usu acquirerentur, tales essent ideae Dei, & moralitatis actionum, sed istae non sunt; ergo. 214 To the argument I reply by denying the minor, whose proof we shall explain. The examples adduced hold good only against those who think that those ideas are present to our minds before all attention. But since, according to our definition, innate ideas are not perceived without some use of reason, the cause to be assigned for so gross and almost incredible an ignorance is this:

> De praecipuis sensationum legibus.

that those men neglected the faculties of their mind and did not apply them to the investigation of the first truths.

> 215 Sit conclusio: lex sensationum est, ut quotiès ab objecto sensibili mutatio quaedam producitur in organo sensorio ritè constituto, totiès in anima oriatur sensatio quaedam particularis huic mutationi respondens. Prob.: illa sensatio mutationi respondet, quae ad arbitrium nostrum variari non potest; sed mutatio facta in organo sensorio ritè constituto non potest ad arbitrium nostrum variari: ergo. Prob. min. quotidiana experientia: si fragor ex. gr. tormenti bellici aurem ferit, illum necessariò percípimus, neque sensationem illam in sonum blandiorem mutare póssum: si faetor nares óccupat efficere nullomodo possumus ut ejus loco, vel odórem suavem, vel faetórem minus molestum percipiamus: ergo.

E X E RC I S E I I I .

> 216 Ex hac generali sensationum lege, quatuor regulae colliguntur. I. Si mutatio in eodem organo, eadem est, sensatio quoque in anima eadem esse debet. II. Si contingat, à diversis objectis sensibilibus eamdem in eodem organo sensorio mutationem produci, objecta eadem adparere debent. III. Si mutatio in organo sensorio diversa est, sensatio quoque in anima diversa esse debet. IV. Hinc si contingat idem objectum diversam in eodem organo mutationem efficere, diversum quoque adparere debet objectum. Ex his fluunt generalia visionis explicandae principia, & opticarum deceptionum fundamenta.

On the principal laws of sensations.

et the conclusion be: it is a law of sensations that as often as some 215

L          change is produced by a sensible object in a duly constituted sense

organ, so often there arises in the soul some particular sensation corresponding to this change. Proof: that sensation corresponds to the change which cannot be varied at our will; but the change made in a duly constituted sense organ cannot be varied at our will: therefore. Proof of the minor, from daily experience: if, e.g., the crash of a cannon strikes the ear, we necessarily perceive it, nor can we change that sensation into a gentler sound; if a stench fills the nostrils, we can in no way bring it about that in its place we perceive either a sweet odor or a less offensive stench: therefore.

216 From this general law of sensations four rules are gathered. I. If the change in the same organ is the same, the sensation in the soul must also be the same. II. If it happens that the same change is produced in the same sense organ by different sensible objects, the objects must appear the same. III. If the change in the sense organ is different, the sensation in the soul must also be different. IV. Hence if it happens that the same object produces a different change in the same organ, the object too must appear different.

From these flow the general principles for explaining vision, and the foundations of optical illusions.

> 217 Opp. 1.: plures producuntùr in organo sensorio ritè constituto mutationes sine ulla animi sensatione: ergo. Prob. antec.: dum interdiù caelum intuemur singulae stellae luminis radios in oculum ritè constitutum immittunt, quibus stellarum imago in oculo delineatur, ac proindè mutationes in organo sensorio producunt: atqui tamen stellas anima non pércipit: ergo. Dist. antec.: plures producuntur sine sensatione mutationes insufficientes, conc. sufficientes, nego. Ad probationem conc. maj. dist. min.: anima stellas non percipit interdiù, id est, anima stellarum perceptiones debiliores ab aliis fortioribus non distinguit, conc., nullas habet stellarum perceptiones obscuras, nego, & conseq.

217 Obj. 1: many changes are produced in a duly constituted sense organ without any sensation of the soul: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: when by day we gaze at the sky, the single stars send rays of light into the duly constituted eye, by which the image of the stars is delineated in the eye, and accordingly they produce changes in the sense organ; and yet the soul does not perceive the stars: therefore. Dist. the antecedent: many changes are produced without sensation that are insufficient, I grant; sufficient ones, I deny. To the proof, I grant the major and distinguish the minor: the soul does not perceive the stars by day, that is, the soul does not distinguish the weaker perceptions of the stars from the other, stronger ones, I grant; it has no obscure perceptions of the stars, I deny; and I deny the consequent.

> 218 Non omnis mutatio facta in organo sensorio sufficit ut anima sentiat, sed requiritur, ut mutatio illa ad cérebrum usque transmittatur, & idcircò necessariam esse diximus mutationem factam ab objecto sensibili, hoc est, ab objecto quod mutationem sufficientem in organo sensorio ritè constituto producere posit. Sed instabis: eidem mutationi in eodem organo sensorio factae, non respondet eadem in anima sensatio: ergo. Prob. antec.: Sol & Luna dum vértici nostro imminent, minores videntur, quàm propè horizontem positi: atqui in utroque loco eandem mutationem in eodem oculo producunt: ergo.

218 Not every change made in the sense organ suffices for the soul to feel; but it is required that the change be transmitted all the way to the brain; and for this reason we said that the change must necessarily be made by a sensible object, that is, by an object which can produce a sufficient change in a duly constituted sense organ. But you will insist: the same sensation in the soul does not correspond to the same change made in the same sense organ: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the Sun and the Moon, when they hang over our zenith, appear smaller than when placed near the horizon; and yet in both places they produce the same change in the same eye: therefore.

> 219 Nego antec., & ad probationem dist. min.: eamdem mutationem in oculo producunt conjunctam cum diversis mutationibus aliis in utroque loco, conc. secus nego, & conseq. Phaenomenon ita explicamus. Id enim circò Lunam & Solem in horizonte majores videri solent quam in meridiano, quia in horizonte simul cum earum imaginibus in oculo pinguntur interjecta corpora terraestria caelique fornix oblongus. At illa objectorum series, dùm Sol & Luna in vertice caeli conspiciuntur, oculum non adficiunt, atque inde est, quod si Solem & Lunam in horizonte per tubum angustum conspiciamus, haud majores videantur, quàm in caeli vertice. Dum ergo dicimus eidem mutationi in eodem organo factae eandem in anima sensationem respondere, propositio intelligenda est de mutationibus singulis seorsim consideratis.

219 I deny the antecedent, and to the proof I distinguish the minor: they produce the same change in the eye, joined with different other changes in each place, I grant; otherwise, I deny, and the consequent. We explain the phenomenon thus. The Moon and the Sun are usually seen larger on the horizon than at the meridian because on the horizon, together with their images, the intervening terrestrial bodies and the oblong vault of the sky are painted in the eye. This series of objects does not affect the eye when the Sun and Moon are seen at the top of the sky; and hence it is that if you look at the Sun and the Moon on the horizon through a narrow tube, they do not appear larger than at the top of the sky. When, therefore, we say that the same sensation in the soul corresponds to the same change made in the same organ, the proposition is to be understood of the changes each considered separately.

> De veri & falsi criterio.

On the criterion of the true and the false.

> 220 Saepe observamus tam luculentèr & perspicuè in pluribus casibus cògnitam nobis esse praedicati cum subjecto convenientiam, ut statim pateat, & adsensum extorqueat. Ex hac summa evidentia persuassum nobis est, nullam unquàm extitisse hominum sectam, qui de omnibus seriò dubitaverit. Quae quum ita sint, quaestionis statum non satis intellígere videntur ii, qui veritatis criterium investigantes, illud in evidentia reponunt, & evidentiam existere contra Scepticos prolixiùs demonstrant. Hi quidem sibi fingunt hostes quos feriant. Nos verò quaestionem hanc sequenti conclusione explicabimus.

e often observe that in many cases the agreement of the predi220

> 222 Veritatis criterium constituunt aliqui in ipsa evidentia. Verùm satis determinatum non est illud veritatis criterium: nam clara perceptio sive evidentia, in dato quolibet casu per regulas Logicae adplicari debet. ita nempè argumentandum est, quidquid clare & distincte percipi potest, illud est verum; sed hoc clare & distincte percipi potest: ergo hoc est verum, id autem fit per regulas Logicae; tradendae ergo sunt regulae, quarum ope judicari posit, adesse evidentiam aut veritatem, illae autem sunt regulae Logicae: quum dicitur ergo, evidentiam esse veri criterium, res perindè se habet, ac si diceretur, veritatem esse veritatis criterium, quod nugari est.

is at once manifest and wrests our assent. By this supreme evidence we are persuaded that there has never been any sect of men that seriously doubted of all things. This being so, those seem not to understand sufficiently the state of the question who, in investigating the criterion of truth, place it in evidence, and demonstrate at length against the Sceptics that evidence exists. These, indeed, invent for themselves enemies to strike. We, however, shall explain this question by the following conclusion.

221 Conclusion: to distinguish the true from the false the rules of Logic suffice, and no other criterion of truth is needed. Proof of the 1st part: he discerns the true from the false who demonstrates that the predicate agrees with the subject; but the rules of Logic suffice for demonstrating this: therefore.

Proof of the minor: a demonstration consists of a chain of syllogisms whose premises are definitions, axioms, and propositions already demonstrated; but

Logic hands down the rules of definitions, establishes the distinction between axioms and demonstrable propositions, delineates the form of syllogisms, and shows, finally, the modes of joining syllogisms together, etc.: therefore. Proof of the 2nd part: if some other criterion of truth were needed besides the rules of

Logic, those rules would not suffice for discerning the true from the false; but we have demonstrated that they suffice: therefore.

222 Some place the criterion of truth in evidence itself. But that criterion of truth is not sufficiently determined: for clear perception, or evidence, must in any given case be applied through the rules of Logic. One must, namely, argue thus: whatever can be clearly and distinctly perceived is true; but this can be clearly and distinctly perceived: therefore this is true; and this is done through the rules of

Logic. Rules must therefore be handed down by whose help it may be judged that evidence, or truth, is present; and these are the rules of Logic. When it is said, therefore, that evidence is the criterion of the true, the matter stands just as if it were said that truth is the criterion of truth, which is to trifle.

Contrary

[p. 72]

> Reffelluntur opposita.

C O N T R A R Y V I E W S A R E R E F U T E D.

> 223 Opp. 1: illud est veritatis criterium quod verum à falso ita secernit, ut veritati adsensum negare non possímus, sed id praestat evidentia, seu quod idem est propositio ista, quidquid clare & distincte percipitur verum est: ergo. Dist. min.: & criterium illud non est satis determinatum per se, sed per regulas Logicae, conc., & determinatum est, ita ut Logícae regulis opus non sit, nego & conseq.: Solutio manet explicata. Instabis: illud non est veritatis criterium quod alio criterio indiget; sed Logicae regulae alio indigént veritatís criterio, nempè ad demonstrandas Logicae regulas opus est evidentiâ; ergo.

223 Obj. 1: that is the criterion of truth which so separates the true from the false that we cannot refuse assent to the truth; but evidence does this, or, what is the same, the proposition whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true: therefore. I distinguish the minor: and that criterion is not sufficiently determined by itself, but through the rules of Logic, I grant; and it is so determined that there is no need of the rules of Logic, I deny; and the consequence. The solution remains explained. You will insist: that is not the criterion of truth which needs another criterion; but the rules of Logic need another criterion of truth, for evidence is needed to demonstrate the rules of Logic: therefore.

> 224 Dist. min.: opus est evidentiâ, quae deinde per Logicae regulas adplicari debeat, conc., quae non indigeat, nego. Omnis dificultas evanescit si quaestionis status rectè intelligatur. Instabis 2: veritatis criterium potest esse principium illud: impossibile est, idem simul esse, & non esse: ergo praeter regulas Logicae saltem aliquod aliud esse poterit veritatis criterium. Dist. antec.: & propositio demonstranda ad principium illud per regulas Logicae redúci debet, conc. secùs nego. Ad objectionem eadem est, quae ad praecedentem responsio.

224 I distinguish the minor: evidence is needed, which must then be applied through the rules of Logic, I grant; evidence that does not need them, I deny. The whole difficulty vanishes if the state of the question is rightly understood. You will insist 2: the criterion of truth can be the principle it is impossible for the same thing at once to be and not to be: therefore, besides the rules of Logic, at least something else could be the criterion of truth. I distinguish the antecedent: and the proposition to be demonstrated must be reduced to that principle through the rules of Logic, I grant; otherwise, I deny. To this objection the reply is the same as to the preceding one.

> 225 Habetis jam, Adolescentes optimi, Logicae praecepta & quaestiones, quae vobis tanquam maxime utilia proponimus; quae si pro ingenio vestro, pro discendi cupiditate, uti par est, adripuéritis, non poenitendum operae pretium vos facturos esse confidimus. Pauca haec sunt, sed pro aetatis genio satis multa. Plura si vultis, ea legendis auctoribus, quos hactenus commendavimus facili negotio comparabitis.

225 You now have, excellent young men, the precepts and questions of Logic, which we put before you as the most useful; if you lay hold of them as befits your talent and your eagerness to learn, we are confident that you will have done work not to be regretted. These things are few, but for the character of your age many enough. If you want more, you will easily acquire it by reading the authors whom we have commended thus far.

## P R E FAC E 

fter Logic, not Physics, as the Peripatetics do, but Metaphysics 1

A         is what the Moderns teach, and rightly so; for since this discipline is

called first Philosophy, and in its first part is occupied with weighing the meaning of words and with unfolding the most generic principles, it must therefore enter into partnership and alliance with the faculty of discoursing. The name of Metaphysics, moreover, altogether unknown to the ancient

Philosophers, is said to have been first used by Alexander of Aphrodisias and

John Philoponus, interpreters of Aristotle. By this name, however, were entitled those writings of Aristotle which, once the Logical, Ethical and Physical works had first been put in order by Tyrannio the Grammarian and a certain

Andronicus of Rhodes,

> [p. 2] ELEMENTORUM RECENTIORIS PHILOSOHIAE PARS ALTERA.

L [p. 2] seemed unable to be referred to any definite class (a).

> ELEMENTA METAPHYSICES.

2 Now, however, by the name of Metaphysics there comes to the mind of Philosophers that discipline which pursues things placed on high, that is, things established above the nature of bodies, or spiritual things freed from all commerce with matter. Hence it is commonly and very well defined by all Philosophers: The faculty which considers all the general affections of being that are common to corporeal and incorporeal beings alike, and which also contemplates incorporeal substances and their affections, as they are perceptible to us by the light of reason alone. There are three principal parts of Metaphysics. The first of them is called Ontology, or Ontosophy, that is, the science of being, and so it treats of being taken in general, and weighs its affections as abstracted by the mind. The second so scrutinizes spiritual substances as to set before us their nature, existence and operations by the light of reason alone. And since there are chiefly two spiritual substances that can be known by us through the light of nature, namely God and the human mind, Pneumatology, or the Science of Spirits, has customarily been divided, quite fittingly, into two parts: that which treats of the human mind is called Psychology, or Pneumatology; that which discourses of God, with reason alone as guide, Natural Theology.

> PRAEFATIO.

3 Accordingly we shall have three parts of Metaphysics, of which the first will comprise Ontology, the second Psychology, the last Natural Theology. The Peripatetic Philosophers handed down Metaphysics in so confused a manner that nothing more obscure can be conceived. We, however, excellent young men, shall give you a Metaphysics, not that old, long and intricate one, but a brief and very expeditious one, such as may sharpen the mind and pave the way for grasping the remaining disciplines.

> 1 Post Logicam, non Physicam quemadmodùm Peripatetici faciunt, sed Metaphysicam tradunt Recentiores, & jure quidem; quum enim haec disciplina prima Philosophia adpelletur, & in vocabulorum significatione expendenda, & in principiis maximè genericis evolvendis prima sui parte versetur, hinc cum facultate disserendi, societatem ac foedus inire debet. Ceterùm Metaphysicae nomen antiquis Philosophis planè incognitum ab Alexandro Aphrodisaeo, & Johanne Philopono, Aristotelis interpretibus, primò usurpatum fuisse traditur. Hoc autem nomine illa Aristotelis scripta inscripta fuere, quae Logicis, Ethicis, atque Physicis â Tyrannione Grammatico, & Andronico quodam Rhodio primùm in or-

Metaphysics

(a) The writings of Aristotle, which were left first to Theophrastus, then to Neleus, were hidden and buried under the earth by his heirs for some centuries. Then, when they were drawn out thoroughly corrupted by damp, they were sold to Apellicon of Teos, who unskillfully filled in the corrupted passages. When Athens had been subdued by L. Sulla, Apellicon’s library was carried to Rome by his order, where first Tyrannio, then Andronicus of Rhodes revised the works of Aristotle and put them in order. See what was said in the Hist. of Philos.

On Being, its species, and its properties.

> 2 Nunc autem Metaphysicae nomine apud Philosophos ea disciplina in mentem venit, quae res sursum positas, id est supra corporum naturam constitutas, seu res spirituales, & à materiae commercio solutas prosequitur. Hinc illa â Philosophis omnibus optimè definiri solet: Facultas quae generales omnes entis adfectiones, corporeis & incorporeis etiam entibus communes considerat; adeòque incorporeas etiam substantias, ipsarumque adfectiones solo rationis lumine nobis perspicuas contemplatur. Tres sunt Metaphysicae partes principes. Illarum prima Ontologia, sive Ontosophia, hoc est entis scientia vocatur, adeòque de ente generatim sumpto disserit, ejusque adfectiones per mentem abstractas expendit. Altera spirituales substantias ita scrutatur, ut earum naturam, existentiam, atque operationes solo rationis lumine nobis exhibeat. Quoniam autèm duae potissimùm sunt substantiae spirituales, quae naturae luminae cognosci à nobis possunt, Deus, scilicèt, & mens humana, ideò Pneumatologia, seu Spirituum scientia in duas partes satis aptè dividi consuevit; illa quae agit de mente humana Psychologia, vel Pneumatologia vocatur, quae de Deo sola dirigente ratione disserit Theologia Naturalis.

he science which knows being in general, or in common, that is, 4

T         separated from all circumstances and accidents, so that from the

contemplation of it as universal a clearer knowledge of any particular being may afterwards arise, is called Ontology, or the science of being. We shall embrace this science in the clearest and most accurate order possible; and since its greatest obscurity arises from the countless and altogether useless questions with which the Arabs and the common Peripatetics have most wretchedly disfigured it, we shall omit those questions as useless, and shall contemplate being itself, its species, and all its properties.

## CHAPTER I

> 3 Itaque tres nobis erunt partes Metaphysicae, quarum prima Ontologiam, secunda Psychologiam, postrema Theologiam Naturalem comprehendet. Peripatetici Philosophi tam perturbatè Metaphysicam tradiderunt, nihil ut obscuriùs cogitari possit. Nos verò, Adolescentes optimi, Metaphysicam vobis dabimus, non illam veterem, longam, intricatam, sed brevem, perexpeditam, quaeque ad reliquas disciplinas percipiendas, mentem acuat, viamque muniat.

On Being in common, and its division. 5

Being is that which is, or can be; hence whatever is conceived by our intellect is called Being, and nothing can be understood, imagined, affirmed or denied to which this general and most universal idea, concept or name of Being does not apply. Being taken universally is divided into substance and

> (a) Aristotelis scripta, quae Theophrasto primùm, dein Neleo relicta fuere, ab ejus haeredibus per aliquot secula sub humo abscóndita fuere, & consepulta. Indè quum extraherentur humore penitùs corrupta, véndita fuere Apelliconi Tejo, qui depraváta loca imperíte supplevit. Subactis Athénis â L. Sulla, Apellicónis bibliotheca ejus jussu Romam delata est, ubi Tyrannio primùm, deindè Andronicus Rhódius Aristotelis opera recensuerunt, & ordine posuerunt. Vide dicta in Hist. Philosoph. [p. 4] METAPHYSICES PARS I.

L2 [p. 4] accident, or into being properly and strictly taken, and a mode of being. Substance, or thing, is the name given to that being which exists by itself, or can exist or be perfectly conceived independently of another being, as a stone, a man, etc.: an accident, on the other hand, or mode of being, is that being which must exist in another, and can neither be nor be conceived except as inhering in and joined to another, as whiteness, roundness, motion, etc.

> ONTOLOGIA.

6 Substance, or thing, is divided into created and uncreated: that is called uncreated which receives from no one the being that it has, as God alone is; created, that which has been produced freely, contingently, by another, that is, by God, as men, stars, etc. Created substances are divided into corporeal and incorporeal. Accidents are divided chiefly into extrinsic and intrinsic. Those are called intrinsic which affect intrinsically and really the thing, the substance or subject itself in which they are found, as motion and figure in a body; extrinsic, those which posit nothing intrinsically, truly and really in the thing, but are only conceived in it by our intellect, and yet are considered by us as beings, of which kind are all relations, privations, and extrinsic denominations.

> DISSERTATIO UNICA.

7 Substance, therefore, can be defined: an essence separated from its modes. A mode, moreover, is that by which a substance is in this or that way, and which in a manner clothes it and makes it perceived by the senses. Hence it becomes manifest that substance is an idea related to the modes from which it is imagined as separated, and therefore that it is an abstract idea: for no substance exists lacking all modes. Therefore those who dispute about substance taken without modes are disputing not about some thing that is outside the mind, but about an abstract idea that exists only in their mind. For we have no other idea of substance than by conceiving a cluster of modes and properties, and adding to them the obscure idea of a nature unknown to us, that is, of a combination, e.g., of parts of matter not known to us, which we think such things contain. (§§. 29, 30, Log.)

> De Ente, ejusque speciebus, & proprietatibus.

8 Accidents, or internal modes, so inhere intrinsically in substance that they can neither be, nor be understood to exist, separated from it: as figure and motion: for where is there figure without a body? motion without a movable thing? External modes, however, do not really exist in the substance, but are conceived by our mind as something that affects it, of which kind are, as we have already said, all relations.

> 4 Scientia quae ens in genere vel in communi, hoc est, â circunstantiis & accidentibus omnibus separatum cognoscit, ut ab universali ipsius contemplatione clarior deindè cujuslibet particularis entis cognitio oriatur, vocatur Ontologia sive scientia de ente. Scientiam hanc clariori, & adcuratiori quo fieri poterit ordine complectemur; quumque obscuritas maxima, ex innumeris prorsusque inutilibus quaestionibus oriatur, quibus illam Arabes & vulgares Peripatetici miserrimè deturparunt, quaestiones illas veluti inutiles omittemus, atque ens ipsum, ejusque species, & proprietates omnes contemplabimur.

9 Therefore substance taken physically and really must have some internal modes. Hence it is inept to ask whether it can be without modes: because even if a substance is at times without this or that mode, yet in this order of things it cannot be stripped of all modes. Taken metaphysically, however, it is plain that it can be without modes. Therefore it is also inept to ask whether it can be without modes; because substance taken metaphysically signifies precisely this, namely a nature separated from modes. Yet since the abstract idea of substance, as of essence, is not the same in all things, but according to the variety

> CAPUT I.

> De Ente in communi ejusque divisione.

> 5 Ens est id quod est, aut esse potest, unde quidquid ab intellectu nostro concipitur Ens adpellatur, nihilque intelligi, effingi, adfirmari, sive negari poterit, cui generalis, & universalissima haec Entis idea, conceptus aut nomen non conveniat. Ens universaliter sumptum dividitur in substantiam, & ac-

> [p. 5]

[p. 5] of things is itself also various, it is at times such as to comprise some modes: which for that reason are no longer to be called modes, but the essence and substance of the thing. But we shall conveniently explain these things by an example.

> cidens, sive in ens propriè & rigorosè sumptum, & modum entis. Substantia vel res dicitur illud ens, quod per se existit, vel existere aut perfectè concipi potest independenter ab alio ente ut lapis, homo &c.: accidens verò vel modus entis, est illud ens quod existere debet in alio, neque potest esse, vel concipi, nisi veluti alteri inhaerens, atque conjunctum, ut albedo, rotunditas, motus &c.

10 E.g., the pen that I am at present moving with my hand in order to write these things can be not moved, if I stop: therefore it can be deprived of motion, and be at rest, without ceasing to be a pen. It cannot, however, be deprived at once of motion and of rest, but must necessarily have one or the other. Likewise it cannot be deprived of all magnitude, figure, and the rest: but it necessarily has one or another. A clock, on the contrary, e.g., comprises, besides the artful construction of its parts, their motion. And therefore, although motion taken in general is a mode of body, it is nevertheless the essence or substance of the clock. Likewise a thunderbolt, besides the inflamed matter, includes a most violent motion. For this reason this motion is no longer a mode, but the essence of the thunderbolt. Therefore, that we may judge rightly of modes, we must first establish in what the nature of the thing consists, lest we unwittingly call a mode that which constitutes its nature.

> 6 Substantia verò vel res dividitur in creatam, & increatam: increata dicitur illa, quae à nullo recipit esse quod habet, ut est solus Deus, creata verò quae liberè, contingenter, ab alio, id est, à Deo producta est, ut homines, sidera &c. Creatae substantiae in corporeas & in incorporeas dividuntur. Accidentia verò dividuntur praecipuè in extrinseca, & intrinseca. Intrinseca dicuntur illa, quae rem, substantiam aut subjectum ipsum, in quo reperiuntur, intrinsecè ac realiter adficiunt, ut in corpore motus, figura: extrinseca verò quae nihil intrinsecè, verè ac realiter ponunt in re, sed in illa solum ab intellectu nostro concipiuntur, à nobis tamèn veluti entia considerantur, cujusmodi sunt, relationes omnes, privationes, & denominationes extrinsecae.

11 Hence internal modes are in reality nothing other than the substance, which is in this or that way: therefore they cannot be separated from it. But it is incredible to say how many logomachies about the nature of modes or accidents are heard in the Schools of certain Philosophers, who, deceived by abstract ideas, to which they are wont to attribute a nature and existence of their own, sharply contend that modes are certain beings which can exist apart from substance. But if they considered the matter with a free judgment, they would plainly recognize that there are no such beings, and that the roundness or magnitude of a golden globe, e.g., is nothing other than gold shaped in this way and having this magnitude. I can indeed consider roundness abstractly, but I cannot understand it as existing without the matter in which it is. If the Peripatetics deny this, let them show us roundness and motion without a subject, and we shall be grateful to them for so wonderful an explanation of the phenomenon. But of these things more fittingly in the Physics.

> 7 Substantia itaque definiri potest: essentia separata á suis modis. Est autem modus id, quo substantia hoc, vel illo modo est, eamque quodammodo vestit, & ut sensibus percipiatur facit. Hinc fit manifestum, substantiam esse ideam relatam ad modos, á quibus fingitur separata, ideòque esse ideam abstractam: nulla enim existit substantia carens omnibus modis. Quare qui de substantia sine modis sumpta disputant, non de re aliqua, quae extra mentem sit, disputant: sed de abstracta idea, quae tantum in eorum mente existit. Substantiae enim, nullam aliam ideam habemus, nisi concipientes cumulum modorum, & proprietatum, adjungendo iis ideam obscuram naturae nobis incognitae; id est complexionis ex. gr. partium materiae nobis non cognitae, quam putamus tales res continere. (§§. 29. 30. Log.)

12 Privation is the lack of a perfection in a subject that is apt and capable of receiving that form or perfection, as darkness in the air, blindness in a man, etc.; and so it is distinguished from negation, which is the privation or lack of a form in a subject that is otherwise incapable of that form, as darkness in an opaque body, blindness in a stone, etc. And so blindness and darkness are conceived by our intellect as if they were some mode, although they are pure nothing.

> 8 Accidentia sive modi interni ita in substantia intrinsecùs inhaerent, ut ab ea nec esse, nec intelligi possint existere separati: veluti figura & motus: ¿ ubi enim est figura sine corpore? motus sine mobili? Externi verò non reapse in substantia existunt, sed á mente nostra concipiuntur veluti aliquid, quod eam adficit, cujusmodi sunt, ut jam diximus relationes omnes.

13 Relation, on the other hand, is a certain order, habitude, or respect of one thing to another, which is conceived in some thing because that thing is ordered or referred to another, as, e.g., if Alexander is referred to Philip, he is called son, although this being a son is found only in the intellect. An extrinsic denomination, finally, is a pure name that is attributed to some thing, although it is conceived by the intellect as some being, perfection or mode inhering in another, as when one is made a judge,

> 9 Ergo substantia physicè & reapse sumpta aliquot modos internos habeat necesse est. Quamobrèm ineptum est quaérere, an sine modis esse possit: quia & si substantia sine ullo vel altero modo interdùm sit, tamen in hoc rerum ordine omnibus modis spoliata esse non potest. Metaphysicè vero sumta, sine modis esse posse perspicuum est. Quare ineptum etiam est quaerere an sine modis possit esse; quia id ipsum significat substantia metaphysicè sumta, nempè naturam sejunctam à modis. Tamen quum idea abstracta substantiae, ut essentiae, non eadem in omnibus sit, sed pro varietate

> [p. 6]

[p. 6] a knight, a nobleman, or is praised or blamed: he receives indeed only this outward word, or denomination, yet something is conceived by us that inheres, as it were intrinsically, in the judge, the knight, the nobleman, the man praised or blamed.

> rerum varia & ipsa; talis interdum est, quae aliquos modos complectitur: qui propterea non amplius vocandi sunt modi sed essentia & substantia rei. Sed haec aliquo exemplo commodè declarabimus.

14 Hence another division of being is drawn, into real being and being of reason. Real being is said to be that which truly and really is, independently of the intellect, or which must be even if the intellect considers nothing, as a rose, a man, a stone: a being of reason is that which is only conceived, is made by and depends on the thinking intellect, and therefore, if the intellect considers nothing, a being of reason cannot be. Here the Peripatetics raise the question whether being itself taken generally, or the concept of being, is univocal with respect to God and creatures; as also with respect to substance and accident, and finally with respect to real being and being of reason: whether, namely, the concept of being applies to them in the same way, and all things are equally being, although they are afterwards distinguished by various properties and differences?

> 10 Ex. gr. Pluma quam in praesentia manu moveo ut haec scribam, potest non movéri, si consistam: propterea motu privari potest, & quiéscere, quin désinat esse pluma. Non tamen privari potest simul & motu & quiete, sed altérutrum habeat necesse est. Item non potest privari omni magnitudine, figurâ, ceterisque: sed unum vel aliud necessario habet. Contrà horologium ex. gr. praeter artificium partium complectitur motum earum. Ideòque etsi motus generatim sumtus sit modus corporis, tamen essentia seu substantia est horologii. Item fulmen praeter materiam inflammatam, includit motum pernicíssimum. Qua de causa hic motus non ampliùs est modus, sed essentia fulminis. Quare ut de modis rectè judicemus, oportet primò constituamus, in quo sita sit natura rei, ne inscîe vocemus modum, id quod naturam constituit.

15 But you see already, from the mere exposition of the question itself, that it is altogether useless and can make us none the more learned. But truly, lest you be altogether ignorant of the more celebrated questions of the Peripatetics, I have decided to say something about them with Corsini. Accordingly, if God himself is compared with creatures, or substance with accident, the more probable opinion seems to me to be that which holds that the concept of being applies to them equally and univocally. For since the common and most general concept of being signifies nothing at all, as we said before, but that which is, or that which has being, and God and creatures have being, they will be contained equally under this common genus of being, as the Scotists maintain.

> 11 Hinc modi interni re ipsa nihil aliud sunt quam substantia, quae hoc vel illo modo se habet: propterea ab ea separari non possunt. Sed incredibile dictu est quot logomachiae de natura modorum seu accidentium audiantur in Scholis quorundam Philosophorum, qui decepti abstractis ideis, quibus propriam naturam, & existentiam tribuere solent, acritèr contendunt, modos entia quaedam esse, quae à substantia existere seorsum possunt. Sed si rem libero judicio considerarent, planè cognóscerent ejusmodi entia nulla esse, nec aliud esse rotunditatem vel magnitudinem globi aurei ex. gr., quám aurum hoc modo figuratum, & hac magnitudine constans. Possum quidem rotunditatem abstractè considerare, sed intelligere existentem sine materia, cui insit, non possum. Si negant Peripatetici, ostendant rotunditatem & motum, sine subjecto, & habebimus illis gratiam de tam mirabili explicatione phaenomeni. Sed de his oportunius in Physica.

16 But if it be said that God exists in a far different manner from creatures, God namely in an infinite and most perfect manner, essentially, necessarily, independently of another, so that he accordingly said of himself (b) I am who am; but creatures in a finite manner, contingently and dependently, on the free will of God, so that all, as Isaiah says (c), all nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity, it can easily be answered: such an infinite interval, by which God, the Best and Greatest, is distinguished from creatures, arises not from the idea of being itself, but from those infinite perfections which are found in God; just as the common idea of soul is attributed univocally to the rational and to the vegetative soul, although these are distinguished by a wonderful difference.

> 12 Privatio est carentia perfectionis in subjecto, quod aptum, & capax sit ad formam illam, vel perfectionem recipiendam, ut tenebrae in aëre, caecitas in homine &c. itaque à negatione distinguitur, quae est privatio sive carentia formae in subjecto, quod alioquin incapax est ejusdem formae, ut tenebrae in corpore opaco, caecitas in lapide &c. Itaque caecitas, & tenebrae ita concipiuntur ab intellectu nostro, ac si modus aliquis forent, quum tamen sint purum nihil.

17 And indeed, if the concept or idea of being is conceived most accurately, it will be seen to be most simple and altogether indivisible, which could not be verified if one idea of being applied to creatures and another to God. Then, the ideas of God and of the creature must be distinguished by means of some character, or difference, which is joined to either concept, or to being;

and

> 13 Relatio verò est ordo quidam, habitudo, sive respectus unius rei ad aliam, qui nempè concipitur in aliqua re, ex eo quod ipsa res ordinetur, vel referatur ad aliam, ut ex. gr. si Alexarder referatur ad Philippum, dicitur filius, quum tamen hoc esse filii in intellectu solum reperiatur. Denominatio denique extrinseca, est purum nomen quod alicui rei tribuitur, licèt concipiatur ab intellectu veluti ens aliquod, perfectio vel modus alteri inhaerens, ut qui ju- [p. 7] dex, eques, nobilis constituitur, qui laudatur, aut vituperatur exteriorem quidem hanc vocem, sive denominationem solum recipit, aliquid tamen à nobis concipitur, quod Judici, equiti, nobili, laudato, vituperato veluti intrinsecè inhaereat.

(c) Ch. 40, v. 17. [p. 7] and therefore that universal and common concept of being, to which those charac‐

> 14 Hinc alia entis divisio desumitur in ens reale, & ens rationis. Ens reale dicitur illud, quod verè, & realiter est, independenter ab intellectu, sive quod etiamsi intellectus nihil consideret, esse debet, ut rosa, homo, lapis: ens rationis illud est, quod solum concipitur, efficitur, & dependet ab intellectu cogitante, ideòque si intellectus nihil consideret ens rationis esse non poterit. Hìc quaestionem movent Peripatetici utrum nempè ens ipsum generaliter sumtum, sive conceptus entis univocus sit respectu Dei & creaturarum, quemadmodùm etiam respectu substantiae & accidentis, denique respectu entis realis, & rationis: utrum nempè conceptus entis eodem modo illis conveniat, & aequaliter omnia sint ens, etsi variis deinde proprietatibus ac differentiis distinguantur?

ters or differences are superadded, must always be admitted. Again, then, it can be asked whether that common concept, to which the differences are not superadded, is one and the same and univocal, or is rather distinguished by those differences? If the first, it will be univocal with respect to its inferiors. If the second, it can be abstracted from the differences, and so be rendered one, simple, undistinguished and indivisible, and therefore univocal as well. What has been said must also be understood of substance with respect to accident.

## CHAPTER II

> 15 Sed videtis jam ex sola ipsius quaestionis expositione eam inutilem prorsùs esse, nihiloque nos doctiores efficere posse. Verumenimverò ne prorsùs ignoretis celebriores Peripati quaestiones aliqua cum Corsinio dicere decrevi. Itaque si Deus ipse cum creaturis sive substantia cum accidente comparetur, verisimilior opinio mihi videtur illa, quae putat conceptum entis aequaliter illis & univocè convenire. Quum enim communis ac generalissimus conceptus entis nihil prorsùs significet, ut antea diximus, nisi id quod est, vel id quod habet esse, Deus autem & creaturae habeant esse, sub hoc communi entis genere aequaliter continebuntur, ut tuentur Scotistae.

On essence, existence, and subsistence.

> 16 Quod si dicatur Deum longè diversa ratione existere quam creaturae, Deum nempè infinito perfectissimoque modo, essentialiter, necessariò, independenter ab alio ut ipse de se proinde dixerit (b) Ego sum qui sum; creaturas verò finito modo, contingenter, & dependenter, à libera Dei voluntate, ut omnes ut ait Isaías (c) ut omnes gentes, quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, & quasi nihilum & inane reputatae sunt ei, facilè poterit responderi: infinitum ejusmodi intervallum quo Deus Opt. Max. à creaturis distinguitur non ab ipsa entis idea oriri, sed ab infinitis illis perfectionibus, quae reperiuntur in Deo, quemadmodum communis idea animae univocè animae rationali, & vegetativae tribuitur, quamvis illae miro discrimine distinguantur.

lthough the concept of being seems altogether simple and uncom18

> 17 Et sanè si conceptus aut idea entis adcuratissimè concipiatur, videbitur esse simplicissima, ac prorsus indivisibilis, quod verificari non poterit si aliqua entis idea creaturis, altera verò Deo conveniret. Deindè idea Dei, & creaturae distingui debent ope rationis alicujus, aut differentiae, quae utrique conceptui, vel enti con-

A           pounded, several attributes, and as it were parts, must nevertheless be

> (b) Exodi cap. 3. ℣. 14.

distinguished in it, which are commonly held and called, as it were, properties of being. Such are essence, existence, subsistence, from which are then derived the distinction of things and the names of hypostasis and of persons, and very many other things of the kind which are treated at length among the Theologians and the Peripatetic Philosophers. We, however, shall set forth all these things as briefly as possible, because, by the now accepted custom of the Schools, to be ignorant of these very distinctions of things, or of words, would seem almost a crime.

> (c) Cap. 40. ℣. 17.

19 Accordingly essence, to begin with it, is nothing other than the first attribute that is conceived in a thing, and from which all the rest proceed as from a root. In the Schools it is commonly defined: that through which a being is, or is conceived to be; or that which intrinsically composes a thing; or that which intrinsically gives being to a thing. Such a principle, which gives being to a thing, is called the essence, the nature, the constitutive of that same thing, with this one difference, that where it is conceived as the source and origin of properties it is called essence, but where it is conceived as the source and origin of the operations which are produced by such a thing it is called nature; most often, however, nature and essence are used indiscriminately.

20 Hence those most celebrated questions which are wont to be agitated in the

Schools with so much apparatus can be briefly settled: namely, whether the essences of things are eternal and invariable, and whether God can bring about contradictories? For although very many think that the essences of things can be varied by God, even against the resistance of our intellect, in such a way that a circle could be turned into a figure endowed with angles, or into a square one, and that God could bring it about that twice two is not four, etc., yet it seems far more probable that the essences of things are so certain and invariable that they cannot be varied even by God.

For

[p. 8]

> jungitur, ideoque semper admitti debet universalis ille, & communis conceptus entis, cui rationes illae, vel differentiae superaddantur. Iterum igitur inquiri potest, an communis ille conceptus, cui differentiae non superadduntur sit unus, & idem, & univocus, an potius à differentiis illis distinguatur? Si primum, erit ille univocus respectu inferiorum. Si secundum poterit á differentiis abstrahi, & unus, simplex, indistinctus, ac indivisibilis, ideoque univocus etiam reddi. Quae dicta sunt intelligi etiam debent de substantia respectu accidentis.

21 For since by the name of essence nothing else is understood but that attribute, or that perfection, which gives being to a thing, it is certainly impossible for that principle to be varied without the thing itself, which receives its being, having to be varied as well; as, e.g., if the equality of the radii and the privation of angles are taken away, the circle too will have to be taken away, or a circle can no longer be conceived or had. And certainly such essences of things are nothing other than the archetypal ideas of things, or those images which God had in his mind from eternity, and in whose likeness he created things in time; and therefore, just as those images, or divine ideas, are immutable, so the essences of things themselves must also be deemed invariable.

> CAPUT II.

22 Existence is commonly defined: the placing of a being or essence outside nothing and all causes; and therefore between essence and existence there is found this difference, that essence applies also to possible things, which are contained in the power of the first or of a second cause, whereas existence applies only to those things which have been placed outside the first or second cause. Since, however, essence and existence apply equally to all substances and to accidents, so that accidents no less than substances, if they are possible, have being, and, if they have been produced, have existing, and since accidents or modes are nonetheless very greatly distinguished from substances, in substances themselves, besides essence and existence, which are common to accidents as well, another perfection must be conceived or admitted which cannot apply to accidents, so that those substances may accordingly be distinguished from accidents as by a constant and most clear difference.

> De essentia, existentia, & subsistentia.

23 This new perfection, which applies to substances alone, is called hypostasis, or subsistence: namely the ultimate perfection, form or act by which a thing, or nature, or essence, is so perfected, terminated, completed, or made its own master, not only so that it does not need another for being and operating, but also so that its operations are attributed to it, or so that it is and operates independently of another; which can belong only to a certain substance, which subsists by itself, and stands under, or is subjected to, accidents. The subject, moreover, the substance or composite, that is endowed with this ultimate perfection, or that subsists and operates by itself, is called a suppositum; and if it is spiritual and capable of incorporeal knowledge, as in God, the Angels and men, it is called a person, which is accordingly defined by Boethius: an individual substance of a rational nature.

> 18 Quamvis conceptus entis omninò simplex, & incompositus videatur, plura tamen adtributa, ac véluti partes in illo distingui debent, quae véluti proprietates entis haberi, vocarique solent. Ejusmodi sunt essentia, existentia, subsistentia, ex quibus deinde rerum discrimen hypóstasis, & personarum nomina deducuntur, aliaque id genùs plurima quae apud Theologos, & Philosophos Peripateticos pertractantur. Nos verò haec omnia quàmbrevissimè exponemus, quòd ex recepta jam Scholarum consuetudine haec ipsa rerum, sive vocum discrimina ignorare, nefas propemodùm videatur.

24 Hence in divine things three hypostases, or subsistences, are found, and therefore also three persons: and since the subsistence of the Divine Word took the place of the created, or human, subsistence in Christ the Lord, or terminated the human nature, which ought to have been terminated by its own created or human subsistence, it appears most clearly that in Christ the Lord there is found a twofold nature, divine, namely, and human, and therefore a twofold will, as the Sixth Synod against the Monothelites

> 19 Itaque essentia ut ab illa exordiamur nihil est aliud quam primum adtributum, quod in re concipitur, & ex quo cetera omnia veluti ex radice proveniunt. In Scholis vulgò definitur id per quod ens est, vel esse concipitur, sive id quod intrinsecè rem componit, sive quod intrinsecè dat esse rei. Ejusmodi principium quod dat esse rei vocatur essentia, natura, constitutivum ejusdem rei, hoc uno discrimine, quod ubi concipitur tanquam fons, & origo proprietatum, vocatur essentia; ubi verò concipitur tanquam fons & origo operationum, quae à tali re producuntur, dicitur natura, plerumque tamen natura, & essentia promiscuè usurpantur.

> 20 Hinc dirimi breviter poterunt celeberrimae quaestiones illae, quae tanto adparatu in Scholis agitari solent; utrum nempè essentiae rerum sint aeternae ac invariabiles, utrum Deus contradictoria efficere possit? Quamvis enim plurimi existiment rerum essentias ita, reluctante licet intellectu nostro, à Deo variari posse, ut circulus in figura angulis praedita, sive quadrata redduci possit, ut Deus efficere possit bis duo non esse quatuor &c, longè tamen verisimilius videtur rerum essentias ita certas ac invariabiles esse, ut nec à Deo variari possint.

> [p. 9]

[p. 9] defined; but only one hypostasis, or divine subsistence, and therefore only one divine person, was found in him.

> 21 Quum enim essentiae nomine nihil aliud intelligatur, nisi adtributum illud, aut illa perfectio, quae dat esse rei, impossibile est certe ut principium illud varietur quin ipsa quoque res, quae recipit esse variari debeat, ut ex. gr. si radiorum aequalitas, & angulorum privatio auferatur, circulus etiam auferri debebit, sive circulus amplius concipi vel haberi non poterit. Et certè ejusmodi rerum essentiae nihil aliud sunt quam archétypae rerum ideae, vel imagines illae, quae ab aeterno Deus in mente habuit, & ad quarum similitudinem res in tempore creavit, ideòque sicuti imagines illae, vel divinae ideae immutabiles sunt, sic ipsae rerum essentiae invariabiles etiam censeri debent.

> 22 Existentia communiter definitur: positio entis aut essentiae extra nihil & omnes causas; ideoque inter essentiam & existentiam discrimen illud reperitur, quod essentia possibilibus etiam rebus conveniat, quae in causae primae, sive secundae potentia continentur, existentia vero iis solum rebus conveniat, quae extra causam primam sive secundam positae sunt. Quandoquidem verò essentia & existentia aequaliter substantiis omnibus, & accidentibus convenit, ut accidentia non minus quàm substantiae, si possibilia fuerint, habeant esse, si producta fuerint habeant existere, & accidentia tamen seu modi á substantiis maximè distinguuntur, in subtantiis ipsis praeter essentiam, & existentiam accidentibus quoque communem concipi, vel admitti debet alia perfectio, quae accidentibus convenire non possit, ut illae proinde substantiae ab accidentibus veluti constanti, clarissimoque discrimine distinguantur.

> 23 Haec nova perfectio substantiis solum conveniens dicitur hypostasis, vel subsistentia, ultima nempè perfectio, forma, vel actus, quo res, aut natura, vel essentia ita perficitur, terminatur, completur, vel redditur sui juris non modò, ut non indigeat alio ad essendum, & operandum, sed etiam ut sibi tribuantur operationes suae, sive ut sit ac operetur independenter ab alio, quod soli certae substantiae convenire potest, quae per se subsistit, & substat, sive subjicitur accidentibus. Subjectum verò, substantia, sive compositum quod hac ultima perfectione donatur, sive quod per se subsistit ac operatur dicitur suppositum, & si spiritualis & incorporeae cognitionis capax sit ut in Deo, Angelis, & hominibus vocatur persona, quae proinde à Boethio definitur: rationalis naturae individua substantia.

> 24 Hinc in divinis tres hypostases, vel subsistentiae reperiuntur, ideòque etiam tres personae: quumque subsistentia Divini Verbi, subsistentiae creatae, vel humanae vices in Christo Domino suppleverit, sive terminaverit naturam humanam, quae propria creata, vel humana subsistentia terminari debebat, clarissimè adparet quod in Christo Domino duplex quidem natura: divina, scilicèt, ac humana, ideoque duplex voluntas ut à VI Synodo contra Monotheli-
