suffer something, according to that common principle, operations belong to supposita, the operations or merits of Christ the Lord had to be of infinite value and dignity, and therefore equal to redeeming infinite men from the guilt or the punishment of their crimes: since they were produced by an infinite person, or divine

Suppositum. But these things we leave to the Theologians, to be explained according to the dignity of the matter, lest we put our sickle into another’s harvest.

## CHAPTER III

On the other properties or attributes of Being, or on Unity,

Truth, and Goodness.

he properties or attributes of being which were explained in the chap26

T           ter above can apply not to every being, but to the individual genera of

being: essence, indeed, is found in all beings, even possible ones, existence in those things which have been placed outside every cause, and subsistence, finally, in substances only. There are, however, other attributes which apply to being so universally that they transcend, or exceed, all the bounds or limits of beings, whence they are called transcendentals; and therefore they embrace not some only, but absolutely all the genera of beings; and three in particular are commonly enumerated by the Philosophers: namely Unity, Truth and Goodness.

27 Unity is nothing other than the lack or privation of division, and for no other reason is the concept of being one and simple except that it cannot be divided into various parts. Since, therefore, unity is opposed to division, as many kinds of unity can be distinguished as there are divisions themselves, or distinctions, found among beings. Distinction or division is reckoned threefold by the

Philosophers: namely generic, specific and numerical. Generic distinction is said to be that which is found between beings that are contained under a different genus or category, as between a circle and a straight line; for the circle is contained under the genus of curvilinear figure, whereas the straight line belongs neither to the curvilinear genus nor to any other genus of figure.

28 Specific distinction is found between beings which, though they are contained under the same genus, are yet of a different species, as between a circle and a triangle, which, though placed under the same genus of figure, yet belong to different species of figure. Numerical distinction, finally, is that which is found

> [p. 10]

M [p. 10] between individuals of the same species, or between those that are contained under the same species and are distinguished only by individuating circumstances and conditions, as circle A, circle B. Generic and specific distinction is conceived to be drawn from the form, nature, or essence of things; whence those things that differ specifically or generically must have a different essence.

> tas definitum est, reperitur: unica tamen hypostasis, vel subsistentia divina, ideòque unica persona divina in illo reperiebatur.

29 Numerical distinction, on the other hand, which is also commonly called material, must, as very many think, be drawn from matter alone, which is accordingly called the principle of individuation, or from material circumstances; whence the Thomists hold that in Angels, because they lack matter, this numerical distinction is not admitted, or that several Angels cannot be found in a single species, but rather that individual Angels differ specifically from one another. Yet just as rational souls, though they are incorporeal, are numerically distinguished from one another by the order or habitude by which each is directed to its own body, so too Angels can be numerically distinguished by the spiritual accidents or circumstances with which they are affected, or at any rate by the varied action of God by which they were created or are conserved.

> 25 Quumque non natura, sed persona sit illa, quae aliquid operari vel pati dicitur, juxta commune principium illud: operationes sunt suppositorum, operationes aut merita Christi D. infiniti valoris, ac dignitatis, ideoque infinitis hominibus à scelerum culpa, vel poena redimendis pares esse debebant, quippè quae ab infinita persona, sive Supposito divino producebantur. Sed haec Theologis pro rei dignitate explicanda relinquimus, ne nos falcem in alienam messem immitamus.

30 Real distinction is that which is found in the thing independently of the intellect. Distinction of reason is that which depends on the intellect. Real distinction is divided into entitative, modal and virtual. Real entitative distinction, which is also commonly called major, is said to be that which is found between various things whose entities are so distinct that one can be separated from the other, or at least one can be perfectly conceived without the other, as between the Moon and the Sun, gold and silver, etc. Real minor, or modal, distinction is said to be that which obtains between a thing and a mode of the thing, which mode cannot be separated from the thing itself, or perfectly conceived without it, as between figure and the figured body. Virtual distinction, finally, which you might rather call the foundation of a distinction than a distinction, is that which is found in a thing which, although it is one and simple, is yet equivalent to several, and therefore gives the intellect occasion to conceive several parts in it; as in God and in his attributes and perfections we conceive the attributes themselves as distinct, e.g., Justice from Mercy.

> CAPUT III.

31 Besides these kinds of distinction Scotus admits another distinction, which he says is formal, actual, and from the nature of the thing: formal, because it is found not between thing and thing, or between a thing and a mode of being, but between various formalities or perfections of the same thing, as between the attributes of God, between the animality and rationality of man, etc.; actual, and from the nature of the thing, because it is found in things actually and in fact, independently of the intellect. Hence arose a most weighty question between the Thomists and the Scotists: by what kind of distinction, namely, the metaphysical grades of the same thing are distinguished, as, e.g., the animality and rationality that are found in man, the grade of vegetating and of sensing that is found in brutes, and universally the genus and difference that are contained in individual things or species.

> De aliis proprietatibus vel adtributis Entis; sive de Unitate, Veritate, & Bonitate.

The

> 26 Proprietates illae vel adtributa entis, quae sup. cap. sunt explicatae, non cuilibet enti, sed singulis entis generibus convenire possunt, sed essentia quidem in entibus omnibus etiam possibilibus, existentia verò in iis rebus, quae extra omnem causam positae sunt, subsistentia denique in substantiis tantummodò reperitur. Alia tamen sunt adtributa quae sic universaliter enti conveniunt, ut omnes entium fines vel terminos transcendant, vel excedant, unde transcendentalia vocantur, ideòque non aliqua solum, sed singula prorsùs entium genera complectuntur, solentque tria praesertim à Philosophis enumerari Unitas, nempè, Veritas, & Bonitas.

> 27 Unitas nihil est aliud quàm carentia sive privatio divisionis, nec alia de causa conceptus entis unicus, & simplex est, nisi quod ille varias in partes dividi non potest. Quoniam ergo unitas divisioni opponitur, totidem unitatis genera distingui possunt, quot sunt divisiones ipsae, vel distinctiones quae inter entia reperiuntur. Distinctio verò sive divisio triplex à Philosophis numeratur; generica nempè, specifica, & numerica. Distinctio generica, dicitur illa, quae reperitur inter entia, quae sub diverso genere, sive cathegoria continentur, ut inter circulum, & lineam rectam, circulus enim sub figurae curvilinae, linea verò recta, neque ad curvilineum genus, neque ad quodvis aliud genus figurae pertinet.

> 28 Specifica reperitur inter entia, quae quum sub eodem genere contineantur diversae tamen speciei sunt, ut inter circulum & triangulum, qui sub eodem figurae genere collocantur, ad varias tamen figurae species pertinent. Numerica denique est illa, quae reperitur

[p. 11]

> inter individua ejusdem speciei, vel inter illa quae sub eadem specie continentur, & solis circunstantiis & conditionibus individuantibus distinguuntur, ut circulus A, circulus B. Distinctio generica atque specifica desumi concipitur à forma, natura, vel essentia rerum, unde illa quae specificè sive genericè differunt diversam essentiam habere debent.

32 The Thomists think that among all these only a virtual distinction suffices. The Scotists, besides this virtual one, admit also a formal one, by which the grades themselves are conceived not as two things or modes (otherwise the distinction would be real) but as two formalities; and therefore that formal distinction is less than the real, but greater than the virtual, or midway between the two. But let the Scholastics see to these things. Distinction of reason is commonly divided into major, minor and minimal. The first is the name given to that by which, in one and the same thing, various concepts are distinguished, of which one is not contained in the other, as justice and mercy, which are distinguished in God. Distinction of reason is minor when the concepts themselves mutually include each other implicitly, as one, good, true, which are conceived in being.

> 29 Distinctio verò numerica quae materialis etiam vocari solet, ut plurimi existimant à sola materia, quae proindè principium individuationis vocatur, vel à circunstantiis materialibus desumi debet; unde Thomistae arbitrantur in Angelis quia materia carent, hanc numericam distinctionem admitti, sive plures Angelos in unica specie reperiri non posse, sed potius Angelos singulos specificè inter se differre. Quemadmodùm tamèn rationales animae, etsi incorporeae sint, numericè inter se distinguuntur ex ordine, vel habitudine qua singulae ad proprium corpus diriguntur; ita quoque Angeli numericè distingui possunt ex accidentibus vel circunstantiis spiritualibus quibus adfecti sunt, aut certè ex varia actione Dei qua creati fuerint, vel conserventur.

33 Minimal distinction of reason, finally, is the name given to that which, without any foundation, and by the mere choice of the intellect, or rather by its weakness or by a bad habit, distinguishes one thing from another, as, e.g., God from the Divinity, man from humanity, etc. Hence this distinction is called a distinction of reasoning reason, because, namely, it depends on reason alone, whereas the major or minor distinction of reason is commonly called by the name of reasoned reason, as if, namely, some ground or foundation of the distinction were found in the thing itself. But these and other things of the kind, which are explained at length by the Peripatetics, are certainly not of such worth that they should be set forth more fully. They had to be hinted at here, however, because the very frequent use of them has crept into Theology itself; and therefore many things cannot be understood unless this meaning of the words is explained.

> 30 Distinctio realis est illa quae reperitur in re independenter ab intellectu. Distinctio rationis est illa quae pendet ab intellectu. Distinctio realis dividitur in entitativam, modalem, & virtualem. Realis entitativa quae etiam major vocari solet, dicitur illa quae reperitur inter varias res, quarum entitates ita distinctae sunt, ut una ab alia separari, vel saltem una sine alia perfectè concipi possit, ut inter Lunam & Solem, aurum, & argentum &c. Realis minor seu modalis dicitur illa quae datur inter rem & modum rei, qui modus ab ipsa re separari, vel sine ipsa perfecte concipi non potest, ut inter figuram & corpus figuratum. Virtualis denique, quam potius fundamentum distinctionis, quàm distinctionem dixeris, quae reperitur in re, quae quamvis unica & simplex sit, pluribus tamen aequívalet, ideòque occasionem praebet intellectui, ut plures in illa partes concipiat, ut in Deo, ejusque adtributis & perfectionibus, adtributa ipsa veluti distincta cóncipimus, ut Justitiam à Misericordia.

34 The second property of being is Truth, namely the aptitude of being itself to be known by the intellect. It is divided into transcendental and formal. The first is the very entity of the thing, insofar as it is conceived by an intellect, especially the Divine one: for since the very entity and essences of things are contained, expressed, in God, or in his archetypal ideas and images, it can be known by God, and therefore conceived as the object or term of the Divine knowledge, which corresponds most perfectly to the thing itself, or to the idea known, and therefore derives its truth from it, and in turn communicates it to it, so that it is called a true idea, or true knowledge. Formal truth, however, is that same conformity of the knowing intellect with the thing known.

> 31 Praeter haec distinctionis genera Scotus distinctionem aliam admittit, quam dicit esse formalem, actualem ex natura rei, formalem quia non reperitur inter rem & rem, sive inter rem & modum entis, sed inter varias formalitates seu perfectiones ejusdem rei, ut inter adtributa Dei, inter animalitatem & rationalitatem hominis &c. actualem verò & ex natura rei, quia actualiter de facto independenter ab intellectu reperitur in rebus. Hinc gravissima exorta est quaestio inter Thomistas, & Scotistas, quo nimirùm distinctionis genere distinguantur gradus metaphysici ejusdem rei, ut ex. gr animalitas & rationalitas quae reperiuntur in homine, gradus vegetandi & sentiendi qui reperitur in brutis, atque universaliter genus & differentia, quae in singulis rebus, sive speciebus continentur.

35 What we have said, finally, about truth can easily be understood also of the last affection of being, namely of Goodness, except that truth is referred to the intellect, and goodness to the will. Transcendental goodness, then, is being itself, insofar as it can be desired or loved by the will; formal goodness, which is also called moral, is the conformity of the object willed and loved with the laws of morals, namely with the precepts and with the archetypal image of the good, which are found in God. And let these things, which have been excerpted from the distinguished Corsini, suffice as said.

## METAPHYSICS

> 32 Thomistae existimant inter haec omnia distinctionem solum virtualem sufficere. Scotistae praeter hanc virtualem, formalem etiam admittunt, qua gradus ipsi non veluti duae res aut modi (alioquin distinctio foret realis) sed veluti duae formalitates concipiantur, ideòque formalis illa distinctio minor est reali, major autem virtuali, sive inter utramque media. Sed haec Scholastici viderint. Distinctio rationis in majorem, minorem; ac minimam dividi solet. Prima vocatur illa, qua in unica, eadémque re varii conceptus distinguuntur, quorum unus non continetur in alio, ut justitia & misericordia quae distinguutur in Deo. Distinctio rationis minor quando conceptus ipsi impliciter mutuò includuntur, ut unum, bonum, verum, quae concipiuntur in ente.

S E C O N D P A R T.

> 33 Distinctio denique rationis minima vocatur illa, quae sine ullo fundamento, & ex solo intellectus arbitrio, sive potius infirmitate aut prava consuetudine unum ab alio distinguit ut ex. gr. Deum à Divinitate hominem ab humanitate &c. Unde haec distinctio vocatur rationis ratiocinantis, quòd nempè à sola ratione dependeat, quum distinctio rationis major, aut minor nomine rationis ratiocinatae vocari soleat, quasi nimirùm ratio quaedam aut fundamentum distinctionis in ipsa re reperiatur. Sed haec aliaque id genus, quae fusè à Peripateticis explicantur tanti certè non sunt, ut uberiùs exponi debeant. Innuenda tamen hic fuerant, quòd frequentissimus illorum usus in Theologiam ipsam irrepserit; ideòque plura intelligi nequeant, nisi haec vocum significatio explicetur.

P S Y C H O L O G Y,

> 34 Altera proprietas entis est Veritas, aptitudo nempè ut ens ipsum ab intellectu cognoscatur. Distinguitur in transcendentalem & formalem. Prima, est entitas ipsa rei, quatenùs ab intellectu praesertim Divino concipitur, quum nempè entitas ipsa & essentiae rerum in Deo vel archétypis ipsius ideis & imaginibus expraessa contineatur, potest à Deo cognosci, ideòque concipi velut objectum aut terminus Divinae cognitionis, quae ipsi rei vel ideae cognitae perfectissimè respondet, ideòque veritatem ab illa sortítur, & vicissim illi communicat, ut idea vera, vel vera cognitio dicatur. Veritas autem formalis est eadem conformatio intellectus cognoscentis cum re cognita.

OR

> 35 Quae denique de veritate jam diximus, de ultima quoque entis adfectione de Bonitate nimirum intelligi facilè poterunt, nisi quod veritas ad intellectum, bonitas autem ad voluntatem refertur. Bonitas autem transcendentalis est ipsum ens, quatenus adpeti vel amari potest à voluntate; bonitas formalis quae moralis etiam vocatur, est conformatio objecti vóliti & amáti cum legibus morum, praeceptis nimirùm, & archétypa boni imagine quae in Deo reperiuntur. Et haec quae ex Cl. Corsinio excerpta sunt dicta sufficiant.

On the Rational Soul.

hat can the loftier sciences profit us, excellent young men, if we are 36

W                 ignorant of ourselves? If we do not know what our soul is, whether it

is spiritual and immortal, and what commerce intervenes between it and the body? And all these cognitions, what do they profit us, if we lose the soul itself, if we do not use its faculties to attain true immortality, namely eternal beatitude?

We shall therefore divide this second part of Metaphysics into two Dissertations.

The first will be on the origin, spirituality and immortality of the human mind; the second on the admirable commerce that exists between the mind itself and the body.

## D I S S E RTAT I O N I 

On the Origin, spirituality, and immortality of the human mind.

## CHAPTER I

On the origin of the Soul, and at what time it is infused into the body. 37

That a true notion of creation may be had (says the celebrated Clarke (d)), one must not picture it to oneself as the generation of some thing drawn out of nothing considered as matter. To create is to give existence

> [p. 13]

(d) De l’Existence de Dieu, vol. 1, ch. 11. [p. 13] to a thing that did not have it before; that is, to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before. All Philosophers admit that no created agent can bring about any of those things which cannot be except through creation. For the power of creating belongs to God alone: For it is not lawful, says St. Augustine (e), to believe or to say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone but God. These things being laid down,

> METAPHYSICES

38 I say 1: the rational soul is created by God alone when it is infused into the little body. It is proved: to create is to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before; but God brings it about that the soul exists, which did not exist before: therefore. It is proved 2: to create is to make something when nothing that intrinsically pertains to it exists beforehand; but it is thus that God makes the soul: therefore. Proof of the minor: the human mind is a simple substance, lacking parts, devoid of composition and divisibility, as we shall see in what follows: therefore it is made without any succession of parts, and with nothing that intrinsically pertains to it existing beforehand: therefore it comes to be by creation alone; but creation belongs to God alone, as has already been said: therefore the rational soul is made by God the Creator.

> PARS ALTERA.

39 It is proved 3: the rational soul is not generable; but what is not generable comes to be by creation: therefore. Proof of the major: what is generable is corruptible, as all admit; but the rational soul is incorruptible, because it is immortal, as will be shown later in Ch. III: therefore. It is proved 4: nature extends only to generating; but what is not is not generated, for there is nothing from which it might be generated, as Hippocrates says very well (f); therefore creation exceeds the power of nature: therefore it cannot be done except by God.

> PSYCHOLOGIA, sive

40 Christian Wolff (g), a celebrated philosopher of our age, admits indeed that the rational soul comes to be by creation from God alone; but, following Leibniz, he contends that the souls of all men were made by God together at the beginning, and each of them enclosed in its own little body. Souls, he says, pre-exist in pre-existing organic corpuscles, from which the fetus is formed in the womb.

> De Anima rationali.

41 I say 2, against Leibniz and Wolff: rational souls were not all created together by God at the beginning of time and enclosed in those organic corpuscles which, likewise made by God at that time, lie hidden in the mother’s womb. It is proved 1: from the Fifth Lateran Council (h), where it was expressly defined that the rational soul, according to the multitude of the bodies into which it is infused, is singly multipliable, multiplied, and to be multiplied: therefore the souls of all men who are to be born until the end of the world were not created by God at the beginning of time, because at that time, although they are multiplied, they are not, however, to be multiplied:

> 36 Quid prodesse nobis possunt sublimiores scientiae, Adolescentes optimi, si nos metipsos ignoremus? Si nesciamus quid sit anima nostra, an spiritualis, & immortalis, quodnam inter ipsam & corpus commercium intercedat? Hae autem cognitiones omnes, ¿quid nobis prosunt, si animam ipsam perdamus, si ejusdem facultatibus ad veram immortalitatem, aeternam scilicet beatitudinem consequendam non utamur? In duas ergo Dissertationes alteram hanc Metaphysices partem dividemus. Prima erit de origine, spiritualitate, & immortalitate mentis humanae. Secunda de admirabili commercio quod inter ipsam mentem, & corpus est.

> 38 Dico 1: rationalis anima à Deo solo creatur, quum corpusculo infunditur. Prob.: creare est efficere ut existat res quae prius non existebat; sed Deus facit ut anima existat, quae prius non existebat: ergo. Prob. 2: creare est aliquid efficere, nullo quod ad ipsum intrinsecùs pertineat, priùs existente; sed ita facit Deus animam: ergo. Prob. min.: mens humana est substantia simplex, carens partibus, compositionis, & divisibilitatis expers: ut in sequentibus videbimus: ergo efficitur sine ulla partium successione nulloque quod ad ipsam intrinsecùs pertineat priùs existente: ergo sola creatione fit; sed creatio soli Deo competit, ut dictum est jam: ergo anima rationalis à Deo Creatore conditur.

42 It is proved 2. from absurdity: once this opinion is granted, Virginity could not be urged upon all women indiscriminately; for since it is not known which women are endowed with animated corpuscles, virginity cannot be urged upon individual women without its being true that it lies in our choice that as many souls should perish as those animated corpuscles contain. For the same reason, too, no woman would be permitted to bind herself by a perpetual vow of virginity unless it were first certainly established for her that no animated corpuscles are contained in her womb; and since all these things are no less false than absurd, it follows that the Wolffian opinion is to be utterly rejected by a Catholic man.

> 39 Prob. 3: anima rationalis non est generabilis, sed quod non est generabile per creationem fit: ergo. Prob. maj.: quod generabile est, est corruptibile, ut omnes fatentur; sed anima rationalis est incorruptibilis quia est immortalis, ut posteriùs Cap. III. ostendetur: ergo. Prob. 4: natura non extenditur nisi ad generandum, sed quod non est, non generatur, non enim est unde generetur, ut optimè ait Hippócrates (f) ergo creatio excedit naturae potentiam: ergo nequit fieri nisi à Deo.

43 For the second part of the question, it should be known that all the ancient Philosophers agree in this, namely that the rational soul is not infused immediately upon conception, but after some time. The most common opinion holds that the rational soul informs the fetus after forty days, because then, and not before, the little body is perfectly organized. So Galen (i). Hippocrates (j), or whoever is the author of the book On the Nature of the Child, teaching a difference between male and female fetuses, said that the former are articulated in thirty days, the latter in forty-two, that is, perfectly organized. But the same Hippocrates, in the book On Flesh, no. 10, assigned a much shorter term for perfection of this kind, saying in seven days it has whatever the body ought to have; and in this way, if the body is complete in seven days, it seems consistent with the opinion of Hippocrates that it is animated on the seventh. Others assert that the human fetus is completed in three days, and receives the rational soul on the third day. Aristotle (k) asserts that man lives the life of a plant, the life of an animal, and that of a man, and hence that the rational soul comes to the fetus after some time, although he did not define that time. These things being laid down,

> 40 Christianus Wolff (g) celebris nostri seculi philosophus fatetur quidem animam rationalem à solo Deo per creationem fieri, verùm Libnitzium sequutus contendit animas omnium hominum, initio simul conditas a Deo fuisse, easque singulas suis inclusas corpusculis. Animae, inquit, praeexistunt in corpusculis organicis praeexistentibus ex quibus fetus in utero formatur.

44 I say 3: with the distinguished Paolo Zacchia (l) and other authors of great name, whom the Most Illustrious Don Feijóo (m) praises and follows: the rational soul is infused into the fetus at the first moment of conception. It is proved by most effective reasons: it can in no way be denied that the fetus, as soon as it is conceived, lives, is nourished, and grows; but it cannot have all these things from any other soul than from the rational one: therefore. ished, and grows, as all agree: therefore at that very instant it is endowed with the rational soul. Proof 2: God and nature always act for an end, God indeed from his own free will, nature from necessity; but the delay of the infusion of the rational soul can have no end: therefore.

> 43 Pro secunda quaestionis parte sciendum est, in hoc convenire antiquos omnes Philosophos, nempè, animam rationalem non illicò à conceptione infundi, sed post aliquod tempus. Communissima opinio defendit animam rationalem post quadraginta dies fetum informare, quia tunc, & non antea perfectè organizatum est corpusculum. Ita Galenus (i). Hippocrates (j) sive quisquis Auctor est libri de Natura pueri, differentiam docens inter fetus masculos, & femineos illos triginta, hos duobus supra quadraginta diebus dearticulari dixit, hoc est, perfectè organizari. Multò autem breviorem terminum ad hujusmodi perfectionem adsignavit idem Hippocrates lib. de Carnibus, num. 10. inquiens in septem diebus habet quaecumque, corpus habere debet, atque hoc pacto si corpus in septem diebus absolutum est, in septimo animari, ex sententia Hippocratis videtur consentaneum. 45 Proof of the minor: such an end would be either the perfection of the body, or this, that it might be able to perform its operations rightly. Not the first; for then the rational soul would have to be infused much later, since at the term of forty days the body has not attained its perfection so as to be evident to the eyes; indeed, after some months it has nothing more than a certain rough delineation of the parts, scarcely perceptible even to the eyes of a Lynceus. Not the second: for as regards the operations proper to the rational soul, neither after forty days, nor after the infant, the ninth month completed, has come forth into the light, is the soul fit to exercise any of them: therefore the delay of the infusion of the rational soul can have no end. We must therefore conclude from these things that, since the conceived fetus lives, is nourished, and grows immediately, and cannot have this from any other soul than the rational one, which can vegetate, and nourish, and communicate life, since it is furnished with all the faculties necessary for accomplishing these things, it is created by God at the very instant of conception and infused into the fetus, and by itself nourishes and increases the conceptus, and communicates life and sense to it.

> 44 Dico 3: cum Cl. Paulo Zacchia (l) & aliis magni nominis Auctoribus, quos laudat, & sequitur Illmus. D. Feijoo (m): in primo conceptionis momentó infunditur fetui anima rationalis. Prob. eficacissimis rationibus: negari nullomodo potest, fetum illicò, atque conceptus est vivere, nutriri, & augeri: sed haec omnia habere non potest ab alia anima quàm à rationali: ergo Prob. min.: absurdum est dicere ut Aristoteles adfirmabat fetum priùs vivere anima vegetativa, postea sensitiva, & tandem rationali; alioquin eae tres simul animae in homine essent, quod nemo sanus dixerit: ergo vita, nutritio, & augmentum fetus non possunt provenire nisi

46 The conclusion is confirmed: either the rational soul can communicate life and sense to the conceptus, or it cannot: if the first, nothing prevents it from being able to do the same before forty days, for it does not acquire those faculties from the body, but possesses them from its own nature. If the second: then the body, even when the rational soul is present, receives life, growth, nutrition and sense from another soul; for it is not likely that all these things are supplied before the fortieth day by another soul, and after forty by the rational one. It is further confirmed: if man does not receive the rational soul before forty days, he will not be a man before the said term; for how would he be a man, not having the form of a man? Will he then be a plant, or a worm, or an insect, or some other animal, or some beast reducible to no genus, or to no definite species of living things, and will he constitute of himself a new species of animal? What, then, will this species be? Let what has been said about the animation of the human fetus suffice: these are the things that seemed to me could be said with probability.

[p. 16] ab unica anima rationali; sed à primo instanti conceptionis vivit, nutritur, & augetur, ut omnes consentiunt: ergo in ipso instanti anima rationali donatur. Prob. 2: Deus, & natura semper operantur propter finem, Deus quidem ex sua libera voluntate, natura autem ex necessitate; sed retardatio infussionis animae rationalis nullum potest habere finem: ergo.

Obj. 1. Creation is the production of a thing out of nothing; but out of nothing nothing comes: therefore the rational soul is not created. I distinguish the minor: out of nothing nothing comes, that is, something is not drawn out of nothing as [p. 16] from a material and pre-existing cause, I grant; that is, it cannot be brought about that what did not exist before should exist, I subdistinguish: if we speak of an agent whose powers are finite, I grant; if the discussion is of an agent whose power is infinite, such as God is, I deny; and I deny the consequence as well. You will say with Toland and Gildon: God communicated divisibility and figure to matter, although God does not have them in himself: therefore an intelligent substance too, namely the soul, can emanate from a non-intelligent substance, such as matter is: therefore it is not created by God. I deny the consequence, and there is a disparity, because God contains in himself most eminently whatever good and perfection there is in matter, and by his power produces all things in matter; but matter can contain neither formally, nor virtually, nor eminently the true and simple perfections of the soul; since in a corporeal and inert being, such as matter is, there cannot be the adequate ground of an intelligent and freely acting being, which is found only in a free, acting, intelligent being.

> 45 Prob. min.: talis finis, vel esset corporis perfectio, vel ad hoc, ut suis operationibus fungi rectè posset. Non primum: quia oporteret multò serius animam rationalem infundi, quum corpus in termino quadraginta dierum non sit adsequutum suam perfectionem, ita ut oculis pateat, quinimò nihil amplius habet post aliquot menses, nisi rudem quandam, & vix Lynceis oculis perceptibilem partium delineationem. Non secundum: nam quod spectat ad operationes proprias animae rationalis, nec post quadraginta dies, nec postquam infans jam nono exacto mense in lucem prodit, earum ullam exercére anima apta est: ergo retardatio infussionis animae rationalis, nullum potest habere finem. Concludendum igitur ex his, quod quum fetus conceptus illicò vivat, nutriatur, & augeatur, id ab alia anima quàm à rationali habere non possit, quae & vegetare, & nutrire, & vitam communicare potest, quum omnibus facultatibus necessariis ad haec peragenda sit instructa, eamque in ipso instanti conceptionis à Deo creari, & fetui infundi, ac per se ipsam conceptum nutrire, & augere, illique vitám, & sensum communicare.

48 Obj. 2. with Antonio Rocco: the soul depends entirely on the body, or matter: therefore it is produced dependently on matter: therefore it is not created. The antecedent is proved 1. because this soul depends on the temperament of this body; otherwise any soul could enter any body. 2. because if the soul did not depend on the body, it would not depart unwillingly when the body perishes and is dissolved: therefore. To the argument I distinguish the antecedent: it depends on the body in order to be, I deny; in order to exercise the office of a form that vivifies and moves the body, I grant; and therefore the soul is not free to enter any body whatever, since it is destined by God its Creator to rule and vivify this one, and is produced under this law, that together with this body it should constitute an individual man. That the soul departs unwillingly when the body is dissolved, however, is a penalty of original sin. The distinguished Berti (n) explains most happily and aptly, by the example of a sailor, how the soul is both dependent on the body and independent of it, which it will not be unwelcome to you to hear.

> 46 Confirmatur conclusio: vel anima rationalis potest vitam & sensum conceptui communicare vel non: si primum nihil obstat, quominùs idem possit ante quadraginta dies, non enim à corpore eas facultates adipiscitur, sed eas ex sua natura possidet. Si secundum: ergo corpus etiam anima rationali praesente, ab alia anima vitam, augmentum, nutritionem, sensum recipit, quia non est verisimile ea omnia ánte quadragessimum diem ab alia anima, & post quadraginta à rationali praestari. Confirmatur ulterius: si homo ante quadraginta dies non recipit animam rationalem, ante praedictum terminum non erit homo, nam ¿quomodo esset homo, non habens formam hominis? Erit igitur planta, vel vermis, vel insectum, vel aliud animal, vel bestia quaedam ad nullum genus, vel ad nullam viventium speciem certam reducibile, & ex se constituet novam speciem animalis? ¿Quaenam igitur erit haec species? Haec circa fetus humani animationem, quae probabiliter dici posse mihi vissa sunt, dicta sufficiant.

49 A sailor is a man destined to steer a ship. Insofar as he is a man, he has no need of the vessel, than which he himself is far nobler, for he can at times lead his life otherwise than by sailing; but insofar as he is a sailor, whose business is to cross the seas by navigation, he certainly needs a ship. When this is broken up, he is forced to lead either a most wretched life on the shore, or a happier one in port. But when the ship has been repaired, he at length returns to his homeland. The soul likewise is a spiritual substance, but it is the form of the body and, as it were, its shipmaster, for it steers and moves it, and, having taken its bearings, tries to bring it into port. As a spiritual substance it is more excellent than the body, and gains no advantage from it: as the form of the body it depends on it, not indeed in order to be, but in order to travel the sea, namely the mortal life. By death the body is dissolved, like a ship by a storm, and the soul, according to its merits, leads a life either wretched or tranquil. The mortal body will rise again to everlasting life, and this resurrection itself is, as it were, the restoration of the wrecked ship.

> Argumenta contra primam conclusionem.

## 50 Obj. 3. with the same: If the rational soul were created, it would not con‐

> ex causa materiali, & praejacente, conc, hoc est non potest effici, ut existat id, quod priùs non existebat, subdist: si loquamur de agente, cujus vires finitae sunt, conc; si sermo habeatur de agente cujus potestas sit infinita, qualis est Deus, nego, & consequentiam. Dices cum Tolando, & Gildono. Deus communicavit materiae divisibilitatem, & figuram, licet easdem in se Deus non habeat: ergo etiam à substantia non intelligente, qualis est materia, substantía intelligens nempè, anima, emanare potest: ergo non est creata à Deo. Nego conseq. & est disparitas, quia Deus eminentissimè in se continet quidquid boni, & perfecti in materia est, & sua potentia in materia omnia producit: materia autem nec formaliter, nec virtualiter, nec eminenter potest continére veras, & simplices perfectiones animae; quum in ente corporeo, inertique, cujusmodi est materia, entis intelligentis, liberèque agentis, adaequata ratio esse non possit, quae solùm in ente libero, agente, intelligente reperitur.

tract original sin from the seed of Adam; but it does contract it: therefore. I deny the major: original stain is not contracted by the son because his soul fell away from the infected soul of the father in his generation, like a part from a whole, as

> 48 Opp. 2: cum Antonio Rocco: anima omninò dependet à corpore seu materia: ergo producitur dependenter à materia: ergo non creatur. Antec. prob. 1, quia haec anima ab hujus corporis temperie pendet, aliàs quaelibet anima in quodlibet corpus ingredi posset. 2: quia si anima non dependéret à corpore, pereunte ac disoluto corpore invita non recederet: ergo. Ad argumentum dist. antec.: dependet à corpore, ut sit, nego, ut exerceat munus formae corpus vivificantis, ac moventis, conc., atque ideò liberum non est animae ingredi quodcumque corpus, quoniam huic regendo, ac vivificando à Deo Conditore destinatur, & producitur hac lege, ut unà cum hoc corpore constituat hominem individuum: Quod autem resoluto corpore anima recédat invíta, poena est originalis peccati. Exemplo nautae felicissimè, aptèque explicat Cl. Berti (n), quomodo anima sit à corpore dependens, & independens, quod non ingratum vobis audire erit.

Rocco and Pomponazzi stubbornly contend; rather, the rational soul is polluted by original guilt from this, that it is joined to corrupted flesh, as water is corrupted in a tainted vessel. How this comes about, indeed, the Theologians, to whom it belongs, explain most clearly. But Rocco insists: accidents are not transmitted without their subject; but the subject of original sin is the soul: therefore if the soul is not propagated from the seed of Adam, neither is sin spread by propagation. I deny the major: for, as Estius very well replies, heresies, vices, leprosy, and other contagions of morals and of diseases pass from one subject into another without the subject being transferred.

> 49 Nauta homo est ad regendam navim destinatus. Quatenùs homo non opus habet navigio, quo est ipse longè nobilior, nam & vitam interdùm ágere aliter, quàm navigando potest; at quatenùs nauta, cujus est maria navigatione tranare utique indiget navi. Hac dissolutá, cógitur, aut in litore misserrimam vitam ducere, aut feliciorem in portu. Refectâ autem navi ad patriam tandèm revertitur. Anima pariter est spiritualis substantia, sed corporis forma, & quasi navicularia, nam illud, regit, & movet, & exploratè ad portum tentat adpellere. Ut spiritualis substantia, praestantior est corpore, neque aliquid commodi ab illo captat: ut forma corporis ab eo dependet, non quidem ut sit, sed ut mare perambulet, vitam nempè mortalem. Morte corpus, ut navis tempestate dissolvitur, atque anima pro meritis vitam agit sive miseram, sive tranquillam. Resurget mortale corpus ad vitam perennem, & haec ipsa resurrectio, quasi dirútae navis instauratio est.

51 Obj. finally: man begets his like; but likeness consists not in matter, but in species, nature and form: therefore the form too, which is the soul, is begotten by man: therefore it is not created by God. To the argument I reply that man begets his like insofar as he so disposes matter that God may put into it the soul by which the human species and nature are perfected. For once the soul has been put into the body, the son bears the image and likeness of the Father, even though the soul is not propagated from him by generation. Nor does that text of

Genesis (o) support Rocco: All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt, and that came out of his thigh. For the sense of these words is: all the men who descended from Jacob by generation, etc. For it suffices that the son descend from the thigh of the father as regards the body alone for the whole son to be said to have descended; for although the body is not the principal part in man, it is nevertheless what meets us immediately in ourselves and what is seen by us; just as a statue too is called the work of the artist, although it depends on the sculptor only as regards its form.

Arguments against the other conclusions. 52

Obj. against the second, with Wolff (p) and Sennert: that God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done, we read in Gen. 2, v. 2: therefore today he creates nothing more: therefore the creation of souls was accomplished by God in the first creation. This is Wolff’s chief argument. But with the great

Augustine (q) we reply that God rested from founding kinds of creatures,

> (n) De Theolog. Discipl. tom. 1. [p. 18] 50 Opp. 3: cum eodem: Si anima rationalis crearetur, non contraheret ex semine Adae originale peccatum; sed contrahit: ergo. Nego maj.: non ideò originalis labes à filio contrahitur, quia ipsius anima, ex infecta anima patris, veluti pars ex toto in illius generatione deciderit, ut pertinaciter contendit Roccus, & Pomponatius, sed rationalis anima originali culpa ex eo polluitur, quod corruptae carni conjungatur, sicut aqua viciato in vase corrumpitur. Id vero quo pacto fiat, Theologi ad quos spectat clarissimè explicant. Sed insistit Roccus: accidentia sine subjecto non traducuntur; sed peccati originalis subjectum est anima: ergo si anima ex semine Adae non propagatur, neque peccatum propagatione diffunditur. Nego maj: nam ut optimè respondet AEstius transeunt de uno in alterum subjectum, subjecto non transfuso haereses, vitia, lepra, aliaque morum, & morborum contagia.

(q) Bk. IV, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis. [p. 18] because beyond that he no longer founded any new kinds. And so, when God is said to create a soul, he is not said to do something that he had not done before. For already on the sixth day he had made man to his own image, which is certainly understood according to the soul. And this he does now, not by instituting what was not, but by multiplying what was. Hence both that is true, that he rested from instituting things that were not; and this is true, that he works until now, not only by governing what he made, but also by creating in greater number, not what he had not yet created, but what he had already created.

> 51 Opp. tandem: homo generat sibi simile, sed similitudo non consistit in materia, sed in specie, natura, & forma: ergo etiam forma quae est anima ab homine generatur: ergo non creatur à Deo. Ad argumentum respondeo, hominem generare sibi simile, quatenùs ita materiam disponit, ut ei Deus inferat animam, qua species, & natura humana perficiatur. Nam inserta anima corpori filius gerit imaginem, & similitudinem Patris, tametsi anima non sit ab ipso per generationem propagata. Neque patrocinatur Rocco illud Genes. (o) cunctae ánimae quae ingrésse sunt cum Jacob in AEgiptum, & egressae sunt de foemore illius. Horum quippè verborum sensus est: cuncti homines qui à Jacob per generationem descenderunt &c. Sufficit enim quod filius tantùm quoad corpus descendat de foemore patris, ut totus filius descendisse dicatur, etsi enim corpus non sit in homine pars princeps, ea tamen est, quae in nobis immediatè occurrit quaeque à nobis conspicitur, sicuti etiam statua dicitur opus artificiis, quamvis non nisi quoad formam à statuario dependeat.

53 Obj. against the third: The presence of the soul is detected more, and more certainly, from the motion of the embryo than from its other operations; but before the fortieth day the embryo does not move, and moreover the female moves later than the male: therefore before the fortieth the embryo does not receive the rational soul, and male and female do not receive it at the same moment of conception. I deny the major of the argument: because the other operations that precede motion cannot be attributed to any other agent than the rational soul, and it is all one to elicit the presence of the rational soul from motion and to deduce it from life, from nutrition, from growth; hence, since the fetus in the womb immediately lives, is nourished, grows, and feels, it must immediately have a rational soul. Besides: what dependence does motion have on the rational soul as rational? One ought therefore to have affirmed that the fetus receives the rational soul when it performs some operation pertaining to the rational soul as rational, not when it begins to move. The minor of the argument, moreover, is false, absolutely speaking. For who will dare to affirm that the embryo does not have some unobservable motion before the fortieth day? Nor, even if all motion were absent, ought one to infer from this that the rational soul is not present.

> Argumenta contra ceteras conclusiones.

54 Much more reasonably, therefore, ought the presence of the soul in the embryo to be inferred from the operations of life and from the formation of the fetus itself; for none of these can depend on any cause other than an intrinsic one, nor can any other intrinsic cause be imagined in the fetus than the soul itself. The difference, moreover, between the male and the female as to the first motion excited in the mother’s womb (if what is reported is true) perhaps consists in this, that the matter from which the male is produced swells with a greater abundance of spirits and obtains a livelier heat. Besides, it has been observed that some males, because of their weakness, move later than females, and on the other hand that some females, because of their strength, move sooner than males; whence the included minor, absolutely speaking, is altogether false.

> 52 Opp. contra secundam cum Wolffio (p) & Sennerto: Deum quievisse die septimo ab universo opere quod patrarat, legitur Genes. 2. ℣. 2: ergo hodie nihil amplius creat: ergo creatio animarum in prima creatione à Deo facta est. Hoc est praecipuum Wolffii argumentum. Sed cum magno Augustino (q) respondemus, Deum requievisse à condendis generibus crea-

55 Obj. 1. The fetus ought not to receive the rational soul unless it is perfectly organized; but this organization is not completed at the same time in every individual, because of the variety of temperaments and powers: therefore the soul is not infused at the very moment of conception. The argument can be answered in several ways. First: by granting that organization is required for the soul to operate, but denying that it is necessary

[p. 19] for it to inform. Second: by saying that God ought not to be subject to nature, so that before he infuses the soul he must wait for the organization of the fetus contrived by nature itself. But it is preferable to satisfy the argument in another way, according to the mind of the Moderns. The most common opinion among the Moderns is that of the perfect delineation of the embryo in the corpuscles lying hidden in the mother’s womb; and once this is granted, it can be denied that the fetus is not perfectly organized before the fortieth.

> turae, quia ultrà jam non condidit aliqua genera nova. Itaque dum dicitur, Deum animam creare, non aliquid facere dicitur quod ante non fecerat. Jam enim sexto die fecerat hominem ad imaginem suam, quod utique secundum animam intelligitur. Hoc & nunc facit non instituendo quod non erat, sed multiplicando quod erat. Unde, & illud verum est, quod à rebus quae non erant instituendis requievit. Et hoc verum est, quod non solum gubernando quae fecit, verùm etiam non quod nondum, sed quod jam creaverat numerosius creando usque nunc operatur.

56 But if by perfect organization our adversaries understand an organization so complete in every respect that by it the fetus has whatever an embryo ought to have, so that, as the eye bears witness, it is furnished with all its members and necessary organs, we shall deny that this organization is necessary for receiving the soul; for if it were so, the reception of the soul would have to be delayed for several months; hence, when the Angelic Master says (r) that the rational soul is infused when the body is disposed, he is not to be understood of this final disposition; otherwise the holy Doctor himself would be asserting contradictory things, which it is wrong even to think.

> 53 Opp. contra tertiam: Ex motu embrionis magis, ac certiùs deprehenditur animae praesentia, quàm ex aliis operationibus; sed ante quadragesimum diem non movetur embrio, & praeterea seriùs movetur femella quam mas: ergo ante quadragesimum non recipit embrio animam rationalem, & mas, & femella non eodem conceptionis momento eam recipiunt. Nego maj. argumenti: quia aliae operationes motum praecedentes alteri agenti tribui non possunt nisi animae rationali, & perinde est elicere ex motu praesentiam animae rationalis, quàm deducere ex vita, ex nutritione augmentatione, unde quum fetus in utero illicò vivat nutriatur augescat, sentiat; illicò animam rationalem illum habere necesse est. Adhaec: ¿quamnam dependentiam habet motus ab anima rationali, ut rationalis est? Oportuit ergo adfirmare, tunc fetum animam rationalem recipere, quum aliquam operationem rationali animae, ut rationali pertinentem edit, non quando moveri incipit. Minor autem argumenti absolutè loquendo falsa est. ¿Quis enim adfirmare audebit non habere embrionem ante quadragesimum diem, motum aliquem inobservabilem? Neque etiam si omnis motus abesset, inde inferri deberet animam rationalem praesentem non esse.

57 For the most wise Master himself (s) asserts that, since the soul is the proper act and form of the body, it must necessarily be produced together with the body; but the body is produced immediately when it is conceived: therefore, according to the mind of the Angelic Doctor, the rational soul too is infused then; and once infused it operates immediately, and thus it is present at the first moment of the conception of the embryo itself; for otherwise it would always be true to say that the body is produced before the soul, contrary to what the Theologians teach with the Angelic Master (t).

> 54 Multò ergo rationabilius inferri debet praesentia animae in embrione ex vitae operationibus, & ex formatione ipsius fetus, neque enim aliquid eorum ab aliqua causa dependére potest quàm ab intrinseca, neque in fetu ulla alia intrinseca causa imaginari potest, quàm ipsa anima. Differentia autèm inter masculum, & femellam quoad primum motum in utero materno excitatum (si vera sunt quae narrantur) in eo fortè consistit, quia materia ex qua producitur mas majori spirituum copia turget, & calorem vividiorem obtinet. Praeterea observatum est, mares nonnullos ob eorum imbecillitatem seriùs movéri, quàm femellas, & alia ex parte femellas nonnullas ob earum robur citiùs moveri, quàm mares, unde inclusa minoris absolutè loquendo falsa omninò est.

58 But you will say: the soul was breathed into the face of Adam when his body was perfect: therefore it ought to be introduced into any man when the body is perfect in every way. I reply that the argument proves nothing: for however perfect our adversaries may wish the embryo to be on the fortieth day, it will never be as perfect as the body of Adam when God breathed the soul into it. Besides: there must be a great difference between a work emanating immediately from God himself and a work entrusted to nature in the generation of man.

If the rational soul were present at the first instant of conception, then when an abortion occurred before the fortieth day the Canons would order that fetus to be baptized; but they do not so order: therefore it is because it is not informed by the rational soul before the fortieth. I reply that in these abortions it is impossible, because of their weakness, that the soul should not be separated from the body at once, and for that reason the Sacred Canons make no mention of baptism; and it was enough if, whenever they give some sign of life

[p. 20] by motion, even if this happened before the fortieth, they should be cleansed in the laver of baptism, at least conditionally; but this in no way prevents us from affirming with the distinguished Feijóo that, at whatever time the abortion occurs, the fetus ought to be baptized conditionally; for according to everyone it ought to be washed in baptism when it is probable that the fetus is animated; but from what has been said it is highly probable, both by the intrinsic probability of the reasons and by the extrinsic probability of authors of great name, that the fetus is informed by the rational soul from the very instant of conception: therefore, at whatever time the abortion occurs, it ought to be baptized, at least conditionally.

Doctor contradictoria adsereret, quod vel cogitare nefas est.

60 Obj. finally: the Laws, Canon as well as Civil, distinguish the animated fetus from the inanimate, and declare it animated only after forty days, and for this reason impose a greater or a lesser penalty on offenders and on those who procure abortion; in confirmation of which the Constitution of Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff, was finally issued, in which it is determined that those who procure the abortion of an animated fetus are subject to the same penalties as true homicides: therefore our conclusion is contrary to the authority of the Ecclesiastical and Secular Laws. To the argument I reply, with Zacchia, praised above, that both the Canons and the Laws speak in the texts cited not from their own scientific knowledge, but from the opinions of the wise men of that age, Philosophers and Physicians, as they have been accustomed to do elsewhere in matters that belong to other professions. Therefore, since the aforesaid wise men had been consulted on that matter, the Canons and Laws, wishing to follow their determination in this, imposed on offenders penalties now greater, now lesser, according to the difference that those men made between the fetus not animated by the rational soul and the animated one. But even with these things granted, we contend that the determinations of the Canons and Laws issued in accordance with justice, and must remain safe and intact, while our opinion on the animation of the fetus at the first moment of conception also remains firm.

> 57 Ipse enim Sapientissimus Magister (s) adserit, quod quum anima sit proprius corporis actus, & forma necessariò simul cum corpore produci debet, at corpus illicò producitur cum concipitur: ergo ex mente Doctoris Angelici etiam anima rationalis tunc infunditur; infusa autem illicò operatur, & sic in primo momento conceptionis ipsius embrionis praesens est, nam aliàs semper esset verum dicere corpus ante produci, quàm animam, contra id quod Theologi docent cum Angelico Mag. (t)

61 For the Canons and Civil Laws always follow the milder opinion in imposing penalties; since, therefore, it was called into doubt whether one who procures abortion always, and at any time whatever, should be punished with the same penalty, and some, of the milder opinion, had judged that he should be punished with a lesser penalty when the fetus is more tender and before the fortieth, while others thought the contrary, the Canons adhered to the former opinion, and with the greatest reason they establish a greater penalty for one who procures abortion after forty days than before, because the former inflicts much greater violence both on the fetus and on the mother than the latter does. For the abortion of a more tender fetus, because of the weakness of the ligaments, takes place easily and with the least discomfort to the mother, whereas the abortion of a more advanced fetus does not take place without evident danger to the mother; whence from Hippocrates (u) and from daily experience we know that abortions are safer

## CHAPTER II

> (u) In Lib. de Nat. Pueri.

It is examined whether the human mind is a spiritual substance, or rather a corporeal one?

he human mind is that which thinks in each of us. By the Scholastics it is 62

T           commonly defined: the first act of a physical organic body having life in potency.

They explain, namely, the unknown by the more unknown. We, however, define it: the principle by which man thinks, or by which he understands the true and wills the good, and is moreover conscious of his own perceptions and volitions. It is called mens [mind], because the power of thinking is preeminent in the soul. It is called anima rationalis [rational soul], or animus, because it is capable of incorporeal knowledge, or reason.

63 That a principle of this kind, or a soul, exists in us is most evident; for nothing can be more manifest than that we think while we think, that we will something when we will, that we perceive, doubt, remember, when we perceive, doubt, remember: therefore that principle exists in us by which each of these operations and acts is carried out in us.

64 By body, or matter, we understand an extended, divisible, solid substance, woven together from various parts of various figures. By a spiritual substance, on the other hand, we understand a substance devoid of matter, or one that excludes extension, divisibility, solidity. The question, therefore, is whether that which thinks in each of us is a substance devoid of extension, divisibility, solidity, etc.?

65 The Materialists, namely unbelieving and most perverse men, maintain that there is nothing in man besides physical sensibility, and hence that it is through this, which is something material and depends on matter, that man understands, thinks, reasons, and consequently that our mind is matter. This most pernicious error is maintained by Spinoza,

Hobbes, Toland (y), nor is Locke very far removed from him. Among the more recent Materialists are counted Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Voltaire and other French Philosophers, with most pernicious little books by which they corrupt Religion and morals; from reading these, as befits a Christian philosopher, you must always abstain. Against these unbelieving and lost men, then:

> CAPUT II.

66 I say 1. The human mind is a spiritual substance, or one distinct and different from matter, or body. The first part is proved, namely that the human mind is a substance. We experience that our thoughts are continually changed in us, and that they succeed one another in a perpetual flux; but the changeable things that are in a being are called modes, and cannot be without a subject: therefore that which thinks in us, namely the soul, is the subject of thoughts. A subject, moreover, does not need another subject in order to exist; and therefore it is a substance: therefore the soul is a substance.

> Expenditur an humana mens sit substantia spiritualis, num verò corporea?

67 The second part is proved: the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter is a substance altogether distinct from matter, and consequently spiritual; but the soul is the principle of thoughts, which can in no way belong to matter: therefore it is a spiritual substance. Proof of the minor: if thought belonged to matter, it would be an intrinsic modification of matter; for since thought is an internal action of the thinking subject, it is an intrinsic modification of the thinking subject; but thought cannot be an intrinsic modification of matter: therefore it can in no way belong to matter. Proof of the minor:

> 62 Mens humana est id quod in unoquoque nostrum cogitat. A Scholasticis vulgò definitur: actus primus corporis physici, & organici potentia vitam habentis. Ignotum scilicet per ignotiùs explicant. Nos autem eam definimus: principium quo homo cogitat, seu quo verum intelligit, bonumque vult, suarumque insupèr perceptionum ac volitionum conscius existit. Dicitur mens, quoniam cogitandi vis in anima eminent. Dicitur anima rationalis, seu animus, quoniam incorporeae cognitionis aut rationis capax est.

> 66 Dico 1. Mens humana est substantia spiritualis, seu à materia, vel corpore distincta, atque diversa. Prob. prima pars, scilicèt, mentem humanam esse substantiam. Experimur cogitationes in nobis continuò mutari, alias aliis fluxu perpetuo succedere; sed mutabilia, quae enti insunt, modi dicuntur, & sine subjecto esse non possunt: ergo id quod in nobis cogitat, nempè anima est subjectum cogitationum. Subjectum autèm, alio subjecto non indiget ad existendum; ideòque substantia est: ergo anima est substantia.

68 Proof of the minor: if it were so, thought would have the properties of matter; it would consequently be extended, divisible into parts, and figured; but this is most evidently repugnant: therefore. Proof of the minor: for who is so mad as to believe that an act of the intellect, e.g. assent or dissent, is spread out over a certain space of place, that it can be cut into two or four parts, and have a round, square, or triangular figure? Therefore thought does not have, nor can it have, the properties of matter: therefore the soul is the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter: therefore it is spiritual, and not matter.

> 67 Prob. secunda pars: principium operationum quae ad materiam pertinere non possunt est substantia prorsus distincta a materia, ac proindè spiritualis; sed anima est principium cogitationum, quae ad materiam nullomodo possunt pertinere: ergo est substantia spiritualis. Prob. min.: si cogitatio pertineret ad materiam esset intrinseca materiae modificatio; quum enim cogitatio sit subjecti cogitantis actio interna, intrinseca est subjecti cogitantis modificatio, sed cogitatio non potest esse intrinseca materiae modificatio: ergo nullomodo potest ad materiam pertinere. Prob. min.:

69 But let us contemplate this matter a little more attentively with the most distinguished Valsecchi (z), and see whether we can persuade ourselves that matter can think. I think, and I consider my thought; I compose several notions, I separate them, I join them. Quicker than it can be said, I pass from heaven to earth, and turn over in my mind a great many most remote things. I weigh the nature, the properties, the relations of these things: I measure motions, spaces, times: I compare these things with those; from the open and clear I make my way by reasoning to the hidden and latent. Nor do I dwell only on the things that are subject to the senses, but I also turn over those that far surpass my senses. I know, and I discourse, about Being, about Order, about the Virtues, about Truth, about Reason, about God.

70 Of these and similar operations, which are called thoughts, I have consciousness, that is, an inner and most vivid sense, through which I know them; I know also that I, who think, and from whom these operations flow, cannot be a lump of stupid and inert flesh, but a self-moving substance, endowed with a power and efficacy of acting, and with that virtue of which matter is not capable.

71 Meanwhile I turn to this matter; I carefully carry out an analysis of it; and I find in it nothing other than extension, solidity, figure, rest, or motion. I cut it into a great many very fine parts. I give them every configuration I can, I impel them in every direction, with every degree of motion: but I never discern in them anything that is in the slightest degree like what I clearly know when I say to think; indeed nature itself draws me back from ascribing this attribute to them: and when I wish to assert that the finest dust and boiling blood can elicit those thoughts and reasonings, a greater force deters me than if I were saying that a circle is square; and when I hear that thought is hard or soft, triangular or pentagonal, this monstrous conjunction disturbs me more than either a goat-stag or a chimera.

72 To speak briefly, I know thought by an inner sense, I know extension clearly, and so far am I from perceiving the former in the latter, or vice versa,

> 68 Prob. min.: si ita esset, cogitatio haberet proprietates materiae, esset proindè extensa, divisibilis in partes, & figurata: sed hoc evidentissimè repugnat: ergo. Prob. min.: ¿quis enim tam amens est, ut credat actum intellectus ex. gr. adsensum, vel dissensum esse certo loci spatio difussum, posse scindi in duas, quatuor ve partes, & habere figuram rotundam, quadratam, aut triangularem? Ergo cogitatio non habet, nec habere potest proprietates materiae: ergo anima est principium operationum, quae ad materiam pertinere non possunt: ergo est spiritualis, & non materia.

73 The same argument is set before our eyes by François Lamy, of the Order of St. Benedict (a). I shall give the whole passage, turned from French into Latin: “What, then, is the principle of these operations? (says the Monk just praised) Will it be the body, or a corporeal soul? Can it ever be conceived that a body, that is, a mass of flesh configured in this or that way, can elicit spiritual notions, perceive justice, wisdom, truth, and perceive and know itself?

> 69 Sed rem hanc cum Clariss. Valsechio (z) paulò adtentius contemplemur, videamusque num possímus nobis metipsis persuadére materiam cogitare posse? Ego cogito, meamque cogitationem considero, compono plures notiones, eas séparo, eas conjungo. Dicto citiùs é caelo ad terras migro, & plurimas remotissimas res animo pervolvo. Harum rerum naturam, proprietates, relationes perpendo: metior motus, spatia, tempora: cónfero res has cum illis, ex apertis, clarisque, ad occultas, & latentes ratiocinando gradum facio. Nec immoror his tantum rebus, quae subjectae sunt sensibus, sed etiam illas pervolvo, quae longe sensus meos exsuperant. Novi, & sermocinor, de Ente, de Ordine, de Virtutibus, de Veritate, de Ratione, de Deo.

74 “Who can seriously believe that a wind, a vapor, a smoke of animal spirits, which is diffused through my flesh and passes through my organs, can judge, that is, perceive the relations that exist between things? Is that thing, boiling and running about through my head, the cause why the animal spirits connect demonstrations with one another, that admirable order of inferences which is sometimes beheld in a single glance?

> 70 Horum & his similium operationum, quae cogitationes dicuntur, conscientiam habeo, hoc est sensum intimum, maximè vividum, per quem ea novi; novi etiam me, qui cogito, & à quo eae operationes dimanant, esse non posse frustum stupidae, inertisque carnis, sed substantiam se moventem, praeditam agendi vi, & efficacitate, & ea virtute, cujus non est materies capax.

75 “Is it, finally, likely that this complex of corporeal organs and animal spirits can consider, discuss, foresee, weigh, will, desire, choose the good? That this being of clay is fit for solving questions and problems? And yet, if the matter is so, why, in solving questions that are somewhat more abstract and difficult, do we stop up the organs of the senses as far as we can, free ourselves from matter, impede its motions, and bring it about that through them it excites in us no impulse from that part which applies itself to the unravelling of the questions? Do we not evidently gather from this that that part is not corporeal?” Thus far he.

> 71 Ad hanc materiam interea memet converto, ejus análysim adcurate instituo, neque in ea quicquam reperio aliud, quam extensionem, soliditatem, figuram, quietem, aut motum. In plurimas tenuissimas partes éam seco. His, omnes, quas quidem possim configurationem do, has impello omnibus directionibus, omnibus motus gradibus: at nihil unquam in his internosco, quod vel tantillum simile sit ei, quod clarè cognosco, quum dico cogitare: imò natura ipsa ab adscribendo illis hoc adtributum me retrahit: volentemque adserere, pulverem tenuissimum, ferventemque sanguinem posse eas cogitationes, & ratiocinia elicere major me vis absterret, quàm si dicerem, circulum esse quadratum: audientemque cogitationem esse duram, aut mollem, triangularem, aut pentágonam, haec monstrosa conjunctio magis me cómmovet, quàm aut hircocervus, aut chimaera.

76 I say 2. Thought does not formally consist in this, that objects act on our organs, or in a certain motion of a most subtle and highly mobile substance, excited in our brain by the things with which we are occupied in thinking. Proof: if by this we understood that objects act on our organs, namely by moving that most subtle substance of the brain, the image of the objects would be impressed on us in no other way than this or that figure is impressed in wax: therefore, just as wax is not conscious of its figure, so we too could not be conscious of the things we know; but this is false to the point of evidence: therefore.

> 72 Ut breviter dicam, intimo sensu cogitationem novi, clarè extensionem novi, & tantum abest, ut illam in hac inspiciam, aut vi-

Proof 1: because, however subtle that substance be supposed, it is matter; but the soul cannot be matter, since it is the principle of operations that can in no way belong to matter,

78 I say 4: most absurd is the opinion of John Locke, who asserts that it is not impossible that matter should think, nay, that it can be brought about by the power of God that matter be endowed with the power of thinking. Proof: thought, or the power of perceiving, is intrinsically repugnant to matter, or body, as stands proved; but the power of God, however true it is that it is circumscribed by no limits, nevertheless cannot extend to impossible and contradictory things, since it cannot make the same thing at once be and not be: therefore Locke’s opinion is most absurd.

> 75 ,, Est ne tandem verisimile, hanc organorum corporeorum, animaliumque spirituum complexionem, considerare, discutere, praevidere, perpendere, velle, desiderare, bonum eligere posse? Ens hoc luteum aptum esse ad solvendas quaestiones, & problémata? Atqui si res ita se habet, cur in solvendis quaestionibus, quae sint aliquantò abstractiores, difficilioresque, obstruuntur, quantum per nos licet organa sensuum, materia nosmet expedimus, ejus motus impedimus, efficimusque, ut per eos nullum ipsa in nobis excitet impulsum ex ea parte, quae ad quaestionum enodationem incumbit? Nonne ex hoc evidenter colligimus, eam partem corpoream non esse? Hactenus ille.

79 It must be noted here, however, that although the spirituality of the soul is most certainly established by Divine revelation, and we could prove it by the most splendid testimonies of the Holy Scriptures and of the Fathers, we abstain from them, because our business is with unbelieving and lost men who set Divine revelation at naught; therefore Philosophical demonstrations must be pressed against them, nor must we allow these weapons to be snatched from our hands, so that we may use them against the most bitter enemies of our Christian Religion. Lastly, I warn you that some Ecclesiastical Writers have at times called the human soul, the
