(x) In the place cited, ch. 47. [p. 56] that all natural composites, and the most adorned and most beautiful world itself, not only could have come to be from atoms running together at random, but were in fact so made, why, I say, do they not also say that if innumerable forms of the one-and-twenty letters were thrown together somewhere, the Annals of Ennius could be produced from them, so that they could afterwards be read? That is certainly less laborious than a single paltry animalcule, not to say than the whole machine of the world itself. Why has not the Annals of Ennius, but even a single verse of Virgil, never been produced in this way? Moreover (as the same Cicero excellently argues (y)), if a concourse of atoms can make a world, why can it not make a portico, a temple, a house, a city, which are less laborious and indeed much easier? Surely the Atheists babble so rashly about the world that they seem to me never to have looked up at this wonderful adornment of the Heaven.

175 Add, with Lactantius (z): If all things arise from chance concurrences of atoms, why has it never happened by chance that those principles came together so as to make an animal of such a kind that it would hear with its nostrils rather, smell with its eyes, see with its ears? Moreover, the Atheists have their throats cut by the very reasoning they employ. They say that it is not repugnant that the world should be made from a chance concurrence of atoms, and that if it is not repugnant, there is no reason why it should not in fact have been made in this way. But against them this same argument is urged thus: It is not repugnant that there should exist a cause full of reason which determined the primordial atoms to that combination which is now found: therefore a cause of this kind in fact exists.

176 Proof 5. For the very contingency of things is, in the judgment of all, a most invincible argument that God exists. For hence it comes about that we are compelled, even against our will, to admit some Being from itself, and necessarily existing, from which the things that exist contingently have afterwards received their being. It is therefore certain that it is evidently repugnant that every being should be from another. For since outside the collection of all beings no being is found, the collection of all beings would be from nothing as from an efficient cause, if every being had from another that it should exist. Therefore there is some being not from another. But what is not from another, and is, is from itself, as is plain: therefore there necessarily is some being which exists from itself.

177 Likewise it is repugnant that the whole collection of beings should be contingent. For if the whole is contingent, the whole so exists that it could equally have not been; and if it could equally have not been, there is no reason why it was determined to existing rather than to not existing, unless perhaps one is pleased to say that that collection determined itself to existing, than which surely (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says) nothing is more absurd, and nothing more worthy of laughter. There is, therefore, a necessary being,

The cavils of the Atheists are refuted.

bj. 1. The existence of God is an article of faith: for, as the Apostle has it 178

O            (b), he that cometh to God must believe that he is: therefore it cannot be

demonstrated by natural reason. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an article of faith in such a way, namely, that it can be known only through revelation, I deny; that is, it must be admitted through faith if it does not become known through reason, I grant; and I deny the consequence. Moreover, that there is no repugnance in the existence of God becoming known to us through means both natural and supernatural is so manifest that it needs no demonstration. Besides, since Divine Faith is an assent given to some proposition on account of Divine revelation as its motive, a man must be certain of the existence of God before he is moved to assent on the authority of God revealing. Hence the sense of the testimony praised above is this:

whoever cometh to God, that is, whoever wishes to embrace the true Religion, must be certain of the existence of God.

179 That it came about either through fear, or through ignorance of causes, or through the frauds of rulers and Legislators, or finally through education, that all men have agreed in some Religion, is falsely and rashly contended by Hobbes (c),

Spinoza (d), Bayle (e), Toland (f) and very many others.

180 They object, therefore, 1: men, because they are weak by their nature and anxious with the expectation of things to come, easily feign fearful things for themselves: therefore it is probable that it was induced by fear that they admitted some

Supreme Deity. I deny the consequence. For just as many incline naturally to fear, so also more incline to boldness: therefore fear cannot be the universal cause on account of which all agree unanimously in some thing. Next, the Atheists confess with

Hobbes (g) that men are lovers of liberty and of dominion by their very nature; but it is impossible that among all men the natural desire for dominion and liberty should be so overwhelmed by empty fear that

181 Obj. 3: men have it implanted by nature itself to investigate the causes of things; but if they have been unable to attain the true ones, they feign supposititious ones for themselves: hence they have falsely persuaded themselves that God exists, so that they might rejoice at having attained the first principle of all things: therefore ignorance and error were the cause why some God was admitted by men. I deny the antecedent and the consequence: for things established on account of ignorance rest on empty and light reasons, and therefore can easily be refuted: therefore it is impossible that all the most skilled men should agree in them. How absurd, then, it is, and how foreign to all reason, that all nations, and those far removed from one another and having no communication with one another, should have been able to agree in one and the same error and kind of fiction!

182 Obj. 4. Since Legislators understood that citizens would be kept in their duty much more easily if they believed that there exists some Supreme Deity by whom they could be punished when they did wrong, it came about by their cunning that Religion was introduced among the peoples and propagated: therefore the origin of Religion must be sought from the Legislators themselves. I deny the antecedent. For it has been found by experience that opinions which are disseminated by the craft of men do not last very long, especially if it comes about from them that no light burden is laid upon all. Therefore, since this consent has always endured, although on account of it men are subjected to more laws, it cannot have had its origin from the cunning of Legislators. Next, barbarous nations too, which were subject to no one, have always agreed in some Religion, and Religion itself had its origin together with the human race.

183 Obj. 5. It very often happens that we hold as most certain what is vain and empty in itself, now on account of prejudices, now also on account of the education and instruction which we had in childhood: therefore Religion too could have flowed from these two principles. (h) On the Nature of the Gods. [p. 59] (i): therefore. Second: no one has ever seen God: therefore we believe the existence of the Supreme Deity from the instruction of our teachers and the education given by our parents. To the first I deny the consequence. For from the fact that some Philosophers have fought against this consent, it is rightly concluded that a greater force for persuading is in it; for from this it is established that this universal consent did not flow from ignorance, error, education or some prejudice, but proceeded from the inner voice of nature, from the reason itself which is inborn in each man, from the natural light itself, which on account of the follies of a few raving philosophers could never be obscured. To the second I distinguish the antecedent: no one has seen him in himself, I grant; in his works, I deny; and I deny the consequence. For who has ever seen the mind? Yet I acknowledge it from its works, because I think, etc.

185 Obj. 6. If the consent of nations is admitted as a firm argument for persuading, many absurdities follow: therefore. Proof of the antecedent. Polytheism was established by the consent of nations; for, if the Jews are excepted, all agreed in it. Second. Each nation, on account of the consent of its forefathers, ought to prefer its own Religion to the Religion of another. Third. No one can be ignorant that many errors were disseminated and various superstitions instituted by the consent of nations: therefore. I reply with a distinction: that in all these things the consent was certain and universal, I deny; that it was inconstant, uncertain and particular, I grant. The consent, therefore, from which we contend that a most firm argument for persuading of some thing is drawn must be such that it embraces firmly and constantly all men of all nations and of all times.

186 Obj. 7. It arises from prejudice that we say there is some order in the world; namely, says Spinoza, from the fact that men found within themselves and outside themselves many things useful to them, e.g. eyes for seeing, plants and foods for nourishment, the Sun for giving light, etc., it came about that they at once judged that all things had thus been prepared and disposed by some agent: therefore from the workmanship and order of the world it is not rightly proved that God exists. I deny the antecedent. For men do not labor under prejudice when they judge, e.g., that the organic parts of the eyes were prepared and disposed by a most wise maker, and did not grow together by some fatal necessity, any more than Spinoza himself (whose cavil this is) would labor under prejudice if, in considering either the structure of buildings or the construction of a clock, he were to suspect intelligent causes by which they were disposed with singular industry; but Spinoza would not labor under prejudice if he suspected that causes of this kind either exist or have existed; nay, he would be held a madman if he contended that all these things had been disposed by some fatal necessity; with how much better right, then, from the wonderful disposition of the whole world

188 Obj. 8. It is shown by several arguments that the world was not founded by God: therefore the existence of God is not proved from his Workmanship. The antecedent is proved: 1. For it cannot be conceived that God, being Eternal, made a mortal world, and that suddenly, when he had rested for so many ages before. What glory or joy did he gain from it, who could never lack glory or happiness? What instruments or ministers did he use? If he created light afterwards, how did he not lie in darkness before? Therefore God did not found the world. Second. God founded the world either for the Wise or for the foolish; but he founded it for neither, for the former are few, the latter wholly unworthy: therefore he founded it for none.

189 Third. There is no order in its parts, of which some are deserted, others suited only for beasts or for birds, as the air, the mountains, the seas, the marshes. The fields, moreover, put forth crops only with unremitting labor, and these are often ruined by hail or by flood: therefore it was not created by a most Wise God. Fourth. The most noxious wild beasts, pestilences, famines, diseases overthrow the Providence of God: therefore. Fifth. The wailing of infants, the nakedness of the body, and the innumerable calamities by which man is more wretched than any animalcule, prove sufficiently that the world was not built by God for his sake: therefore the world was not founded by God, and consequently the existence of the Supreme Deity is not well proved from the Workmanship of the world.

190 I reply: I deny the antecedent; and to the first proof I deny the antecedent as well, to which the Epicureans too must reply, who posit eternal matter although they attribute to the world a beginning and an end. Moreover, in eternity, where, as St. Augustine says (k), “there is no creature by whose changeable motions times are carried on, times can by no means exist,” and elsewhere (l): “If before Heaven and earth there was no time, why is it asked what thou wast doing then?” Nor did God need ministers or instruments, which betray the weakness of a craftsman; nor did he who always was the true light ever lie in darkness. To the 2nd I deny the minor. For God founded the universe first for his own sake, then for the sake of the wise. But that others are

191 To the 3rd I deny the antecedent. For there is no part of the globe from which some advantage does not come to man. The mountains supply purer air, the woodlands pastures, the rocks metals and marbles. Rivers feed fish, water gardens, adorn and fortify cities. The sea contributes clouds and rains to the fertility of the fields, and carries goods across from the remotest shores. Heat and cold too are of use, for the latter makes the earth pregnant, the former ripens the crops: therefore, etc. To the 4th and 5th I deny the antecedent. For hardships, and death itself, are the wages of original sin. But since the Atheist mocks these things, I reply 2.: by these things men are led to contempt of earthly things and to praiseworthy industry; they are warned to live sparingly and not to hasten death upon themselves by excessive venery and wine. Of wild beasts, moreover, there is none which does not furnish us either help, or food, pleasure or remedy. To the last I deny the antecedent. For wisdom with weakness is better than even the greatest strength without reason. Thus far Fr. Buzzi.

192 Obj. 9. It is not certain that the visible world exists: therefore the existence of God too will be uncertain. Reply 1: I deny the antecedent. For there is more than one argument by which the existence of bodies is established against the Idealists. Reply 2: I deny the consequence. For the existence of the Supreme Deity is demonstrated also from the fact that a contingent being exists, namely the human mind itself, whose existence the Idealist cannot deny without holding that no one can have certainty even of his own existence; and how false this is, not to say more, there is no reason for me to show at length.

> 0. mali,

193 Obj. 10. From the fact that a contingent being exists, it cannot be gathered with certainty that a necessary being exists: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: a necessary being can exist without a contingent being existing: therefore, in turn, a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I reply with the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: I deny the antecedent; to its proof I let the antecedent pass and deny the consequence. The reason for the difference is evident. For since in a contingent being there is no sufficient reason why it should exist rather than not exist, a contingent being cannot exist unless there is also a necessary being in which its sufficient reason is contained. The case is the contrary when we speak of the necessary being. For this is such that it comprises the reason of its own existence.

194 You will say: the existence of a contingent being is not necessarily connected with the necessary being; otherwise the contingent being would exist necessarily: therefore a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I distinguish the antecedent: that is, it is not of such a kind that a necessary being cannot be had without a contingent one being had, I grant; that is, a contingent being can exist without a necessary one existing, I deny; and I deny the consequence. It is true that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that the necessary being could not exist unless there existed

> (1) Li. XL, Confess caps 134. 0 

> [p. 62]

[p. 62] a contingent being. For a contingent being is not produced necessarily. But it is false that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that it is altogether repugnant that a contingent being be had without a necessary one being had. For since the necessary being holds the reason why the contingent exists, it is a contradiction that a contingent being should exist without a necessary one existing; just as the conflict is evident in this, that there should be an effect without a cause existing.

195 Obj. finally. It is evidently not repugnant that there be a process to infinity in efficient causes: therefore it is evidently not established that a cause must be admitted which is the first of all. Passing over the antecedent, I deny the consequence. For the existence of God has not been demonstrated by us from the fact that an infinite series of causes is repugnant. For whether it is repugnant or not, it is always true that a cause existing from itself must be admitted, since it cannot be that the whole collection of beings should be in such a way that it could equally have not been. That God, the Best and Greatest, exists is therefore beyond doubt. For (I shall conclude in the words of Cicero): “For if reason is on my side, if events, if peoples, if nations, if Greeks, if Barbarians, if our forefathers too, if, finally, this has always been so thought, if the greatest Philosophers, if the Poets, if the Wisest Men, who established Commonwealths, who founded cities: are we waiting until the beasts speak, and are we not content with the agreeing authority of men?” (m). And let what has been said of Natural Theology and of the whole of Metaphysics suffice.

thics, or Moral Philosophy, has been instituted for directing

E          and perfecting morals, so that by love of virtue and flight from vices we

may attain true felicity and beatitude: there is no one who does not know this. Hence it is deservedly wont to be called the art of living well, the medicine of the mind, the investigator of virtue and the expeller of vices, the art of life, the mistress of morals. It can be defined, and very well: the knowledge of the good, or the science showing the way to arrive at the highest good and at the enjoyment of it. But since we feel that we are not only Philosophers but Catholics too, and glory in this wonderfully, I would deservedly incur the reproach of the Learned if I set the medicine of the mind before Youths not even to be tasted, as they say, with the tips of the lips.

For countless things would present themselves for us to say, if we had a mind to embrace everything that we see explained by the Ancients and the Moderns in setting out the science of Morals; we shall, however, select the principal and, as it were, the chief heads, so as to embrace the nobler precepts of morals in a briefer and clearer order. Since, moreover, no one can attain the highest good, namely God, and the enjoyment of Him, unless he observes his duties toward God, toward himself and toward others, unless he cultivates virtue and detests vices, the whole of Ethics can very well be reduced to two, as it were, supreme heads. First, therefore, we shall discourse on Duties; then we shall touch on a few things concerning virtue in general and its causes and signs. For the prescribed limits of the Elements do not allow us to draw out the discussion any further. Let there be, then,

2 Duties of this kind are derived both from reason and from Revelation. For in the present providence of things the light of reason is dim and weak, and therefore, lest it err, it needs the protection of another light. Now the duties which man must perform by reason and Revelation either regard God, and are those of Religion; or are referred to man inasmuch as he is his own guardian; or regard man inasmuch as he is related to others, and are called those of Society; or inasmuch as he is related to the Commonwealth, and are named the duties of the Citizen.

He must be adored. By the name of Religion we understand the worship of love, of obedience and of service, to be rendered to Him to whom it is due. And hence the true Religion, which is the Catholic one, excludes all impiety and superstition. I call impiety both the neglect and the contempt of Religion, each of which directly conflicts with the light of reason; superstition, on the other hand, is either a worship arising from erroneous opinions about God, or one shown to a thing to which it is not due, or one shown indeed to God, but in ways and rites not consonant with His perfections. Hence Atheism, and Pantheism, and Polytheism, and the Mahometan superstition, and Jewish obstinacy, and every sect whatever proscribed by the Catholic Church, are excluded.

4 And from this it follows that there is the highest obligation to embrace the Catholic Religion, inasmuch as it alone is the true revealed Religion. For in it are found the signs of credibility, of which the chief are: the holiness and unity of its doctrine; then also the probity of life of its principal, and above all of its first, preachers and propagators; the signs that testify that God is speaking, such as miracles and prophecies fulfilled in deed; the testimony of the Martyrs; the continual succession of the Interpreters of Religion and of the Judges of controversies. Such a Religion, in no way overcome by the wicked assaults of the most abandoned men, has stood immovable and constant from the beginning of things down to these times in which we live: it is therefore the work of God Himself.

5 Yet who would have brought his mind to believe this, most accomplished Young Men, had not the thing itself demonstrated it, to the very great disgrace of our times? A crowd of men has arisen who have resolved, not to call back the ancient superstitions, but, by disseminating the impiety that is the opposite of superstition, to eliminate Religion from the face of the earth after so many centuries, and to thrust God Himself, its author, down from Heaven. Among the more notable leaders of this design are counted Hobbes, Spinoza, Toland, Bayle. 6 For my part I would not dare to decide (I use the words of the most distinguished Valsecchi) which feeling ought rather to be aroused in a wise man beholding this crowd, whether that of indignation, or of contempt, or rather of pity. Ah, wretched men! Do you think you have so much strength that you judge yourselves able, by bringing out a few little pages, to refute the consensus of so many centuries, to convict the whole human race of error, to stifle the voice of nature, and to wage war on the Supreme Deity? Will that Religion which neither idolatry, then dominant, nor the cruelty of Tyrants equipped with the arms of the whole Roman empire, nor the acumen of so many Philosophers practiced in all the arts of disputation could overwhelm, be subdued by avarice, pleasure, the manners and bearing of a world corrupted by every desire and made effeminate? 9 The Atheist denies that God exists; the Deist (c) says that He exists, but does not care for human affairs. The Naturalist fights against both, and defends with all his might both Providence and God. But this man, since he will recognize nothing in God except what he himself can grasp with so dull a wit, offers himself to be pierced by the weapons both of the Atheist and of the Deist. Helvétius gives man a soul of the same kind as horses and wolves have, and strips it of all freedom. Rousseau makes it free and spiritual: but the primeval, original condition of man, in his opinion, differs in nothing from the origin of wolves and horses.

Among the latter, however, some hold that in the other life he is to be punished with no torments; others will have it that there will be those torments which the law necessarily prescribes; others laugh at these laws, these penalties, as the pure and simple fictions of Poets and of Kings. (c) A Deist, or Theist, is the name given to one who indeed grants that God exists, but professes no Religion, no worship. The Deists disdainfully decry all Religion and divine Revelation as mere fables, and prattle that it is enough if God is adored in the simplicity of nature and of the heart.

(d) The definition on which Spinoza’s system rests is the definition of substance conceived in these words: By substance I understand that which is in itself and is conceived through itself: that is, that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed (Ethics, Pt. 1, Def. 3). Now these words, that which is in itself, can have a twofold meaning. I. That which is in itself, that is, which is from itself, excluding a cause that produces it. II. That which is in itself, [p. 6] religiously imitates its illustrious leaders in this point: having learned lying from them, it has also learned this, to reject what it has approved and always to contradict itself.

to that is, which is through itself, excluding a subject that sustains it. Modes, e.g. motion, shape, etc., do not exist from themselves, because they need a cause by which they are produced; but neither do they exist through themselves, for they require a subject in which to inhere, e.g. a ball. But the most perfect Being exists through itself and from itself. For it does not need a subject by which to be sustained, nor can it even have a cause by which it is produced. A horse exists through itself, since it inheres in no subject; but it does not exist from itself, since it has had a cause by which it was produced. Spinoza used the ambiguous expression exists in itself, and will have it proper to substance to exist from itself, excluding a cause that produces it; but this is what everyone denies, and what that circumcised philosopher nowhere proved in his book. Let us pass to the other parts of the definition and, with the torch of the distinction just given going before us, uncover his fraud. By substance I understand that which is in itself, and he adds, and is conceived through itself. If Spinoza believes that the concept of substance is so absolute that it implies no relation to a subject that sustains it, as motion implies one to the movable, he thinks truly, but this helps Pantheism not at all. What then does he mean? This, namely: that the concept of substance is so absolute that it removes from itself every relation to a cause that produces it; but this is altogether false, and this he will never prove. The same must be said of the other words that follow, which the impious Apella adds to explain the definition of substance just given, that is, substance is that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed. For if he means that the concept of substance must exclude from itself a relation to another substance to which it is referred, as an effect to a cause, we deny it, nor will he ever prove it. The crafty Hebrew, however, understood this; for from this one false principle he derived his whole Pantheistic system, and he wished to include in that definition, as its foundation, that which was the head of the whole controversy: namely, that it is of the essence of substance that it exist from itself, excluding any cause whatever, and that there can never be conceived in a substance a relation of effect to another substance as to the cause that procreates it. [p. 7] to Rome, from the age of Augustus to the age of Louis. A passage is made from the Caribs of the Antilles to the Hottentots of Africa; from these to the northern Greenlanders; thence to the wild men of other remote regions. Hence the laws of regions of the world so unlike one another are now examined, now their customs are compared with one another, now their turpitudes are recounted, now irreligion is celebrated with applause. Chinese antiquities carry greater weight with them than sacred Genesis. Diodorus, Strabo and Tacitus are cited as more expert in Jewish antiquities than Moses himself. Horace, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius are brought forward as incomparable teachers of wisdom.

14 Libertine youths stand fixed in their gaze as they read such a heap of erudition, such a variety of matters, such confidence in deciding. They admire Philosophers of this kind as oracles of wisdom. Religion, whose foundations and whose system they have never meditated, wavers in their minds. These teachers, for their part, think that they have in fact achieved what they intended, and by their rapid and turbulent loquacity have really shown that the Catholic Religion is a fiction, the Gospel a jest, its Martyrs madmen, that the Holy Fathers know nothing at all, and that all true Catholics are a herd of fools, useless, nay pernicious to Society and to the Commonwealth.

18 As regards God, since He is most excellent and rightly and deservedly claims for Himself the supreme right and the supreme authority over all things, everyone understands that He is to be honored with as great a homage and veneration as is owed to the Best Founder and the most Loving Preserver of things. There are many things by which we testify our homage toward others, and indeed love is the chief proof of our homage. For by it it comes about that we cultivate in a wonderful way, with zeal and devotion, those whom we judge worthy of our benevolence. There can therefore be no doubt that God, the Best and Greatest, who by right of dominion is to be worshipped by us, is to be loved above all else and cherished supremely. Nor indeed is there only one reason by which we are driven to do this. For God is that highest good which, if it were seen with the eyes, would arouse (as Plato says of Wisdom) wondrous loves of itself. For whatever is good for us in this life we understand to proceed from Him alone, and we are to receive eternal beatitude in the other life from the enjoyment of Him.

19 Hence we are taught by Sacred Scripture that God is to be loved with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with all one’s strength (g), so that, if our heart, kindled as it were by a perpetual and restless flame, could be consumed as a victim of love, that love would scarcely, nay not even scarcely, be equal to repaying in some measure the love of a most loving Father. With all the powers of the mind, therefore, we must strive to love God above all things; and since God is charity, and is a fire, and came to cast fire on the earth, and wills nothing else but that it be kindled (h), we ought to ask Him Himself with tears and outpoured prayers that the ardor of divine charity may be kindled more vehemently in our hearts, consume all our affections, and at last make us a victim acceptable and pleasing to God.

21 That filial love, therefore, by which we love God as a Father, ought to rouse us to hope with certainty from Him for all the goods that will profit us; and therefore we ought to ask and entreat of Him help, and aid in adversity, as the Redeemer Himself very often invites us to pray and to ask: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. By divine counsel, however, He admonishes us to ask in the name of Christ Himself: If you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you.

22 But not even from the invocation of God and from prayer can we abstain, whether Rousseau will or no. For this is the first part of our duty, in which we certainly cannot fail without bringing on ourselves the greatest inconveniences and losses. For since we are afflicted by so many and such great evils, it is granted to us to be refreshed in them only by the power and wisdom of the Supreme Deity. Immortal thanks, too, are not only to be felt toward God, but also to be rendered to Him. For who, heaped with innumerable benefits, would think himself exempt from performing this duty? And if, endowed with the single benefit of creation and conservation alone, we would owe God very much, what must we judge of that condition of life in which far more has been imparted to us?

23 But these are the internal duties of Religion. Concerning the external ones, the following seem to us to be laid down, as it were in summary. God is to be adored not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion, as we said above. And indeed there is nothing in us that is not the gift of God, and therefore subject to Him in every respect. Therefore the external members of the body too must serve Him. To this argument another is added, and that a very weighty one, taken from the very condition of our nature. For if the acknowledgment of the Deity is the necessary bond of natural Society and of the civil state, the worship of that same Deity will also be supremely commended to both conditions of men. But it is certain that neither Society nor this Civil form can subsist without sensible operation; wherefore, in order to establish it, an external and sensible worship must also be added. From the law of rendering external worship other duties follow. The first is that we speak of God and of Divine things only in the most honorable way. The second, that by all external signs we manifest our internal duties for the example of others. The third, that we also explain the knowledge of Divine things to others, so that in turn one may profit another. Finally, that we promote the glory of God with all piety and zeal.

But although we are bound to both, the perfecting of the mind must nevertheless be greater and more careful, by as much as the mind itself is more excellent and nobler than the body. Now the care of the mind is perfected by the amendment of the intellect and of the will. Whatever, therefore, seems to regard this amendment must be performed by a Christian man above all, with all zeal and diligence. And since the vices of the intellect are more easily removed by the study of the disciplines, as the errors of the will are more safely amended by the exercise of the virtues, we shall have to take refuge in both. Nothing, however, among the aids just mentioned, can be offered or devised that is more apt for procuring the cultivation of the mind than an attentive and vigilant moderation of our affections.

25 The principal affections are Love, Hatred, Desire, Joy, Hope, Sadness, Distrust, Boldness, Despair, Pleasure, Ambition, Avarice, Anger, Shame, Weariness, Envy, Derision, Jealousy, immoderate Love of self, Emulation, by which we see human minds enticed, moved or excited, so that from them all the virtues or vices arise as from most abundant springs. [See what was said in the Logic, bk. 2, ch. 5.] Hence in every kind of life we have this precept: that we correct the motions of the mind that do not obey reason. As for the body, since no one is Lord of his own life, whatever Voltaire may blurt out, neither can anyone exercise an absolute dominion over it. And indeed such custody of the body must be kept as is required in order neither to destroy it nor to impair it. All of which, however, is to be understood and performed always without prejudice to the business of Religion.

26 There have not been lacking those who thought that, in order to avoid grave harm, and above all to escape an ignominy more shameful than death itself, it was lawful for them to inflict death on themselves. But it is certain that this in no way agrees either with the prescriptions of the law of nature or with Christian laws. For there is no necessity of nature why we should claim for ourselves, against the will of its very master, that dominion too which is proper to God alone, and to Princes, who act in God’s stead on earth. Add that those are injurious to Providence and distrust the Divine Goodness too much who, in the extreme straits of affairs, complain that they have been deserted by the most loving Father of lights; not to speak of the virtue of Fortitude, which certainly shines out in adversity the more, the more bravely evils are endured.

27 The remaining duties to be observed by man toward man are these. That the human race is generated for mutual Society, whatever Rousseau, still living and the talk of men, may think to the contrary, is ascertained among all. For what would organs fit for speaking profit, or to what use would affections for helping others serve, unless we were destined by nature itself, namely by God, the most wise author of nature, to enter as it were into one great Society? We are therefore joined by a mutual bond of friendship

> [p. 11]

[p. 11] and benevolence. And just as all that is honorable lies in observing it, so all deformity and baseness lies in breaking and violating it.

28 From this friendship, moreover, two kinds of duties are derived. The first, that we offend no one by word or deed; the second, that we help our fellows with beneficence as far as we can. And indeed the injury of others, which is forbidden by that natural law, what you would not have done to you, do not do to another, can extend very widely. For since there are goods of the mind, of the body and of fortune, we can be harmful to others in three ways.

In discharging this duty, moreover, there is no one who does not see that the nature and condition of the children must be followed.

31 As for those things that are referred to the goods of fortune, I explain much in few words thus. Whatever things are placed in the possession of others, and procured from outside for their preservation and advancement, cannot be violated except with a transgression of the law of nature. For although no things are private by nature, they nevertheless become so by ancient occupation, victory, war, compact, condition, lot.

32 That excellent name, therefore, which has fallen to each man through the exercise of the virtues, can be injured by another neither privately nor publicly. In this matter, if we falsely charge the words or deeds of others as crimes, we are both guilty of calumny and sin against justice. If, on the other hand, we make manifest to another what is a vice and a sin in someone else, which is indeed true but hidden, we are already acting against mutual benevolence. But nothing is more shameful, nothing fouler in the Society of men, than inconstancy in words and compacts. For since the chief foundation of Justice is Faith, once this virtue is removed, Justice too, and together with it sociability, must collapse. Wherefore, if the faith given to anyone must not be violated, by the same reasoning every license of deceiving another by a lie has also been taken away. This indeed we understand of every kind of lie, so that whether it is done to the detriment of another, or you lie for the advantage of yourself and of others, you will be judged a violator of both rights, namely the perfect and the imperfect. Concerning beneficence and liberality, I think that all the duties derived from this head are contained in that principle: whatever you would have done to you by others, do also to others. Thus the omission of these is to be referred not to injustice, but to inhumanity

33 It will therefore be the duty of a prudent and honorable Citizen to embrace his Country and the Prince himself with sincere love; humbly to obey his rule, his laws and his ministers; to win over the minds of all by eminent charity, munificence, sweetness of manners, justice, and all the virtues; to outshine others in talent, skill, the liberal arts, good faith, prudence, care of the household, solicitous education of children, piety and religion; to shrink from public honors and dignities for which he knows himself to be unequal, but to administer those he has merited, and those offered of their own accord, sedulously, diligently and faithfully; finally, to provide diligently, by counsel, strength and resources, in prosperity and adversity, for the common welfare, liberty or safety of the Citizens and of the Prince; and, where the debt of the office laid upon him or a grave calamity shall have demanded it, steadfastly to pour out honors, fortunes, children, and life itself in a sweet and becoming death.

35 Virtue, moreover, is (says the most distinguished Genovesi (k)) whatever perfects nature and renders it more apt for attaining its end; as, on the contrary, vice is what makes it more hindered with respect to its end, or draws it away from it. But since the affections of human nature are certain more vehement impulses by which we are driven toward our end, the whole nature of virtue and its function are placed chiefly in this, that

36 Now the ends of our nature regard either the present life only, or the future one as well. The virtues that perfect men for the happiness of the future life and direct them toward it are called Theological virtues, about which it is for Theologians to discourse; those, on the other hand, that train the same man for holily cultivating and preserving society, and produce the tranquillity and security of society, are called Civil virtues; and finally whatever virtues perfect man for the tranquillity of a private or solitary life are named Monastic and Ethical virtues.

37 But here a grave and ancient question arises for us: can virtue be acquired? For there are those who think that virtue comes wholly from nature, and not also from art, discipline and exercise. For our nature, they say, is necessarily driven by the temperaments, so that we can neither root them out nor change them. There are some who, endowed with a sanguine temperament, are carried away as if against their will into jests, buffoonery, love affairs and the other pleasures of the body; whoever would curb them must change their whole nature. Others are endowed with a melancholic temperament, so that on that account they are perpetually restless, least of all satisfied with themselves, turbid, grim, savage. He who would make them tame must overturn the fibers, the vessels, the fluids, the whole structure of the human body, and the constitution of nature. Some are by nature timid and pusillanimous, others irascible; some soft and inert; others avaricious; others by nature ambitious; some sly and fraudulent. When we wish to compose these to virtue, we must begin from the first Elements of nature. Add that the constitutions of human nature, so diverse according to climate, if they are not wholly born of it, yet depend on it very greatly. Thus these men think they conclude that virtue, unless it be from nature, can in no way be acquired, or else is a dissimulation of nature.

38 They are mistaken, however, and they feign to be untamable those things in human nature of which none is not patient of the rein. For in the first place, the temperaments have more force for receiving than for acting morally. They move nature by reason, sense and imagination, more easily indeed and more promptly, or more slowly and with more difficulty, than if they were absent; they do not always elude the command of reason. And just as softness or hardness in wax is an ease or a difficulty in receiving letters, not the force that carves them, in the same way the temperaments bring it about that we are stirred more promptly and easily, or with more difficulty and more slowly, by certain images of things, but not that we are perpetually impelled against our will. Next, let them have the force of acting physically: they certainly cannot have the force of acting by moral necessity; for they do not necessarily drag freedom to moral malice, even though they often entice it not lightly.

39 Wherefore, if we strive to amend reason, to purge the imagination, if we measure exactly the goodness or malice of things, if we discern the true relations of things to our nature and our ends,

> [p. 14]

[p. 14] we shall indeed be able to be stirred by them somewhat more vehemently toward vices, or to be held back somewhat from conceiving virtue, but in no way to be driven to the former, or drawn back from the latter, against our will. Nor can there be any greater argument that those things can become instruments of virtue than what experience teaches: that very many have so subjected them to themselves and to reason that, while they felt themselves either more vehemently agitated or hindered by a great force, they meanwhile either curbed them or drove them on with goads. I say that there is no one, however depraved, who, if he would be candid, would confess that he is carried to vices against his will; no one so very wicked that he cannot be bent to what is honorable and to virtue. Hence Horace said very elegantly and admirably (l) that

40 I would not indeed deny that climates have some influence on temperaments and manners; but that they act necessarily, that I affirm to be false. M. de Montesquieu (m) strives to prove that the diversity of climate has more power over us than moral diversity, nay that the latter has almost no power over us, and that the opinion of metempsychosis is proportioned to the climate of the Indians in the same way as the Religion they profess is proportioned to the Spaniards. Elsewhere (n) he affirms that it appears of itself, if we wish to speak in human fashion, that limits have been prescribed by the diversity of climate both to the Christian Religion and to the Mahometan. In this Work climate performs the same office as motion in this universe of things, and it is the cause of the things that are done by us. Since such is the foundation of this Work, what must the things be that are deduced from it?

> nim NEN

41 But that no necessity can be brought upon the will by the diversity of climates, as I said above, has been found by experience. For how diverse are the climates in which either one and the same Religion is kept, or now one Religion, now another; or in which the true one has suddenly come into esteem, the ancient and ancestral one being cast aside, or the contrary? Do not men in one and the same climate, in London for example, most constantly profess Religions altogether different from one another? And what of the fact that we do not find the same manners in the same nation at different times? Unless someone wishes to say that the manners and pursuits of the Greeks and Romans who once were are the same now; that the same peoples who once ran wild in barbarism or savagery are now humane and virtuous; or, on the contrary, that those are savage who were humane, or soft who were brave, or unjust who once held most tenaciously to right, or impious who were pious. And let what has been said suffice.

42 But since the virtues are not born with us, as is evident, it will rightly be asked at this point: what are the efficient causes of the moral virtues? And there seem to be five in all: God, talent or temperament, education, exercise, precepts. And in the first place, the first source of true and perfect virtue can only be the first cause of all things: for from Him our essence and nature are, by the same they are both preserved and perfected, and they are led to their ends most powerfully and most wisely. Moreover, no one but God can know most accurately the ends of rational natures, the means to the ends, the proportion of the means to the end, and the powers necessary for this. God alone, therefore, can be the first giver of true and perfect virtue.

43 Talent, or nature and temperament, contributes chiefly two things to moral virtue. First, the faculty or aptitude for receiving virtue, for otherwise we should never attain virtue. Second, the impulse and inclination toward virtue, which is a certain perfection of that natural aptitude. The third and fourth causes of virtue are education and exercise; for by education and exercise our nature is at length bent toward virtuous habits, as tender plants are brought to bear fruit by continued cultivation. He who said that the civil man is nothing other than a heap of habits contracted by education and exercise pronounced a word worthy of a philosopher. The man of Nature, namely, differs as much from the Civil man as an animal, so to speak, from a man.

44 But the precepts of doctrine, which are the fifth cause of virtue, contribute very greatly to education and exercise. For if those precepts are attentively received and very often gone over again, so that they are turned into sap and blood, they acquire such force for refashioning nature that they seem to be a second nature. But of these let us now discourse more accurately. The precepts to be observed by one who wishes to rouse and exercise himself to virtue are of two kinds, some general, others special. Of these we treated in the preceding chapter. The general ones we shall set forth here.

45 The first precept is that we implore with assiduous prayers the divine help by which we may receive strength for cultivating virtue. For God is also the first efficient cause of virtue, and in the divine Scriptures the fear of God is called the beginning of Wisdom. The second precept is that the signal beauty of virtue and its most abundant fruits be kept continually before our eyes. Socrates used to say that if honorableness and virtue showed their face without a veil, they would kindle incredible flames of love in us. Among the fruits of virtue, moreover, the chief are: I. Tranquillity of mind, which proceeds from virtue alone. II. True praise and glory, which can be expected not from vices but from virtue alone, even in this depravity of morals in which nearly all of us live. III. True utility, since vices can feign utility, but cannot furnish the true kind. IV. True nobility; for nobility

46 The third precept is that you set before yourself, to be pursued in virtue, not only middling things or things easier to do, but that you always aspire to its highest summit, and to the virtue that is called heroic; for unless you do this, you will scarcely cling to its lowest part. The fourth precept is that we perpetually paint all the vices to the mind in vivid colors, and accustom ourselves to shudder at them. For it can scarcely be told how much force the horror of vices contributes to establishing virtue. The fifth precept is that we weigh to which vice we are more prone, whether because of temperament, or of education, or of the manners of the age, so that we may draw ourselves farther away from it. And to this above all the man who loves virtue must give his effort. Elegantly Horace (o):

47 The sixth precept is derived from the preceding one. Namely, since there are certain vices proper to the ages of life, as intemperance and rashness in adolescents and youths, ambition in men of mature age, avarice and querulousness in the old, these must above all be restrained and avoided, lest, once they invade us, they throw our whole moral life into confusion. The seventh precept is that you flee idleness worse than a dog and a snake: for it is, as it were, the sink of all the vices, and so the especial enemy of virtue. Wherefore the man who loves virtue must apply himself to labor. And since labors are twofold, of the mind and of the body, the labors of the body are indeed to be undertaken according to each one’s condition; but the mind is never, or rarely, to be removed from serious occupations. Men devoted to the study of letters will themselves do something worth the effort if they learn some honorable art, worthy of the freeborn, and exercise themselves in it in their spare hours. We know from their Lives that excellent philosophers of the last age practiced with pleasure either sculpture, or painting, or the art of optical glasses, or of clocks. Among the labors of the mind, moreover, are the studies of letters; those who seriously give themselves to these have no time to spend on vices. It is reported that Newton, when asked whether he had ever given his attention to love affairs, answered that no time had been left him from his philosophical meditations in which to think about that matter.

48 The eighth precept is that we not only read most attentively the histories of men illustrious in virtue, but also choose honorable, virtuous and sincere friends, and converse with them most familiarly. For indeed, both from reading the lives of illustrious men and from the conversation of virtuous men something continually passes over into the mind, by which we are gradually shaped to virtue. Besides, with virtuous friends we cannot fail to be virtuous, and to be perpetually bent toward virtue: for all men, however shameless, fear the reproof and the judgments of grave and honorable men. Excellently Seneca (p): The greater part of sins is taken away, if a witness stands by those about to sin.

Sed ia re morali: id in primis maximi inomenüti est, sedulo &ecum reputare coram Deo nos esse; & opcrári, Dei veró oculum vindicem esse, Dco enim piena suat omnia. Id vero cüm in omnibus vittis adhibendum est, tüm praecipue in iis, ad quae sumus naturá pro- «liviores. Alexander Macedo. (ut refert. Plutarchus.) , quum semel invisisset, Darii Persarum Regis filias aetate. florentes, ac formá pulcherrimas, noluit secundà invísere, quia sibi ab illis metuebat: Dotcres, inquit, oculerum. suat. - mE

49 The ninth precept is that, if a witness grave in holiness of morals, and one who inspires shame and reverence, is not always present, at least some perfect image of him should perpetually hover before the mind: for it draws the mind very greatly away from vice and impels it toward virtue. But in moral matters this is above all of the greatest moment: to reflect carefully within oneself that we are, and act, in the presence of God, and that the eye of God is an avenger; for all things are full of God. The tenth precept is that we flee all occasions of vices, and most vehemently resist their beginnings: because, namely, it is always easier for a man still whole to resist a vice that is only creeping in than for a man already seized and weakened by vice: for his strength gradually decreases, and the vice grows in the same proportion. And while this is to be applied in all vices, it is so especially in those to which we are by nature more inclined. Alexander of Macedon (as Plutarch relates), having once visited the daughters of Darius, King of the Persians, in the flower of their age and most beautiful in form, refused to visit them a second time, because he feared for himself on their account: They are, he said, torments of the eyes.

50 The eleventh precept is that what Hippocrates wisely pronounced concerning the health of the body, consider nothing small, nothing to be despised, we should refer with better right to the mind; for very often a small spark neglected has stirred up a great conflagration. The twelfth precept is that we institute daily and carefully an examination of our deeds, words, or thoughts. Seneca testifies that he was accustomed to rule his whole life by this precept, and never to take sleep until, as a severe censor of himself, he had weighed all his words, deeds and thoughts, forgiving others much, himself nothing. There is in the golden poem which is attributed to Pythagoras a remarkable passage on this matter, which it is worth the effort to hold in undying memory. In Latin it runs thus:

When first you wake from sleep, as you leave your bed,

Arrange in your mind what must be dispatched in the coming day.

When black night, coming on, takes from things their color,

Do not admit sleep through your sweet eyes

51 The last precept, finally, is that we think of ourselves most modestly, and consider not so much how far we have advanced as how far we still have to advance. For nothing so obstructs progress in virtue as arrogance and a great opinion of ourselves: since no one will strive to arrive where he thinks he has already arrived. Therefore what Plato said of the intellectual virtues, many would have arrived at knowledge, had they not thought they had already arrived, you can say with greater right of moral virtue. For this reason we must beware lest we be captivated by praises and, growing proud, turn aside from the right path of virtue. Many other precepts could be handed down; but if those which we have set out above are turned into nature by practice itself, they suffice for governing early Adolescence (for whose benefit we undertake this labor). But this must now be explained: by what arguments can we know whether we have advanced in virtue or not? Here are the principal ones.

52 The first argument is the love of virtue itself. He, namely, may know that he has advanced in virtue who loves virtue intensely. And he will recognize that he loves virtue if he impatiently seeks an occasion of exercising it; if he is held by a great desire for it; if he is delighted by the conversation of virtuous men; if he shudders at the presence of vicious ones: in a word, it is discerned that we love virtue by the same signs by which it is known that we love any other thing whatever. The second sign is if one perseveres constantly in virtue in the face of the mockery of others, and is not greatly disturbed in mind. And to obtain this it is necessary not only to grow hardened in virtue, but also to weigh carefully that the greater part of men is corrupted by vices; and that therefore the virtuous man must needs displease many, be often exposed to envy, be torn by calumnies. Let him reflect within himself beforehand that these things will come, so that he is the less disturbed when they happen.

53 Indeed, from this a third argument of progress in virtue can be drawn: for to displease the wicked is a great argument of goodness. Thus that Philosopher of whom Laertius speaks, when it had been reported to him that he was being publicly praised, said: wretch that I am, what great evil have I committed? The fourth sign is if we listen with a glad mind to rebukes and reprehensions. The reason for this is that virtue makes the mind not insolent, fierce, savage, contemptuous of others, but gentle and most easy to deal with. Therefore where meekness is lacking, as may be seen in worthless fellows, it is a manifest argument that one has made either no progress, or very little, in virtue. Elegantly Plutarch: full ears of grain bend down, empty ones stand upright.

54 Now the fifth sign that we have advanced in virtue is if, in the face of the difficulties [p. 19] which virtue offers in prospect, we do not yield timidly, but go against them boldly. To kindle this ardor, the fruits of virtue must be perpetually considered. The sixth sign is if adversities are borne with an even mind. For indeed, he who is so disturbed by even the smallest evils that he is miserable has not advanced even a finger’s breadth. And this is what the Stoics taught, that distress does not befall the Wise man. Excellently Cicero (q): “He who is brave,” he says, “must likewise be great of soul; he who is great of soul, unconquered; he who is unconquered must look down upon human affairs and judge them to be placed beneath him: but no one can look down upon those things on account of which he can be affected by distress. From which it follows that the brave man is never affected by distress. But all wise men are brave; distress therefore does not befall the wise man.”

55 The seventh sign is if the virtuous man despises enticements to vice: for if he is easily moved from his purpose, he has made either no progress or little. For vicious men are above all wont to adorn their vices with the most beautiful appearances, so that they may seem less vicious, and to take away from others the horror of vice: to make it respectable by custom, to excuse it by the weakness of human nature; to traduce and deride the virtues as the figments either of weak minds or of enthusiasts; to call those wise who have learned to deceive others cunningly for the sake of private advantage, and those fools who do not know how. If you by no means allow yourself to be taken in by them, know that you have advanced in virtue.

> (4; Tusc. 5. Cap. z7..

56 I set down as the eighth sign of progress in virtue if those devoted to letters take up most eagerly, out of all studies, those that are useful to themselves and to society, and bid farewell to the rest, or greet them in passing. For who is so mad as to affirm that the interminable questions which are disputed in the Schools with such contention of minds, and which smell of the old oil of the Arabs, will be useful to himself or to Society? The last sign by which one can know that he has taken a great step in virtue I hold to be this: if, namely, he feels himself so peaceful in mind, and is so secure in Divine Providence, content with virtue, that he does not anxiously and over-solicitously ask what will be tomorrow, nor is much disturbed by care for the time to come. You therefore, if you are wise, forbear to ask what will be tomorrow. Do you cultivate virtue? For the rest, be tranquil.

57 And let these things suffice for the present: they are few, but for the scope of Elements they will already seem too many to most. It seemed good to us to devote this effort to a most beautiful discipline, neglected hitherto by I know not what fate in the Schools of our America, not without the greatest loss to Youth and detriment to Philosophy. These things are more useful than to fight sharply over the Being of Reason, over the Connection of God with the possibility or impossibility of possibles, and over six hundred other things.

I had long since resolved, and had promised you, excellent Young Men, that I would not speak on physical matters before I had handed down to you Geometrical Institutions, very brief indeed, such as the narrowness of the time required. By good fortune I had brought away with me from Italy a little Book, small indeed in bulk, but one which I should believe would be sufficient for our purpose, and of benefit to you above all for cultivating and advancing physical matters rightly and in order. For whoever will wish to treat seriously of corporeal nature, let him, in short, learn Geometry thoroughly above all things, as diligently as he can: otherwise he will be pursuing not Physics, nor Philosophy, but the smoke and shadow of Philosophy. But those who think themselves Physicists, worthy of so great a name, because all day long they exhaust their brains on long hundreds of syllogisms in a row, as though they wished to entangle the Nature of things, and the Supreme Maker of Nature, in their own fabrications and foolish questions, to their utmost disgrace and sloth: let them see whether it would not have been better for them to have kept away from things abstruse and clouded over with much darkness. For it is shameful, and wholly unworthy of a Philosopher, to wish to discourse about what you do not know; more shameful to prefer to obey custom rather than to embrace the truth that lies in the open sun; and most shameful of all to envy bitterly others, whose minds are not so perverse, and who preside over the apprenticeship of Young Men and over their right instruction. But be that as it may, here is the Author’s Preface, to be placed at once before your eyes. For thus he writes.

principles of demonstrations, were collected by Euclid of Alexandria, about the Year 280 before Christ, a Man greater than all praise, so that by them access might be opened to the whole of Mathematics and to the other natural disciplines. Most young men, however, deterred by their difficulty, having scarcely greeted Mathematical studies from the threshold, and lacking either in wit or in constancy, turn their backs and cut themselves off from all hope of obtaining the fruits of a more solid science; not only because they are left destitute of the first and simplest demonstrations of natural things, but because nothing so sharpens the edge of the mind, and prepares it for perceiving the other disciplines more easily and more rightly (for which use chiefly Plato said Geometry was to be learned), as Geometrical exercise, which opens the surest way of investigating truth.

For this reason we set forth the Geometrical Elements, especially those which will be of very great use to Natural Philosophy (which others have furnished excellently in other ways), in a briefer, and perhaps also a clearer, method. And in the first book we set forth the figures which are contained by straight lines; in the second, curvilinear figures; in the third, the proportions of figures; with great hope indeed of being of help (which is the aim of our Institution), since experience has taught that these principles have helped young men much.

> X Geometriae Elementis alia sunt Principia, quae sola nominum explicatione constant; ala ex iis deducta, ad praxim pertinentia, quae Problemata dicuntur; alia ad Veritauis cognitionem ordinata, quae Theoremata adpellantur. Primo igitur Liber hic Principia dabit; Secundó Problemata circa fizuras Re&ilineas; Tertió Theoremata selectiora-

In the Elements of Geometry, some things are Principles, which consist solely in the explanation of names; others, deduced from them and pertaining to practice, are called Problems; others, ordered to the knowledge of Truth, are named Theorems. First, then, this Book will give the Principles; second, Problems concerning Rectilinear figures; third, the more select Theorems.

## CHAPTER I

Principles.

> Principia.

Principles are either definitions, or Common notions, which either concern the consideration of truth, and are called Axioms, or concern the carrying out of a Work, and are usually named Postulates. We propose each of them here, with explanations added to some, where there is need: so that by these, too, they may be rendered clearer to learners, and the Theorems may afterwards be demonstrated more briefly.

> Rincipia vel sunt definitiones, vel Communes notiones, quae aut circà veritatis considerationem versantur, & Axiomata dicuntur , aut. circà Operis effeéctjionem , & Postulata nun.

In these we depart somewhat from the common Method, so as to begin from the things better known.

I. A Body is that which has a threefold dimension, namely Length, Breadth and Depth.

> M Corpus esr, quod trinam habet dimensionem Longitudinem scilicct, Laritudinem, & Profundicztem.

II. The Extremity of a Body is the surface, in which Length and Breadth alone are considered.

> II. Ex:remum Corporis est superficies, in. qua sola Lonzitudo, & Latitudo. consid-ratur.

III. The Extremity of a Surface is the line, in which Length alone is considered.

> IH. Extremum Superficiei esc linea, in qua sola eonsideratur Longitudo.

IV. The Extremity of a Line is the Point, in which neither Length, nor Breadth, nor Depth is considered.

> IV. Exiremum Lineae est Pun&um, in quo nec Longitudo, ncc. Latirudo , nec Profu-d:tas. consideratur.

And hence a Point is usually defined as that in which there is no Part.

VI. A straight Line is the Shortest from one point to another.

> Hinc Lineae re&ae, quae iisdem pundciis terminantur, sunt aequales, & omninó congruunt inter se. Et lincae curvae, aut quoinodocumque inflexae majorem habent longitudinem, quam Rectà, si iisdem Punctis terminentur,

Hence straight Lines which are bounded by the same points are equal, and wholly coincide with each other. And curved lines, or lines bent in any manner whatever, have a greater length than a Straight one, if they are bounded by the same Points.

> VII. Plana superficies est ,, cui ex omni parte. Recta. linea potest adcommodari: estque ab una linea ad aliam brevissima.

VII. A plane surface is one to which a Straight line can be fitted in every direction; and it is the shortest from one line to another.

> VIIi. Angu!us in superficie est. Duarum linearum post unum €ommune punctum mutua Iaclinatio. B .

VIII. An Angle in a surface is the mutual Inclination of Two lines beyond one common point.

> IX. Angulus Reüilineus dicitur, quit ex rectis lineis componte tur: Curvilineus, qui ex curvis: Mixrus, qui ex una curva, alte» ra i1ecta, .

IX. An Angle is called Rectilinear which is composed of straight lines; Curvilinear, which of curved ones; Mixed, which of one curved and the other straight.

> X. Angulus Rectus est, quum Re&a linea, quae Perpendicularis dicitur, aequaliter utrinque inclinatur. super aliam Rectam.

X. An Angle is Right when a Straight line, which is called Perpendicular, is inclined equally on either side upon another Straight line.

> XI. Angulus obtusus esc major Recto.

XI. An obtuse Angle is greater than a Right one.

> XIL Angulus Acutus est minor Recto,

XII. An Acute Angle is less than a Right one.

Note 1, that when only two lines meet at one point, the Angle can be designated by one letter. But since it often happens that several lines are united at the same point, to avoid equivocation the Angle is usually designated by three letters, of which the Middle one indicates the Angle; the first and third letters, taken in whatever order, designate the lines containing the Angle. As in Figure I of the Theorems, Plate II, the Angle DAB is Right, because the Perpendicular line BA is inclined equally on either side, by a Quadrant of a Circle, upon the line DE: and so the Measure of the right Angle DAB is the Quadrant DB of a Circle, whether larger or smaller. The Angle DAG is Obtuse, whose Measure is the Arc DG, greater than a Quadrant. The Angle DAF is Acute, whose Measure is the Arc DF, less than a Quadrant.

> Nora 2, quód quum quilibec Circulus dividatur à Matlicmaticis in 360. pattes, quas gradus adpellant; Angulus rectus dici so* let Angu!us 9o. graduum; (quae est quarta pais Circuli / Angus lus obtusus major 9o gradibus; Angulaos acutus minor go. gradie bus. Hinc Anguli recti;sunt omnes inter se aequalcs; ad: oque quam plures Aoguli sunt uni, vel pluribus rectis sumihter aequales; erunt & inter. se aequales,

Note 2, that since every Circle is divided by Mathematicians into 360 parts, which they call degrees, a right Angle is usually called an Angle of 90 degrees (which is the fourth part of a Circle); an obtuse Angle, greater than 90 degrees; an acute Angle, less than 90 degrees. Hence right Angles are all equal to one another; and so, when several Angles are equal to one or to several right angles alike, they will also be equal to one another.

Note 3, that lines make a greater or a lesser Angle, not when they are longer or shorter, but when, with the same length of each, they recede more or less from each other. Hence if two lines AD, AL (in the same Figure) are each equal to the two AE, AN, and their extreme Points D and L are as far apart from each other as E and N, the Angles DAL and EAN will be equal. And conversely, if the Angles are equal, the extreme points will be equally distant. On the other hand, when D and M stand farther apart from each other

> [p. 6]

[p. 6] than E and N, the Right Angle DAM will be greater than the Acute Angle EAN.

XIII. Parallel lines are those which stand apart from each other by an equal space everywhere, and, however far they are produced, never meet so as to make an Angle.

Inclinationes.

As in Figure II of the Theorems, Plate II, are the Lines CD, AB, between which the same Perpendicular CA, DB falls. And if any other line cuts them, as the line GP, the Parallel lines are inclined equally toward it on either side: for if they were inclined more toward the middle secant on one side or the other, e.g. toward I, M, they would approach each other more on that side, and so would not be Parallel. Hence the Two Angles L and N together are equal to the Two Angles I and M together: because the Inclinations are equal on either side.

> .XIV. Figura est Quantitas; quae sub uno, vel pluribus termi: nis continetur,

XIV. A Figure is a Quantity which is contained under one or several bounds.

> Scilicec, quae clauditur vel una. Linea curva , ut Circulus : vel una curva, altera recta, ut Semicirculus: vel pluribus rectis, ut Triangulum.

That is, one which is enclosed either by one curved Line, as the Circle; or by one curved and the other straight, as the Semicircle; or by several straight ones, as the Triangle.

> XV. Circulus est Figura plana, unius Lineae circuitu compre: hensa, quae Circumferentia dicitur, seu Peripheria: ad quam om: nes rectae lineae du3ae ab uno medio Puncto sunt aequales.

XV. A Circle is a plane Figure, comprehended by the circuit of one Line, which is called the Circumference, or Periphery: to which all straight lines drawn from one middle Point are equal.

> XVI. Hoc autem medium Circuli Punctum vocatur Centrum.

XVI. And this middle Point of the Circle is called the Center.

> XVII. Diamster est Linea ducta ab uno puncto ad aliud circumferentiae, transiens per centrum , & secans Circulum in duas par. tes aequales.

XVII. A Diameter is a Line drawn from one point of the circumference to another, passing through the center, and cutting the Circle into two equal parts.

> XVIII. Redilineae Figurae sunt , quae reGis lineis continentur: Trilaterae, quae tribus: Quadrilaterae, quae quatuor: Multi- Jaterae, quae pluribus.

XVIII. Rectilinear Figures are those which are contained by straight lines: Trilateral, which by three; Quadrilateral, which by four; Multilateral, which by more.

> XIX. Triangulum, secundüm Latera consideratum , est. Aequilaterum, quod tria latera habet aequalia: u£ i2 Fig. V. con. 11. AH I.

XIX. A Triangle, considered according to its Sides, is Equilateral, which has three equal sides; as in Fig. V, Plate II, AHI.

> XX. sosceles seu. AEquicrure, quod duo tantüm latera habet aequaila; ut in vadem Figura, ABC. /

XX. Isosceles, or Equal-legged, which has only two equal sides; as in the same Figure, ABC.

> XXI. Scalenum,; quod tria inaequalia habet latera; s; iz eadcm Figura, BAL.

XXI. Scalene, which has three unequal sides; as in the same Figure, BAL.

> XXIX Triangulum, secundüm Angulos consideratum , est Rectangulum , seu Orthogonum, quod habec unum Angulum Rectum; ut in Fg. III. 1con. III, 4€ B.

XXII. A Triangle, considered according to its Angles, is Right-angled, or Orthogonal, which has one Right Angle; as in Fig. III, Plate III, ACB.

> XXHI. Obtusapgulum, seu Amblygonium , quod habet unum Angulum Cbiusum; w iz eadem Fig. AEB.

XXIII. Obtuse-angled, or Amblygonal, which has one Obtuse Angle; as in the same Fig., AEB.

> XXIV. Acucangulum, «eu Oxygonium, cujus omnes Auguli sunt Acuti; u£ in eadcm l'ig. ADB.

> XXVI. Rhombus, cujus latera omnia aequalia, sed Aoguli non rectis. Fig. VII. Icon. I.

I.

From any Point to any point a Straight Line can be drawn.

II. A straight Line can be continued in a straight line as far as you wish.

III. From any center at any interval a Circle can be described.

IV. Any line can be divided into Equal or Unequal parts.

V. To any Straight line another can be placed, Equal or Unequal, Perpendicular or

Parallel.

## §. III

Axioms.

I.

Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other.

And things which have a common measure are equal.

And what is greater or less than one of equals is also greater or less than the other of the equals.

II. If to equals you add equals, or something common, or take them away from them, the things that remain are equal.

III. If to equals you add unequals, or take them away from them, the things that remain are unequal.

IV. Things which are double, triple, or half of the same thing, or of equals, are equal to each other.

And whenever two things are equally exceeded by the same thing, or equally exceed it, they are equal.

V. Things which mutually coincide with each other are equal.

VI. The Whole is greater than its Part.

And it is equal to all its parts taken together. And the Part which is equal to all the other parts taken together is the Half of the whole.

## VII

> "E: LIB. T. GEOMETRIAE.

VII. Two straight Lines do not enclose a space.

> VII. Daae rectae Lineae spatium non comprehendunt.

That is, to enclose a space on all sides, at least three straight Lines are required.

> Scilicet ad. claudendum .uudique spatium, saltem. cres. Lineae rectae requiruntur, E /

VIII. Two straight Lines do not have a common segment, or Part.

> VIII. Duae rectae Lineae mon habent commune segmentum , seu Partem. mE zs . . Scilicet duae rectae lineae, quae angulum efficiunt, non pos. sunt continuari ia unam rectam, nisi inflectantur.

That is, two straight lines which make an angle cannot be continued into one straight line unless they are bent.

> "Problemata.

Problems are Propositions which teach how to do some Work concerning Lines,

> Roblemata sunt Propositiones, quae docent Opus aliquod facendum circa Lineas, Aogulos, aut Figuras. Praecipua, ad TeCtilineas Figuras pertinentia, hic proponuntur, eorumque demonsirauones solüm indicantur, exceptà primà: tum quia hae facilé :ex positis: Principijs, aut demonstrandis Theorematibus deducunciur; tum quia Problemata non sunt Principia ad ceteras ves» ritates ostendendas: sed ut Hypotheses supponi possunt. Quae Methodus Disceotibus videtur magis adcommodata, ne sub. initium perturbentuts sed post demonstrata Theoremata in. Problematum dee monstrationibus inveniendis exerceantut. -

Angles, or Figures. The principal ones, pertaining to rectilinear Figures, are proposed here, and their demonstrations are only indicated, except for the first: both because these are easily deduced from the Principles laid down, or from the Theorems to be demonstrated; and because Problems are not Principles for showing the other truths, but can be supposed as Hypotheses. This Method seems better suited to Learners, so that they may not be thrown into confusion at the beginning, but, once the Theorems have been demonstrated, may exercise themselves in finding the demonstrations of the Problems.

To make an Equilateral Triangle.

> Periatur. Circinus- intervallo datae lineae AB: tum ab. utraque lineae extretitate fiant, Circino invariato, duo arcus.. se secantes.in «C:.demü a ex Pundto C ducantur lineae CA, & CB, quae £onsciruent Tria gulum AEquilaterum ABC. 005 Ad demou:strandam, perficiatur circulus A C F, & BC E. Let the Compass be opened to the interval of the given line AB; then from each end of the line, with the Compass unchanged, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C; finally from the Point C let the lines CA and CB be drawn, which will constitute the Equilateral Triangle ABC.

> . Ad efficiendum Triangulum Isosceles, aperiatur semel cireinus majori, vel minori intervallo, quàm data linea; & deinde fiant arcus, ut, supra. Si veró dum fiunt arcus, semper varietur circint. intervallum, fiet. Triangulum Scalenum; BIEN ?, » Ji

For the demonstration, let the circles ACF and BCE be completed.

Demonstration. The line AC is equal to the line AB, because they are drawn from the center to the circumference of the same Circle: from definition XV. But the line BC is also equal to the same line AB, by the same definition: therefore the lines CA and CB are equal to each other: from Axiom 1; and so the Triangle ABC, consisting of three equal lines, is Equilateral.

To make an Isosceles Triangle, let the compass be opened once to a greater or a lesser interval than the given line; and then let arcs be made, as above. But if, while the arcs are being made, the interval of the compass is changed each time, a Scalene Triangle will be made.

Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

To make an oblong Rectangle.

At the end of AB let a perpendicular greater or less than it be drawn: then from the end C let an arc be made with the interval of the line AB, and from the end B let an arc be made with the interval of the line CA, intersecting the former arc at D: finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and a Rectangle longer on one side will be had. From the same Theor.
