At the end of the line AB let an unequal line CA be drawn, at an angle that is not right: then from the end C, with the interval of the line AB, let an arc be made; and from the end B, with the interval of the line CA, let another be made, intersecting the former at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhomboid will be had. From the same Theor.

Hence it is evident how a Parallelogram may be made equal to any Trapezium whatever. For let the Trapezium be divided into two Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite Angles HI, to which let Parallels be drawn through the vertices L and M: then, HI having been bisected at N, between the same Parallels, upon a base BG equal to the half HN, let the Parallelogram FBDG be made: which will be equal to the Trapezium LM, inasmuch as it is equal to the two Triangles HLI and HMI, which compose the Trapezium. From the same Theor.

Theorems.

> J CAPUT III.

A      Theorem is a Proposition demonstrating some property of quantity. Its prin‐

> T heoremata.

cipal parts are three: the Proposition itself, which proposes the truth to be shown; the Preparation, which arranges the lines sometimes necessary for the demonstration; the Demonstration, which concludes the proposed truth from the Principles laid down, or from Theorems.

> T eorema. est Propositio, proprietatem aliquam quaatitatis demonstrans. Tres praecipuae sunt ejus partes: Propoe $iti* "psa, quáe proponit veritatem ostendendam: Praep;- giz2,. quae .4sp»onit lineas quandogne necessarias ad demonstra tionem : Demonstratio, quae ex positis Principiis, aut Theorce matibus propositam veritatem. conciudit.

Twelve Theorems selected from the 1st and 2nd books of Euclid are proposed in this chapter, with Corollaries, or inferences, added, which follow easily from the Theorems: some of these are contained in the propositions of Euclid, others lie outside Euclid; the order of that Author has been varied somewhat, so as to keep, if it please Heaven, a clearer method. For, beginning from Angles and Lines, we come to the properties of Triangles, and from these to demonstrating Quadrilateral figures.

> Daodecim in hoc capite ex ir. & 2. Euclidis libro selecta "Fheoremata proponuntur, adjectis Corollariis,seu illationibus, quae ex Theorematibus facilé descendunt : quorum alia in Euclidis propositionibus continentur, alia extra Euclidem sunt; ejus Authoris. ordine noonihil variato , ad. clariorem, si Superis placet, mecho« dum retinendam. Initio quippe facio ab. Angulis, & Liaeis, ad Triangulorum. proprietates, & ex iis ad figuras. Quadrilateras demonstrandas devenimus. -

But lest the Number of the more notable Propositions of Euclid, as it is commonly used by Mathematicians, should lie hidden, we shall place it at the foot of the page. The Principles, however, from which the Demonstrations descend, we shall not always indicate, because they are so clear that they may be supposed present to the mind.

> Ne veró. Ninerus insigniorum Euclidis Propositionum, quals passim à Mathematicis usurpatur lateat; illum. ad pagimae fi.. em adponemus. Priucipia tamen , unde Demonstrationes desrendunt, non semper indicaoimus; quia tam clara sunt; ut animQ praesentia supponantur.

> LIBER II.

The four Theorems just demonstrated are very well explained by numbers, which you have in Clavius and others. Of these, however, the last two, although very useful for practical Geometry, are nevertheless not necessary for the following Propositions, after which they can be gone over again, if they seem rather difficult to anyone. In the Demonstrations that follow, moreover, when the Book is not indicated, the one under discussion is understood.

## BOOK II

> "De Figuris curvilinets.

On Curvilinear Figures.

> ; Nter figuras, quae curvá lineà continentur; primuni habet in Geo« metria locum, Circulus, qui solus uno, ac certo. Circini ductin perficitur. Ejus tres praecipue mirabiles proprietates considerat:

Among the figures that are contained by a curved line, the first place in

> Aristoteles. cap. 2. Mecbanicarum. quaestionum: Prima. est, quód circu-- Jus fit ex linea. mota, & quiescente: dum enim linea tota circums ducitur ad circulum: efficiendum, ejus. extremum. in. pencto: centri: quiescit. Secunda est; quód singula lineae: puncta, quamvis continua ,.

Geometry is held by the Circle, which alone is completed by one sure sweep of the Compass. Aristotle, in ch. 2 of the Mechanical Questions, considers three especially wonderful properties of it. The first is that the circle is made from a line that is moving and at rest: for while the whole line is carried round to make the circle, its end rests in the point of the center.

> dum linea circumagitur,. insequali velocitate moventur: majus enim spatium percurrit punctum , quod: magis à centro removetur. . , Tertia. est, quód Peripheria, circulum $gmbiens, constat quodammodo. ex conirariis, & extremis sine medio: ex. concavtp nimirum, & convexo; inter quae Rectum ita medium est, oc AEquale 1brer magnum, & parvum. Nam quemadmodum linea, ut ei: magna fiac parva, priüs debet fieri. aequalis; jta, ut ex^ concava fiat convexa, priüs. debet fieri reéta. Idque eó: mirabilius est, quod £a contrar'3 insunt. lineae, nullam. Jatitudinemy habenti, qualis est "Circuli Periphieria. : : c : . , De Cuculo igitur agit Euclides tertio, & quzrto Iibro Ele-mentorüm: & nos hic tum. Problemata, quae ad Circulos, & Figuras circulo inscribend*s pertinent: tum: Theoremata, àd eorum: Proprietates. investigandas. uulioras. praejactis. principijs. trade «mRus,.

The second is that the single points of the line, although continuous, are moved with unequal velocity while the line is carried round: for the point that is farther removed from the center runs through a greater space.

The third is that the Periphery that surrounds the circle consists in a certain manner of contraries, and of extremes without a middle: namely of the concave and the convex; between which the Straight is a middle, just as the Equal is between the great and the small. For just as a line, in order to become small from great, must first become equal, so, in order to become convex from concave, it must first become straight. And this is the more wonderful in that these contraries are found in a line having no breadth, such as the Periphery of the Circle.

Of the Circle, then, Euclid treats in the third and fourth books of the Elements; and here we, having laid down the principles, shall deliver both the Problems that pertain to Circles and to Figures to be inscribed in the circle, and the more useful Theorems for investigating their properties.

To draw a Tangent.

First, if a Tangent is to be drawn to a given Point in the Circumference, as A: let the semidiameter AD be drawn, at whose extremity A let a perpendicular be raised in this way. With the interval of the Semidiameter AD let the circle be cut from A at B, and through B let the indefinite line DF be drawn, which from B, with the same interval of the semidiameter, is to be cut at F. When FA is joined, the perpendicular will be Tangent to the circle. From Theor. I & V.

Second, if from a Point F outside the circle a straight line Tangent to the circle is to be drawn: let the line FD be drawn to the center of the Circle, and let it be bisected, as at B; then from B, with the interval of the half, namely FB, let the Periphery be cut at A. (Having made, for the demonstration, the semicircle FAD.) The line FA will be Tangent to the circle. From the same.

> Entagonum circulo inscribitur, ductis duabus diametris ad ans guios reclos A B, C D: deinde semidiameter E B. diw:datur bi. fariam in F: intervallum F C transferatüc ex F. in G; eritque C G, latus Pentagoni. ex Tbcor. at right angles: then let the semidiameter EB be bisected at F: let the interval FC be transferred from F to G: and CG will be the side of the Pentagon, from Theor. XI, bk. III. The side of the Decagon, moreover, will be the line GE, from Theor. X, bk. III. > Si in circulo, cui est inscriptum Pentagonum, inscribatue etiam Trigonum regulare: ita , ut vertex Trigoni congruat cuilibet vertici Pentagoni , distantia minima inter angulum Pentagoni, &G Trigoni erit latus Quindecagopi.

If in a circle in which a Pentagon is inscribed a regular Trigon is also inscribed, in such a way that a vertex of the Trigon coincides with some vertex of the Pentagon, the least distance between an angle of the Pentagon and one of the Trigon will be the side of the Quindecagon.

> . . Figurae veró omnes Circulis circamscribuntur, $i priüs inscribatur Circulo Figura quaesita: & deinde per vertices anguíoe zum ejusdem Figurae, Circulo inscriptae, ducantur Tangentes, quae Similem tiguram circa circulum consticuent.

All Figures, moreover, are circumscribed about Circles if the Figure sought is first inscribed in the Circle; and then through the vertices of the angles of that same Figure, inscribed in the Circle, Tangents are drawn, which will constitute a similar Figure about the circle.

> , Possunt quoque istae, aliaeque omnes Figurae Circulo ine scribi, Circuli Quadrante diviso in gradus 9o. Sumantur enim ia Quadrante tot. gradus, quot conveniunt quaesitae Figurae; Si see cundum eos circulus dividatur, dabuntur arcus, quos ejus figu. sae latera subtendunt, & ejusdem Anguli ad Cenuum comprehendunt.

These and all other Figures can also be inscribed in a Circle when a Quadrant of the Circle has been divided into 90 degrees. For let as many degrees be taken in the Quadrant as belong to the Figure sought; if the circle is divided according to them, there will be given the arcs which the sides of that Figure subtend and which its Angles at the Center comprehend.

> . Ut autem cognoscatur, quot gradus conveniant singulis Figuris dividantur 360. gradus circuli per numerum laterum Figurae coustruendae ; & Quotiens dabit .gradus quaesitos. Ex. gr. Trigofo conveniunt 120 gradus circuli; quia 560, diviciper 5, dant 120.

But in order to know how many degrees belong to each Figure, let the 360 degrees of the circle be divided by the number of the sides of the Figure to be constructed; and the Quotient will give the degrees sought. E.g., 120 degrees of the circle belong to the Trigon, because 360 divided by 3 gives 120.

> Possunt etiam similes Figurae sine circule construi supra datam lineam, inveniendo angulum, quem duo lateta Figurae coustruendae comprehendunt; qui dici solet Angulus ad Circumfereniiam.

Similar Figures can also be constructed without a circle upon a given line, by finding the angle that two sides of the Figure to be constructed comprehend; which is usually called the Angle at the Circumference.

> Is autem invenitur, subtrahendo ex 180 gradibus circuli an- ' £ulum ad ceutrum. Ex. gr. S1 quaeratur. Trigoni angulus ad circumferentiam: quum ejus angulus ad centrum inventus sit. graduum Xao; his subtraClis ex 180, remanent éo gradus pro angulo Trie £oni ad circumferentiam ; quem scilicet ejus Figurae Jatera com- Prehendunt : ut. videre est in adposita Tabella.

This, moreover, is found by subtracting the angle at the center from 180 degrees of the circle. E.g., if the angle of the Trigon at the circumference is sought: since its angle at the center has been found to be of 120 degrees, when these are subtracted from 180, there remain 60 degrees for the angle of the Trigon at the circumference, which, that is, the sides of that Figure comprehend: as may be seen in the adjoining Little Table.

The Angle in a Semicircle is Right. (a)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameter AD be drawn.

Dem. The angle CAD is equal to the angle ACD; and the angle ABD is equal to the angle DAB, since they are opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V of the first book. Cor. When the line AE is drawn, it is plain that the angle BAE, having for its base an arc greater than a semicircle, is Obtuse; and the angle GAB, standing upon an arc less than a semicircle, is Acute.

> I. Das est magnitudo minor, quae metitur majorem,

§. I.

> . Dividitur Pars 10. Aliquotam, & Altiquantam. Pars aliquota dicitur, quae aliquoties repetita adaequat suum totum: ut 4 adaequaté contibecürs n 8, 12, 16, &c. Pars aliquanta. dicitur, quae aliquoties repetitá non adaequat suum totum, sed velipsum excedit , velab eodem deficit: ut 4 in 65,7, 9, &c. Definitur hic so/üm pars aliquota, quae metitur, & adaequat totum; tum quia ejus praecipuus usus est in proportionibus demonstrandis: cum quia pars ali» Quanta proprié noa dicitur pars, sed partes totius 5 Dam numerus 4: ex. gr. dicitur Guae tertiae. numeri 6.

Definitions.

> 4l. Muluplex magnitudo est, quam met'tur minor.

A    I. part is a lesser magnitude that measures a greater.

> Scilicet Magnitudo mulriplex dicitur comparata cum sua parte aliquoti, quai. pluries adaequaté continet; ut 6 continet 2.

Part is divided into Aliquot and Aliquant. An aliquot part is so called which, repeated a number of times, exactly equals its whole: as 4 is exactly contained in 8, 12, 16, etc. An aliquant part is so called which, repeated a number of times, does not exactly equal its whole, but either exceeds it or falls short of it: as 4 in 6, 7, 9, etc. Only the aliquot part, which measures and exactly equals the whole, is defined here; both because its chief use is in demonstrating proportions, and because an aliquant part is not properly called a part, but parts of the whole; for the number 4, e.g., is called two thirds of the number 6.

> Iii Rotio, seu (ut alus placet) Proportio est Modus, quo una quanutas aliam ejusdem generis continet, vel ab ea condaoetur.

II. A multiple magnitude is one that a lesser measures.

> Ejusdem autem generis dicuntur. ea, quae multiplicata se possunt mutuo superare: hinc inter Deum, & Crearuram, Finitum, & Jufiojtum nuila proporttos quia non se possunt mutuo Superare- Si» militer inter angulum contingentiae, & rectilineum ; quia angulus conuüngeatiae quantumvis auctus, non superat an2ulum rectiliucuak

That is, a magnitude is called multiple when compared with its aliquot part, which it contains exactly several times; as 6 contains 2.

III. Ratio, or (as others prefer) Proportion, is the Mode in which one quantity contains another of the same kind, or is contained by it.

Those things, moreover, are said to be of the same kind which, when multiplied, can exceed each other: hence between God and the Creature, the Finite and the Infinite, there is no proportion, because they cannot exceed each other: likewise between the angle of contingence and a rectilinear one; because the angle of contingence, however much increased, does not exceed a rectilinear angle.

[p. 31]

> . Kàtignalem, dicuatur Incomaensurabiles.

Proportion is divided, 1, into rational and irrational. That is called rational which can be expressed by numbers: as double, triple proportion, etc. That is called irrational which cannot be expressed by numbers: such is the proportion of the diameter to the side of the square; for by no number can it be expressed by how many parts the Diameter exceeds the side of the square (whoever does not know this, says Plato, is to be counted not among men but among the brutes). And quantities that have a rational proportion to each other are called Commensurable; those that have an irrational one are called Incommensurable.

> —«. DEFINITIONES. 3r

Proportion is divided, 2, into the Proportion of Equality, which obtains between equal things, and of inequality, which obtains between unequal things: of these, when the greater contains the lesser exactly, it is called multiple proportion, as in definition 2. When it contains the lesser and, besides, some aliquot part of it, it is called superparticular proportion, as 6 to 4. When it is greater by some aliquant part, it is called superpartient proportion: as 8 to 5. But if the lesser is referred to the greater, the particle sub is prefixed: as 2 to 4 is subduple proportion.

> Dividitur 1. proportio in rationalem, & irrationa]em. Rationalis dicitur, quae numeris exprimi potest: üt. prcporco dupla, tríe pla, &c. IV. Proportionality, which is also usually called Proportion and Analogy, is the Comparison and Similitude of Ratios, or Proportions.

> Dividitur 2. Proportio in Proportionem AEqualitatis,, quae intercedit inter aequálio; X inacgualitadis, quae intercedit. 10ter inaequalia: ex iis ve.ó quum major continct adaequaté. minorem , dicitur proportio multiplex; uc in definitioue 2. Quum contiuet mie norem, & insuper aliquam ejus partem aliquotam, dicitur propos:io supernaturalis, ut 6 ad 4. Quum est major aliqua parte aliquanta , dicitur proportio. superparteus: ut 8 ad y. S1 vero annor ad. mas jortem referatur, praeponitur pardicula sub: ut 2 ad 4 est propore 110 subdupla.

It is divided first into Arithmetical and Geometrical. Arithmetical proportion is the Equality of the excesses among several quantities: as 1, 2, 3, 4, which numbers all exceed one another by unity; or 1, 3, 5, etc., which exceed one another equally by two.

> IV. Proportionalitas, quae & Proportio, & Znaloeia dici solet est Racioaum, seu Proportionum Coinparatio, & Sinil tudo,

Geometrical proportion is the similitude of the excesses among several terms that contain one another in the same way: as 1, 2, 4, 8, etc., which likewise exceed one another in double ratio; or 1, 3, 9, 27, etc., which are in triple ratio.

> Dividitur. primó 1n. Arithineticam, & Geometriam. Arithinetica proportio est AEqualitas excessum inter pluies quantitates z UC I. 2, 3, 4: qui numeri omaes se excedunt unitates vel i, 5, f» &c. aequaliter se excedunt. binario.

There is, besides, Harmonic Proportion, which does not pertain to the present matter.

> Geometrica proportio. es; similitudo. excessuum. inter. plures: terminos, qur eodeu; modo se contineut: ut I, 2; 4, 8, &c. cub similiter se excedunt. in. dupla rauene- vel tr, 3, 5», 27, &c. qui sunt in ratione tripla.

Proportion, or proportionality, is divided secondly into discrete and continuous. It is discrete when there is some interruption between the terms: as if you say, 8 is to 4 as 6 to 3; there is an interruption in the middle terms, because 4 is not to 6 as 8 to 4.

> Est praeterea Proportio Harmonica, quae ad rem. praesentem:

Proportion is called continuous when there is no interruption: as if you say, 1 to 2, as 2 to 4, as 4 to 8, as 8 to 16, etc.; for in these terms the earlier are referred to the later in the same way, with no interruption made. This continuous proportion is also usually called a progression: and if it goes from the lesser to the greater, it is called an increasing progression; but if from the greater to the less, a decreasing progression.

and [p. 32] are called homologous to each other, just as the two consequents are to each other: e.g., if it is said, as 4 to 2, so 6 to 3: 4 and 6 are called antecedents and homologous to each other; 2 and 3 are also called consequents homologous to each other.

VI. Proportion, moreover, or Proportionality, consists in at least three terms;

Because proportionality is the comparison of two relations, each of which requires two terms. For if the Proportion is continuous, three terms suffice, because the second is repeated: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 4 to 2. But if the Proportion is discrete, four terms are required: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 6 to 3.

VII. Compound Proportion is that which is produced by the multiplication of proportions.

As duodecuple Proportion is that which is produced from sextuple and duple proportion, because twice six make 12.

Hence the Proportion of the extremes is said to be compounded of the proportion of the Means: as if there are 20, 10, 2, the Proportion of 20 to 2 is decuple, compounded of the duple proportion of 20 to 10 and the quintuple of 10 to 2.

VIII. But when Magnitudes are continuously proportional, as 27, 9, 3, 1, the First is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and the triplicate to the fourth, and so on.

Double and duplicate ratio are very different; for Proportion is double or triple when one quantity contains another twice or three times. But Proportion is duplicate or triplicate when between several magnitudes there intervene two or three continued proportions. Thus, because between 27, 9, 3 there intervene two triple proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 3 the duplicate proportion of that which it has to 9. And because between 27, 9, 3, 1 there intervene three similar proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 1 the triplicate proportion of that which it has to 9.

IX. Similar Figures are those that have their angles equal, each to each, and the sides about the equal angles proportional.

In these, moreover, the sides opposite equal angles are called homologous: [as in Figure 6, Theor., Pl. V] the side GE homologous to the side NL, and the side ED homologous to the side LH.

X. Reciprocal Figures are those that have their sides mutually antecedent and consequent.

That is, mutually double and half; triple and subtriple, etc., as in Figure 1, Theorems, Pl. V, are the Rectangles X and Y: for the Rectangle Y has the side GA double the side AD of the rectangle X, and reciprocally the other side AF half the side AB of the same rectangle X.

Axioms.

In place of Axioms I put most of the Propositions of Euclid’s bk. 5, of which

Geminus, the illustrious Mathematician, seems to have spoken in Proclus, bk. 3, ch. 1, where he says: Others have devised demonstrations even of indemonstrable things: they have tried to prove things that are known to all by less known Means.

I. If two quantities are equal to each other, they will have the same proportion to one third thing, or to equal things: as 8 and 8 contain 4 twice in the same way. (a)

II. If two things have the same proportion to the same third thing, or to equal things, they will be equal to each other. As, if the number 4 is contained twice by two numbers, these will be equal to each other, namely 8 and 8. (b)

III. Of unequal quantities, the one that is greater has a greater proportion to the lesser, or contains the lesser more times.

As the number 8 contains the number 4 more times than the number 6 does. And that which contains the same quantity more times is greater: and that which is contained more times is less. (c)

IV. Proportions that are equal, the same, similar to the same one (they signify the same thing by different names) are equal, the same, similar to each other. (d)

V. If single magnitudes have the same proportion to single magnitudes, all together will also have the same proportion to all together.

That is, twice the double will also be double to twice the half; three times the double to three times the half, etc.

Hence all the antecedents together are to all the consequents as the single antecedents to the single consequents: as, if 4 has to 2 the same proportion as 6 to 3, namely double: 4 and 6 together will also have a double proportion to 2 and 3 together. (e)

VI. Similar parts, that is, those that are contained equally, are to each other as the wholes containing them. That is, as 2 to 3, so twice 2 to twice 3; three times 2 to three times 3.

Hence if similar parts are added to or taken from similar wholes, what remains is similar. (f)

VII. If, as the whole to the whole, so the part taken away to the part taken away, the whole will also be to the whole as the remainder to the remainder. (g)

VIII. If equals are added to equal proportions, the wholes will be equal.

> .. Hinc quum multiplicatio sit multiplex additio, si aequales pree portiones per aequales multiplicentur, totae erunt a-quales: ut si duae proporiienes duplae, singulae mulüplicentur per triplam proe portionem; anibae erunt sextuplae.

As, if to the two numbers 4 and 4, in double proportion to 2, there is added to each 6, which number is in triple proportion to the same 2, there will be 10 and 10 in equal, quintuple proportion to 2.

> $. III.

Hence, since multiplication is multiple addition, if equal proportions are multiplied by equals, the wholes will be equal: as, if two double proportions are each multiplied by a triple proportion, both will be sextuple.

> Proportionum zdrgumentattones.

Arguments about Proportions.

> Athematici, nec non Philosophi omnes ad proportiones infe- . rendas, sex modis arguendi utuntur, querum veritas, vel ex se, vel ex positis Principijs facilé paret. E :

Mathematicians, and also all Philosophers, use six modes of arguing for inferring proportions, the truth of which is readily plain either of itself or from the Principles laid down.

> I. Ratio inversa, seu conversa esc Mutatio antecedentis in. con« sequens, & consequentis in antecedens: ex. gr. ut antecedens 9'ad consequens 5, ita antecedens 6 ad consequens 2: ergo convertendo, ut 5 ad 9, ita 2 ad 6.

I. Inverse, or converse, Ratio is the Change of the antecedent into the consequent, and of the consequent into the antecedent: e.g., as the antecedent 9 to the consequent 3, so the antecedent 6 to the consequent 2; therefore, by converting, as 3 to 9, so 2 to 6.

> Patet ex se: quia si antecedentes aequaliter praecontinent cons sequentes, etiam consequentes aequaliter praecontinentur ab ante. «edeniibus, - M. Ratio alterna, seu permutata est comparatio antecedentis cum antecedente. & consequentis cum consequenti ; ex. gr. ut 9 ad 5, ita 6 ad €. ergo alternando, seu permutando, seu vicissim; ut 9. ad 6, ita 3 ad 2. (a)

It is plain of itself: because if the antecedents contain the consequents equally, the consequents are also equally contained by the antecedents.

> Patet ex Axiom. VI.: quia partes similes sunt inter se, ut tota: & tota, ut partes similes. :

II. Alternate, or permuted, Ratio is the comparison of antecedent with antecedent and of consequent with consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by alternating, or by permuting, or conversely, as 9 to 6, so 3 to 2. (a)

> In proportione tamen alterna debent esse quatuor termini ejusdem generis; nam si duo primi fuerint diversi generis à duobus secundis, non valet alternando: quia inter res diversi generis, nul ja est proportio. Ex defiiione lll. —— 0

It is plain from Axiom VI: because similar parts are to each other as the wholes, and the wholes as the similar parts.

In alternate proportion, however, the four terms must be of the same kind; for if the first two are of a different kind from the second two, the argument by alternation is not valid: because between things of a different kind there is no proportion. From definition III.

IV. Division of ratio is the comparison of the excess of the antecedent over the consequent to the consequent itself: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by division, as 6 (the number by which 9 exceeds 3) to 3, so 4 (the number by which 6 exceeds 2) to 2. (a)

> Duae quantitates sunt in ratione inversa, seu reciproca quum pri» müs & quàrtus termings proportionis Geometricae perünent. ad unam quantitzretm, secundus veró. & tertius ad aliim spectant. On the one side 27, 9, 3;

On the other 18, 6, 2.

The argument runs thus: as 27 to 9 on the one side, so 18 to 6 on the other; and as 9 to 3 on the one side, so 6 to 2 on the other: therefore, from equality, as 27 to 3, so 18 to 2. (c)

And this indeed is called an ordered ratio, because the proportion of the first with the second, and of the second with the third, is compared in order on each side. But if this order is not kept, it is called a disturbed ratio: as if there are set down (d)

On the one side 12, 6, 2;

On the other 24, 8, 4.

The argument runs thus: as 12 to 6 on the one side, so 8 to 4 on the other; and as 6 to 2 on the one side, so 24 to 8 on the other: therefore, from equality in disturbed order, as 12 to 2, so 24 to 4. It is called a disturbed ratio because on the one side the proportion of the first with the second is compared, on the other that of the second with the third.

Each argument is plain from the definition itself and from Axiom 8, because in both cases the proportion of the extremes arises from equal intermediate proportions, whether these are taken in order or in disturbed order.

“Since, however, what has been said about proportions by the celebrated Author is apt to cause difficulty to young men, I have therefore thought it opportune to set these things forth and explain them again, perhaps more clearly.

If one quantity is referred to another, e.g., a number to a number, and attention is paid to the manner in which the former contains the other, or is contained in the other, that relation of the one to the other is called a Geometric Ratio; the number which is referred is called the antecedent, and the number to which it is referred is called the consequent of the ratio. But if the antecedent is divided

Cc 2                                      by

(a) Prop. 17.

(b) Cor. prop. 19.

(c) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 22.

(d) Prop. 23. [p. 36] by the consequent, the quotient is called the exponent of the ratio. Now the Quotient, or Quotient number, is that which denotes how many times some number is contained in another. Thus in the ratio 8 to 2 the number 8 is the antecedent, 2 the consequent, and the quotient 4 is the exponent of the ratio; and 4 is the quotient because 2 is contained four times in 8.

If the antecedent equals the consequent, the ratio is one of equality, as 4 to 4.

If the first quantity contains the second twice, the first is said to be to the second in double ratio; if three times, in triple ratio, etc.; and the one that is contained is said to be in subdouble, subtriple ratio, etc. Thus, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to another of 4 feet in double ratio, and the line of 4 feet to the line of 8 feet in subdouble ratio.

The equality or likeness of ratios is called Proportion, and it is expressed in this way: 8 : 4 :: 6 : 3, or 8 : 4 = 6 : 3; that is, 8 is to 4 as 6 is to 3, or, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to a line of 4 feet as a line of 6 feet is to a line of 3 feet. These four terms, or numbers, are proportional, and this proportion is called Geometric because it is an equality of ratios. The following, however, is Arithmetic: 4 is to 3 as 2 to 1, because the excess of the first antecedent with respect to the first consequent is the same as that of the second antecedent with respect to the second consequent.

Two ratios, then, are equal to each other when the antecedent of the first contains its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second contains its own, or when the antecedent of the first is contained in its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second is contained in its own. Thus the ratio 12 to 6 is equal to the ratio 48 to 24, and the ratio 3 to 6 is equal to the ratio 50 to 100. Two equal ratios, then, make up a Geometric proportion.

Two quantities are said to be in direct ratio when the first and third terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, and the second and fourth terms of the same proportion relate to another. Let us suppose, e.g., that Peter has 100 of wisdom and 100 of study, but that Paul has only 50 of Wisdom and 50 of study. Peter and Paul will have Wisdom in the direct ratio of their study: I shall say, therefore, that the Wisdom of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the study of Peter is to the study of Paul. In this proportion the first and third terms belong to Peter, while the second and fourth relate to Paul, as is evident. This ratio is therefore called direct.

Two quantities are in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio when the first and fourth terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, while the second and third relate to another. If Peter, e.g., has 100 of knowledge and 50 of study, and Paul has 50 of knowledge and 100 of labor, the knowledge of Peter and the knowledge of Paul will be in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio. I shall say, therefore, that the knowledge of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the labor of Paul is to the labor of Peter. The first and fourth

> [p. 37]

[p. 37] terms of this proportion belong to Peter, the second and third relate to Paul, as is self-evident.

>  PROPORT. ARGUMENT. 97. tus terminus hujus proportionis. pertinent ad Petrum, secundus & tertius ad Paulum spectant,ut per se patet. —

The ratio which arises from the multiplication of several ratios with one another is called a compound Ratio. Thus, if there are the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5, and you multiply the antec. 8 by the antec. 3, and the conseq. 4 by the conseq. 5, the ratio of the product 24 from the antecedents to the product 20 from the consequents is said to be compounded of the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5.

> Rari» illa quae oritur éx multiplicatione plorium rationum inter se, dicitur Ratio composita. Sic si fuerit ratio 8 ad 4 & 53 ad $ multiplices autem antec. 8 per antec. 5. & conseq. 4 pir con-seq. $, ratio producti 24 ex antecedentibus ad productum :o ex consequentibus, dicitur composica ex rationibus 8 ad 4 & 3 ad ;.

If there are several quantities, of which the first has the same ratio to the second as the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, then the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Likewise it is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Thus if, e.g., there are four lines, of which the first is of 16 feet, the second of 8 feet, the third of 4 ft. and the fourth of 2 ft., and you ask the ratio of the first to the second, I shall say that it is double, or as 2 to 1. But if you ask the ratio of the first, of 16 ft., to the third, of 4 ft., I shall say that it is twice double, because it is compounded of the ratio of the first line, of 16 ft., to the second, 8, which is double, and of the ratio of the second, namely 8, to the third, 4, which again is double; whence the ratio of the first to the third is the duplicate of the ratio of the first to the second, or is twice double, or in a word quadruple. And the ratio of the first to the fourth, or 16 to 2, is the triplicate of the ratio of the first to the second. And so it must be compounded of the double ratio, which is that of the first to the second, and of the quadruple ratio, which is that of the same first to the third; and thus it is twice quadruple, or, in a word, octuple.”

## Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

> PROBLEMA V. (Fig. 5.)

To divide a line in extreme and mean ratio.

> Lintam exirema , «c media vatione dividere.

Let the line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio, that is, by finding in the same line the mean and the extreme proportionals. At A let a perpendicular AC be placed, equal to half of the whole AB; then let CB be drawn, and from it let CD be cut off, equal to the line CA; and let the remainder DB be transferred from A to E; and the line AB will be cut proportionally at E, so that the greater part AE is a mean proportional between the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Moreover, the square on the line AE will be equal to the rectangle of the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Because of its outstanding uses this was called by the ancients the Divine proportion. From Theor. VIII of this book, cor. I.

Let there be given three figures, circular or rectilinear, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, BC, DE. Let AB, BC be set at a right angle and produced indefinitely, and let AC be drawn; then let AC be transferred to BF, and DE to BG. The line FG will be the diameter, or homologous side, of a figure similar and equal to the three together upon the lines AB, BC, DE. If the lines AB, BC are taken as equal, the figure upon AC will be double the similar figure upon AB or BC; and when AC is transferred to BF, the figure upon FC (which is here understood to be drawn) will be triple; and when FC is transferred to BH, the figure upon HC (were it drawn) will similarly be quadruple the figure upon AB; and so on to infinity. To subtract a similar figure from another, or to diminish it, or to enlarge it in any proportion whatever.

> .. PROBLEMA VILI. ( Fig. 8. )

Let there be two similar figures, rectilinear or circular, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, CB. Upon the greater line BC let a semicircle be made, within which let another line be fitted equal to the line AB; then let the straight line AC be drawn, which will be the side of the figure sought: the figure by which the similar figure upon BC exceeds the figure described upon AB. From the same Theor.

Hence it is plain how any figure whatever is to be diminished to a given proportion: e.g., let a third part be taken away from the figure described upon BC. Having made the semicircle, let BC be divided into three parts, and then at the intersection of one third, DC, let a perpendicular DA be erected; finally let AC be drawn. The figure upon AC will be the third part of the similar figure upon BC, and the figure upon BA two thirds of the same. From the same.

To convert any Figure whatever into an equal Rectangle.

Theorem XI. (Fig. 11.) The Square of the side of the Pentagon, AC, is equal to the two Squares together of the side AB

of the Decagon and of the side FC of the Hexagon. (a)

Prep. Let the arc AC of the Pentagon, of 72 degrees, be bisected at B; whence the arcs AB, BC of the Decagon will each be of 36 degrees. Then let a perpendicular FD be drawn which bisects the line and the arc AB at D; whence the arcs AD, BD will each be of 18 degrees, and the whole arc CD of 54 degrees.

Dem. Since the whole angle F of the Pentagon is of 72 degrees, and the equal angles FCA, FAC are each of half of 108 degrees, the remainder to two right angles, they will each be of 54 degrees, as is also the angle EFC, whose arc DC is of 54 degrees: therefore, since the two Triangles AFC and EFC have the angles EFC and CAF equal, and also the angle C in common, they will be equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the larger triangle is CA to CF, so in the smaller, CEF, is the same CF to CE; therefore the Rectangle made of the extremes CA, CE is equal to the Square made of the mean CF, the semidiameter, or side of the Hexagon. By Theor. I, cor. 3.

Again, since DF is perpendicular to AB, which it bisects, the sides AE, EB will be equal, by Theor. IV, bk. 1, and the angle ABE equal to the angle EAB, to which the angle BCA is also equal, because of the isosceles triangle ABC: therefore the two triangles ABC and AEB are also equiangular and proportional: therefore, as the whole AC to AB, so the same AB to AE: therefore the rectangle made of the extremes AC, AE is equal to the square of the side AB of the Decagon.

II. Circumferences, Chords and Arcs are to one another as the radii. For let the arcs CD, FE be similar, e.g. a sixth part of a circle: since the angle B is common, and the sides CB, DB are equal, as are also FB, EB, the triangles FBE, CBD will be similar: by Theor. III, cor. 2; therefore the chord CD will be to the chord FE as the radius CB to the radius FB; and, dividing the arcs equally at G and H, CG will be to FH as CB to FB; and, continuing the bisection, CP will be to FR as CB to FB: but to equal arcs correspond equal chords, by Theor. IV, bk. 2; therefore the arcs also have the same ratio as the radii; and all of them together, that is, the circumferences, are to one another as the radii.

IV. Circles also have the duplicate proportion of the radii; for the Triangles BCD and CFE have the duplicate proportion of the radii CB and FB, by the preceding Cor. Let the arcs be bisected at G and H. The similar Triangles inscribed, CBG and FBH, will also have the duplicate [proportion] of the radii. Likewise, the bisection being made again at P and R, M and N, all the similar triangles inscribed in the circle will have the duplicate proportion of the radii: by the preceding Cor. But the circles are equal to the whole sum of the triangles that can be inscribed in them (for if any space were left over in the circle, another triangle could be inscribed by bisecting the arc; and so the sum of all the triangles would not be understood to have been inscribed, contrary to the hypothesis); therefore circles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their radii. Hence whatever was said in the Corollaries of Theor. VI on similar rectilinear figures must also be applied to circles. (a)

> - - Mw PI

Moreover, just as Surfaces, which consist of a twofold dimension, namely breadth and length, have, if they are similar, the duplicate proportion of the Diameters, or of the homologous sides, so similar bodies, such as two whole spheres, have the triplicate proportion of the same, since they are made of a threefold dimension, namely breadth, length and depth. For example, if the Diameter of the earth is quadruple the Diameter of the Moon, the surface of the Earth will be four times quadruple, that is, sixteen times the surface of the Moon; and the whole terraqueous body will be four times sixteen, that is, sixty-four times, greater than the body of the Moon. Likewise, since the diameter of Venus appears as the tenth part of the diameter of the Sun, its apparent circle will be the hundredth part of the whole circle of the Sun; and so, when Venus comes between us and the Sun, it will appear like a spot on the Sun. And whoever knows these things has the most open access to all the natural disciplines.

3 The objects of Physics are Body, Space and Motion; what is understood by these I shall indicate in a few words. Whatever thing we can behold with the eyes, or grasp and feel with the hand, and which resists pressure, we call Body. The extension of the universe, in which bodies are placed and move freely, we call Space. The transfer of a body from one part of space into another we call Motion.

4 All the positions, motions, changes and actions of bodies which are observed by the senses, whether by one or by several, are called Phenomena. It is agreed that all bodies are moved according to certain laws or rules. A law of nature, moreover, is that norm according to which God willed certain motions to be performed always, that is, on all occasions; hence, e.g., every plant produces its own seed, from which a like plant, not a different one, is born again; hence every animal begets from itself one like itself. A heavy body freely left to itself falls downward of its own accord. By means of these laws we understand what happens naturally and what miraculously. For those phenomena are natural which are observed constantly in the same manner when bodies are placed on similar occasions; but there are miracles when phenomena occur contrary to those laws.

5 But if something happens according to the laws of nature, yet beyond what is usual, or contrary to what is owed to such a nature, it is called nonnatural: as a fever, which so agitates the beating both of the heart and of the arteries that they are said to be in a nonnatural state. What surpasses the forces and laws of nature is called supernatural. Thus if the Sun, e.g., while it is at noon, were rolled back toward the east, this is supernatural, because it cannot be brought about by any forces of nature, as is evident. There are, however, certain things which, even though they are above nature, can nevertheless be judged only by a man cultivated in good Philosophy and well practiced, whether they are natural or beyond nature. Hence we must judge cautiously of unusual things, lest we take for miracles things which are not such. This warning is most useful, so that we may meet the foolish multitude of the unlearned, and indeed also of those who, though learned in other matters, yet, because they are without good Philosophy, are prone to give credence to any chattering little woman who tells of some miracle.

The usefulness of Physics. 6

The dignity, certainly, and the excellence of Physics can be understood amply enough even from this alone, that the study of this discipline extends as far as nature itself. And indeed, who will deny that it is by far the worthiest thing now to contemplate the vastness of the heavens and the mass of the bodies running their courses in them by a fixed law, now to penetrate into the hidden recesses of the earth, to search out the origin of metals and stones and the almost infinite variety of plants and animals, and finally to consider the majesty of God shining forth in this universe of things? Hence Seneca (b) valued this contemplation so highly that he did not hesitate to say: unless I were admitted to these things (the more secret things of nature), it would not have been worth while to be born.

7 Then delight and the sweetest pleasure spring from this study of nature. For whom would a science not delight in which there is never lacking the occasion both of discovering and of contemplating new and wonderful effects, as so many shining testimonies of the supreme Maker of things? Who could behold the most diverse kinds of innumerable animals, terrestrial, aquatic, flying, insects, the wondrous variety of the other things, their beauty and their fitness for definite uses, without a noble pleasure of mind? What of the fact that those very things which commonly fill the unskilled with dread afford the physicist a most delightful spectacle? Thus, while the rude multitude is shaken by an empty fear of eclipses, the Philosophers

Such advantages, however, and innumerable others which I silently pass over, you will seek in vain in the School of the Peripatetics, if we may call Physics that discipline in which most things have customarily been taught everywhere against the observation of nature and against plain experiments. But it is a pleasure to hear the excellent mathematician and physicist Tomás Vicente Tosca, the glory of our Spain and a most distinguished ornament of the Congregation of the Oratory of Valencia. Let them hear a Spaniard, those who, steeped in contemptible prejudices, falsely suppose that the Physics of the Moderns is cultivated only by heretics, and judge it impious that it should be set before studious youth and commended to them: a race of men born for the ruin and destruction of the good arts.

11 “I know not, certainly (so speaks the most illustrious Tosca (e)), I know not, certainly, by what fate, and that an unhappy enough one, the School of the

Peripatetics has now for some centuries back been so given over to metaphysical speculations that it seems to neglect physical things altogether: books come out daily, to the point of nausea, which pursue the last fine points of the being of reason, but pass over altogether the nature and causes of the wonderful effects of nature that meet our eyes every day. Nothing was once held more pleasant (says Luis Vives

(f)) than the contemplation of this garden of nature: but now the inquiry into natural things is so entangled in metaphysical abstractions that upon them, as upon a weak foundation, there rises nothing but a vast edifice of assertions and of dissenting opinions, or rather a cross is set up, on which minds are tortured rather than delighted by so great a pleasantness of natural things.

12 “It is surely most to be lamented by what windings those have made a labyrinth of the whole of philosophy who treat physical things not physically, as is fitting, but with metaphysical precisions remote from all sense and experiment; it is to be lamented again that minds otherwise lofty, while they desire to satisfy their hunger for knowledge, are fed for at least a whole three years on the empty food of beings of reason alone, not without the greatest loss to youth, their minds being held back, namely, lest they go on to better things.

13 “To better things, I said. For who would doubt that the study of natural things is far more excellent than those metaphysical questions, not to say trifles, over which it is customary in the Schools to contend sharply in perpetual litigation, and for the most part about words? Certainly, when God willed to disclose to Job the incomparable eminence of his wisdom, he put to him a great many questions, and wonderful ones, taken from the storehouses of natural philosophy, as is manifest from the whole of chapters 38 and 39; but of those things which are made so much of in the Schools, not a word.

> ^ L JH uL

14 “He could, however, have asked him a great many things about the being of reason: namely, whether and how it exists, what its fabric is, what powers or what acts concur in its construction; whether, moreover, it can be produced by God, or by the Angels, or by the bodily senses? About precisions, too, he could have inquired whether they are only formal, or objective as well? About lacks, moreover, whether there are any? nay, whether there are even lacks of lacks? and likewise whether the essences of things are really distinct from their existence? But about these and other like things, deep silence.

15 “Moreover, in Wisdom, ch. 7, Solomon commends the knowledge bestowed on him by God, not because God taught him that huge crowd of formalities, distinctions and reflexions, but rather because he disclosed to him the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements, the beginning, and ending, and midst of the times, the alterations of their courses, and the changes of seasons, the revolutions of the year, and the dispositions of the stars, the natures of living creatures, and rage of wild beasts, the force of winds, etc.” Thus far Tosca. What do those men say to these things, who are little or not at all studious of physical things? 16 There will not be lacking, therefore, men who will try to throw you down at the very entrance and to call you away from the reflections you have undertaken, by dinning again and again into your ears and minds that this kind of Physics is new, obscure, and wrapped on every side in mathematical coverings; but, despising the raillery of the detractors, apply yourselves diligently to the most beautiful study of nature, and do not let yourselves be led away by the talk of the unskilled. It is true indeed that without the aid of Geometry no worthy progress can be made in Physics; but you have sufficiently experienced this aid in what has gone before, when you went through such Geometrical Institutions as were needed. For those Elements of Geometry set out above as briefly as possible suffice for a fuller understanding of our Physics.

But since it has been the custom of all physicists to indicate at the outset the sect to which they had sworn, there will perhaps be some who demand this of us as well, asking: Do we follow Descartes, or Leibniz, or Newton, or someone else? To them we answer in these few words. We profess that our judgment is free, so that we will swear to the sect of no Philosopher; for we think there has been no sect that saw every truth, and none that did not hold something of the truth. Therefore to gather into one body the truth scattered among individuals and dispersed through the sects, this we judge to belong properly to our undertaking. But it is well, on the very threshold, to set down the rules of philosophizing.

§. VI.

On the Rules of philosophizing. 19

While we try to explain phenomena and to investigate the laws of nature, it will be necessary to attend scrupulously to the following rules of philosophizing prescribed by the most illustrious Newton (i). The first is as follows.

20 No more causes of natural things ought to be admitted than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their phenomena. For if a cause is merely possible, it can never be held to be true, however apt and suited it may otherwise have been to producing the effect. That the same effect can arise from several causes is a matter beyond doubt; but of so many causes not more than one really exists and operates, and it alone is to be investigated by physicists, because it alone is the true cause of that effect. Those Philosophers are surely to be spurned who strive to derive natural effects from their own hypotheses and from causes feigned at pleasure, little concerned about the existence of those causes. Hypotheses, therefore, are in that case to be banished from Physics; for, as Musschenbroek very well says (j), whatever is gathered from them is inconstant; from them useless controversies are stirred up; phenomena are feigned so that the hypotheses may be strengthened and defended.

21 Unless perhaps we must agree with the most illustrious Perrault (k), who, not altogether unreasonably, rules on hypotheses very much in this manner. He contends that hypotheses bound by fixed laws are suited to the investigation of truth, being led by this reason: that from hypotheses laid down beforehand we strive in the most fitting order toward the thesis, and it is plain that a great many things which at present we hold as certain were once among the number of hypotheses. Now the laws by which the method of hypotheses ought to be restricted would chiefly be these, namely: Let the hypothesis flow from natural things and arise from phenomena observed again and again, but let no position be fashioned at whim, toward which nature herself is dragged by I know not what tricks; let the proposition, assumed not without foundation, correspond exactly not to one or another phenomenon only, but to all of that kind; let it, moreover, dissent from no phenomenon of another kind that has been ascertained and is of tested certainty, and likewise from no evident principle; finally, let it generate conclusions of such a kind as are held sober and consonant with the tenets of the saner Philosophers, and proceed by sure consequence from the assumed foundation of the doctrine. The second rule of philosophizing is this.

22 Of natural effects of the same kind the causes are the same. This rule is easily derived from the first. For (by the first rule) nature is simple and does not abound in superfluous causes; therefore to attribute effects of the same kind, or wholly alike, to different causes is altogether repugnant to the simplicity of nature. Thus the descent of heavy bodies in Europe and in America is to be attributed to the same cause. By like reasoning, since anatomical observations show the same instruments of respiration in all men, we rightly conclude that the cause of breathing is the same in each. But one must carefully beware lest from merely external characters we pronounce boldly on the perfect likeness of effects. Thus certain lethal plants imitate the external appearance of wholesome plants,

23 The qualities of bodies which cannot be intended and remitted (that is, neither increased nor diminished) and which belong to all bodies on which it is possible to make experiments, are to be held for qualities of all bodies universally. That is, those which persist always the same and invariable in bodies, however the condition of time and place may vary, and whatever change or alteration bodies may undergo; such as solidity and figurability: for there are other qualities which can be intended and remitted, and of this kind are gravity and the force of attraction. For when the distance of a body from the center toward which it tends, either by gravity or by attraction, is diminished, the forces of gravity and of attraction are increased, and they are diminished when the distance is increased, as can be found by experiment in iron attracted to a magnet. These are the rules of philosophizing which we shall use from here on.

## §. VII

> Inulti efie nec debemus; nec vero póífumus,

Division of Physics. 24

Following the method now accepted among men most practiced in teaching this discipline, Physics has customarily been marked out in a twofold treatment, namely under the name of General and of Particular. The General considers body taken generally and the principles of natural composites, and likewise comprehends the phenomena pertaining to them, as also their causes. The Particular examines the single kinds of bodies and demonstrates their forces, properties and operations. We shall perform both at once, since we neither ought, nor indeed are able, to be lengthy.

The first thing to be asked in this dissertation would be whether bodies exist, so that it might first be established that the thing whose nature we undertake to inquire into exists. But since our consciousness persuades us of their existence, we propose this, as a kind of postulate, to be granted by our adversaries, holding it for certain that a most certain matter is only made more obscure by a superfluous inquiry. Bodies, therefore, exist. But concerning their essence the opinion of Philosophers is not one and the same.

2 The excellent Philosopher René Descartes, wonderfully versed in the mathematical disciplines, placed the nature of corporeal substance in extension; for he says (l): we shall perceive that the nature of matter, or of body regarded in general, does not consist in its being a thing hard, or heavy, or colored, or affecting the senses in any other way, but only in its being a thing extended in length, breadth and depth: which

Aristotle also asserted, for in Bk. 3 of the Physics, text 43, body is, he says, that which has dimension in every direction. But let us set out the state of the question. The question, then, asks: what is the formal reason of physical body? that is, which of all those attributes that belong to body (as impenetrability, extension, divisibility, etc.) is so first in the body itself that from it, as from a root, all the rest proceed? 3 I say first, against Descartes and Aristotle: the essence of body is by no means placed in actual extension, or in threefold dimension. It is proved. Who will deny that God, Best and Greatest, can destroy the whole mass of air which is enclosed between the earth and the Moon? But then the very same extension would remain, and yet no corporeal substance would be left: therefore. But Descartes denies that this can happen: for he thinks that if, e.g., the air of this little room were destroyed, the walls themselves would touch one another, since those things are said to be joined which are separated by no intervening body; or he thinks that in this hypothesis a most manifest contradiction is contained, since that space would indeed be void, as is supposed, and at the same time not void, because there would always be threefold dimension in it, and therefore body itself.

> ' quam :e(lentia. perfecta corporis phyfici, ut ipfi contendunt: quemadmodum. quia figura circulo & triangulo communis eft, non poteít haec fola alterucríus effentia haberi; eflentialiter igitur corpus phyficum aliquid aliud habere debet, per quod à (implici extenfione , & à corpore mathemático. diflinguatur. C.

4 But who does not see that Descartes here imposes upon us, since he proves the same by the same, and assumes in place of a principle what had been placed in controversy? For he contends that a void cannot be made by God for no other reason than that body would always remain in that space, extension, namely, remaining, which according to him is the essence of body; and that is the very thing under dispute. Next: although it is certain that two bodies touch each other when no other body lies between them, yet it is not necessary that those things touch which are separated by no body. Descartes, therefore, confuses physical body with mathematical body. But who does not see that what constitutes physical body must be one thing, and what constitutes mathematical body another; or that the nature of the body which is contained in our imagination alone is one, and that of the body which is also found in the very nature of things is another? Thus what constitutes a Geometrical line is that it have length without breadth; and yet the essence of a line which is found really and physically in the nature of things need not consist in length alone without breadth.

5 The Cartesians could indeed reply that mathematical body differs very greatly from physical body, but not by reason of extension, which is essentially common to both. But they ought also to take note of this: that then extension could no longer be held to be the complete essence of physical body, as they themselves contend; just as, because figure is common to the circle and to the triangle, it cannot be held to be the sole essence of either of them. Essentially, therefore, physical body must have something else, by which it is distinguished both from simple extension and from mathematical body.

T H E O B J E C T I O N S A R E A N S W E R E D.

7

Obj. 1, for the opinion of Descartes: when threefold dimension is understood, all the other things that are in body being cut away, body is understood; for spirit is not understood, as is evident; and between body and spirit there is no middle: therefore the formal reason of body is threefold dimension. The argument could very well be turned back against the adversaries, and prove against them that the formal reason of body consists in impenetrability. Reply: I distinguish the antecedent. Body is understood according to its more obvious property, I grant; according to its essence,

I deny; and I deny the consequent. Body is surely understood by the very fact that a substance divisible into integral parts is conceived; and yet the Cartesians will not say that divisibility into parts so belongs to body that it is in no way to be distinguished from its formal reason.

8 Obj. 2. Whoever are willing to attend to the idea of body are forced to admit that they conceive body in no other way than as a substance extended in every direction: therefore the formal reason of body is not different from threefold dimension.

The argument proves too much: for in the idea of body not only threefold extension, but also actual impenetrability presents itself. Reply: I deny the consequent; for since the greater part of our ideas is acquired by sense [§. 14, Log.], and it is certain that the inmost attributes of things become in no way known to us immediately through the ministry of the senses [§. 29, Log.], it remains that the formal reason of body is not that attribute of it which occurs to us in the idea of body that we drew in in the time of infancy, but that attribute can most rightly be called only the more obvious property of body.

9 Obj. 3. St. Augustine, addressing Evodius, says (n): I ask you whether you think there is any body that does not, in its own measure, have length, breadth and depth? ….. If you take this away from bodies, in my opinion they can neither be perceived by the senses nor rightly be judged to be bodies: therefore. Reply: these words must be understood of bodies as to existence, since certainly without some extension no body could be sensible; but not as to essence: just as body cannot indeed exist without figure, and yet no one would say that its essence is placed in figure. We do not deny, however, that extension is one of the properties of body; we contend only that it is not the first attribute in body.

10 Obj. 4. No body can exist, be seen, or be conceived without threefold dimension: therefore extension is the formal reason of body.

(n) Bk. On the Magnitude of the Soul, no. 6.

The consequent does not follow; because neither can any finite body be conceived without figure, nor man without the capacity for knowledge, and yet these ought by no means to pertain to their essence. You will say: if the essence of body is constituted in threefold dimension, the spirituality of the rational soul is most clearly proved, as was shown in the Psychology: therefore. Reply: in our opinion on the essence of body the argument for the spirituality of the soul has the same force; for just as, from the fact that the rational soul cannot have actual extension, Descartes rightly infers that it is incorporeal, so we, from the fact that the rational soul does not require to have extension, very well infer that it is of a different nature from body.

11 Obj. 5. When we wish to conceive in the mind that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we imagine a certain extension: therefore extension itself is conceived by us not as a property, but as the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent; and from the phantasm of our imagination the essence, or formal reason, of body is well gathered, I deny; is wrongly gathered, I grant; and I deny the consequent. The argument proves that matter was already existing before the creation of the world: for we conceive extension: therefore, according to the Cartesians, we conceive body: therefore that body was existing from eternity, which is absurd.

> rimus, quod illa fit diyerfae naturde ac corpus. — «s 5.

12 But the Cartesians insist: of nothing there is no extension, no property, no quality; but when we conceive that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we conceive it as extended: therefore we conceive something, and not nothing itself, and consequently we conceive some body. But in this argument (as the Most Illustrious Pierre Daniel Huet (o) very well notes) Descartes is deluded: for he ought to have observed that properties, or qualities, are of two kinds, some positive, others negative; that of nothing there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. For we say that nothing is incorruptible, that nothing is like nothing, that nothing is contrary to being, that the world was created by God out of nothing, etc. But these properties are mere negations, namely of corruption, of difference from nothing, etc. Likewise, when we imagine that the wine which is contained in some vessel is reduced to nothing by God, no other body being admitted into the place of the wine, it must be said that the space which was occupied by the wine remains void, and that it will be of the same amplitude and extension as the wine was before; and we shall deservedly attribute extension to this void space, but a negative one: for when I say that that empty space which is inside the vessel is of one square foot, it will be just as if I said that in that space of a foot there is no body; and this extension of a foot, of the void, or of nothing, will be the negation of body in a space of a foot.

in the natural exigency of occupying place impenetrably. Proof of the conclusion: the formal reason of physical body is rightly constituted in that from which the other attributes are derived as from a root, as all agree; but such an attribute is natural impenetrability, or, what is the same, radical impenetrability: therefore. Proof of the minor: from it flows the entitative extension of body; for that is called entitatively extended which comprises several parts united among themselves in such a way that the whole entity of one exists outside the entity of another; but several things cannot be conjoined among themselves in this way unless they are naturally impenetrable: therefore.

15 There follows solidity, by virtue of which bodies either cannot be compressed, or can be constrained by our forces only to a certain degree. Then mobility; because, if bodies did not resist bodies, we could scarcely think of the motion which we experience in things. Then divisibility, measurability, and the capacity to receive any figure whatever follow from natural impenetrability. Secondly: it seems evident that such an exigency cannot be demonstrated of body a priori; for there is nothing in body from which, as from a principle, or root, its natural impenetrability could be deduced; for body is not impenetrable because it is extended, but on the contrary it is entitatively extended because it is impenetrable.

16 Obj. 1. Impenetrability belongs also to Angels. For an Angel can be in place in such a way that it excludes any body whatever from it; [p. 14] therefore impenetrability cannot be the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent. If impenetrability is taken for the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, as it is taken in the question, I deny; if it is taken for a free power of non-penetration, I grant. The impenetrability of body is such that, because of it, a body cannot by the forces of nature subsist together with another in the same place, and by its very essence it always requires to occupy the place in which it exists with the exclusion of every other body. But an Angel is of such a nature that it does not fill place, although it can freely repel any body whatever, by its own force, from the place in which it is.

17 Obj. 2. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel: therefore body is not distinguished from spirit by impenetrability; and for that reason the formal reason of body is not well placed in natural impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel through its own defect, I deny; by reason of the Angel, I grant; and I deny the consequent. Body by its nature seeks to exclude from its place everything that fills place. Hence, since a spiritual substance is not repletive of place, neither is it of such a kind that body could expel it from its place. Moreover, since it is evident from what was taught in the preceding place that the impenetrability which is in body does not belong to Angels, there can be no doubt that body is sufficiently distinguished from spirit by radical impenetrability.

18 Obj. 3. One body can by divine power be together with another in the same place: therefore body can be deprived of impenetrability, and so etc. I deny the consequent; for although some body may by a miracle be stripped of actual impenetrability, yet it always requires to have it, nor can such an exigency ever be taken away from it; in exactly the same way as, although actual heat may be taken away from fire, and downward motion from a stone, or be impeded by God, yet the power, nay even the exigency, remains, by which, once the obstacle is removed, those bodies would actually produce their proper effect.

19 Obj. 4. An extended thing can arise only from extended things: therefore extension is an attribute of body prior to impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent: and these extended things are apt for composing body by reason of their impenetrability, I grant; and they are not so, I deny. For indeed, just as this does not prevent the extended thing from being, of its own kind, something composite, so it does not prevent the aptitude of the parts for composing it, namely their natural impenetrability, from being an attribute of the composite itself prior to its entitative extension: for natural impenetrability is nothing other than the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, and the parts of body are rendered apt for constituting an extended thing through this impenetrability of theirs.

20 You will say: the principles from whose union the entitatively extended whole arises are not body if taken separately, but principles of body: therefore the formal reason of corporeal substance is not

> [p. 15]

[p. 15] different from extension, but is extension itself. I deny the antecedent; because the parts constituting the extended thing, taken separately, are material, or corporeal, substance (for they are not spirits): therefore the formal reason of corporeal substance is different from entitative extension: therefore, if the reason of material substance is different from extension, the reason of body too will be plainly different from it.

21 Obj. 5. The essence of body is explained better through the collection of all its attributes than through natural impenetrability, so that body is called a substance by its nature impenetrable, extended, divisible, mobile, and apt to receive any figure whatever: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: and this is the state of the question, I deny; and it is not, I grant. I explain the solution: however much the properties mentioned may be proper affections of bodies, and, thus collected, may belong to body alone, this does not prevent its being asserted that among those very ones listed there is some one attribute which occurs in the first place in bodies, and from which the remaining properties found in them flow. Certainly it cannot come into controversy that general properties so inhere in body that they in no way belong to a thing distinct from it, since that cannot even be called into doubt; and this notion, as it is obvious to anyone, so need not be discussed at length by a Philosopher.

On the Principles of natural body.

## CHAPTER I

General notions of principles. 22

Intrinsic principles of a natural composite are all those from which the composite itself is essentially constituted. Thus the rational soul and the body are intrinsic principles of man. These are either primary or secondary. Primary are those from which the composite itself is so constituted that they themselves are in no way composed, together, of others into which they could be resolved; or, as the Scholastics say, which are made neither from one another, nor from others, but all things are made from them. Those are called secondary principles which do indeed constitute a natural composite, but themselves too coalesce essentially from others. Thus the organic body is a secondary principle of man, since it so constitutes man that it itself too, together with

C [p. 16] others, is essentially composed. Moreover, the intrinsic principles of things are either metaphysical, or artificial, or sensible.

23 Metaphysical are those which, after the manner of metaphysical things, cannot be reached by sense, but only grasped by the intellect. Artificial are those which, disposed and conjoined by a certain wonderful artifice of nature, compose natural body in such a way that all its sensible affections and operations arise from the magnitude, figure, motion, etc. of the parts, and can be suitably explained from these. Sensible, finally, or Physical, are called those which can really be separated from one another by a true resolution of bodies, and be discerned with the aid of the senses. It is established among all Philosophers, the Ancients as well as the Moderns, that any natural composite which can be produced and destroyed by the forces of nature consists of a twofold essential principle; of which one is determinable and is called matter, the other determining, and is named form. For it is certain that natural changes of one composite into another as to substance take place: for who would deny that food, e.g., is changed into chyle, this into blood, and blood into the other parts of the organic body; of which one is surely converted into another on such terms that nothing sensible remains out of which each of them essentially coalesces?

24 Now it is certain that a composite which is changed by the forces of nature is neither made by creation nor reduced to nothing. It is certain, therefore, that there is something from which, as existing, all things are made, and which is therefore common to all; and this is rightly designated as the determinable principle, or matter. In a not dissimilar way, since, as is plain, natural composites differ from one another as to substance, but are in no way distinguished by that part which is equally common to all, it is made manifest that there is something else in bodies which is called the determining principle, that is, form. Wherefore, if matter is taken for the subject from which, as previously existing, natural composites are produced, and form precisely for that by which each composite is the very thing that it is, and is distinguished from the rest as to essence, it is plain indeed that no question can be raised concerning the existence of these principles between the Peripatetics and the Moderns. But just as these same principles, so taken, are contained in abstract notions and are by no means objects of Physical consideration, so they contribute nothing to explaining the nature, affections and operations of physical things.

25 The whole business, therefore, that this matter involves consists in this: that it be made plain what the physical nature of these principles is; namely, what physically is that from which, as pre-existing, as from a determinable subject, natural composites are produced by created causes, and what is that by which each composite is what it is, and is essentially distinguished from any other? The Peripatetics gave us nothing on this matter, content to have considered matter and form metaphysically. But the Moderns, having rejected the scholastic subtleties, are wholly engaged in setting out openly the physical nature of these principles; whence it appears how falsely the common Peripatetics

> [p. 17]

[p. 17] say that neither matter nor form is admitted by the Moderns. These things, then, being established, let us look at the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics.

t must be supposed that any natural body can be considered in two ways: 26

I       both inasmuch as it is generated, or, as the Peripatetics speak, in fieri, and

inasmuch as it has already been generated, or, as they themselves say, in facto esse. The principles of natural body, inasmuch as it is generated, are three according to Aristotle (p): matter, form, and privation: for generation is a certain passage from substantial non-being to that substantial being, in which passage three things necessarily concur, namely the terminus a quo, or the privation of that being; that being which is acquired, which is form; and that from which the thing constituted through that being is made, which is matter. The principles of natural body already made, or in facto esse, are only two, namely matter and form, as was said above. In addition, they say that union is a certain form, or substantial mode, a part ut quo, whose office is to bring it about that a certain complete substantial whole is constituted from matter and form.

The Thomists generally deny that this union is distinct from matter and form; the others hold the contrary, and acknowledge it as a true modal entity. Nay, indeed, there are some to whom another union of that very union, which they call unition, seems to need asserting. But these things, like most others, are not of such importance that they ought to be set out by me at greater length.

27 The Peripatetics teach, besides, that prime matter is a simple, incomplete substance, the first foundation of corporeal things, and the first subject of natural transmutations.
