28 From what has been said they infer: that prime matter is a subject indifferent to many forms, and indeed not modal, but absolute; for if it were an accident, it would be received in another subject, and consequently would not be the first subject: that it is simple, that is, not composed of subject and form, for then it would not be the first principle; this, however, does not prevent its being composed integrally of extended parts. They infer also that it is incomplete, that is, that it is ordered to constituting a whole together with another substantial part: that it is ingenerable and incorruptible; for since generation is the production of a thing from a presupposed subject, and corruption the ceasing of a thing while the subject remains, and since matter, which is the first subject, can neither be presupposed by itself nor remain when destroyed, it can therefore neither be generated nor be corrupted. That it is naturally indestructible, because God destroys no substance except at the demand of a stronger enemy, and there is nothing in things hostile to matter.

> Leibnitzii, u

29 As regards form, they say that it is an incomplete substance, which as first act completes and informs matter, so as to constitute natural body in a determinate species. It is called incomplete, because together with matter it is determined to constituting the composite; it is called act, because it determines the potency of matter to a certain complement and to a certain species of composite: and it is called first act, that it may be distinguished from accidents, which are acts of matter, but secondary ones. The

> 30 y Eibnitzius admittit in natura vim aliquam infenfbilem, . I & entia abilracto: atque hac de caufa in claffe. co* . 7 rum ei; qui izerapbyficaes five infen[ióiiia corporum prin.

Peripatetics affirm that all composites consist of matter and form so explained. From what has been said they infer: 1. that the specific difference of bodies is taken not from matter, as being the same in species in all, but from form. 2. that substantial form is produced anew in every generation, and destroyed in corruption (the rational soul excepted), prime matter remaining, which is incorruptible. 3. that all forms (the rational soul excepted) are educed from the potency of matter, either by a created cause, if a proportionate one is present, or by God alone, as author of nature. So far the system of the Peripatetics.

## CHAPTER III

The System of Leibniz is very briefly set out and refuted. 30

> [p. 19]

Leibniz admits in nature some insensible force, and abstract beings: and for this reason he is in the class of those who, as the principles of bodies, metaphysical, or insensible, ones [p. 19] have laid down. The elements of all things, according to him, are monads, or simple, ingenerable and incorruptible substances created by God. Every monad represents the whole universe, and so is in a certain way all things; but just as we do not sufficiently discern remote things with our eyes, so it comes about that not all the things that are in any given monad are distinctly represented. His complete system was published in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (s). But who could grasp with his mind that any monad whatever, that is, a being devoid of parts, represents the whole totality of things? Nor is it my intention to reproach Leibniz with the use, in explaining his opinion, of words beneath which no distinct idea lies, which Hartsoeker has done in full (t); nor to show that the monadology is not far removed from the error of idealism, which has been done expressly by Jac. Frider. Müller. It will be enough to have touched upon these few things.

They are, moreover, of this kind.

Axiom II. That system is to be preferred to the others which is simpler, and explains the properties, effects and phenomena of natural body from fewer principles. Beings, assuredly, are not to be multiplied beyond necessity; likewise, what can be done by fewer things ought not to be done by more, as all Philosophers agree. Wherefore neither the principles of things nor the causes of effects are to be multiplied, unless an undoubted reason demands it, as was said above [§. 20.]. Axiom III. That system is to be judged the better which unfolds the more of the things that must be taken into consideration among Physicists. For the whole of Physics is engaged in this: that the affections, effects, etc. of natural things be explained, as many of them as possible, and as well as possible.

## 33 On the reason given for this axiom is founded Axiom IV. That system is to be

> 29 ELEM. REC. PHILOSOPH. P. IV.

preferred to the rest which not only uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, but also sets forth in particular the nature of bodies, their affections, and the causes of effects, as far as this can be done, perspicuously and lucidly. For general ideas produce only an obscure knowledge of particular things, and do not explain natural things in the best way, which is the task of Physics. Hence, if to someone asking, e.g., why does heat rarefy bodies and cold contract them? the answer is given that this is the nature of heat, and that the nature of cold, a response unworthy of a Philosopher is given. Similarly, to dispatch someone who asks about the various effects of nature with the general term quality is the mark of a small and lowly wit, as the most illustrious Rohault (u) says. Hence follows Axiom V. That doctrine excels the rest which asserts or posits nothing that cannot be sufficiently grasped in thought or explained. For

34 Axiom VI. That system must prevail in Physics which pursues the doctrine of natural things in a manner suited to the nature and method of this discipline. To this may also be referred, as certain further rules, the following, which are extremely useful. I. One must not have recourse to the first cause, or God, when a second cause can be had. II. While the sensible causes of effects are unknown to us, let no insensible and equally unknown cause whatever be asserted. III. On those questions one must not dwell, or must altogether abstain from treating them, whose solution either will never be found, or, if perchance it is found, makes us none the more learned. IV. The same is to be said of those controversies which depend on the inscrutable counsel of God and are known to Him alone who made all things, and which therefore, as Tertullian rightly says, are to be learned either from God or from no one. These things being established,

36 To make this clearer, suppose the following case. Let someone ask, e.g., from what, as from intrinsic principles, does a house come together? And let me answer that it comes together from the matter and the form of the house: that the matter, moreover, is that from which the house is made, and the form the act by which the matter is determined to compose a house. With this answer I have certainly spoken the truth, but I have not made the questioner more learned; and therefore he will rightly ask again what, namely, that matter is from which the house has been made, or likewise what that act is which is called the form of the house. We do not, therefore, come away from the school of Aristotle more learned in those things which pertain to the first beginnings of natural things; and therefore the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics serves almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy, not because it is false, but on the contrary because it is too true, and teaches nothing beyond those things which cannot be unknown. For who can ever doubt that all composites are made of matter and form? But after we have learned these things we can give the cause of no phenomenon: therefore it serves nothing toward learning Physics thoroughly.

37 I say secondly: the Peripatetic system of the principles of natural body is to be altogether neglected in Physics. Proof: for if in natural Philosophy that system is rightly neglected in which natural things either are not explained or the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, the Peripatetic system certainly cannot have a place in Physics, by Axioms III and IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected. The first part of this proposition, although it has already been proved by us above, is proved more fully and to the point of evidence. For suppose the question arises why fire, e.g., is endowed with certain qualities which we experience, while water, on the other hand, obtains other affections? You will receive no other answer from a Peripatetic than this: namely, that these things follow from the fact that fire has one substantial form, water another; and if someone insists by asking what those forms are, by what law they produce diverse effects and demand diverse accidents? these philosophers reply at once that this is the nature of the form of fire, that it requires such affections, and that on the contrary the nature of the form of water itself is another; which is indeed against Axiom IV.

38 The second part of the proposition is evident; for when a Peripatetic is asked why heat and cold, e.g., produce a diverse sensation? they point to no other cause than that these qualities are diverse, of an altogether diverse nature. But who will deny that by these little ways of speaking the phenomena of things are by no means explained, and that the unknown

> [p. 22]

Epicurus erred when he admitted the atoms themselves as uncreated and mobile of themselves; and he shows that this too was a mark of desperate madness in Epicurus, that he believed the world to have been generated from a fortuitous concourse of atoms and to be governed by no counsel of the Divine mind, or Providence; for, as

> (7 . pue— m

Cicero observed, there is nothing so hidden, so admirable and divine, that among these men the throng of atoms does not accomplish it (c). Although, therefore, it cannot be denied that a great many things in the opinion of the Atomists have been devised happily and usefully, yet the system, or hypothesis, of the Atomists does not seem acceptable as a whole, since it is altogether uncertain whether there can be corpuscles of this kind which are extended and at the same time indivisible; and therefore it is contrary to Axiom V.

## CHAPTER VII

The system of Descartes is set forth and refuted.

irst, Descartes (d) posits a matter created by God, simple, homogeneous, 42

F         measurable in three dimensions, and extended everywhere. This matter

God divided into particles as nearly equal to one another as possible, cubical, so that they touched one another on every side with an immediate contact excluding all void. On the parts thus divided God the Creator impressed a most vehement twofold motion: one by which the individual portions were moved about their own center, the other by which several together were moved about a common center. To the portions of matter thus driven round in a circle Descartes gave the name of vortices, from vertendo [turning]; and hence, secondly, he teaches that from that agitation and twofold motion of matter, the angles of the particles having been worn away, three elements of different kinds arose, of which the first contains the most minute parts; the second, globules, into which the square particles were shaped once their angles were removed; the third consists of the coarser parts, irregular, with various angles.

45 I say, therefore: the Cosmogony of Descartes (that is, the formation of the world devised by Descartes), or the system of vortices, cannot have a place in

therefore. The antecedent is evident. For in the first place this system fails at that first origin of the three elements. For if no void is possible, as Descartes would have it, even by Divine power, then, when matter was divided into cubic parts and each of those parts was moving about its own axis and about the center of the universe, it certainly cannot be conceived how some empty space would not then be intercepted between parts of this kind, a space, namely, that would not then be filled by any subtle matter, since this had not yet come forth from the wearing of the angles.

## APPENDIX

The Newtonian system is touched upon lightly. 47

Of the system of the most illustrious Newton it is necessary to set forth some things, though very briefly. It differs from the elements of Descartes, besides other things, in the primordial particles of bodies, inasmuch as Descartes asserts them to be friable, Newton hard and solid, so that they cannot be broken by any forces of nature (e). Of the Newtonian system the principal head

> [p. 25]

(e) Opticks, Qu. 31. [p. 25] head is the attractive force: by this they understand the virtue, or principle, of that action which cannot be explained by the ordinary forces of bodies, namely pressure and impulse; and the action itself by which bodies approach one another is called by them attraction. This they hold to be universal and mutual, both of great bodies and of the smallest particles of matter.

48 Some philosophers, the French especially, say that although Newton’s system would have vague and uncertain hypotheses driven out of Philosophy [§ 20], some of the Newtonians nevertheless do no less themselves, by admitting an attractive force. For they do not know whether a force of this kind is a cause or an effect, nor can they by its help give the reason of the phenomena. 49 And elsewhere (g) he speaks thus: “I use the words attraction, impulse, or propensity of whatever kind toward a center indifferently and promiscuously for one another, considering these forces not physically but only mathematically. Hence let the Reader beware of thinking that by words of this kind I anywhere define the species or mode of action, or the physical cause or reason, or that I attribute forces truly and physically to centers, which are mathematical points, if perchance I should say that centers attract, or that there are forces of centers.” So that for this reason Nollet (h) said that attraction, once it passed from the hands of Newton to his followers, was greatly despoiled of its simplicity.

50 And as regards the second, namely that by the help of attraction the reason of the phenomena cannot be given, M. Pluche (i) strives to show it by very many arguments. Let them explain, he says, by the help of attraction: why does the huge mass of some building, which compared with a feather possesses an almost infinite attractive force, not draw to itself a little feather fluttering in the air? or why is a stone falling beside a tower attracted by the earth rather than by the tower, which is nearer? For although (as the Newtonians say) the attractive force of the earth exceeds any other attraction by an immense amount, who will deny that, if an increase is added to this virtue, it will act with a greater effort? Let there be added, then, to the attracting forces of the earth the attractive force of a steep mountain, as of a part joined to the terraqueous globe. 53 Chymia, which by the Moderns is also called Chemia, that is, the art of resolving bodies, is said to have been invented by Hermes, and is therefore also called Hermetic. It was greatly illustrated, not only with a view to preparing medicines but also to explaining the principles of natural things, by Theophrastus Paracelsus, called the Father of the Chemists. The chemists, then, are the Spagyrists, or Empirics, who are occupied with the analysis of bodies and seek nothing else by their art and operations than to unfold the principles joined and bound together in mixed bodies and, once unfolded, to subject them to the senses themselves. The object of this art is every sensible body, and it is divided into three classes, or kingdoms, or families, as they themselves speak, namely the animal, the vegetable and the mineral. And what they draw out of these, chiefly by the help of fire and through menstrua, or dissolvents, those are for them the principles of bodies, according to their axiom: that anything is constituted of those parts into which it is resolved. Their principles are numbered five, namely Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, Water and Earth. The first three are called active, the last two passive.

54 Mercury, or spirit, is a subtle, penetrating and volatile liquor, which usually comes out of bodies first when fire is applied; on which, according to its greater or lesser dose, the growth and corruption of bodies depend; and from which the motions of all mixed bodies immediately proceed. Hence it is plain that the mercury of the chemists is a substance far different from quicksilver, which is otherwise also called mercury. Sulphur they call a certain fat, oily substance, through which mixed bodies that abound in it are able to catch flame. Salt is a savory substance [because it is the origin of savors], which can be diluted by water and liquefied by fire. It is divided into fixed and volatile, acid and alkali: the former does not fly off in the fire, though it is dissolved and melted; the latter flies off and is dissipated by heat. It is called acid because, placed on the tongue, it affects and twitches it with a certain sense of sharpness known to all. Alkali is that which is of a looser texture and of a taste as it were burning, and broken up by many passages; whence, if it is mixed with an acid, it produces a great ebullition. Therefore every body is called alkaline which cannot be mixed with an acid without exciting a great effervescence.

55 Water, which is also called phlegm by the chemists, is a fluid substance, extremely moist, odorless, insipid. Earth, lastly, the damned earth, which is also called caput mortuum, is not much the concern of the chemists, who almost neglect it; it is a dry, fixed, insipid, solid and powdery substance, which remains after the said liquors and the fixed salts have been extracted. These are the five elements of the chemists, which

What is to be determined about the system of the

I   say, first: The physical nature of matter seems to consist in this, that it is a substance impenetrably extended, consisting of primordial parts that are most minute, and these homogeneous as regards substance, but unequal and diverse as regards bulk, figure, motion and like affections. Proof, by parts. The physical nature of the matter of natural bodies is placed in that by which it has the capacity, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite, and which it is known to have both by reason and, so far as is permitted, by the experience of the senses; but by this very fact, that matter is a substance impenetrably extended, it has, and is understood to have, whatever is required for it to be able, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite: therefore. [p. 29] spirit of sal ammoniac, imbued so great a quantity of water with a blue color, and that a conspicuous and saturated one, that it contained 256806 parts equal to that little grain. The most learned Fr. Francesco Lana testifies [r] that as much gum lac as would suffice to fill a walnut shell tinges with an intense color such a quantity of water as is enough to imbue a thousand paper leaves on both sides with the same color. Since, then, on any one leaf a thousand millions of colored points can conveniently be marked, there will be on all those leaves 1,000,000,000,000 visible colored points, distinct from one another. These things certainly prove that the parts of matter are most minute. Next, that these smallest parts are unequal in their magnitude, and diverse in figure and motion, is manifest from this, that this inequality and diversity of the most minute parts must be asserted in order that the sensible qualities and operations of any natural body may be rightly and conveniently explained.

> (1) Magift. Nat. & Arc. Tom. 1. tract. 1. cap. 1. Qbf. 3.

59 These most minute parts of bodies, finally, can certainly be homogeneous, and not diverse as regards substance, since it is by no means required that they be substantially diverse in order that from their union bodies may emerge whose sensible qualities are diverse from one another, and whose operations are quite dissimilar. For composites can be made from those primordial parts of matter whose sensible qualities and operations are quite diverse from one another, although the parts themselves differ not at all from one another as regards substance: for since they are of unequal magnitude and diverse figure, they can be artfully disposed among themselves in diverse ways; finally, some of them can be moved in diverse directions within the whole that they constitute, and others be at rest in it, which quite suffices for bodies endowed with dissimilar qualities to be capable of being composed of them: therefore those parts can certainly be homogeneous.

60 I say, second: The essential, or substantial, form of natural bodies devoid of life, if it is regarded physically, is nothing different from that disposition, congruence and proportion of the particles of which the bodies themselves are composed intrinsically and as to their essence. Proof: given a certain disposition, proportion, etc., of the parts of matter, and everything else taken away, a corporeal being, or a substantial composite specifically distinct from others, is understood perfectly well: but by substantial form nothing else is understood than that ground by which this composite is actually such, specifically different from others, and by reason of which it has these special effects and properties: therefore. The major is proved by the example of a plant: given precisely a certain disposition, organization, etc., in the particles of matter, an excellent account is had of how the nutritive sap is sucked up, distributed, etc., and why such a vegetating body is a plant and not a stone, etc., without there ever being need to recur to anything else in order to explain these phenomena, these attributes of the plant: therefore.

(r) Magisterium naturae et artis, vol. 1, tract. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 3.

[p. 30]

> jo ELEM. REC. PHILÓSOPH. P. IV...

61 The same reasoning holds in the remaining bodies. For if (as Du Hamel rightly says (s)) we wish to designate the form and species of gold, we shall adduce its properties: that it is the most ductile of all, that it is not dissolved in aqua fortis as silver is, etc. And a skilled goldsmith, when he has seen those qualities come together in some body, will not doubt that it is true gold, nor will he be anxious whether there is in it some absolute form of gold. For were that form withdrawn, so long as those endowments remained, it would be pure gold: and the same is the reasoning for all bodies; therefore the essential, or substantial, form of bodies devoid of life is nothing different from a certain aggregate of sensible qualities, which arises from a certain disposition, motion and other affections of the parts of matter. To these is added that, from a substance extended, impenetrable, mobile, divisible, yet everywhere like itself and uniform, things most dissimilar can spring up if it is variously configured, determined, modified.

65 From what has been said you will infer I. That in our opinion form is not an absolute entity, but something modal and relative: for that texture, proportion, combination, etc., of the parts of matter, in which form consists, are mere modes. You will infer II: that if this name substance is taken for a being existing by itself, the essential form of natural composites devoid of life (for we are speaking only of these) is not entitatively a substance, as is self-evident. You will infer III, that the said form, properly speaking, is neither produced, nor made, nor generated, as the Angelic Doctor excellently says in very many places; for everything that is made, says St. Thomas (u), is always a composite, but form is not a composite. We are by no means speaking of the rational soul, which is truly and properly the form of man, and is created by God alone.

> 07 MEE ftit,

66 Material form, therefore, or essential form, is not produced, nor made, nor generated, but the composite is: for since the said form is nothing else than that disposition, proportion, texture, etc., and these are nothing else than something modal, form cannot be made except improperly, inasmuch, namely, as it is so denominated from the production of the composite; for when the parts of matter are joined, variously disposed, etc., which is for the composite to be composed or generated, there are necessarily in them those presences, dispositions, etc., which we call form; form, therefore, is not made otherwise than insofar as the composite is made or generated, which can best be set out in an artifact. You will infer IV. that for form to be contained in the potency of matter is nothing else than that the parts of matter can be variously disposed and conformed. You have an analogy in a statue, which, before it is made from wood, is contained in that wood in potency, inasmuch, namely, as the wood can be formed into a statue.

67 You will infer V. That matter and form are really distinguished, not indeed entitatively, since form is not an entity but something modal, as we have said, nor by the major real distinction, but by the minor real distinction, or modal distinction. When the idea of one thing positively and completely excludes the idea of another thing, then we say that they are distinguished by a major real distinction; thus body and soul are distinguished. The minor, or modal, real distinction is that which is found between a thing and the mode of the thing itself, as the distinction of body from figure, which has already been stated in the Ontology too. But everything that does not subsist by itself

(x) Philos., vol. 3, bk. 1, tract. 3, prop. 35. [p. 33] in bk. 1 of the Physics, text 64, he says: It is manifest from what has been said that everything that is made is always composite. The Angelic Doctor defends this very point in the places cited [§. 65]. Indeed, this very thing is shown most clearly also by the testimony of Cicero, who, since he knew Greek to a marvel, and understood Aristotle and Plato and the others, whom he had read attentively, much better than even all the common Peripatetics gathered into one, says in more than one place that the Peripatetics and the Academics differ in names but agree in substance; and since it is clearer than daylight that the Academics in no way admitted such substantial forms, we must say that Aristotle, in expounding physical things, never took refuge in such forms.

70 Proof 2. Whatever is produced outside God is produced either by creation or by generation; but substantial forms are produced neither by creation nor by generation: therefore. The minor is proved as to its second part: if forms were generated, they would be made out of something existing in them; but this can be nothing else than matter: therefore they would be made out of matter existing in the forms themselves: therefore the forms themselves would coalesce out of matter and form. I will frame the same argument about the form of the form, and so on to infinity: therefore, to avoid an inconvenience of this kind, it must necessarily be said that form is neither generated nor made, and consequently is not an absolute entity, as the Peripatetics contend.

71 They reply: the form is truly not made when the composite whose form it is is generated, but is educed from the potency of matter, and therefore is not created. But against this: for to be educed from the potency of matter does not befit a form that is entitatively a substance: therefore either that form is not entitatively a substance, or it is created when the composite is produced. The antecedent is proved: that a form is educed from the potency of matter is nothing other than that it is so made that it is necessary, at least in the natural order, that a subject exist in which it is produced and conserved: therefore a form which is educed from the potency of a subject necessarily depends on it in becoming, in being, and in being conserved, which is the same as saying that the form inheres in the subject; but to inhere in a subject befits only a physical accident, because a physical accident inheres in a subject and depends on it, at least by the forces of nature, in becoming, in being, and in being conserved: therefore, taking substance as it is taken by the Peripatetics, namely for a being existing by itself, a form that is a substance in this sense cannot be educed from the potency of matter. For to exist by itself and to inhere in a subject are wholly opposed modes of existing, as is evident.

72 Proof 3. Every substantial entity really distinct from others can properly be made and generated; but form, according to Aristotle and St. Thomas, cannot properly be made and generated [§§ 65 & 69]: therefore it is not a substantial entity, but only a mode modally distinct from matter. Proof 4. If the said entitative forms were given, they would be annihilated in the destruction of the composite; but they are not annihilated: therefore. The major is proved: an entity which ceases to be according to its whole being is annihilated,

73 They reply that the said forms are not annihilated although the composite is destroyed, because their subject remains. For annihilation is the ceasing of a thing with no subject remaining; destruction, on the contrary, is that in which the subject always remains, as is clear from the definitions. But against this: for these very definitions are arbitrary, and by no means consonant with common notions. For who, unless he clings tooth and nail to Peripatetic prejudices, would not grasp that a thing goes into nothing when it no longer exists in the nature of things? And what does it matter that the subject (namely a wholly different thing) remains, so that we should use the word not of annihilation but of destruction? as though there were in reality some difference whether we speak in this way or otherwise. We shall therefore be offering mere words, and Philosophy will not be advanced a nail’s breadth by these circumlocutions and logomachies.

## T H E A R G U M E N T S O F T H E P E R I PAT E T I C S A R E A N S W E R E D

74

Obj. 1, against 1. It implies a contradiction that the parts of matter should be homogeneous, or of the same nature, and should differ from one another as to figure, bulk, etc.: therefore either they do not differ from one another, or they are not of the same nature. I deny the antecedent: for although the parts of matter do not differ as to substance, since all are homogeneous, they differ nevertheless in their artful dispositions, and no repugnance is found in this: for all admit that very many molecules, or parts, of gold, certainly of the same nature, can by art differ in affections of this kind, while some are made cubical, others spherical, etc.

75 Obj. 2. If the parts of matter differ from one another as to bulk, figure, etc., then matter is not indifferent to receiving all forms: therefore it will not be a determinable principle. The antecedent is evident: for one body, e.g. air, by the very fact that it has dissimilar properties, must also comprise particles, by which it is constituted, different from those of fire. Reply: by the very fact that the most minute parts are apt for a most diverse combination among themselves and demand none in preference to another, it is sufficiently understood that matter is indifferent. The four and twenty letters we use differ in figure and magnitude; yet who would deny that of themselves they are indifferent to being gathered into definite words, or to being bound by no laws, to being constrained into verses by the laws of meter, or to composing a more freely flowing speech? We by no means contend that it belongs to the notion of matter that the very same parts which are in one composite should, with no change at all supervening, constitute any other.

76 Obj. 3. It belongs to matter to be the first subject of all natural changes, and of bodies of incredible variety and discrepant [p. 35] from one another; but matter, which is everywhere of the same kind and not of diverse nature, cannot accomplish this: therefore. I deny the minor. For all variety must be derived from the varied disposition, combination, etc., of matter, that is, from form. Thus from the juices of the earth, by the mere percolation of their parts transmitted through the fibrils of a tree, bark, flowers and fruits are born. From foods likewise chyle, blood, bones and flesh, which differ greatly from one another, are formed by the mere transposition of parts, a new order, etc. Accordingly the variety of bodies coheres most aptly with a matter homogeneous as to substance.

77 You will insist. If the parts of matter are supposed homogeneous, from their addition and conjunction there would not result some new essence, but a certain homogeneous integral whole, which would not be of a different nature from one part of it; just as, when we add water to water, we do not make another essence, but extensively increase the same essence of water that is found in any drop; but this is against experience: therefore. It is confirmed: if a musician joined two voices like each other in all respects, he would by no means make a diapason; for this it is necessary that they be of diverse nature, the lower, namely, double of the higher: therefore the same must be said in our case.

78 To 1, I deny the consequence: for in order that a composite specifically different from others may be produced, it suffices that the parts of matter be of diverse nature, not indeed substantial, but only modal; that is, it suffices that they be diversely figured, diversely extended, etc.; which is very different in the addition of water to water: for what is added is of altogether the same nature as the other, namely of the same figure, of the same state, namely of fluidity; and from the addition no new combination is made, no new texture, and consequently no new form and essence, but only the same water becomes more extended.

Quemadmodum 3taque ípecies hujus confonantiae diapaíón ex vocum combinatione coalefcic, folo. motu, & magnitudine diverfis, ita ex materiae particulis magnicudine, figura, &c. diverfis cunctae rerum fpecies exurgere poffunt.

79 The confirmation of the argument, however, rather confirms our opinion; for the voices that compose a diapason do not differ essentially, but only accidentally, namely in quantity and motion: for the lower is greater and moves more slowly, the higher shorter and quicker; for the diapason, or octave, consists in this alone, namely that the lower voice moves twice as sluggishly as the higher, so that the latter performs two vibrations in the time in which the lower completes only one. Just as, therefore, the species of this consonance, the diapason, coalesces from the combination of voices diverse only in motion and magnitude, so from particles of matter diverse in magnitude, figure, etc., all the species of things can arise.

80 Obj. 4. If we say that matter is a substance consisting of parts diverse in bulk, figure, etc., it is not the essence of matter that is explained by us, but body itself: therefore. The antecedent is proved: it is the nature of matter that it is not complete; but the particles of which matter consists are complete: therefore. I distinguish the minor: they are complete in the character of matter, I grant; in the character of a natural composite, or sensible body, I deny. By us only the essence of matter physically considered is set forth:

> [p. 36]

[p. 36] in the character of matter it is something complete; but in the character of sensible body it is not completed except by the form, which arises from a certain complex, order and proportion of the parts.

> Argumienta contra. fecundam Conclufionem.

81

Obj. 1, the principal argument of the Peripatetics. In the Sacrament of the Altar the accidents of bread and wine remain, but the substantial form of bread and wine does not remain: therefore the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of accidents. I distinguish the major: the accidents remain, taken in the

Peripatetic sense, for accidental forms, or absolute qualities inhering in a subject, I deny the major; in the Theological and Dogmatic sense, taken for species, which in an ineffable and plainly miraculous way deceive us, I grant the major. And, having roundly granted the minor, I distinguish the consequent: the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of Peripatetic accidents, I let the consequent pass; besides the aggregate of accidents such as are so called by the Moderns, that is, besides the texture and combination of the molecules of corporeal matter, I subdistinguish:

where such a texture and combination is really given, I deny; where it is not really given, but nevertheless so appears to the senses as if it were truly given, I grant.

82 The matter comes back to this, that we understand the accidents of bread and wine in the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar not to be true corporeal qualities, abstracted from the body of the bread and wine and left without a subject connaturally proper to them, but mere appearances (if I may so speak), or species of bread and wine, under which the most true Body and the most true Blood of Christ the Lord lie hidden. We, therefore, taught by the Orthodox faith, deny that the substance of bread and wine lies beneath them after the consecration; but, taught by Philosophy, we shall deny that those things which appear are true accidents.

83 It is, therefore, a Dogma of the Catholic Faith that in the Venerable

Sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ the Lord exist truly, really and substantially. So it was expressly defined in the Council of the Lateran (y), in that of Constance (z), in that of Florence (a) and in that of Trent (b), against Berengar,

Calvin and other impious Innovators, who dogmatize no less falsely than wickedly that Christ the Lord is contained in the Eucharist only in sign, or figure, or virtue. It is also a Catholic Dogma that by virtue of the Consecration there takes place a real conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the blood, of Christ the Lord; which altogether wonderful and singular conversion the Catholic Church transubstantiation most

84 It is also altogether most certain that the most Sacred body of Christ the Lord (and the same must be said of his blood) is in the Eucharist Sacramentally, namely in such a manner as, although we can scarcely express it in words (as the Council of Trent wisely admonishes), we must nevertheless most steadfastly believe to be possible to God (d). That mode of existing, indeed, has no example in created things, and is full of miracles, and is therefore deservedly called Sacramental, that is, a mode which belongs to the Sacrament alone. Let these things that have been said suffice for the Peripatetics to see that the most Sacred Dogmas of our Religion are kept safe and sound by us.

> (d) Seff. (5. Cap. 1.

85 But since they leave no stone unturned to brand the opinion of the Modern Philosophers on non-substantial forms as heretical, and to persuade the unlearned that the Catholic Dogma of Transubstantiation is overthrown once the opinion of the Moderns is posited, it is worth the trouble to add some things, so that they may see that they have no right whatever to think us guilty of violating the faith. In the first place, then, I should have to count very many Catholic Philosophers who most steadfastly defend the opinion on forms in the very words in which it has been set forth and proved by us, without their Works ever having been proscribed by the Church; nay, they have been approved with the highest praise by great Theologians. Let it suffice to name some. Klaus, Macko, Regnault, Paulian, Scherffer, Lanis, Corsini, Hamel, Purchot utterly explode the substantial forms of the Peripatetics. From the family of the Minims, Maignan, Saguens and Jacquier; from the illustrious family of the Minors, the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia, who suffices for a thousand; from the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, the celebrated Tomás Vicente Tosca, and very many others from the French Oratory.

> (c) De Loc, Lib. 8.

86 What of the fact that this doctrine is publicly defended throughout all Europe, and at Rome especially, in the Universities and Colleges, before the Roman Pontiff himself? Let us now hear the illustrious Melchior Cano. I think (says the celebrated man) that the testimony even of many Scholastic Theologians, if other learned men contend against them, is of no more weight for producing belief than their reasoning; that is to say, that in a Scholastic disputation a Theologian ought not to be overwhelmed by the authority of the greater number, but that if he has a few Men with him, provided they are weighty ones, he can surely stand against very many (e). Among the Theologians, moreover, there are not a few who expressly teach that the opinion of the Moderns on non-substantial form agrees perfectly with what the Church holds concerning the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, and that it can therefore, without harm

87 But it is better to hear the most learned Theologian of the illustrious family of the Preachers, Hyacinthe Serry [m]: “Why should I relate other things” (says the celebrated man)? “Are the systems of the recent School to be subjected to the rash censures of certain Theologians? Most philosophers now, following Descartes, place the essence of physical body in the extension of quantity, and hold that substance itself is in no way distinguished from quantity; and the Church, as I know for certain, permits them to philosophize thus. Why then do you brand them with censures? And those whom the common Mother cherishes as sons, do you curse as heathens and publicans, because they seem to you perhaps to shake the faith of the most holy Eucharist? Your study and zeal for the House of God I praise highly and commend: but I would have it be according to knowledge. You will be by far a better Theologian if you reconcile the system permitted by the Church with the faith of the Eucharist.

> Inn

88 “This will perhaps be done not unfittingly if you say that the conversion of the substance of bread which is wont to take place in the Sacrament of the Eucharist has been defined by the Church, but that the mode of the change has not been so defined; and that the Mystery stands just as well if, the substance being changed together with the quantity, only the external sensations produced in our senses remain (as Descartes thinks), as if, the substance alone being changed, the true quantity remains with the other accidents, as the Peripatetics judge. And that for this reason the Fathers of Trent used the word species for what remains when the substance has been taken away, when they could have named them accidents: namely, so that by the word species they might signify simply those sensations which both Cartesians and Peripatetics profess to be produced in our senses alike, whether the quantity, being undistinguished from the substance, perishes, or, being distinct, does not perish. If you do not say this, but charge the Cartesians with violating the faith until the Church passes sentence against them,

89 “For it is not enough” (says the celebrated Cano) “for passing sentence of heresy to have touched upon the heresy itself by suspicion; but a certain comprehension is needed, so that we may judge of errors without error” (n). “Let the Peripatetics therefore cease” [I use the words of the celebrated Muratori] “to leave no stone unturned whereby they may defame the Modern Authors of new opinions, though these have nothing at odds with our Holy Religion, and tear their books to pieces, proscribe them, and present them to the Supreme Tribunals of the Church to be pierced through” (o).

90 Further, it must not be passed over in silence that that opinion too is held by many Peripatetics to be heretical which denies that quantity is really distinguished from corporeal substance. This censure, then: is it true or false? If true: then the Most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly, Auriol, Ockham, Biel, Melchior Cano, who deny that real distinction of quantity (p), are heretics, which surely no sensible person will say of such great Men: then likewise all those Scholastics are heretics, especially of the School of the Scotists, who think the quantity of bodies is to be placed not in their entitative extension but in their impenetrability, chiefly for this reason, that extension is not an absolute accident really distinct from corporeal substance, but substance itself is of itself entitatively extended, that is, with every accident excluded.

> ' F tum.

91 Then the Subtle Doctor himself is a heretic, who (q) steadfastly maintains (as the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia says) [r] that continuous permanent quantity consists in extension, that is, in the order of the parts in the whole, as Father Hiquaeus, the Commentator of Scotus, says. But if that censure is false (as in truth it is): then that one too must by the same right be held entirely false which the very same men pronounce on the opinion that denies absolute accidents. For what the Church understood by the name of species, or what at length their physical nature may be, has nowhere been handed down by her, just as it has nowhere been defined by her either that quantity too is comprehended under the name of species.

This error, then, the Council condemned; it did not say that the existence of accidents in the Peripatetic sense is a Dogma.

93 It is therefore established by Faith that under the species of bread and wine which present themselves in the Eucharist there is contained, not the nature and substance of bread and wine, but the true Body of Christ the Lord. But that the aforesaid species are absolute accidents, as the Peripatetics contend, the Church has nowhere defined: nor has any question of this kind ever been raised in the Church; nay rather (u), I nowhere read that the existence of the species in the Eucharist was doubted, which no one but a blind man or a madman could have denied. And so much on the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist. Let us dissolve the other arguments of the Peripatetics.

94 Obj. 2. If a natural composite devoid of life were composed essentially of particles of matter differing among themselves only in mechanical affections, it would not be one per se but one per accidens, as consisting by no means of an act per se and a potency per se: but this is false, just as it is also manifestly false that there is no difference whatever between natural and artificial composites: therefore. Dist. maj.: it would not be one per se, if by this name is understood a whole made of a double semi-substance, I grant; if a whole is understood which is primarily and per se intended by operating nature, I deny the maj.; and in the same way dist. the min.; I deny the conseq. In the opinion of the Moderns, which is also ours, the natural composite is one per se, and is more than sufficiently distinguished from the artificial one.

95 For it is one, because it is undivided in itself and divided from everything else. It is one per se, because the particles which constitute it are united together by the diverse intention of operating nature: whereas in an artificial composite the parts which constitute the artificial whole are coupled together by the direct intention of the artificer. It also consists of an act per se and a potency per se. For the mechanical affections are in matter by the direct intention of nature, and by the same intention they determine the matter itself to constitute a composite one in species. Nor do I think that anything else can be understood by the name of potency and act per se without a manifest begging of the question, as I shall say below.

96 Inst.: every natural composite is one substantial whole: therefore its essential form must be entitatively a substance; for otherwise it would in no way be distinguished from an accidental composite. Dist. antec.: it is one substantial whole, that is, intended per se by nature, I grant; in another sense, gratuitously devised by the Peripatetics, let it pass; and I deny the conseq. I call a substantial whole, then, that which, whatever at length the essence of the component parts may be, is regarded by operating nature primarily and per se when it acts; an accidental whole, on the other hand, that which either is not regarded by nature, as an effect by its cause, but only by art; or is regarded by it not primarily, but secondarily

only

97 For what, I ask, do those words mean: One per se, a whole per se, a substantial whole? What do these mean: act per se and potency per se, or a whole being composed of act per se and potency per se? For if by the name of one per se, etc. a composite is understood which arises from a double semi-substance, what is in question is assumed as if certain, or the same is shown by the same, as they say. For to say a natural composite is one per se is just the same as to say a natural composite arises intrinsically from a double substance, or the form of any natural composite is entitatively a substance. But if by the name of one per se is meant that which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, it is plain that nothing can legitimately be inferred from this which would in the least favor establishing the existence of the forms of the Scholastics.

98 Obj. 3: one natural composite is distinguished substantially from another: but to be distinguished substantially is the same as to be distinguished by an entity which is a substance: therefore its essential form is entitatively a substance. Dist. maj.: it is distinguished substantially, that is, essentially, or in respect of something pertaining intrinsically to their essence, I grant; that is, by an entity which is a substance, I deny; and the conseq. For substance can be taken in two ways: first, for the essence of a thing; second, for an entity which does not need a subject in order to exist. Taken in the first way, those things are distinguished substantially which differ among themselves by something pertaining intrinsically to their essence. Taken in the second way, those things differ substantially which are discriminated among themselves by an entity that is a substance. That natural composites differ essentially is certainly true; that their difference arises from the form, all admit; but that they are distinguished substantially, namely by a form which is entitatively a substance, this must be proved by the Peripatetics, not assumed without hesitation as though it were most certain. For in this lies the question, as is plain.

99 Inst.: things that differ by a form which is entitatively an accident differ accidentally: therefore, for natural composites to differ substantially, they must differ by a form which is entitatively a substance. Dist. antec.: things that differ by a form, etc., differ accidentally, if that form does not pertain to the essence of the things compared with one another, I grant; if it pertains to their essence, I deny; and the conseq. For no one is unaware that a white thing, e.g., differs no less essentially by whiteness from everything that is not white than a man

F2 [p. 42] is distinguished essentially by rationality from that which is not a man. And the reason is that whiteness pertains intrinsically to the essence of a white thing no less than rationality does to the essence of man. Artificial dispositions, therefore, although considered in themselves they are accidents, nevertheless, because they essentially constitute a natural composite, bring it about that the composite itself is distinguished essentially, or substantially, from any other.

100 They urge: a natural composite is essentially a substance: therefore its form cannot be an accident; for it cannot happen that a substance be composed of an accident. Dist. antec.: it is essentially a substance by reason of the matter, I grant; by reason of the form, if it lacks life, I deny; and the conseq. A natural composite devoid of life, then, is not a substance except in the way in which man is called a corporeal substance; namely, just as man is not a corporeal substance except by reason of matter, and by no means by reason of form, so a natural composite which lacks life is a substance not by reason of form but only by reason of matter; and just as it is not repugnant that man should consist intrinsically of body and spirit, so it implies no contradiction that a natural composite should be essentially composed of substance and accident as of parts.

101 Obj. 4. If a form which is entitatively a substance is taken away, there is no longer any substantial generation: for matter is not generated: therefore a form which is entitatively a substance must necessarily be admitted. Dist. antec.: there is no longer any substantial generation, if by this name is understood the production of a composite whose form is a substance, I grant; if by this name is meant a composite which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, I deny the antec. and the conseq. For just as a natural composite can be regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, and so be one per se and a substantial whole, although its essential form is not entitatively a substance, so this very thing does not prevent its production from being rightly called substantial generation. But if this does not please the Scholastics, let them prove that substantial generation occurs in nature in the sense in which they themselves take it: for otherwise they hold as certain what is in question.

102 “To show,” says a most renowned man (x), treating of this matter, “that this argument is a mere begging of the question, we need only lay bare the equivocation that lies hidden in the word generation. For if by generation we understand the natural production of a new whole in nature, such as is the production of a chick from an egg, then rightly and deservedly it must be said that in this sense there is generation; but from this it could not be inferred that substantial forms also exist, since the disposition of the parts effected by nature is able to produce these new wholes and these new natural beings. But if by the word generation

[p. 43] is understood, as is commonly done, the production of a new substance which had never existed before, namely of a substantial form, the very thing will be supposed which is in question, since it is clearer than daylight that one who denies substantial forms cannot grant that nature produces such things. Nay, so far is anyone from being driven by this argument to admit substantial forms, that he ought even to draw from it a wholly opposite conclusion, in this manner: if there were substantial forms, nature could produce anew substances which did not exist before; but nature does not produce such things anew; for such a production would be a kind of creation: therefore there are no substantial forms.” Thus far the praised Author.

103 Obj. 5. There is in every natural composite, not even excepting those which lack life, an active principle of diverse operations; but this principle cannot be anything but a substantial form, as it is taken by the Scholastics: therefore we must admit a form of this kind in every composite. Reply by denying the min.: for the active principle, if any exists in natural composites which lack life, is nothing but the subtler portion of those corpuscles of which the composite itself essentially coalesces: for there is no purely corporeal operation in nature which is not wholly accomplished through the motion of the subtlest corpuscles.

104 They say: it is evident that there is in each natural composite a force by which they recover their congenital qualities. For it is plain that heated water recovers its former coldness as if of its own accord: therefore some substantial principle, wholly different from the artificial dispositions of matter, must be admitted in them. Reply by denying the antec.: for it is manifest that the parts of a tree’s bark, if they have been somewhat scorched by a torch brought near, no longer recover their power of attracting moisture; that an egg violently shaken becomes wholly unfit for incubation; that an apple bruised in some part gradually rots. Nor does the example of heated water prove anything. For, as we shall say in its place, the recovery of coldness arises from without. But if it sometimes happens that some composite recovers lost qualities, we judge that this is to be derived solely from the living substance which is in it.

105 Obj. 6. Prime matter is not a physical and substantial act, because it is pure potency; but this act is the form: therefore prime matter is entitatively not the form: therefore the substantial form is entitatively distinguished from matter. Granting the whole argument, I deny the last conseq.; for although prime matter in itself is entitatively not form, yet from this it by no means follows that the form is entitatively distinguished from matter; for since the form is not an entity but a mode, it is only modally distinguished from matter.

106 Obj. 7. If form were nothing entitative, but only modal, creatures would produce nothing anew, and there would be no created agent,

> [p. 44]

[p. 44] but this must not be said: therefore. Proof of the conseq.: for a created agent does not produce matter anew, since it presupposes it; nor the form, which is neither generated nor produced: therefore it produces nothing. I reply that created agents produce neither matter nor form, but only the composite: for creatures, as St. Bonaventure excellently says (z), only bring it about that what was in one mode comes to be in another mode.

108 Obj. finally: once our opinion is posited, there is no difference between alteration and generation; but there is one, for in alteration only qualities are produced, in generation a substantial form must be produced: therefore the substantial form is a semi-substance distinct from matter, as the Peripatetics maintain, following the opinion of the Arabs, against the doctrine of Aristotle. Reply: I deny the maj.: for in alteration the same sensible body remains which was there before, since only a few accidents perish from it and a few newly arrive, as when water from hot becomes cold, or when wax from yellow becomes white, or from soft hard. But in generation either all the accidents perish, or, if some remain, they are not enough for the sensible body to be called the same: e.g., when wax has been dissolved into smoke, it cannot be called the same body, although perhaps certain accidents which were before in the wax, e.g. the odor, remain in the smoke, because these few accidents are not enough to constitute wax.

109 Inst. If the matter stands so, generation and alteration are not distinguished except according to more and less; but more and less do not change the species, as the common axiom of the Schools has it: whereas diverse forms constitute diverse species: therefore the substantial form of a body devoid of life is not an artificial disposition of the parts. Dist. min.: more and less do not change the species where only a few accidents perish, I grant; where all or nearly all perish, I deny. But when a new form is given, nearly all the accidents which were in the former subject are destroyed, and new ones succeed, as when from wood comes fire, from wax smoke, etc. Hence a new species then results; for smoke is of a different species from wax, and fire from wood; for those things are judged to differ among themselves in species in which there appears so great a diversity

from the fact that the said principles can be drawn out of individual bodies by means of resolution; which indeed, as regards vegetables and animals, no one will call into controversy who has observed the manifold operations of the Chemists and the diverse condition of the parts dissolved by them. An obvious experience in the burning of green wood declares this very thing: for the spirituous and most agile particles, released as it were from their bonds, are roused into flame and, torn away from the rest, fly off entirely; the sulphurous, or oily, ones feed the flame, and are gradually raised up, concreting into the part of soot; the saline ones partly go off into smoke, sharply stinging the eyes, partly settle in the ashes; the watery ones burst forth at the very beginning like the tiniest buds, to be dispersed into vapor; earth, finally, remains as survivor once the salts have been drawn out.

113 These things surely indicate that there reside in iron certain peculiar endowments, an active and at the same time subtle substance, to which the Chemists give the name of spiritus rector, and which we, consistently with what was said above, think to be the elemental fluid of fire, bound up in a certain ratio, quantity and texture with the other principles constituting iron: at least the same solution shows that such a principle is present in this metal; and hence we deduce by legitimate reasoning that water likewise is comprised in it, as being what all kinds of salts give off in evaporation. Obj. 1. The Elements of the Chemists are not found in mixed bodies in the form in which they themselves set them out to us: therefore they ought not to be sensible principles of bodies. The antecedent is proved: for fire by its action brings it about that the parts of a body show themselves after the resolution in another form and state than they were in the mixture; and therefore they must be considered as new substances, as it were, produced by fire: therefore. Reply by denying the antec. of the proof: for, as we shall say in its place, the whole nature of heat consists in a swift, disturbed and expansive motion impressed on corpuscles; and nothing else is effected but, first, an expansion, then a disturbed agitation of the parts in the body, when it conceives heat. Moreover it is evident that by means of the disturbed and expansive motion of the corpuscles which enter the pores of a natural composite no new substance can be entitatively produced, but only that the texture is loosened and the bond dissolved by which the component particles of the composite itself are held united together; and therefore the destruction of a natural composite, [p. 47] which is effected per se by the action of fire, or heat, consists not in the production of some new substance, but only in the dissolution of the bond by which the component parts are tied together.

116 I said that fire, or heat, effects nothing else per se, when it destroys a natural composite, than to dissolve the component parts. For I do not deny that it happens not rarely that some new substance, which had not been in the composite, is produced by the action of heat. But this is entirely per accidens; for a new substance comes to be if the heat is more vehement than the dissolution of the parts requires. For the particles, agitated beyond measure by too great a heat, are so mingled together, those of diverse kinds, that new concretions emerge from it, and hence new substances seem to be produced; but this does not prevent the aforesaid substances from being found in mixed bodies; for from bodies of the same species salt, sulphur and mercury, likewise of the same character, are perpetually extracted, which would surely not happen with such constancy if those substances were produced entitatively by heat; for what is effected by chance happens rarely.

117 Obj. 2. If salt, sulphur and mercury are secondary principles of the composite, the principles will be plainly innumerable, namely as many as there are species of those same things; but this is absurd: therefore. Maj. proved: for, to make mention of salt alone, there will be nearly as many salts differing from one another as there are composite bodies; for salt extracted from ash wood is caustic, that is, it corrodes by burning the flesh to which it is applied; extracted from other woods, it is not so: therefore. Dist. maj.: the principles from which the essential difference of the things themselves is taken will be plainly innumerable, I grant the maj.; those by which they are specifically distinguished, I deny the maj.; and dist. the min.: it is absurd to constitute as many principles by which things differ as there are species of the things themselves, I deny; to constitute as many genera of all the principles as there are genera of composites, I grant the min.; and I deny the conseq.

120 And what forbids us to say, rather, that in the very act of combustion the fatty, saline, vitriolic-acid and earthy parts, which are the elements of iron, fused into one and joined together, coalesced into true iron? So that, consequently, the extraction of iron from ashes and clay is a true making of it. An argument for this may perhaps be what the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris (g) record: namely, that those composites which burn less readily and give off smoke more copiously, such as herbs and the harder woods, yield iron in their ashes in greater quantity than those which flare up suddenly and give off a more brightly shining flame.

121 Nor perhaps is the origin to be sought elsewhere of the granules of iron which, drawn out of a calcined human calculus by the most renowned Lister, were exhibited to the Royal Society of London (h). 122 Obj. 4. It is established by experience that sulphur especially, and mercury, are resolved into earth and water, as the most renowned men Du Hamel (j) and Du Clos attest: therefore sulphur and mercury are not of that condition of which they must necessarily be in order to be rightly and deservedly held for principles of things. Passing over the antec., I deny the conseq. For since those are laid down as secondary principles of a natural composite, their composition from others does not prevent them from being legitimately held for principles of this kind. However the matter may stand, then, concerning the composition of salt, sulphur and mercury, our assertion will be safe by this alone: that any natural mixture whatever, when it is corrupted by the action of heat, is resolved into earth, water, salt, etc., by their mere separation.

124 Moreover, the argument must also be answered by the Scholastics. For if there can be no part in a mixture which is not mixed, there could also be no essential part in a composite which is not essentially composite: therefore matter and form must necessarily be composed essentially of other principles, which likewise must be essentially composed of others, and so on, so that it would be true, namely, that there is no part of a composite which is not composite; but this is absurd: therefore it is absurd also that there is absolutely no part in a mixture which is not mixed. Finally, note: not all the sensible principles are found in every composite, nor always in equal quantity, since experience teaches us that some bodies abound in salt, e.g., but contain less oil and mercury; in others earth holds the chief place; of others the greatest part is sulphur.

## 130 I say, first, against many Scholastics: the magnitude of body does not

> J CAPUT II. . De Figura, &Situ corporum.

consist formally in its impenetrability. Proof: it is plainly established that any two bodies agree in impenetrability in such a way that, if they are considered in respect of it, one can in no way be discerned from the other: therefore either the magnitude of body is not formally placed in impenetrability, or any two bodies whatever are equal to each other; but this manifestly opposes the truth: therefore the magnitude of body by no means consists in its impenetrability.

> 53 Xtenfio cujufvís corporis terminis, five fuperficiebüs, quae materiam corporis propriam incladunt, limitatur. Ordo ille, & pofitio quam inter (e habent fuperficies; volumen corporis termipantes,

131 I say, secondly: the magnitude of body is nothing different from the entitative extension of the body itself. Proof: the magnitude of body is formally that in respect of which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or unequal to it; but it is by entitative extension that one body is said to be equal or unequal to another: therefore the magnitude of body is nothing different from its entitative extension. The maj. is evident: for two bodies a palm in length are judged equal for this reason, that the extension of both is the same; whereas bodies of which one is a palm and the other two palms in length are called unequal, because the extension of both is not the same, but the one is exceeded by the other in respect of it. Confirmation of the concl. It is agreed among all that rarefaction is motion toward greater, and condensation motion toward lesser quantity; but rarefaction is motion toward greater extension, and condensation toward lesser: therefore.

132 They reply: the magnitude of body consists indeed in extension, but in solid, or impenetrable, extension. But against this: because, when impenetrability is prescinded and extension alone is posited, the foundation of equality and inequality is had: therefore impenetrability in no way pertains to the formal notion of magnitude; just as, for altogether the same cause, it is certain that the hardness of a body does not concern magnitude. Surely hardness does not pertain to the formal notion of magnitude for this reason, that two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally hard: therefore neither does impenetrability concern magnitude in any way, since two bodies can be unequal and at the same time equally impenetrable.

## CHAPTER II

On the Figure and Situation of bodies.

he extension of any body is limited by terms, or surfaces, which en133

T         close the matter proper to the body. That order and position which

> [p. 52]

the surfaces bounding the volume of the body have among themselves [p. 52] is called figure, by which a body is said to be spherical, cubical, etc. The exterior conformation of a body, then, is called figure, which namely does not pertain intrinsically to the nature of the thing, and can be common to altogether diverse bodies; but the figure of the parts themselves, constituting a body definite in its kind, which in wax, e.g., must doubtless be other than in iron, is called configuration. Situation is a certain posture, order, combination, texture, or artificial disposition of the molecules themselves in the whole which is intrinsically constituted of them.

134 The surfaces of bodies can be varied in altogether manifold ways. This prodigious variety of figures, moreover, is confirmed by innumerable experiments of the Physicists, of which we shall select the more useful. Keep some drops of the best vinegar on a fragment of glass for some hours, so that they partly evaporate; then look at them through a microscope: you will observe innumerable salts, nearly all pointed. If you keep vinegar in some vessel exposed to the air for some weeks, and more quickly in summertime, you will see with the microscope innumerable, as it were, most tiny eels running about hither and thither. From these, however, it is plain that the sharp taste of vinegar draws its origin not from the eels, as some have thought, but from diverse salts.

135 Put a drop of pure water on glass, and in it dissolve thoroughly a little common salt reduced to powder; after all the water has evaporated of its own accord, observe the drop with the microscope: you will see the salt reduced into crystals of cubical figure. If you dissolve sugar in the same way, you will observe crystals of nearly round figure. Richard Mead, in his Mechanical Account of Poisons, placed upon glass a very small part of the venomous juice which is emitted from the tooth of a viper when it bites, and in a short space of time it was changed into most slender and extremely sharp crystals, which were so rigid that they remained for a month without any change. From the figure and hardness of this poison, then, is to be derived its untamable nature, which sometimes scarcely yields to remedies opportunely applied. If a portion of crushed pepper is kept for some days in a vessel full of water, innumerable animalcules of diverse kind and diverse figure are observed with the microscope.

136 Insects figured in other ways are detected in stagnant water into which bits of cut hay, of chaff and of various plants have been thrown: certain animalcules are seen like globules, others longer and turning themselves round in a circle; in some, feet are distinguished; some are seen ringed like worms; and, in a pleasant spectacle, the greater are often observed to pursue the lesser so as to devour them.

137 If you collect the parts emitted spontaneously, or drawn out of bodies by art with the help of fire, you will notice that they are of the same nature, and produce the same effects, as the bodies themselves. Thus the vapor of water, collected, gives water; the vapors of sulphur and of camphor restore sulphur and camphor anew. But these things would not happen if the parts of bodies did not

> [p. 53]

[p. 53] have, and when released did not preserve, the same figure. The parts of water and of other vapors can be observed if bodies evaporate in a small room closed on all sides, into which only a ray of the sun passes to illuminate the vapors. In this way it became known that the parts of water are perfectly round. Many other things worth noting are found in the writings of Leeuwenhoek, Robert Boyle, Martin Lister, Erasmus Bartholin and John Freind, which Authors you will be able to consult when you have the means and the leisure.

>  haberent, nec folutae coníervarent eandem figuram. Aquae, & alio.

138 Since, then, any part whatever of matter, or of body, has its peculiar figure, necessarily, while the parts of some body are actually separated, its surface must be increased. For when the parts are disjoined, and each is contained by its own surface, because it has figure, those internal surfaces of the body by which the parts touched one another become visible, and, together with the old surface under which the whole body was contained, compose the entire surface of the body cut into parts. When, therefore, a body is divided into several parts, its surface is increased while the same mass, or solidity, remains. Wherefore, since the same matter remains and the surface of the body is increased by the continued separation of the parts, the surface will acquire a greater ratio to the matter of the body.

Hac ratiore innotuit partes. aquae clle perfecte :otundas. Plura alia notatu digna reperiuntur in ícripris Leuwenheex, Roberti Boyle, Martini Lyfler, Eraími Bartholini , Johannis F:ieind, quos Auctores ubi copia erit, & otium fuppeut confülere poteftis.

139 From this, moreover, are explained several phenomena which are very often observed when some fluid, such as air, fire or water, acts upon bodies. The action of fluids follows the ratio of the surface of the body; for the greater the surface of the body, the greater the quantity of fluid that acts upon the body. Hence it is excellently explained why a wind which cannot lift a cubic foot of marble carries up in a moment of time several cubic feet of sand to a remarkable height, namely a weight a hundred times greater than the first. For a cubic foot of sand is the same as a cubic foot of marble cut into as many parts as there are grains of sand; but the wind can exert a greater force on marble in powder than on a cubic foot of the same; it will therefore lift a cubic foot of sand, nay several feet of sand, and will not be able to raise a whole foot of marble.

Nam quum fejunguntur partes, & quaelibet propria contineatur fuperficie, quia figuram habet, fuperficies illae 1nternae corporis, quibus fe mutuo .

140 In the same way is explained the very great medicinal force of quicksilver, or mercury, for driving out stubborn diseases. A drop of mercury is easily resolved into innumerable most tiny globules, as will be plain if you throw upon it the rays of the sun collected by a concave mirror or a crystal lens. Wherefore its surface will quickly be increased to a wonderful degree within the body, and, this being increased, the mercury will more easily be driven by the fluids of the body into the vessels, and with the force acquired will expel the morbid matter from them; or it will easily open for itself an entrance into the smaller vessels, and so will at least deplete them, whence the circulation of the fluids will become more unimpeded, by which the body recovers from long-lasting diseases. Mercury, then, does not operate by its own weight, as most think, but by its divisibility.

141 From the figure and situation of bodies many phenomena can be explained [p. 54] and these no less useful than pleasant to know, of which we shall set forth only some, so that from those which are now to be set forth by us very much light may come to what we shall afterwards say on Statics and Hydrostatics. All bodies, then, are seen to have a certain gravity; hence it comes about that stones, e.g., descend until they are held up by meeting other bodies. They begin to be held up, moreover, when their center of gravity is prevented from descending. The center of gravity, moreover, is the point placed in any heavy body by which, if the body is suspended, all its parts will keep whatever situation you have given them, and so will be in equilibrium. E.g., if a staff or an iron rod is suspended by a thread at its middle part, and each part of it is in equilibrium, that point from which it will be suspended will be its center of gravity, since its parts on either side will be of equal weight.

142 But if that rod is not everywhere homogeneous, that is, of the same nature, suppose if in one part it is of iron and in the other of wood, its center of gravity will not be in the middle of its extension, but will recede from it toward that part of the matter which is denser. Wherefore the center of gravity and the center of magnitude, or of extension, do not always coincide in the same point, but only when the matter of the heavy body is homogeneous: e.g., in an iron globe the center of extension, or its middle point, which is equally distant from the individual points of the surface, can also be conceived as the center of gravity, since the matter in the iron globe is everywhere homogeneous.

143 Now, when a heavy body tends downward, namely to the center of the earth, which they therefore call the center of heavy things, since all heavy things strive toward it, its motion, or descent, is directed along a certain line on which the center of gravity always stands; and for this reason it is called the line of direction, and is defined: the straight line which is understood to be stretched from the center of gravity to the center of heavy things. Now the Axioms are these. First: A heavy body resting on another remains at rest, if the body on which it lies prevents its center of gravity from being moved downward. For since the whole gravity of the body is as it were collected in one point, it cannot happen that the body moves downward if its center of gravity cannot move downward.
