144 Second: a heavy body resting on another slips, if its center of gravity is not supported by that on which the body itself rests. For if the center of gravity is not supported, nothing prevents the center itself from tending downward, as the law of nature requires, and consequently the whole body from moving downward. A heavy body, then, can never fall unless its center of gravity falls. But that center cannot fall as long as the body is so placed on a horizontal plane that the line of direction is conceived to pass within its base. Third axiom: The center of gravity of any heavy body cannot ascend except violently; for it is against the law of nature that a heavy body should tend upward as it were of its own accord.

145 Let a heavy solid A rest on the horizontal plane D E (Fig. I) by its plane surface m n x, and let its line of direction a b fall within its base m n x. I say that it can then in no way happen that the body A slips downward. For it is evident that the center of gravity a is supported by the plane D E on which the body A rests; but a body cannot fall if its center of gravity cannot move downward [§. 43]: therefore the body A will not fall down. But let there be another body H G (Fig. II) whose line of direction Cd falls outside the base F G; it is understood that it will at once fall toward the side e, because, while the whole body is carried with a circular motion about F, its center of gravity C is continually descending: therefore it must needs fall [§. 144]. Moreover, the center of gravity C is not supported by the plane D E, since the line of direction Cd runs outside the base F G: therefore it is necessary that the body H G should tumble down [§. 144].

146 Hence the reason appears why some leaning towers do not fall, such as those of Bologna and Pisa, observed by me while I was traveling through Italy in the year 1767. The Bologna tower is square, 130 feet high (1). The Pisa tower is round, 138 feet high. The plumb line of the Bologna tower stands off from the base by an interval of 9 feet, while the plumb line of the tower of Pisa runs outside the base over a space of 15 feet. Yet they remain firm and stable, because the line of direction of each is within the base, and therefore neither can tumble down. Hence it also follows that slender bodies, such as a needle, for example, can by no means stand upon their point, for its base is too narrow; whence any inclination, however slight, any impulse of the air, however small, suffices for its line of direction to run outside the base.

148 By means of the motion of the center of gravity it is also explained how it can happen that a body, while ascending, continually descends, which at first sight seems a Paradox. Let a triangle A B C (Fig. IV) be constructed of three pieces of wood, whose base C B is equal to the axes of two cones joined together by their bases G F. Under the base C B let two supports C D, B E be placed, shorter than the radius of the base of the cones G F. If those two cones are set upon the extremity A, they will seem to ascend into C B, where the elevation is greatest; yet the center of gravity will descend.

149 That this may be understood more plainly, consider the plane A B b (Fig. V) in which the center of gravity a of the two cones is found. This center is raised above the horizon by as much as the line a b, which is equal to p F. If the cone advanced upon F D, the center of gravity a would describe the line a p parallel to the horizon F D. But the cone in the IV. figure moves along the two planes B A, A C in such a way that its vertex x x is in B C, or in C (Fig. V): therefore in the motion of the cone the center of gravity a describes a C, that is, it continually descends, so that when it arrives at C, its center of gravity will have descended by as much as is marked by p C; but the motion of bodies is determined by the motion of their center of gravity: therefore if the center of the cones descends, as has been demonstrated, the cone must ascend. It is necessary, then, that the double cone should ascend along the two planes of the IV. figure.

150 The knowledge of the center of gravity and of the line of direction is suited to explaining many other things. A man, for example, who sits in such a way that his legs make a right angle with his thighs, and his thighs too are at a right angle with his trunk, will not be able to rise unless he first inclines his shoulders or draws his foot back, so that the line of direction may fall within the base of the feet. If a man stands touching a wall with his shoulders and heels, and resting on the ground only with the tips of his feet, he will not be able to bend himself unless he puts a foot forward; otherwise, when he bends, he must needs fall, because the line of direction then falls outside the base.

T           doubt, so it ought by no means to come into question here; the

Physicists consider only this: how far does that divisibility extend? This contemplation is indeed of the highest moment in Physics, and for that reason the modern Physicists have instituted very many experiments and have illustrated this subject in published writings. But can matter, body, or the physical continuum be divided to infinity, or must one at last come to a stop at indivisible parts? It is a controversy which, as Fr. Regnault says (m), has from the very rise of Philosophy tormented famous and most elegant wits without fruit. We shall approach the matter with this design: that, having set forth the state of the controversy, we may candidly expound what can seem certain in it.

153 That, then, is called a continuum which results from parts so joined that their extremities are one, that is, belong to altogether the same substance, as are the parts of wood, which compose the same single substance of the wood.

That, however, is called contiguous whose extreme parts are together, as when hands, or two bodies, touch each other. The parts of some composite are also said to be placed in succession, or placed side by side, when particles of another body, e.g. of air, lie between them, as are the grains in a heap of wheat. Those parts are called aliquot which, repeated some number of times, exactly equal the whole. Thus the foot is an aliquot part of the fathom, because, repeated six times, it exactly equals the fathom.

154 Those parts are called aliquant which, repeated any number of times, never exactly equal the whole, but either exceed it or fall short of it: thus a part four feet long is an aliquant part of the fathom, because if it is taken twice it exceeds the fathom, while taken once it does not yet equal it. Proportional parts are those which decrease in continued proportion; thus the fathom can be divided into two halves, and either of these into two others, and so on. The

Peripatetics and very many Cartesians judge the parts of the physical continuum to be divisible to infinity. Those who follow Epicurus and Gassendi defend the contrary opinion.

(m) Entret. Physiques. Entret. I. [p. 58] extended: therefore every body is always, and to infinity, divisible. The Epicureans reply by distinguishing the major: everything extended taken mathematically, they grant; taken physically, they deny. That is said to be extended mathematically which is considered only by reason of its dimensions, without regard to the condition and nature of the extended subject; that, however, is called extended physically which is considered as a certain physical substance endowed with a definite nature and condition. Whatever is extended can be divided mathematically and by the mind, but not always in reality itself and physically, since there can be a certain simple substance not composed of parts, namely the atom, which is the first subject of which all sensible bodies consist, and the last into which they are resolved. Thus far the Epicureans and Gassendists.

156 These, moreover, argue thus against the Peripatetics: If matter were divisible to infinity, a tiny body, such as a grain of wheat, would contain within itself infinite parts in act, for a body is conceived as divisible only into those parts which it contains; but this is manifestly contradictory: therefore matter, or the continuum, is not divisible to infinity. The Peripatetics reply by distinguishing the major: if matter were divisible according to aliquot parts, a tiny body would have, etc., they grant; if it is divisible only into proportional parts, each of which includes infinitely many others within itself, they deny. You have the state of the question.

157 But all these things (as Purchot and Klaus very well observe) (n) are of such a kind that, if only the reasons, and not the replies, are weighed, they seem on both sides to carry the force of demonstrations. So that it may therefore be permitted to pronounce this one thing: it is uncertain whether corporeal magnitude can always be divided, or whether all its division at last terminates in indivisible parts; which we assert all the more fittingly as we know the more certainly that for the advancement of Physics it is altogether the same whether the parts of the continuum are posited as indivisible or as divisible to infinity; for, for the principles of natural body and for explaining the phenomena in general, it suffices to show that any bodies whatever can be split into parts so minute that reason itself is astonished, which is to be proved by us as clearly as possible in the following proposition.

158 I say, therefore: bodies are actually divided, and can be divided, into utterly minute parts in an altogether stupendous manner. 159 Fill the vial A (Fig. VI) with a bent neck, which is called an Aeolipile, with rose water or any other fragrant water; put a fire under it, or the case B, in which there is spirit of wine with a lighted wick; the water will soon evaporate through the slender neck, and the odor will be diffused through the whole room, however large. After two or three minutes remove the vial from the fire and stop it up: the diminution of the water will scarcely be sensible, so that a very small quantity of it has been dispersed through the whole air of the room. Now, by a calculation made by the learned Fr. Giovanni della Torre (p), a man most perspicacious in searching out the secrets of nature, it has been ascertained that that very small portion of water which evaporated in the space of three minutes is resolved into 3,583,180,800 particles sensible to the nostrils, which truly surpasses all comprehension.

160 The odors of the fragrant fields of the island of Ceylon are carried toward approaching ships even at a distance of ten leagues. A tiny particle of musk so imbues other larger bodies — clothes, gloves, books — with its odor that they keep the odor for a very long time, and yet continually never cease to give off odoriferous parts. Many similar things are related by Boyle, Keill, ’s Gravesande, and other Physicists. Since, then, with so many odorous particles perpetually flowing off, no sensible loss of substance can be observed in many cases, these effluvia will have to be incredibly subtle.

161 Secondly, it is shown from tinctures. The said Boyle relates that he found by experience that if a grain of copper, dissolved and mixed with spirit of wine, is poured into a lamp whose wick, made of plume alum, is not consumed, a flame tinged with a blue color is produced for a whole half hour; and so new particles of copper continually succeed one another and produce the same color in the flame: so that we cannot sufficiently wonder by what means that particle of copper could have been cut up so minutely as to supply always new color, that is, always new particles.

162 Thirdly, the same is proved from the ductility of gold; for, as the most celebrated Physicist Réaumur (q) testifies, a cubic ounce of gold is beaten out by the gold-beaters into more than five hundred times a hundred thousand square leaves of the utmost thinness; but, what altogether surpasses every power of the imagination, if one of these leaves is wrapped round a silver cylinder and covers its whole surface, and the cylinder is then drawn gradually through several successively narrower holes until it is reduced to the thickness of a very fine thread, or of a hair, the surface of this very long thread will nevertheless appear gilded everywhere, which

163 Fourthly, an abyss of minuteness in matter is demonstrated from microscopic observations. Fr. Lana Terzi (r) relates that he observed a very white animalcule which had been invisible to even the most perspicacious eyes, and which, placed under a microscope magnifying twenty-seven million times, appeared equal to a grain of wheat: with a very swift motion it scarcely covered the length of a grain of wheat in twelve seconds of time. What, then, must be the wondrous subtlety of the steps, of the feet, of the eyes, of the pupil, of the blood, of the animal spirits in an animalcule of this kind! The same must be said of those very fine animalcules which are seen in cheese with the help of a microscope. How tiny, moreover, is the pupil of those animalcules, through which nevertheless far finer rays of light pass? How tiny are those parts which can be called animal spirits? If we consider these things, we must needs confess that something greater, and more than our faculty of imagining can present to us, lies hidden in the smallest things.

At his infinitae. propémodum minores. effe debent partes fluidi , quod per canaliculos decurrit , nempe faneuis, lympha, & fpiritus animales. ; Quanta in vilifsimo animalculo portenta, Divinaeque Omnipotentiae argumenta !

164 That most skillful investigator of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, observed in water kept for some days, with the help of an exquisite microscope, very small animalcules, thousands of which do not exceed the size of a globule of common sand. Now since any animalcule whatever is an organic body, let us weigh for a little how delicate and subtle must be the parts necessary to constitute it and to preserve its vital action. It is not easily conceived how in so narrow a little space there can be comprised the heart, which is the fount of life, the muscles necessary for motion, the glands, the stomach and intestines, and innumerable other members without which an animal cannot exist. Moreover, since each of the members mentioned is also an organic body, they cannot lack other parts necessary for their actions. They will therefore consist of fibers, little membranes, tunics, veins, arteries, nerves, and similar little canals, whose minuteness far surpasses the powers of the imagination. But almost infinitely smaller than these must be the parts of the fluid which runs through the little canals, namely the blood, the lymph and the animal spirits. What prodigies in the meanest animalcule, and what proofs of the Divine Omnipotence!

> &ac liquida innumeris poris pertufa (uot. Probatur: admittenda. eft fumira illorum corporum porófitas, quam facta in unoquoque cor. . pos

fluid, or soft, or hard. Pores arise, moreover, from the joining together of the smallest corpuscles that constitute visible bodies. For these, on account of their figures, can scarcely ever be so joined that they fit one another altogether and leave no cavities and openings to be occupied by some subtle matter foreign to the body.

Imagine, e.g., that the smallest corpuscles which compose some body are spherical:

then every three spheres will touch one another in three points and will leave a triangular space in the middle; wherefore there will be in the body innumerable triangular pores of this kind, filled with some very subtle matter.

168 It will be the same if the smallest component corpuscles are laid down to be of other figures, except that pores of very different figures as well must necessarily arise from the joining together of those corpuscles. Pores, moreover, are for the most part so very small that they are not perceived by the senses. We must not, therefore, abide by the judgment of the senses in determining how much solid matter is found in any body. For it can happen that two bodies equal in bulk seem to contain the same quantity of matter beneath their surface, and yet in one of the two scarcely any matter is found. These things laid down,

169 I say: all bodies, whether large or small, hard as well as liquid, are pierced through with innumerable pores. Proof: the greatest porosity of those bodies must be admitted which experiments made in each body demonstrate:

The minor is proved; and, to begin with diaphanous bodies, their very great porosity is more than sufficiently established from the fact that they transmit light, whereas, if these bodies were not pierced through with innumerable pores, they would deny passage to the rays of light. Wherefore air, water, glass, crystal, diamond and the other pellucid stones must be filled with innumerable pores; for pellucidity cannot be understood unless an easy passage lies open for the rays of light to the opposite points of the surfaces. Hence it is evident that crystal, e.g., contains almost nothing whatever of solid matter.

170 Now, since the smallest parts of all bodies appear in some measure pellucid, as is observed with the microscope, it follows that opaque bodies too are not devoid of their pores; for if the smallest parts of which they grow together are porous, the bodies composed of those smallest parts must also be porous. Let us now speak of particular bodies.

> :Bimno f[oiidae continere.

171 That woods, however compact and hard, are porous is argued by the manner of their nourishment, which could not take place unless the woody fibers were perforated, so that, namely, they can allow passage to the sap ascending from the roots. Earthenware vessels, though baked and hard, are so porous that they easily drink in the particles of a liquid poured into them, and keep its odor a very long time. There are also thick and compact stones which transmit water, and from them are made mortars through which water is strained, that it may be purged of its muddy parts. Magnetic effluvia pass through wood, glass and metals: for if iron, or small fragments of steel, are placed on some plate of glass, wood or metal, and the magnet is moved in any way whatever below the plate, you will see the iron stirred by the motion of the magnet.

172 The hardest marbles, too, are penetrated by very many fluids, by spirit of wine, by spirit of turpentine, as the most distinguished Dufay testifies in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (z). The most distinguished Homberg (a) discovered that a salt extracted from mixtures of quicklime, distilled vinegar, saltpeter, sea salt and common sulfur penetrates iron no otherwise than water permeates paper.

Suitable for this use will be mutton fat, wax heated until liquid, or common varnish laid on several times. Certainly Nollet (b) found by experience,

This practice serves those who sail the sea for a longer time, and also for bringing into our kingdoms foreign birds, which would not be carried alive across so many stretches of land and sea without the greatest trouble.

174 I will also describe for you, so that the porosity of bodies may appear more clearly, the ink which is commonly called sympathetic by the Chemists. It is usually prepared in this way. Let one ounce of litharge be taken and mixed with five or six ounces of distilled vinegar, and let it be filtered through paper in the usual way. This liquor, which is called by the Chemists vinegar of Saturn, or impregnation of Saturn made with distilled vinegar, is to be used for tracing characters, which you will no more perceive than if you had written with water; but if another liquor is applied, to be prepared by an artifice presently to be described, the characters at once become visible. Let one ounce of orpiment therefore be taken and mixed with two ounces of quicklime; let water be poured onto the mixture: there will be had a second liquor, with which some paper inscribed with the characters previously traced is to be moistened; even with a hundred sheets of paper placed in between, the particles of this liquor at once pass through the many sheets of paper, and you will read, splendidly black, the characters which before escaped the eyes, and you will marvel.

175 But you will marvel more that quicksilver itself also passes through the pores of wood: for if a little cylindrical vessel C B A (Fig. VII) is made, and a glass tube about three feet long, furnished with a screw E at D, is inserted into it, which is filled with quicksilver through an opening in the base of the little vessel fitted with a wooden screw, then, the little hole at D being opened and the screw E removed, so that the pressure of the external air upon the quicksilver may not be intercepted, the mercury bursts out through the pores of the wood at G F in a delightful spectacle; and if the part G F from which the quicksilver flows out is observed with a microscope, little round holes arranged in order present themselves, to be looked at with no less delight, as Thümmig reports in the Institutions of the Wolffian Philosophy (c).

176 The porosity of fluids too is easily gathered from the fact that certain fluids imbibe one another. Let a vessel be filled to a height of three inches with oil of vitriol, let as much water be added to it, then let it be closed, so that nothing may evaporate in their effervescence: when the fermentation has subsided, you will have not six inches of height, but a smaller number. Moreover, if within any vessel there are two inches’ height of sand, and you mix with them two inches’ height of water, you will have not four, but only two inches of matter. I should be long if I wished to describe here all the phenomena that could adorn the present subject.

178 Manifold, therefore, is the necessity and use of pores in nature. First, in the generation of plants, while the little seed of the plant is unfolded by the heat and moisture entering it; similarly in the production of animals: namely, a hen sitting on an egg hatches the chick by no other means than by the heat that enters and penetrates the pores of the shell. Secondly, in nourishment, since through them suitable nourishment and juices are sent off to the single parts. Thirdly, to omit the rest — fermentations, namely, various rarefactions, magnetic motions and other effects, for producing and explaining which these minute interstices contribute wonderfully — they are of the greatest use for excreting harmful and superfluous humors in animals, which is effected by perspiration, of which we shall treat in the following chapter. And thus far of porosity, which is a property common to all bodies.

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

179

Obj. 1. If all bodies are pierced through with innumerable pores, then we do not know the absolute weights of bodies: for the quantity of matter is unknown, and hence also the weight, which is proportional to the quantity of matter; but this seems contradictory: therefore. I grant the major, deny the minor:

for no perfectly solid body can be found, as is manifest from what has been said; and if one could indeed be found, the quantity of matter in each body, and hence its absolute weight, would at once become known, namely by comparing some given portion of matter with an equal volume of different bodies.

180 Wherefore, since such a perfectly solid body is nowhere found, those idle

Philosophers indulge in superfluous conjectures who attempt to determine the quantity of matter by fictitious hypotheses; nay, it is most probable that this whole universe consists of a very small quantity of matter. But you will say: at least gold will be a perfectly solid body: therefore what we have said thus far is false. I deny the antecedent: for gold of itself transmits water, not to say mercury, whose parts are doubtless subtler, as the most distinguished Martini testifies (d); for a hollow golden globe filled with water, and then, with great force compressed,

181 Obj. 2. If the porosity of bodies were so great, the organs of the senses would perpetually lead us into error, and God, Best and Greatest, would perpetually deceive us by false sensations; but this illusion is contrary to the

> ^ CAPUT V. -—

Divine veracity: therefore. I deny the major: for very many fallacies of the senses can be called back to examination and corrected by philosophical reasoning, and the senses must not be rashly believed, as we said in the Logic. The judgment of truth is not in the senses, says St. Augustine. God, Best and Greatest, therefore by no means drives us into the error of the senses; for it pleased his infinite Goodness to grant to men only those cognitions which can lead to the just uses of this life and to the ultimate end, namely eternal life.

> De tranfpiratione corporum, -

C H A P T E R V.

On the transpiration of bodies.

he effluvia of a body are said to be certain very subtle corpuscles 182

T          which burst out of the pores of the body and are scattered in every

direction as if in a circle. The motion, moreover, by which a body emits effluvia is called Transpiration. For a body is said to transpire which exhales a very subtle substance. The Atmosphere of a body is the space occupied by its effluvia diffused as if in a circle around the body itself; so that, if the body X (Fig. VIII) diffuses outside itself effluvia which fill the space A B C

D and hence surround the body itself, the space comprised by the outermost surface A B C D will be the atmosphere of that body (namely, the sphere of its exhalations, or of vapor). All bodies, therefore, which emit effluvia are endowed with an atmosphere. These things being established,

183 I say, therefore: there seems to be scarcely any mixed body in nature which does not either continually transpire, or (though it is not the same thing)

from which certain outflowings do not fly off. I said that to transpire and to emit outflowings are not the same: because the first belongs only to bodies endowed with animal or vegetable life, the other also to those devoid of life. It is proved by observations and experiments. For just as there is no sensible body which lacks pores and which does not contain something of a very subtle substance, so likewise none

184 Truly no other reason is given why plants, while the air is very hot, droop and wither, but, when the air has cooled, begin to flourish and revive, than that this hidden expiration, brought about by the heat, robs the plants of a huge quantity of corpuscles; whence it comes about that the fibers are exhausted and slackened, lose their firmness, and, through the lack of the corpuscles and of the spirits which sustain the little tubes of the fibers, are at length forced to yield to the forces of gravity; which shines forth most of all in the heliotrope. Not to mention to you the odor which vegetable bodies above all diffuse in every direction.

185 As regards very many mixed bodies, e.g. wine, spirit of wine, and others of this kind which abound in active substance, it is evident that, if they have been exposed to the free air for a considerable time, such mixtures are much weakened, a manifest sign that much active substance has been lost through the flying off of a very subtle vapor. That the weight too is in some cases sensibly diminished, the said Fr. Lana Terzi (e) shows by many experiments. Of camphor that eminent man Robert Boyle (f) speaks thus. When I had weighed camphor in an exact balance, in the space of a few hours it suffered a visible loss of its weight through the flying off of corpuscles: he also records a remarkable evaporation which he observed in apples, as well as in bodies covered with a firmer integument, such as eggs, which became manifestly lighter from day to day, and in other bodies which he had kept long in the balances, observing the decrease of their weight.

186 Effluvia emanating by exhalation for the most part retain the same color, taste and odor which the bodies themselves from which they fly off possess. Thus, to omit the rest, Fr. Lana Terzi confesses that when he was preparing a salt from wormwood and touched his tongue with his hand, although his hand had previously in no way handled the wormwood, he nevertheless perceived exactly the same taste which belongs to the plant itself, namely from the exhalations of the salt adhering to his hand. Another, who had taken every day a very little spirit of vitriol mixed into his drink, noticed that the keys he carried with him, well polished to brightness, had contracted blackness and rust, although they had never been touched by this spirit. A girl afflicted with jaundice imparted the color of a citron to the clothes she wore and to the silver coins she carried for use.

187 From what has been said it is inferred, 1. That there is scarcely any mixed body which is not surrounded by its own atmosphere. For every body that emits effluvia is endowed with an atmosphere. It is inferred, 2. That there exists no mixed body whose internal, subtler particles are not affected with a continual motion, although a motion of this kind may be very slight and can hardly be perceived by the senses. For since the ethereal matter, placed in continual motion, permeates even the most compact body, plucks away its fine parts and excites a certain exhalation, it seems evident that there is in bodies an intestine agitation of certain subtle parts; nor does this come to rest in those smallest particles alone which first flow out through the body, but others too receive an impulse; for the subtle matter, having entered through the pores and being agitated, continually urges and impels other particles that form the sides of the pores, whence it comes about that it plucks away now this, now that particle from the rest of the body and, the bond being broken, carries it off with itself.

188 It is inferred, 3., with Robert Boyle (g) and Lana Terzi (h): that there is no natural composite all of whose parts are entirely at rest. It is plain both from what has been said and from this, that since there is no body which is not at length corrupted as if of its own accord, there is certainly none of these whose internal, subtler parts are not continually moved. But let us say a few things about insensible transpiration in the human body from the most learned Sanctorius (i).

189 Sanctorius was the first to reduce the insensible perspiration of the human body to calculation, having spent 30 years in observing it; from his observations it has pleased us to note down some things. Insensible perspiration carries off more from the body in the space of 24 hours than all the sensible evacuations together in 15 days. This is aphorism 4 of Sect. 1 of the Medicina Statica of Sanctorius. Healthy men in winter transpire 50 ounces within 24 hours; likewise, within the same time, out of 8 pounds of food taken, perspiration carries off 5 pounds. Aphor. 6. The quantity of insensible perspiration suffers some variety according to the variety of nature, region, season, age, and diseases. Aphor. 7. Any cold, even the slightest, which we suffer while sleeping at night, impedes perspiration. Aph. 50. One of the frequent causes which in summertime impede perspiration is frequent agitation of the body in bed. Aph. 51.

(i) Medicina Statica. [p. 68] assert that there is little or no usefulness in these matters; but again I say to you: do not be led by the talk of the unskilled. Let us, however, return to the point from which we digressed.

191 The most distinguished Dodart (j), Member of the Royal Academy of Paris and physician to the King of France, established by experiments carried out over a space of 33 years that transpiration is far greater in youth than in any other age (k). From what has been said it is manifest that a very rapid change takes place in our bodies, and that the hardest parts of our body are subject to this perpetual vicissitude; and indeed there is no bone in the animal body so hard, so compact, that it is not nourished, and hence that it is not changed, and does not lose part of itself and recover a new one.

192 Who, then, will not marvel at the hand of Almighty God, which in the structure of our body has disposed so many very subtle instruments necessary for nourishment and evaporation! But let us contemplate a little more attentively the single stages of human life and the different states of our body; for these things have more usefulness than quarrelling sharply about the appetite of matter and other trifles of the common philosophy. In childhood the parts are very tender, abound in water, and are perforated with innumerable little canals, which anatomical injections indeed demonstrate in the bones, membranes, cartilages and tendons, and in the skin itself. Hence it comes about that the force which is the principle of motion in the animal body extends the softer parts more easily. With the progress of time the parts become more robust and are solidified, and this goes on until at length the forces of the heart are no longer sufficient for extending the solids.

193 Nevertheless the cellular tissue still remains easily flexible and in many places admits fat and blood; hence adults become fatter up to a certain time, and yet they do not grow. In advanced age the cellular tissue becomes thicker, the bones of old men stiffen, the excretory vessels are compressed, the secretions are diminished, the blood is dried up and deposits a kind of earthy humor in the single parts of the body. Hence all the parts are observed to be harder; hence bony crusts are found on the surface of the bones, and above all in the vertebrae.

(j) In Ozanam, Recreat. Mathematiques, vol. 3.

(k) Of the same Dodart the said Ozanam relates a fact not unfittingly to be brought forward here: namely that at the beginning of Lent Dodart weighed 116 pounds and 1 ounce, then spent the time of the holy fast living chiefly on legumes. Then on the Saturday of Holy Week, examining the weight of his body again, he found that it did not exceed 107 lb. and 12 oz.; that is, in the space of 46 days he had lost 8 lb. with 5 oz., namely the 1/14 part of his substance. Having afterwards resumed his accustomed manner of living, after 4 days he had gained 4 pounds in weight. Whence it is plain that in 8 or 9 days he would have recovered the integrity of his former weight, and that what is dissipated by fasting is thus easily repaired.

I also deny the major: for the fact that the fluids necessary for living do not burst out through the pores of the human body is to be traced back to the different figure of the fluids and of the pores, whose variety had to be such as to prevent the exit of the necessary fluids in the state of a healthy body.

Therefore the Divine Goodness is to be praised again and always, which so composed the admirable structure of our body that we might live, and live as long as God himself willed, to pass thereafter to immortal life.

Therefore. I deny the minor: for although the matter of our body has flown off through insensible transpiration, although it has even passed into the substance of a carnivorous beast or of a barbarous man, God will discern it and restore it to the body whose it will be. Not all the particles which from birth until death constituted our body through its different ages will rise again with us; for then we should be raised up as monsters of enormous size.

body is called rare which under great dimensions contains little matter; dense, 198

> ^ - - - " 22ís H exis - £s

A           however, which has much matter under small dimensions; thus water filling

half a little vessel and boiling when brought near the fire is called rare, because for so great an extension as it then has there is in reality little aqueous matter; wax, on the contrary, first heated and afterwards cooling, is dense, because it contracts into a smaller space. Hence rarefaction is the motion by which a body, the same quantity of matter remaining, is extended into a greater space. For if something of the same matter is added, e.g. water to boiling water, it will not be rarefaction but augmentation. Condensation is the motion by which a body is reduced to a smaller space without anything of its matter being taken away; for if anything is taken away from wax, e.g., it will not be condensation but diminution.

199 A rare and a stretched body agree in this, that under a greater extension they contain little matter; they differ, however, in this, that the stretched body requires to be brought back to a smaller extension, but not the rare body, precisely, that is, on account of its state of rarity. Similarly a dense and a compressed body agree in this, that under a small extension they have much matter. But the compressed body requires a greater extension, not, however, the dense, namely by reason of its density.

The compressed body requires a greater extension: for the particles composing it have been reduced to a smaller space by an extrinsic cause; but the dense body is so constituted by some intrinsic cause that it does not require a greater extension; and this cause can be the binding together, the new interweaving and the fixing of the particles composing that body; and once this is in place, even with

200 I say: the rarefaction of bodies consists in this, that the pores of the body are dilated; condensation, however, in this, that the same pores are constricted; upon which dilatation there follows an entry of particles and of insensible corpuscles, as upon the constriction their expulsion. Proof: a body is said to rarefy when, its matter not being increased, its volume grows and occupies a greater space; to be condensed when, its matter not being diminished, its volume decreases and the body fits a smaller space [§. 198]; but it is evident that the volume of a body is increased without its matter growing, by the very fact that the pores in it are dilated, and that the volume of a body decreases without anything being taken away from its matter, by the very fact that the pores are narrowed: therefore. That in the physical sense, moreover, there cannot be rarefaction without the entry of insensible corpuscles, fiery, ethereal or others, is plain; because, since (as will be said) there is no sensible void, and so every sensible space is full of some very subtle matter, it follows that when the pores are dilated, the bulk of the whole body being sensibly increased, this matter, being very subtle, enters and fills them. One must reason about condensation in the same way, proportionally.

201 Confirm.: In physical matters that opinion is to be preferred to the others which is easy to grasp, does not bring in mysteries almost surpassing the human intellect, and in which an account is most easily given of the phenomena occurring in the motion of rarefaction and condensation [Axiom. III, IV & V, §§. 32 & 33]; but such is our opinion: therefore. The minor will shine forth both from what has been said thus far and from the solution of the objections, and is also proved by induction from experiments and by their explanation. For it is explained why water congealed into ice occupies a greater space than in its natural state. The Florentine Academicians, to examine this exactly, chose a glass tube closed at one end, which they filled with water to half its height, then immersed it in finely crushed snow until the water was turned into ice; whereby it came about that the dilated water rose in the tube and occupied a greater space in it than when it was fluid.

202 Moreover, with a most exact balance they examined the weight of water before freezing, and of the same water once frozen, and found that the unfrozen water weighed more than after freezing. The reason of these things, moreover, is this: since the particles of water on one side adhere to one another by congelation and embrace one another more tightly, they leave on the other side innumerable and quite notable pores, which are filled chiefly with aerial matter; and since this cannot escape through the narrower pores of the water that is freezing, it is dilated; whence it comes about that ice, which is a kind of aggregate of coagulated water and of air thus dilated and enclosed in those little bubbles, becomes more extended than the water itself was before freezing.

Obj. 1. On our opinion no fitting account can be given of the phenomena observed in a vessel which is made of copper, has the shape of a pear or an apple, and has for its little stem a tube ending in a tiny opening; this vessel is called an

Aeolipile. Filled with spirit of wine to a certain quantity and set upon a fire, it will exhibit a fountain of spirit of wine leaping up, and if you bring a candle near it, the liquor springing out will be set alight (Fig. IX). Similarly, if it is filled to half with water and set near coals, it will throw out vapor through the little canal with great vehemence and noise (Fig. X): nay, the vapor will drive the water contained in the

Aeolipile to a height of 20 feet. These things being established, the argument is formed thus.

205 If rarefaction takes place through the dilatation of the pores, then, when water or spirit of wine is rarefied in the aeolipile, the little vessel itself must necessarily be rarefied just as much, since it is nearer to the fire than the liquor contained in it; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Nor are several other things explained more aptly: as that a glass globe (Fig. XI), full of a drop of water or of spirit of wine and closed on all sides, bursts with a crash when brought near the fire; similarly, that chestnuts not cut open, put into live coals, burst with a noise; especially since it cannot be said that the external air, which would have to rarefy the water, permeates the pores of the glass globule. But these arguments can be explained without difficulty. I indeed assert that the aeolipile is somewhat dilated, and also rarefied, by heat; but since it is more solid and consists of more compact matter, it has parts more cohering and fixed into one another; whence, for its pores to be rarefied as much as the liquor contained, a greater force of heat is required than that which suffices for dilating the pores of water or of spirit of wine, bodies, namely, that are liquid and therefore cohere less among themselves.

206 Nor can the other phenomena be explained any less easily. Certainly the bursting of a glass globe arises from the rarefaction of water, or from vapor. The bursting of chestnuts thrown into the fire is likewise brought about by moist particles shut up within the shell, which are rarefied by the heat and seek an outlet. Nor should you wonder that so great a force is attributed by us to vapor, since it is established that rarefied vapor has a greater force than gunpowder, which, shut up in a like little glass globe and of the same weight as the drop of water, does indeed shatter the globe, but with a far smaller crash; and since, moreover, it is known from Nollet (n) that water converted into vapor forms a volume 14000 times greater.

207 Obj. 2. In condensation subtle matter is excluded; therefore no subtle matter is then introduced. I deny the consequence: for since the subtle matter which is introduced joins and binds the parts of the body more tightly to one another, it is the cause of the pores being contracted, and consequently of the other subtle matter, which was contained in them, bursting out; but what is excluded is more than what is newly added, and therefore the dense body occupies less space than it occupied before condensation. The other arguments which the Scholastics are wont to raise are very easily dissolved by distinguishing a twofold signification of rarity and density: one in which this twin change of bodies is taken metaphysically and insensibly, the other in which it is taken physically and sensibly.

208 Obj. finally: when a spark of fire falling on a heap of gunpowder kindles and rarefies it, that motion or rarefaction can proceed neither from the dilatation of the pores nor from subtle matter. For what is it that impels that matter, or agitates it with such force that by mere contact it imparts so great an agitation to the gunpowder? Whence comes its force, so that it throws down citadels themselves, as we see in mines? I reply that this effect is to be referred chiefly to the dilatation of the pores and to the elastic force of the kindled powder; for the kindled powder, which demands a greater place, pressing against the walls on every side, bursts out on the side where it is less resisted: the successive dilatation of the powder increases the force of the percussion. The force of the powder by which it propels a ball from a cannon is also to be attributed to the fiery particles, joined with the elasticity of the air and of the niter; for these so many springs strive in every direction with the utmost force, and since the resistance of the ball is less than that of the hinder part of the cannon, it therefore hurls even a ball of several pounds to a notable distance. And of such great effects in the powder the principal cause is saltpeter, on account of its elasticity; whence, as Kircher says, if a cannon is filled with powder made of sulphur and charcoal alone, without niter, and the powder is kindled, it will not expel the ball from the cannon, the spring, namely, being wanting.

On the Fermentation of bodies.

ermentation seems to be nothing other than an intestine motion of a mixed 209

F          body, by which its subtler and more active parts loosen its texture, attenu‐

ate the coarser particles, and agitate them in such a way that a certain effervescence and ebullition is observed in the whole mixture. The explanation of fermentation can best be derived from two principles, namely from acid and alkaline salts: for since the particles of an acid salt, on account of their rigidity, intrude themselves only with violence into the pores of an alkaline salt and into alkaline materials, the ethereal matter impelling a great part of them, and compress the fiery and airy particles lying hidden in the pores, it comes about through these violent concussions, with the spring both of the fire and of the air coming to their aid, that the passages into which they rapidly rushed are broken open, and that the alkaline particles are impelled by the help of the rarefied air and of the fire and are scattered in every direction; and this scattering of the diverse parts is followed by that swelling observed in fermentations which, if it forms something like bubbles of vapor, is called ebullition, and if it is joined with sensible heat, effervescence.

210 In general it can be said that that intestine motion of fermentation is excited by spirituous particles which, contained and compressed within coarser and more solid ones, burst out, when these are scattered and cut to pieces, as from an opened prison, unfold themselves more freely, and by their motion agitate the other parts, variously mix them together, and disturb them. 211 Fulminating powder is a mixture composed of three parts of niter, two of salt of tartar, and one of sulphur, each reduced separately to powder and then mixed together. This, put in an iron spoon over a candle or live coals and heated to a certain degree, is suddenly dissipated with a horrible detonation, and sometimes bursts the spoon. The action, namely, of the fiery corpuscles insinuating themselves carries the spicules of the niter into the salt of tartar, and the dilatation of the internal air brings about that violent agitation from which the detonation arises. Father Regnault gives as the cause of the bursting of the spoon that the force of the powder is not only borne in every direction, but is moreover driven into the spoon by the resisting upper air, the more powerfully the greater the speed and vehemence with which the dissipated powder strikes and moves the air. From these things the phenomena of fermentation are explained.

212 First: if spirit of niter is poured onto mercury or tin, an effervescence and a very hot ebullition will follow; for the acid particles of the spirit of niter, aided by the spring of the internal air, rush rapidly into the alkaline particles of the mercury or of the tin; hence they communicate agitation in every direction, whence effervescence, ebullition, sensible heat. Secondly: if oil of tartar is mixed with spirit of niter in which iron filings have previously been dissolved, the fermentation will take fire; for the acid particles communicate motion and agitation in every direction to the alkaline ones, and this motion is greater than that which is produced by simple heat; this motion in every direction, moreover, is produced by the spirit of niter, which meets in the iron filings a great many obstacles that must be overcome by it. Other explanations of the phenomena can be seen in the Dictionary of Physics published in French by Father Paulian (p).

213 Thirdly: the fermentation of quicklime when water is poured on it arises for this reason. In the making of lime the heat breaks the fibers of the stone, enlarges the pores, and makes new ones; these interstices and pores are filled with subtle matter and fiery corpuscles; then, when the lime begins to cool, the outer air penetrates into its many passages and is condensed by more and more air coming in after it; and so, if water is poured on, it violently pervades the very dry lime, and by its agitation the fiery particles and the mineral salt lying hidden in the pores and left behind after calcination are loosed and freed from their prison; whence, the little fires acting with greater force, and the acid particles of the salts also thrusting themselves into the pores of the alkali, the parts of the lime, forced to yield, are separated and scattered: hence the effervescence and sensible heat. On this matter, among others, Willis (q), Boerhaave (r), François Bayle (s) and Father Lana (t) may be consulted.

214 Hence, fourthly, can also be explained the phenomenon of the burning powder, which is also called the pyrophorus powder. Let powdered alum be put in an earthen dish with a third part of its weight of honey, or flour, or sugar, and, the dish being set over coals, let these powders be stirred for a long time until they are thoroughly dried and turn dark. Then let them be pounded in a mortar and dried again, and this until the parts of the powder no longer unite but remain separate. Then let this powder be put in a small long-necked matrass (u), which is buried up to the neck in sand; the matrass being lightly stopped with paper, let the vessel be exposed to a fire increased by degrees, until the lower part of the neck glows red and no more smoke comes forth; when the fire is put out, let the powder be placed in a phial well closed, so that it is not exposed to the air, and kept for use.

215 The property of this powder is that even the smallest portion of it, exposed to the air, takes fire spontaneously, without noise. In the course of time, however, it loses this force, and when it does not take fire quickly, it often takes fire when it is moistened with the breath. The reason of these things is given. When it is exposed to the fire to be roasted, it is then intimately pervaded by the fire, and acquires the power of retaining fire, as an alkali does. As soon as it is exposed to the air, it draws in the air’s moisture, and so the latent, compressed fire acquires the force of expanding itself and is rendered sensible, as in lime moistened with water; hence in the course of time it loses this force, because the fire flies off; and if there has not been too much moisture in the air, it takes fire when moistened with the breath.

216 I cannot, however, pass over the different chemical vegetations that belong to this subject. Among these the most celebrated are the tree of Mars and the tree of Diana, or Philosophical tree. The first is set forth by Lemery the son in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (x). Into a glass vessel (Fig. XIII.) in which there are iron filings, pour spirit of niter upon them; a huge effervescence and ebullition will arise. The spirit will be tinged with an intensely red color on account of the dissolved iron, and many red fumes will arise. When the effervescence, by which the parts of the iron are raised to the upper regions, has subsided, throw into the liquor oil of tartar per deliquium; a moderate effervescence will arise, by which the liquor will be greatly swollen; a little after, on its sides and on the lip, countless branches and shrubs will arise, which without any visible effervescence will rise above the liquor and the lip, and fall down on the outside, as is shown in the figure. In another vegetation Lemery employed, in place of the spirit of niter, a spirit produced from the red vapor which spirit of niter gives off in effervescence, and he used this in another experiment to dissolve iron, and a more distinct vegetation

217 That these phenomena may be explained, it must be observed that spirit of niter divides iron into very small parts and associates itself with them, and these parts are the smaller the more the spirit abounds in the sulphur of the iron. That sulphur, moreover, can divide metals is well established. Now let oil of tartar, which is an earthy alkali, be added: the parts of the nitrous acid do not cohere so closely with those of the iron that they cannot enter with their points into the cavities of the alkali; hence arises the effervescence, which the bubbles of air continually bursting from the liquor display. Since, however, the acid parts are united with the iron, they cannot rush into the alkali with very great force, and therefore the effervescence is not so sensible as that which arises if oil of tartar per deliquium is put into simple spirit of niter; but in our experiment the acid particles of the niter partly enter the alkali, partly cohere with the particles of the iron.

219 The tree of Diana is produced easily and expeditiously by the method handed down by Homberg in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (y). Take four drachms of silver filings (z), and let an amalgam (a) be made with two drachms of mercury, without fire. Dissolve the amalgam in four ounces of aqua fortis, and throw the solution into a vessel with 18 ounces of common water; then shake the water, and put it away in a well-stopped phial. Whenever you wish to use it to produce the tree, take an ounce of this water and put it in another phial; into this put a common amalgam of gold or of silver of the size of a pea, which should be semifluid, or of the consistency of butter: after two or three minutes threads will begin to come forth from the amalgam that has settled to the bottom of the vessel, which will put out lateral branches, will grow little by little, and will be formed into small silver shrubs, as is depicted in Figure XIV; and within a quarter of an hour this, together with the amalgam to which they adhere, will harden and become white. Behold the tree of Diana made in a short time, which was formerly completed only by a long operation.

221 If the solution is too dilute, the trees will be produced more slowly, but the branches will be more conspicuous. If the solution is stronger, then the trees will arise denser and less perfect. If the amalgam put in, of the size of a pea, is hard, it will be dissolved by the solution, and the tree will arise as in Fig. XV. A vegetation is also made by means of rainwater, which can be very well explained on our view. In rainy and thundery weather collect a determinate quantity of water running down from a roof. Keep it: after several days it will deposit a greenish matter to the height of two lines, which in hot weather, or when placed near a fireplace, will swell, will produce bubbles, then filaments and green branches, some of which will rise as far as the surface of the water; when the heat ceases they will settle again to the bottom; when the heat returns they will sprout again.

222 Each branch will have at its extremities bubbles of air, as though they were fruit. This vegetation, unless perhaps you prefer (which I allow) that very true seeds fall to the earth together with the water, is easily explained by means of effervescence; for the matter is first inflated, and on account of the effervescence air is expelled, which is visible, and this raises and distributes the matter into branches and shrubs, which, on account of their charming green color, wonderfully imitate the natural vegetation of plants. These things are rather curious. You will find many others in the celebrated Authors often praised by me.

224 Time, then, to begin with it, is indeed very easily conceived, but can scarcely be explained or defined by us. “For what,” says the great Augustine (b), “what do we mention more familiarly and more knowingly in speaking than time? And we understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it also when we hear another speaking of it. What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know: yet I say confidently that I know that if nothing passed away there would be no past time, and if nothing were, there would be no present time.” Aristotle, however, wishing to define time, says that it is the number of motion according to before and after (c). This definition is deservedly wont to be censured by the Moderns; for it can more probably be said that motion itself is the number and measure of time, since we are certainly accustomed to number or to measure the duration of time by some motion, such as that of a clock or of the sun.

> 215 Res etiam non modó quum moventur, fed etiam dum quiefcunt, tempori fubjiciuntur, atque aliquo tempore ccatiientur, ideoque tempus dici deberet aequaliter numerus, & meníura metus, Gr quietis, .& quemadmedüm tempus dicitur. ab Ariftotele quiauerus cujefcumque totus, 1ta quoque dici deberct mumeres cujuf- «umque quietis. 225 Things, moreover, are subject to time not only when they are moved but also while they are at rest, and are contained in some time; and therefore time ought to be called equally the number and measure of motion and of rest; and just as time is called by Aristotle the number of any motion whatever, so it ought also to be called the number of any rest whatever. What of the fact that the number or measure of things is not the thing itself numbered or measured, just as the fingers by which days are numbered are not the days themselves, nor is the ell by which cloth is measured the cloth itself? — to omit many other things, which can be seen in the Philosophia Sceptica written in the Spanish language by Doctor Martínez (d). Hence the Aristotelian definition of time is deservedly censured as faulty, or obscure, or rather false.

226 More clearly, then, time can be described as the successive duration of mutable things; from which definition is understood the notable difference between eternity and time: for in eternity no parts can be distinguished, since it embraces all the differences of times in an admirable way; whence it is quite fittingly defined by all Theologians, with Boethius: the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life. We, indeed, by no means possess this mortal life of ours all at once: for what has passed was indeed possessed by us, and what remains to come will be possessed, and only that fleeting instant which is present to us is possessed by us; and just as a sphere rolled over some plane always touches it

227 But to the immortal God the whole of His interminable life is so present that nothing of it has passed away, and nothing of it is ever past. Aevum, which is conceived as lying between eternity and time, is excellently described as the duration of a created, permanent being, dependent on God, and by its own nature incorruptible. Such is the duration of an Angel and of the rational soul.

A          rounding body, that is, the first and interior surface of a body containing

another body. This interior surface is called concave, and the exterior convex. Here is an example. The terraqueous globe is circumscribed on every side by the air: here three things are to be considered, the air itself, its concave surface, and the convex surface of the terraqueous globe, which is contiguous to the concave surface of the air. Aristotle therefore says: the place of the Earth is not that surrounding air, nor the convex surface of the earth, but that concave surface of the air which surrounds the earth. Descartes embraced the opinion of Aristotle. For he too expressly teaches (f) that the external place of a body can be taken for the surface which most closely surrounds the thing located.

229 This surrounding surface he calls the external place, so as to distinguish it from the internal, namely from space, which in his opinion is distinguished from the substance of the located body not in reality but by thought alone. For in truth, says

Descartes (g), the extension in length, breadth and depth which constitutes space is plainly the same as that which constitutes body.

230 I hold as certain, in the first place, that no body really exists which does not exist in some place. Whether, however, it can be brought about by Divine power that some body should exist nowhere, let the common Philosophers, who take the greatest delight in the philosophy of possibles, weigh in the scales. I likewise hold as an ascertained matter that place is not in a place, and so that place is not one of those things that exist in a place. For if it were so, by the same reasoning the place of the place also would be in a place, and so on to infinity. It is ascertained also that none of those things which are moved locally can be held for the place of bodies. For only that which exists in a place can be moved locally. I judge, finally, that the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves singly so exist that they fill one part of it altogether equal to their extension, are moved in it while it is itself wholly immobile, and by it, primarily and of themselves, mutually exclude one another, so far, namely, that several cannot by any means be placed together in the same part by the forces of nature. For all admit that bodies fill the place which each occupies, that they equal it, and that they are on that account impenetrable, because each of them excludes another from that place in which it is. By the name of space nothing else is understood but a negative extension, wholly immobile according to its threefold dimension, in which existing bodies are now placed, and which, if they were reduced to nothing, they would leave behind. This negative extension is called by St. Augustine a spacious nothing, by others an interval. These things being laid down:

231 I say 1. Space is really to be admitted, if it is shown to be possible. It is proved: for since space is not something real and positive but a pure nothing, it cannot be the term of a productive action; therefore, if it does not exist, it certainly cannot be possible either, since what does not really exist and is possible can be produced, at least by God. Wherefore either space is not possible, or, if it is possible, we must necessarily say that it really exists.

Since, therefore, it is a most certain thing that the contact of two spheres can take place at one point only, it remains evident that the two bodies A, B will touch each other only at the point C, and consequently that their convex surfaces will be distant from each other, or that a straight line can be drawn from the point a to the point b, and so of the others. Between such convex surfaces, however, no body would really be had, since it has been supposed, namely, that only the two bodies A and B were created by God: therefore between those surfaces there would then be a pure interval, or space; and therefore space is possible in which no body at all exists.

233 I say 3. Space is really to be admitted, namely a negative extension, altogether different from corporeal substance. Proof: space is really to be admitted if it is shown to be possible [§. 231.]; but it is established with mathematical evidence that space is possible [§. 232.]; therefore it is really to be admitted. Moreover, the existence of space is clearly gathered also from the fact that the extension of the world is not infinite. For it cannot be finite unless outside its bounds there is space which could be occupied by other bodies. That the world is by no means without limits is the opinion of all those who hold it for an ascertained matter that no being besides God is infinite. From what has been said it becomes manifest that all bodies exist in space, that each fills one part of it, plainly equal to its extension, and that they are moved in it while it is wholly immobile.

234 It is established also that, since any two bodies really resist each other, it seems that something must necessarily be admitted in which, while one of them exists, the other can by no means be by the forces of nature. That this, however, is nothing other than space seems perspicuous, since, even if no surrounding surface whatever existed, nay, if one were impossible, any two bodies would be naturally impenetrable, inasmuch as they would still be bodies. I do not deny that secondarily and accidentally two bodies, because they are impenetrable, cannot be contained by one and the same concave surface; but space, in which bodies exist, is the only thing from which the bodies themselves primarily and of themselves, by reason of their natural solidity, mutually exclude each other.

235 I say 4, against the Peripatetics: bodies are not in a place because they are circumscribed by the concave surface of another body. Proof: if it were so, that body which is contained by no circumambient surface would exist nowhere: therefore, since the outermost Heaven is comprehended by no external body, it really is outside its own nothingness without existing in any place; but it is false that a body can exist without being somewhere [§ 230.]: therefore bodies are not in a place because, etc. That the outermost Heaven, moreover, is nowhere, once the opinion of Aristotle is admitted, none of the Scholastics can deny without most openly opposing Aristotle himself. 236 It is confirmed: once the opinion of Aristotle is laid down, it must be said that a body exists in the same place as long as it is contained by the same circumambient surface, which is false; for from this it follows that the same body can at the same time exist in the same place and be moved locally, as is evident in the case of water contained in a glass vessel. For it is moved together with the vessel when the vessel itself is carried elsewhere, and yet the surface by which it is circumscribed is not changed: therefore a body is not in a place because, etc. 2. The concave surface of the surrounding body also exists in a place, and it too is moved at the same time when the body is carried elsewhere: therefore the place of bodies cannot be set in it without our being forced to say that place is not locally immobile, and that place itself at the same time exists in a place, contrary to what we have said [§. 230.]

237 I say 5. The place of bodies is the space occupied by the bodies themselves.

Proof: each body really exists in space, fills one part of it equal to itself, and is moved in it while it is wholly immobile [§. 230.]; but by the name of place nothing else is understood than that in which each body is in this manner [§. 230.]: therefore. It is confirmed: the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves so exist that each, by reason of its natural solidity, primarily and of itself excludes any other whatever from that in which it is [§. 230.]. But this is nothing but the space which each occupies [§§. 233 and 234]: therefore. Secondly: the concave surface of the surrounding body cannot be held for the place of the contained body [§. 235]; but when this is rejected, space alone remains which can be taken for place: therefore the place of each body is space itself.

239 Obj. 2: Space is either something real or a pure nothing. If the second: then it is wrongly called extended, measurable, etc., because of nothing there are no properties. If the first: then something besides God is immense and unbounded; but this is absurd: therefore there is no space. I reply that space is not something real and positive, but, as St. Augustine says, a spacious nothing. It can be called real inasmuch as it does not depend on the intellect. For with no intellect thinking, the points a, b (Fig. XVI.) are distant from each other. Space is called extended, measurable, etc., in plainly the same sense in which a shadow is called extended and measurable, inasmuch, namely, as an extended and measurable body can be placed in that space. Of nothing, moreover, as we have said [§. 12], there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. Since these things are so, it is vainly asked by the Scholastics whether space is a substance or an accident. For it is manifest that only the real and positive is that which can rightly be divided into substance and accident. Nor does it help them that space is not something feigned by the intellect, for neither is a shadow anything of this kind, and yet none of the Scholastics will say that it is a substance or an accident. Nor does it stand in the way that space is called imaginary, as though it depended on the imagination; for it is so called because we imagine its dimensions after the manner of corporeal dimensions, which fall under the senses.

240 Obj. 3. Against the fourth and fifth: it is an undoubted thing that place must be something real, but space is not of this kind: therefore. I distinguish the major: something real, namely not feigned by the intellect, I grant; that is, some positive being which can be produced by a real action, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished by the same solution, I deny the consequence. For it is true that place cannot be something altogether imaginary, but from this it does not follow that it must be some real positive being: for it would follow either that some real being could exist without being anywhere, or that place itself also exists in a place. That reality, therefore, is in space which can legitimately belong to place.

242 Obj. finally: a body is referred to the things which are around it; that is, we judge that a body is in the same place as long as it keeps the same distance from the surrounding bodies: therefore this relation will be the place of the body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is referred so that its situation may be defined, I grant; so that we may be certain that the body itself is in a place, I deny; and the consequence. The situation of a body is nothing else but a certain respect resulting from the fact that the body itself has a certain position among those things with which it is compared, and which are regarded as immobile, and holds a determinate distance from them; but it is false that the body must be referred to the surrounding bodies in order that it may be certain to us that it exists in a place. For just as it does not depend on them in order to be outside its own nothingness, so it has no need of them in order to exist in some place. Therefore the Moderns divide place into absolute and relative; the first they call that part of space which the body occupies. The second, which we have just called situation, they also call apparent and sensible. From what has been said the following Corollaries are deduced.

> abeatur. U

243 First: The absolute place of bodies is nothing real and positive. For space is nothing of this kind. Second: A body can change its absolute place without changing its relative place. For a man sitting in a ship which is moving keeps the same situation in it, as is evident; but at the same time he continually changes his absolute place, since together with the ship in which he is his body occupies a different part of space at each moment. Third: The division of place into natural and violent is to be understood of relative place only. For since space is perpetually uniform with itself, it is all the same to a body whatever part of it it holds, and therefore any absolute place whatever is natural to a body. On the contrary, a body is in a violent place if among other bodies it does not keep that situation which it ought to keep so that that disposition of them may stand which God established at the beginning of time. Thus the earth would be in a violent place if it existed above the water, since the constitution of the world requires that it be held below it.

245 A vacuum or void, taken properly, is called a space comprehended by surfaces and as it were bounded, in which there exists absolutely no body, whether fluid or solid, whether conspicuous or inconspicuous, by which it is filled. I said deliberately taken properly, for in common speech a vessel is also wont to be called empty which is occupied by no body conspicuous to us, although it is filled by an inconspicuous one. From this definition the following Corollaries are deduced. First. There is no vacuum if no space exists within the universe which is not occupied by some body. Second. Nor is a vacuum sufficiently proved from the fact that all sensible bodies whatever are demonstrated to exist in space. For all can be in space without intercepting some portion of it which is occupied by no body: but conversely, and let this be the third Corollary, it is proved that space exists, if a vacuum is shown to exist or to be possible. For by this very fact it is manifest that a negative extension exists.

246 The vacuum is wont to be divided by Philosophers into the coacervate and the disseminate. The first is some notable space within the circuit of the universe, occupied by absolutely no body. Disseminate vacuums, on the other hand, is the name given to the little spaces intercepted by the corpuscles of water or of air, which are no longer filled with air or other body, but are wholly empty, or altogether devoid of every body; or very small, insensible little vacuums shut up within the texture of matter, almost as, between a great many grains of wheat, there lie very small spaces in which there is nothing of wheat. Three questions about the coacervate vacuum are wont to be weighed by Philosophers. First: is it possible? Second: does it really exist in the world? Third: can it be obtained by the forces of nature alone? That the coacervate vacuum is so repugnant that it cannot be had even by Divine power is the most open opinion of Descartes (n). The contrary, however, is held by all those Moderns with whom it is a settled principle that body is distinguished from space.

249 It is also false that those bodies touch each other between which no body is really interposed. For the physical contact of two bodies requires not only that no body be had between them, but also that none, not even the smallest, could be interposed between them without their being moved from their place. That this may be more openly evident, consider Fig. XVI. It is certain that it is wholly repugnant that those two spherical bodies A, B should touch each other along their convex surfaces: therefore the points a b, e d, m n, x y will not be contiguous to one another; but then nothing real and positive would be had between them: therefore it is false that two bodies touch each other by the very fact that nothing real and positive, or no body, really exists between them.

250 The celebrated Antoine Le Grand (p) is therefore mistaken when he says: A possible substance cannot be an actual medium dividing and separating bodies; since it is perspicuous that in that hypothesis the points a, b of the globes A, B would be really distant from each other only through a possible substance. Nor does what he objects help him, namely that nothing in the world would then be united, for this reason, to be sure, that between the parts of a body which are united some medium is possible which might separate them. It does not help, I say, because for two things to be really separated from each other it is not enough that some medium be possible between them; it is further required that some medium be possible between them such that, if it were really interposed between them, they would not be forced to change their situation. Thus the points a, b of the globes A, B are really distant from each other, because, although in the hypothesis made above they intercept nothing real, they can nevertheless intercept it without obtaining a situation different from the one they have. Nor does it help the Cartesians to reply that in the proposed case of the vessel body still remains, since extension, namely, remains, which according to them is the essence of body. For, as we have already said [§. 4.], this is a most open begging of the question, and it can be very strongly attacked, following Tosca (q), in this way.

252 I say 2.: a coacervate vacuum does not really exist in the world. Proof: the existence of a coacervate vacuum in the world can neither be proved by experience nor demonstrated by reason: therefore it does not really exist. Proof of the antecedent:

not by experience, for those experiments which are wont to be brought forward to persuade us of it by no means prove the existence of a vacuum, as we shall see later; nor is its existence shown by reason, for the arguments which are reckoned the principal ones are of no strength, as will be evident from the solution of the arguments:

therefore.

253 I say 3.: a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature. Proof: for since, from what has just been said, there is really no notable space within the circuit of the universe occupied by no body, no notable space can be deprived of every body unless either the body which was in it is reduced to nothing, or it comes about that the same place is filled at the same time by two bodies; but it is manifest that neither can be done by the forces of nature: therefore a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature.

vessel there is actually a body: therefore. Proof of the minor: what exists and is not a spirit is a body; but space in the vessel exists and is not a spirit: therefore. I distinguish the major: what exists and is not a spirit is a body, if it exists by a physical and real existence, I grant; if it is only equivalent to a physically existing thing, I deny; and the consequence. Space, however, where it is posited as empty of every body, although it does not exist by the physical existence that belongs to bodies, nevertheless exists in such a way as to be in a certain manner equivalent to a really existing body, inasmuch as it is endowed with the capacity of receiving one.
