256 Obj. 3, against the second, with the great Newton: if there is not actually a coacervate vacuum, then the spaces of the heavens would have to be actually full; but they cannot be full, for thus the motion of the comets and planets would be retarded; nay, ever since the beginning of the world, from which they have been moving, their motion ought to have been growing languid: therefore. I deny the minor and its included proof: for in order that the stars may continually pursue their motion, nothing else whatever is required than that the matter filling the planetary heaven should not sensibly resist the stars. Moreover, the substance of light, diffused on every side through the circuit of heaven, in which the globes of the planets and comets are moved, does not, according to the excellent Newton himself, bring it about that their courses are disturbed, or that the motion itself grows gradually languid: therefore by the same reasoning those spaces of the heavens could be filled with another body, most fluid and most subtle, without the perennial motion of the stars being either disturbed or retarded even in the least. These things, however, which we have said about the coacervate vacuum do not prevent us from admitting the disseminate vacuum with the celebrated Gassendi.

> 2$6 Opp. s. contra iecundam cum magno Newtono: fi actu non datur vacuum coacervatum , tunc caelorum fparii actu deberent effe plena; fed non poflunt eíle plena, nam ftc cometarum, & planetarum motus retardaretur , imó jam inde á mundi principio,

257 For it is more probable that very slender spaces are interspersed among corporeal things, to which we give the name of disseminate vacuum, since it is perspicuous that the most subtle matter itself, which pervades all things, is interrupted by empty spaces of this kind. For since it is most fluid, and not perfectly continuous, it must consist of particles touching one another at very few points and really dissociated; and those interstices are filled by no body. For if some subtler substance is asserted, one of two things must follow: either this matter of which we are treating will not be the most subtle, or, since the same difficulty recurs once this subtler fluid is admitted, the doctrine of matter divided to infinity and decreasing in fluidity will have to be admitted. Finally, if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies, no local motion could take place in the nature of things. For in order that some body be moved, e.g. through the air, it is necessary that the moving body push the air in front of it into another place; but it could not push it into another place if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies: therefore. The major is evident: for (as Tosca argues) a body cannot be moved without entering into the place of the air in front of it; but it cannot enter into it while the air in front persists there, for otherwise there would naturally be penetration: the moving body must therefore push the air in front of it in order to be able to move. The minor is proved: for the moving body cannot push the air in front of it into another place unless there is a place, forward or backward, upward or downward, or at the sides, that can be occupied by that air which is to be pushed; but if no little vacuums exist, there is no occupiable place, since all are full: therefore.

Let there be a little glass tube A C (Fig. XVII.), hermetically sealed at one of its ends, and let its length be greater than two and a half feet; let it be filled with mercury, then let the mouth through which it was filled with mercury be stopped with a finger; let the tube, thus closed by the finger, be inverted, and let its end, together with the stopping finger, be put into some vessel also well filled with mercury; after the immersion let the finger be removed and the mouth of the tube opened, and at once the mercury will descend from the tube into that vessel, not, however, all of it, but it will remain in the tube itself up to the height A E, which varies with the variety of time and place: therefore the upper part of the tube, E C, left by the mercury, is altogether empty: therefore a coacervate vacuum can be had by the forces of nature alone.

259 I reply that it is false that the upper part of the tube left by the mercury is filled with no substance whatever. For since glass is furnished with innumerable little pores, as we have already said, the mercury cannot desert any part of the tube without the most subtle ethereal substance entering the pores of the glass and filling that part of the tube. Certainly that upper part takes on heat if it is brought near a fire, and is suffused with light, which would by no means happen if there were no substance there: for a vacuum, since it is nothing but the absence of body, is not capable of heat or of light; and light cannot be propagated unless either a substance is diffused through that space, or the substance which is already in it is most strongly urged in a straight line by the luminous body, as we shall demonstrate when we come to speak of light. Besides, if the part C E is altogether empty, I should like to know why the whole tube is not emptied? For it is not contrary to nature that the whole should become empty, if it is not contrary to the laws of nature that the part C E should exist plainly empty.

262 Motion is defined by Aristotle: the act of a being in potency toward a new place, insofar as it is in potency toward it. It can, however, be described more clearly: the passage of a body from place to place, or: the state of a body which is actually carried from place to place, or the continual acquisition of place. For a body is said to be moved locally when it passes from one place into another in such a way that it ceases to be in the one because it is made present to the other. For local motion, therefore, it is necessary that the movable cease to be present to one place from the fact that it is made present to another. Local motion is divided into absolute and relative. Absolute motion is the migration of a body from one absolute place into another, or from one part of space into another; relative motion is the migration of a body from the vicinity of those things which are around it and are regarded as if immovable, into the vicinity of others which are likewise considered as entirely at rest.

Neceffe eít igitur ad motum localem, ut mobile ex eo definat efe praefens uni loco, quia praefens alteri efficitur. Dividitar motus localis in «2fo'utumi, & relativum. 263 Thus a man sitting in a ship is moved with absolute motion while the ship is carried along by the winds, but not at all with relative motion, if he is referred to the parts of the ship. He is moved with absolute motion, since he successively occupies one part of space after another; but he is not moved with relative motion, since he keeps the same distance from the parts of the ship. Descartes, just as he admits no place other than the relative, so acknowledges no motion but the relative. But besides the relative, an absolute motion too must be admitted, as is proved by the same reasons by which it was shown that, besides the relative place, an absolute place, namely space, must be admitted.

264 Rest is the permanence of a body in the same place; and indeed, if a body remains always in the same relative place, the body rests relatively; but if it remains always in the same absolute place, the body rests absolutely. Wherefore a body can rest relatively and be moved absolutely, as happens to a man who sits in a ship while it is driven by its sails. Conversely, a body can be moved relatively although it rests absolutely: as if someone walks in a ship toward one part with exactly the same velocity with which the ship is carried toward the opposite part; for because of the man’s twofold equal motion, the one contrary and proper, the other common — namely the one by which the man walks, which is proper, and the other by which he is carried along, which is common — it comes about that he always stays in the same absolute place.

266 Just as a body is said to be moved with simple motion when there is only one power that determines it to motion, but with compound motion when it is determined to motion by several powers at once, and indeed according to different directions, so direction is twofold: one simple, the other compound. The simple depends on one impression only, as the descent of the globe A (Fig. cited); the compound proceeds from several impressions. Thus if the globe E (Fig. XIX) is impelled at the same time by the globe A in the direction A F and by the globe B in the direction B

D, the globe E will follow neither of these, but will keep to the diagonal line E G.

267 Celerity, or velocity, is that affection of a movable by which it runs through a given space in a given time; whence it corresponds to the dimension both of space and of time, and so is the relation which space has to time. For if two bodies pass through the same space in different times, that one proceeds with greater celerity which reaches the goal in less time, while that which arrives at the same goal in a longer time goes with less celerity. Conversely, if two bodies measure out unequal spaces in exactly the same time, we declare that the one which described the greater space went more swiftly, and the one which traversed the smaller space less swiftly.

268 From this it is easily understood that in the concept of velocity two other concepts are contained, the one of space, the other of time, to such an extent that, the time remaining the same, if the space described is increased or diminished, the velocity of the motion is also proportionally increased or diminished; while, the space traversed remaining the same, if the time is increased or diminished, the velocity in turn is diminished or increased in the same ratio. Wherefore to those who ask, what is velocity? the answer must be that it is the relation which the space described has to the time elapsed meanwhile, and so its measure is had if the space described is divided by the time consumed in describing the space; or, what is the same, the quotient of the space which a body runs through with uniform motion in a certain time, divided by that time itself, best designates the value of the celerity with which the body is moved in that time.

270 This is to be understood only when bodies are moved uniformly; for if the motion is non-uniform, since the body is not moved with the same celerity during that whole time, that variable celerity cannot be designated by a constant quantity. A body, moreover, is said to be moved uniformly if it is moved continually with the same celerity, namely, if in equal times it runs through equal parts of space. It is said to be moved non-uniformly if the celerity of its motion is not always the same, namely, if in equal times it is carried through unequal spaces. Thus the motion of the body A will be uniform if it runs through 5 feet in the 1st minute, then 10 feet by the 2nd, then 15 feet by the 3rd, and so on. Conversely, its motion will be non-uniform if in the 1st minute it is carried through the space of a foot, but in the remaining ones through a space not of a foot, and not by a constant law at all times, but with the magnitude of the space always varied non-uniformly.

271 That motion is accelerated whose celerity is continually increased; retarded, that whose celerity is continually diminished. If in equal times equal increments of velocity are added, the motion is called uniformly accelerated, just as, if they fall away in that proportion, it is named uniformly retarded. And these are the chief divisions of motion. There follows now the third property of motion, which is called quantity; but before we explain it something must be said about Forces.

272 Force is the faculty or power which either induces motion in a body, [p. 95] or would induce it if an obstacle were removed; and this, following the most learned Leibniz, Philosophers divide into living and dead. They call that force living which actually induces motion in a body, as is gravity in a descending stone; that force, on the other hand, they say is dead which actually lacks its effect, but which, if an obstacle were removed, would drive the body to motion, as is the same gravity in a globe held up by a thread, which rests so long as it is held up, but when the support is removed at once begins to descend downward. This same force is also called initial force, conatus or nisus toward actual motion.

273 By quantity of motion (which the Moderns also call momentum) we understand the force or impetus which bodies, out of the state of rest, can exert against obstacles set against them; and so, in defining the quantity of motion, attention must be paid both to the velocity with which the body is moved and to the mass, or quantity of matter, of the body itself. For let there be two bodies A B having equal quantities of matter, and let them be carried against an opposed obstacle with equal velocity: each body will exert the same impetus against the obstacle, for there is no cause why the one should exert a greater force than the other, since both the masses and the velocities are supposed equal; and if the impetuses are equal, the motions, or quantities of motions, will likewise be equal.

274 But, the equality of the masses remaining, make the body A be carried more swiftly and the body B more sluggishly: then the impetuses of the bodies A and B exerted against the obstacle will by no means be equal, but the impetus of the body A, which is moved more swiftly, will be greater, and the greater, the greater the velocity with which it is carried against the obstacle. And since impetus and motion are one and the same, it follows that the motions, or quantities of motion, of two bodies A and B whose masses are equal are to each other as the velocities of those same bodies. But if, the equality of the velocities remaining, the masses of the bodies A and B are supposed unequal, neither will the impetuses exerted by them against the obstacle be equal, but the impetus of that body will be greater which contains the greater quantity of matter, and the greater, the greater the quantity of matter; whence both the impetuses and the motions of equally swift bodies will be in the ratio of the masses.

275 From these Theorems there follows directly the third, which runs thus: the momenta, or quantities of motions, of bodies whose velocities as well as masses are unequal have a ratio compounded of the simple ratios of the velocities and of the masses. So that, therefore, when a twofold motion of any bodies whatever is proposed, it may be understood which of those motions must be held the greater or the smaller, first the gravity, or mass, of each body must be accurately ascertained, then the velocity, or celerity, with which each is moved, or the spaces which are traversed by each body; then, the mass of each body being multiplied by the celerity of the body, the product of them will exhibit the quantity of motion which belongs to each body: and this

276 The quantity of motion, therefore, is not to be estimated from the celerity of the movable alone. For since motion belongs both to the whole body and to each of its parts, it cannot, as we have already said, be estimated otherwise than by multiplying the mass of the body into the velocity. For let, e.g., the mass of the body A be 4, its velocity or celerity 6. In this case each part of the body A will have 6 degrees of celerity, and consequently also 6 degrees of impetus or motion: the impetus, therefore, or force of the whole body will be equal to 6 degrees of impetus repeated four times; or, what is the same, if 4 is multiplied into 6, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 24. Likewise let the mass of the body B be 3, its velocity 8; let 3 be multiplied into 8: the quantity in the body B will be 24. From which it can easily be understood that the same quantity of motion is found in each movable. The momentum of a given body can therefore be regarded as a rectangle whose base represents the mass of the body itself, and its height the body’s celerity. For a rectangle arises from multiplying the base into the height, as was said in Geometry.

277 But if the gravity in the body A is 4, the velocity 5, and the mass in the body B is 3, the velocity 8, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 20, in the body B 24: whence the quantity of motion will be greater in B than in A. From this, moreover, it can easily be deduced that the quantity of motion itself must correspond to the motive power; and therefore, if a certain force is required for a body of 1 pound to be thrown to a distance of 100 feet, a power twice as great will be required for it to be thrown in the same time to a space of 200 feet. Just as, by the same reasoning, it appears most manifestly that if a body of 10 pounds is thrown in some determinate time by a certain force to a distance of 30 feet, exactly the same force and impetus will be required for a body of 20 pounds to be thrown through a space of 15 feet.

278 And therefore, universally, the motive power will be the greater, the greater the quantity of motion in the body that is moved; and the quantity of motion will be the greater, the greater the gravity or mass of the body, and at the same time the celerity with which it is moved. Thus in the former example, since the quantity of motion is the same in each body, it manifestly appears that each of them will be moved by an equal force or power; but if, as happens in the other case, the quantity of motion is greater in one of the two bodies, whether this inequality arises from the gravity or rather from the celerity, a greater motive force or power is also required. All of which must be observed most accurately, since from this, as from a most abundant source, almost the whole of Statics and Mechanics is derived, as we shall show in what follows when occasion is given.

279 From what has been said it is manifest that the force or impetus, or motion, or momentum (for all these are one and the same) of any body can be increased in three ways. 1. By increased velocity, an example of which we have in the iron balls which engines of war, by the force of gunpowder,

> [p. 97]

[p. 97] discharge against the walls of besieged towns, which balls strike the walls themselves with great impetus because of the great velocity with which they are carried. 2: By increased quantity of matter; an example of which we have in battering rams and other machines of war which were in use among the Ancients; for these, although they advanced most slowly, yet had an immense mass, and so afforded great use for assaulting walls. 3.: By increased velocity and quantity of matter together, in which case the impetus becomes immense, since the increment comes to the momentum from a double cause, namely from the velocity and from the mass.

281 As to the first, let there be two straight lines A B, C D (Fig. XX.), divided into as many equal parts as you like, e.g. into nine. On the first line let there be supposed a body of one foot, on the second another body of one foot, perfectly homogeneous with the former; then let these bodies be supposed to run through, within the same time, the same number of parts of their lines. In this hypothesis I say that the motive forces applied to those movables are perfectly equal to each other. For the effects produced are altogether alike, and consequently their productive causes must be judged altogether alike.

283 I say that the impetuses applied to those bodies are likewise equal to each other: which I show thus. Impetuses, or forces, or quantities of motions are equal to each other when their effects are equal: but in this example the effects are equal. For the effect of the first power is to carry the body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B, namely as far as the point 3; and the effect of the second motive power is to carry, in the same time, the body of one foot through nine equal parts of the line C D, or as far as the point 9: but these effects are equal.

286 I.    W       hen the spaces run through by homogeneous bodies are equal to each other,

and the times within which they were traversed are likewise equal, then the velocities are equal to each other. II. When the spaces run through are unequal, but the times equal, then the velocities are to each other as the spaces run through. III.

When the spaces run through are equal to each other, but the times unequal, then the velocities are to each other reciprocally as the times; that is, the shorter time indicates the greater velocity, and the greater the smaller. IV. When the spaces run through are unequal to each other, and the times likewise unequal, then the velocities are to each other as the quotients of the spaces divided by the times.

R U L E S F O R T H E Q UA N T I T Y O F M O T I O N S .

287 I.    I   f the masses or homogeneous bulks are equal to each other, and their velocities

are likewise equal, then the quantities of the impetuses applied to those movables are equal to each other: because in this case the effects are perfectly alike, as was proved. II. If the homogeneous bulks or masses are equal to each other, and their velocities unequal, then the quantities of motions, or of impetuses, are to each other as the velocities. III. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities equal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the masses, or bulks. IV. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities likewise unequal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the products arising from the multiplication of each bulk by its velocity.

On the Newtonian laws of Nature. 289

> . CAPUT II.

Philosophers call a law of nature a most universal rule which has place in all the vicissitudes and changes of natural things. And since every vicissitude of nature proceeds from motion, it comes about that the exercise of the laws of nature shows itself chiefly in the motions of bodies. Since Philosophers had disputed much about these laws of nature, at length Newton reduced everything that had been said before on this argument to three principal heads, which today are commonly called by Philosophers the Newtonian Laws of Nature.

## LEMMA

Motion, so far as lies in itself, is directed along a straight line, nor does it desert it unless it is turned aside from it by some extrinsic cause. The reason is that the straight line is the shortest of those which can be drawn from point to point, or from the term from which to the term to which, and is also the simplest: for it is not divided into various species, as the curved line is: therefore motion along a straight line is shorter and simpler; but nature in all things affects brevity and simplicity, undertakes nothing in vain, rejects superfluities, and works all things with the greatest possible economy: therefore motion is directed along a straight line rather than along another. This being established, before we propose Newton’s Laws of motion, some things must briefly be said by us about the force of inertia. By this name we understand that force in each body by which every body, so far as lies in it, perseveres in its state either of rest or of motion, or a certain force implanted in matter, by which it comes about that each body strives to maintain and preserve its own state.

291 For if a body rests, that rest in the body would last forever, if no impetus were made upon it. And likewise a body once moved would be moved perpetually, and would suffer no retardation from the resistance of the medium. For every body that is moved is moved in a medium resisting it; whence the body cannot continue its motion except insofar as it overcomes this resistance; and it cannot overcome it except by dividing and separating the parts of the medium, nor can it separate these parts except by spending against them some part of the impetus which it had for moving itself; since, therefore, the impetus is gradually diminished in the movable, its celerity must be diminished proportionally, and at length be reduced to nothing.

292 But beyond this resistance of the medium there is also in the body another Resistance, namely insofar as the body, in order to preserve its own state, struggles against the impressed force. For when the body B at rest receives a blow from the moved body A, the body B is not moved without the body A losing something of its force; wherefore there is in B a force breaking the impetus of the body A, which is called the force of resistance. These things being supposed, the first Newtonian law is usually proposed thus: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly and in a straight line, unless it is compelled by some impressed force to change that state. This law is founded on the force of inertia, because of which it comes about that individual bodies strive to preserve for themselves that state in which they are actually placed.

293 A body at rest will never cease to rest of itself, but in order that it be placed in motion an external force must intervene. Conversely, a body that is moved will never cease to be moved, if we suppose the resistance of all the surrounding bodies overcome and reduced to nothing. Nor are the common Peripatetics to be heard here, who teach that moved bodies by their own nature affect rest, or also tend from motion to rest, contrary to what their Prince Aristotle (a) teaches, led chiefly by this reason, that they see the motion of thrown stones gradually grow languid and at length cease altogether. For if thrown stones at some time desist from motion, this must indeed be imputed to a double cause. The first, because, driven downward by gravity itself, they at length strike against the earth. The second, because the air resists their motion; for if a stone were thrown in a vacuum, and moreover if it were destitute of all gravity, without doubt its motion would never grow languid, but would last forever.

For at the beginning they are without doubt moved along a straight line [§. 290.]; and if at the beginning the course is rectilinear, then, because of the force of inertia, which makes bodies always preserve for themselves the state in which they are placed, projected bodies will perpetually persevere

(a) Bk. IV, Phys., text 69. [p. 101] in that course, and will never deflect from the rectilinear path. For if they described a curve, they would then be changing their direction at every moment, which conflicts with the inertia of matter, because of which it cannot assign itself any determination. That they must be moved uniformly, moreover, comes from the same force of inertia; for in order that the motion be accelerated or retarded, a new force must come in which either helps or hinders that motion, a force which, however, we suppose removed.

295 Besides: a body is of itself so indifferent to motion and rest that, if it once rests, it rests forever, but if it has once been placed in motion, it is moved perpetually: therefore, if it has once been determined to motion, it will not return to rest by itself alone; or if it rests, it will not be roused to motion by itself alone: therefore, once incited to motion, it will need a new determination in order to be called back to rest, and conversely. Moreover, a body which was created spherical by God always perseveres spherical, and one that is once square always maintains its figure, until this figure is changed by some cause: therefore likewise a body which once rests will always rest.

296 From what has been said you will gather, 1.: that a body cannot be understood to be carried around a square, a pentagon, or any other polygon whatever, unless at each angle occasional causes of the changed determination of such a body are conceived. For after that body has described one side, it would be understood to be carried along the same line continued, unless there were an obstacle turning it aside along the second side; and so on consequently at the end of each side. Since, therefore, the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of sides indeterminate in number, if some body is moved circularly, there must be conceived either perpetual obstacles, or the same one continued, by which the determination of the movable is perpetually changed.

297 But that you may understand more clearly that the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of infinite sides, consider the circumference of a circle (and what we are about to say of it can be applied without any trouble to all the other curves), and understand described in it first a triangle, then a square, afterwards a pentagon, then a hexagon, and finally a decagon, all of them, however, regular.

298 It is manifest that of all the figures now described the triangle departs most from the circumference of the circle; for the square comes somewhat nearer to it, the pentagon somewhat more, the hexagon still somewhat more, and the decagon indeed much more. But if you understand a regular figure inscribed in the circle consisting of infinite, that is, indeterminate sides, each of which is nevertheless as small as possible, then its declination from the circumference of the circle will be null; and so the perimeters of the circle and of the other curves can be held as rectilinear figures of infinite sides, each of whose sides is infinitely small.

299 Imagine now a body moved in the circumference of a circle, and [p. 102] then it will in truth be moved in a rectilinear figure of infinite sides, each of which is infinitely small. Therefore, if in the first particle of time the body describes one of these sides, thereafter, every external force being set aside, it ought, because of the force of inertia, to be moved uniformly along that same side produced further, which side touches the circle. Wherefore, if we see some body revolve in the circumference of a circle, it must be said that there is some force acting perpetually on the body, which draws it back from its rectilinear course and gradually bends it into the remaining sides of the polygon.

300 This force of a body of receding from the center is called centrifugal; that by which the body seeks the center, centripetal: both are called by the common name central. Hence you will gather 2. that a body moved circularly and afterwards left to itself, or with the obstacles removed, must be carried along the tangent of the circle, which is the small side continued; whence is deduced this general rule, which is the foundation of the whole system of the world: A body moved circularly strives at every moment to recede from the center of its motion; and indeed the more vehemently, the more vehemently it is agitated. This rule is confirmed by experience.

301 For if you have whirled a stone, e.g., circularly in a sling, as soon as you let go one cord of the sling it will slip away now upward, now downward, now horizontally, now in any other determination, according as the tangent begins from that part of the circumference in which the stone was left to itself; and moreover that stone runs out the farther, the more vehemently it was whirled round. But if a body is moved in an infinite circle, or also in a straight line, into which an infinite circle in any case passes, then, since the deflection of the tangent from its circumference is null, as is plain, there will likewise be no centrifugal conatus, or force of receding from the center.

302 But you will say: a body once placed in some state must of itself persevere in that state; but a body moved circularly was placed in some determinate state: therefore, left to itself, it will always be moved circularly. I deny the minor. For a body whose determination is continually changed should not be said to be placed in some determinate state, but rather should be said to be placed in a perpetual change of state. Now the determination of a movable moved circularly is perpetually changed, as evidently appears when a body is moved around some polygon.

303 You will insist: the determination of a movable along a circular line should be called its single state just as much as its determination along a straight line. I deny the proposition: the difference is that the beginning of translation is a straight line, but not a curved line. For the beginning of motion is translation from point to point. Now that translation can be made without deflection, and so along a straight line, as was proved.

304 From what has been said it follows that, although it is natural, that is, consonant with the laws established by God, that some body carried

> [p. 103]

[p. 103] and left to itself be moved in a straight line, it is nevertheless no less natural that the same body, first carried along a straight line, should afterwards be moved away from its determination as often as obstacles occur to prevent its being moved in a straight line. The permanent disturbance, therefore, or inflection of motion in a body which is moved along a circular line, is against the natural requirement of the initial motion impressed along a straight line, according to which the body at each instant begins to move itself; but this disturbance or inflection is not against nature, because the nature of a motion already begun does not require absolutely not to be disturbed, but only not to be disturbed in the absence of some obstacle which requires the disturbance. But let us now propose the second law of nature.

305 The second law is: the change of motion is always proportional to the motive force impressed, and is always made along the straight line along which that force is impressed. For since motion is generated in bodies by motive force, this is certain, that the motion begotten in a body is proportional to the motive force itself, to such a degree that, if some force generates a certain motion in a body, a double force will generate a double motion, a triple force a triple one; and generally, one force which is to another force as the number 100 to 1 will generate a motion which will be to the motion begotten by the other force as the same number 100 to 1; but for this to be true, equality of the times is postulated. That the motion must be made along a straight line has already been demonstrated above.

306 There follows the third rule: To action reaction is always contrary and equal. That is, to the action destroyed the resistance is always contrary and equal. That this law may be understood, let us suppose a horse having a force as 100 drawing a stone tied to a rope, which has a resistance as 50. I say: the horse does not draw the stone with the force which it has as 100, but with a force as 50. The rule, thus understood, is demonstrated: for while some body acts on another, its force tends to overcome the resistance of the second. The acting body, therefore, will not spend all its force, but only that part which is required for overcoming the resistance of the second body. The portion of the motive force which it spends is called Action, and the resistance which the other body opposes is called Reaction. Action, therefore, will have a contrary and equal reaction, which is the 3rd law of motion.

307 There are some who think that the falsity of this law can be shown from this, that, if it were accepted, no motion would ever take place in nature. For let the body A be moved toward the body B at rest. Now, if the reaction of the body B on A is as great as the action of A on B, no motion will follow in B; but we see that it is moved; therefore it is false that reaction is equal and contrary to action. Bah, what a rotten sophism! For in reasoning of this kind there is nothing that ought not to be rejected. For this law of nature does not hold that the resistance is equal and contrary to the motive force, but the reaction to the action, two things which are enormously distant from each other. Force is all the efficacy which there is in a body for acting, speaking absolutely.

Action, however, is only that portion of the motive force which the body spends while it acts. Bodies, therefore, do not always spend all the force they have in producing an effect, but only that which is required for equalling the resistance of the body tending in the contrary direction; and so motion must indeed be made through a force as great as the excess of the action over the reaction, or resistance, has been.

> ..De Motuui legibus, quae in corporum -colli(ione locum habent.

308 The objection, therefore, is futile. For in order that two bodies acting on each other should rest, it is required not only that the actions be equal, but also the forces applied by them. They will rest, namely, when they have equal forces and apply all the force they possess; for in this case, since nothing of their forces remains to them, and these are supposed equal, they will destroy each other mutually, and no motion will arise. Thus, if a horse wishes to draw a weight equal to the whole force which it possesses, it will certainly strive to move the weight with its whole force; but since this weight is equal to the force of the horse, it will destroy that force, and no motion will arise. But if the weight is less than the horse’s force, then it will apply only that part of its own force which equals the resistance of the weight to be overcome, and thus, since a portion of force still remains to it, it will carry the weight along with it.

309 It will not be out of place to note here, since we shall use the name of elasticity in many places, that by the name of elastic motion we mean that by which bodies stretched, compressed or bent are restored to their former figure and situation once the power stretching, compressing or bending them is removed. This force of bringing itself back to its native state we honor with the name of Elasticity, elastic virtue, or elater; and if this restitution is accomplished with the same force by which the body was moved from its state, the elasticity is called perfect; otherwise it is called imperfect.

C H A P T E R I V.

On the Laws of Motions which have place in the collision of bodies.

And would that he had given us truer laws!

311 When one body runs into another, it imparts motion to it in the collision:

> "Leges motus in collifione: corporum claterii mE expertium. ]

nature accomplishes this by certain laws, in which the principles of Dynamics are contained. It must be noted, however, that the collision of two bodies can take place in three ways. First: if one runs into the other entirely at rest. Second: if they are carried toward the same part, but with unequal velocity, such that the one which is moved faster overtakes the other with its motion, or impels it. Third: if they meet each other from opposite parts. Now since the ratio of motions is one in non-elastic, or inert, bodies (under which name both perfectly hard and perfectly soft bodies are comprehended), and another in elastic ones, we shall propose the laws of each kind observed in collision. And of the first, indeed, for the threefold case, we give three laws expressed in as many Propositions by Nollet (b).

If a body at rest is impelled by another, the celerity of the impinging body is divided between both in proportion to the masses.

313 Namely, since the impelling body imparts motion to the one at rest solely in order to remove the impediment to its own motion, and since for this to happen it is necessary only to share out the force in proportion to the mass of each — for if the bodies taken together are understood to be divided into equal parts, and the whole motion likewise into as many equal parts, and equal parts of motion are assigned to equal parts of each body, it will be plain that in this way it comes about that equal parts of the two bodies, endowed with an equal quantity of forces, will follow the same direction with equal celerity, without some being an impediment to the motion of others — accordingly, if a body runs into another at rest and equal to it in mass, it will communicate to it half of its velocity; if the other is half as large, two thirds; if double, it bestows on it one third part of its celerity.

If two bodies with contrary motion meet each other, the motion is extinguished either in both or at least in one. If after the collision some part of the motion has survived, each will be moved toward the same part, according to the direction of the one which was endowed with the greater force, such that the quantity of motion common to them is equal to the excess of the one over the other before the collision.

> (c) Entret. Dbyf. Tom. 1. X. Entret. IV. Kegle, & XII. Eatret, 0 01v. Regle. 0 2. son NENNEN ,

317 Namely, if the quantities of motion before the collision are equal, since they are diametrically opposed to each other, it will come about that in the impact they destroy each other. Hence Fr. Regnault thinks that this same rule holds only in soft bodies, but not in hard ones, because these seem to have to be reflected after the impact just like elastic ones, since no compression of the parts is effected. (c) But with the most illustrious Fortunato da Brescia we think that this happens in bodies of both kinds; (d) for although, if a perfectly hard body runs into another similar one entirely at rest, it rebounds after the impact, as we said above, what happens here is yet a very different thing; for a hard and immovable plane only prevents the incurring body from pursuing its motion in its own direction, and brings it about that the direction of the incident body is changed in the impact; but it by no means extinguishes any impetus in it by a contrary force, as happens when two bodies meeting each other from opposite sides collide. If the forces before the collision were unequal, their equal parts, since they are opposed to each other, destroy each other in the collision: and therefore the body which is the stronger will act with the excess of its forces on the other as on one at rest, and accordingly (by the Law of the first case) they will proceed with equal celerity.

319 For since the masses of the bodies are equal, if the celerity of the incurring body is = 6, half of it is communicated to the one at rest in the impact, the other part remaining to the impelling body (by the Law of the first case): which is what would happen if the bodies were destitute of elater. But since the elastic motion corresponds to the compression, this to the percussion, and the percussion to the direct motion which the body obtains in the collision, therefore the half celerity acquired in the impact is doubled by the equal restitution of the compressed parts:

> 3:3 Sit A fuübdüplum quoad maffam ipfius B; & incurrat celepue

accordingly the impelled body, once the collision is completed, will be moved with celerity = 6, namely with the velocity = 3 communicated in the impact, and with the celerity = 3 supplied by the elater. The incurring body, on the contrary, since it retains half of its celerity, while at the same time the compressed parts after the impact restore themselves with equal celerity but in the opposite direction, must therefore have its motion extinguished, and must rest after the impact.

320 Law II. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, likewise elastic, but of smaller diameter, which is at rest, each is carried toward the same part once the collision is completed; but the celerity of B will be greater than the celerity of the body A.

321 Let A run with celerity = 6 into B, which is half of it as to mass, and at rest.

Since A imparts to B celerity in proportion to the mass of each, and so, since it is double of B, one third of its celerity, that is: the celerity = 2 (by the Law of the first case of non-elastic bodies), these degrees, because they are doubled by the restitution of the elater, will make B be moved after the impact with celerity = 4 along the direction of A. The body A, on the other hand, the celerity = 2 having been transferred into B, loses as much elastic motion in the contrary direction: it therefore follows the other only with celerity = 2.

322 Law III. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, of greater diameter, of the same nature, and at rest, B will be roused toward the direction along which A was carried before the impact, but A will go back after the impact.

Since the equal velocities with which the bodies are borne in opposite directions cancel each other, the whole velocity of body B will be destroyed in the impact, and the velocity of A itself will be = 6 − 4 = 2. Now half of this is communicated to body B, as though to a body at rest; but in the direction in which A itself was moving, that is, the direction in which B must be reflected. Therefore after the impact no more than a force = 1

But body B, since it acquired four degrees of velocity for rebounding by the force of the velocity with which it first met the other: obtained one degree of velocity, going back along the same line, from the excess of the greater velocity of the other body, and, on account of the compression of one simple degree that was made, is increased once more by one degree of velocity along the same line; for that reason body A will rebound with a velocity = 4, body B with a velocity = 6, and so with the velocities exchanged.

334 Law III. If body A, of greater, and B, of smaller diameter, both elastic, meet each other directly with equal velocity: B will always rebound after the impact; but A will sometimes continue its motion, sometimes stand motionless after the collision, sometimes be reflected.

335 B rebounds, since in the restitution of its parts it recovers the whole force it had lost; and it is endowed with a force twice as great as that which body A communicated in the impact. A will sometimes be moved along the same line; for it can happen that the force with which it ran directly into the other body is greater than the forces of the spring. Sometimes it stands still; for it happens that the force with which the compressed parts restore themselves is equal to the direct motion surviving after the impact, and that they extinguish each other altogether. Sometimes it is reflected: namely, when it happens that the restitution by the force of elasticity of the parts exceeds the force that is left over from the direct motion after the impact.

a ball falls at the angle ABD (same Fig.) on the line, or surface, DBE, it will so rebound on the other side, along the line BC, that there is formed the angle EBC, which is called the angle of reflection, equal to the angle DBA, which is called the angle of incidence. Hence that celebrated principle, that the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. It is demonstrated: nature always operates by shorter lines; therefore a body in motion that is capable of reflection, falling on a resisting body, falls and is reflected along shorter lines; but the lines AB, CB, which are the lines of incidence and of reflection and form equal angles, are shorter than the two others AF, FC, and than all the rest that can be drawn between the same end points [from Geometry]: therefore the ball will describe the shorter and equally inclined lines AB, CB, rather than the longer and unequally inclined AF, FC.

339 The perfect equality of the angles of incidence and reflection can be maintained only if the reflection takes place on a very highly polished surface, and neither roughness nor the situation of the parts stands in the way of this equality, nor is the motion of the mobile body in any way diminished in the contact, or percussion. For if the surface is rough and uneven, or distorted in any way whatever, the mobile body will be twisted aside from it, rebounding in various ways according to the varied situation of its parts, or their roughness.

But where it is a question of the reflection of light in mirrors, since that reflection takes place in clean and polished bodies, it can be taken as a principle, so to speak, that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

## CHAPTER VI

On Refracted Motion and its laws.

hat we have so far set forth about the reflection of motion and 340

W                its laws will certainly bring a great deal of light also to the things

that remain to be said about the other property of motion, namely refraction. For just as, if some mobile body falls on another body that is immovable and impenetrable, it loses its former direction of motion and acquires an entirely new one; so too, when a mobile, passing from one body, runs into another body of unequal resistance or density, it does indeed penetrate it, but is so bent and inclined that it acquires a new direction of motion; whence refraction is very well defined: the inflection, or curving, of motion by which a mobile body, on account of the greater or smaller resistance of the body which it enters obliquely, from the straight line which it was describing

342 But if the ray had issued from the point F, placed in the water, then on reaching the surface of the air it would no longer describe the straight line FH, but would rather be so inflected along AB as to recede not only from the point H, but also from the perpendicular BI itself. Hence in Dioptrics these are assumed and shown as the most certain laws of refractions: If a ray passes from a rarer body, or medium, into a denser body and medium, its motion will be so inflected as to approach the perpendicular; but if from a denser into a rarer, it recedes from the perpendicular itself.

343 But if not a ray of light but any other body, as e.g. a ball of lead or of ivory, were to descend from the air into water with an oblique motion, it would so inflect its motion as to recede from the perpendicular, just as, conversely, if it came out of water into air, it would approach the perpendicular. Therefore the motion of light and that of another body must be distinguished most accurately, lest refraction be thought to be performed by one and the same law in light and in other bodies. But for what reason all bodies whatever, if you except light, must be so refracted as to recede from the perpendicular will easily be understood if it is observed that water, as a denser body, resists motion more than air, which is lighter, and that therefore the motion impressed on the ball becomes in some degree more sluggish while it is entering the water.

344 And since it is easily detected by experiment that water resists perpendicular motion more than horizontal, of the two motions of which the oblique one is composed the perpendicular will become more sluggish, and the horizontal will be increased, and so the ball will recede from the perpendicular. But since a ray of light moves more easily in water, crystal and other bodies whose pores, or solid parts, are more stable, than in air, inasmuch as the parts of the air and the interstices formed by them are agitated by a perpetual flux, the ray itself will meet less resistance in water than in air, and so will be refracted by approaching the perpendicular.

will understand how widely the elements of motion, and their use for the conveniences of human life, extend, so that it ought to seem a wonder to no one that the greatest effort has been spent on this subject by most excellent men. Relying, therefore, on certain principles of the Mathematicians, and with a previous knowledge of them, we shall survey Statics with a philosophical eye. Let there be, then, an unfolding of the notions in order.

346 Statics is that part of Physics which discourses on the equilibrium of heavy bodies. If it is concerned with the weight of solid bodies, it is called Geostatics, or

Statics without any addition; if it treats of fluids, it is named Hydrostatics. We shall treat of the former first, with the most distinguished Michael Klaus, and then pursue the other, after general notions have first been indicated.

347 Power is the name given to any cause producing motion. Weight is that which is moved by the power, or resists motion. In what sense living force and dead force are to be taken we indicated above [§. 272.]. To distinguish the matter more carefully here, some call the moving force joined with actual motion, whatever it may be, living force; but that which merely sustains a weight, with only some striving toward motion impressed on it, they hold for dead force. Momentum is usually the name given to the force of a gravitating mass. Equilibrium is the equality of momenta with one another, and their mutual compensation.

348 Homogeneous bodies are those all of whose sensible parts are of the same nature; heterogeneous, on the contrary, those whose parts are diverse as to nature. Heavy bodies, whether fluid or solid, are held to be homogeneous when their gravities are proportional to their volumes; but heterogeneous heavy bodies are those which are not allotted gravities proportional to their volumes.

349 One center is that of heavy bodies, another of gravity, another of magnitude, another of motion. The first is the common center of the universe and, in comparison with terrestrial bodies, the center of the earth, to which they are borne. The second is that point, placed inside or outside the body, about which parts of equal momenta, or equiponderant parts, stand on every side, as, long before Father Schott (h), Pappus of Alexandria (i) and Stevin (j) had more or less explained. Thus in bodies that comprehend all their parts united, the center of gravity is placed within the bodies themselves; but in a ring, a half-ring, a concave sphere or hemisphere, it is constituted outside, e.g. at the intersection of the diameters, a point from which a body suspended, even by thought alone, maintains equilibrium. The third, which is also named the center of figure, is that point in the magnitude, or extension, such that, if some plane, freely imagined, passes through it, the body is divided and cut into equally great parts, whether they are of the same weight or of different. This coincides with the center of gravity in regular homogeneous bodies, but is different in irregular and heterogeneous ones. The center of motion will be set forth a little below.

350 The line of direction of heavy bodies is the straight line drawn from the center of gravity of the body itself to the center of heavy bodies, and perpendicularly to the horizon [§. 143]. It has obtained this name because it directs the descent of heavy bodies, so that the center of gravity, and the heavy body itself, never departs from it. It is also called the diameter of gravity, because, passing through the center of gravity, it divides the body into two equiponderant parts.

351 The beam is the name given to a straight, rigid and inflexible line which can revolve most freely about one point of itself that is altogether immovable. Such is the line AB (Fig. XXIII.), if it is conceived as entirely rigid and void of weight, and freely revolvable about the immovable point F.

352 The center of motion is that immovable point about which weights suspended from the extreme points of a rigid line can move freely. Such (Fig. cit.) is the point F, if the weights A and B applied about it, while it stays altogether unmoved, can be moved. This point is also usually called the point of suspension, because the bodies hung from it, altogether immovable as it is, hang freely together with the beam. The same point also goes by the name of center of the fulcrum; for the Greeks it is called Hypomochlion, as if you were to say:

354 Conversely, moreover, when a heavy body is at rest, the plane on which it stands perpendicularly will be parallel to the horizon. From this shines forth the artifice of exploring, by means of a pendulum, whether a plane is parallel to the horizon or, on the contrary, inclined. Heavy bodies standing with a plane surface on a horizontal plane remain unmoved if the line of direction falls within the base; but they collapse if that same line strays and falls outside the base [§ 145]. The reason is manifest: for in the former case the line of direction is sustained by the underlying plane; not so in the other. Moreover: if in the former case the body ABDC were to topple (Fig. XXV.) while the line of direction EF is contained within the base CD, it would have to be turned and revolved about the extreme point D of the base, and so the center of gravity E would have to ascend along the arc EG above the horizontal line EH, which conflicts with the action of the gravitating cause, and does not happen except when forces opposing gravity are at work. 355 From the consideration of the center of gravity it is likewise deduced why those things stand erect more firmly and more securely which rest on a broader base; and so why we ourselves, while we stand on both feet, remain safely, but on the contrary totter easily when supported on one alone; for in the former case the base is ample enough, and twin props sustain the body; but in the second it is narrow, and much narrower still when we press the floor only with the heel, so that the line of direction easily runs out beyond the base. Hence too are derived the rules of dancing, of walking, and of regulating the motions of the body. The very conformation of the animal body shows this same principle of equilibrium: the paired parts, distributed equally, occupy the sides, so that they are separated from the middle by an equal interval, while the single parts hold the middle place. Nor is this equilibrium evident in men only, but in brutes as well. For the wings of birds add an equal weight to them on either side: those which are allotted a longer neck are also furnished with longer feet, which they stretch out backward in flying; while they take their rest supported on one foot, they hide the head under the wing that lies crosswise opposite. We pass over countless things of this kind (m).

> (m) Vid. Borellum de motu animal. Camus, des Forces mouvane . « tes. Paidies. De viribus moventibus. (n) Euclid. Lib, 3. Prop. 18. ME

356 It is likewise seen from this doctrine why bodies touching a horizontal plane, even at a single point, remain in that place only when the line of direction passes through that point. In this way a homogeneous sphere BC (Fig. XXVII.), placed upon the plane MN parallel to the horizon, stands unmoved; for its center of magnitude a coincides with the center of gravity, and the straight line aE drawn from the center to the point of contact E is perpendicular to the tangent and to the plane MN (n): hence the line of direction passes through the point of contact, or base. But since (Fig. XXVIII.) the straight line xa, which is drawn from the center to the point of contact a, is perpendicular to the inclined plane AB, and so cannot stand perpendicularly on the horizontal plane DB: therefore the straight line xe, which hangs perpendicularly over the horizon and is the line of direction, cannot pass through the point of contact a, or base: the sphere therefore will come to rest at no point of the inclined plane. Here you have a phenomenon common enough, but a cause not commonly enough known.

The velocities of two heavy solid bodies hanging freely from the extremities of the same beam are directly to each other as their distances from the center of motion.

359 For it is well established that body B (Fig. XXIX.) cannot be moved along the arc BD without body A being depressed at the very same time along the arc AC. But the velocities of two bodies set in motion are to each other as the spaces traversed by them in the same time [By the Laws of velocities]: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as the arc AC to the arc

BD. But the former arc is to the latter as the distance AE to the distance BE, or as the radii of the circles, as is known from Geometry: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as AE to BE, that is, as their distances from the center of motion E.

Heavy bodies whose weights are equal, and which are placed, hung up, at an equal distance with respect to the center of motion, remain in equilibrium. If the weights are unequal and the distances equal, they do not remain in equilibrium, but the one that is endowed with the greater weight [p. 118] will be depressed. If the weights are equal and the distances unequal, they do not stand balanced, but the one that is removed further from the center of motion preponderates.

361 The first part is evident: since bodies equal in weight are posited, and an equal distance from the center of motion is had, and so an equal velocity of each (for since, by Princip. I, the velocities are as the distances, if these are equal the velocities too must be equal), therefore the quantity of motion in both is equal, or the momenta are equal: they will therefore stand unmoved in equilibrium (by the Def. of equilib.). The second part is shown: since the distances of the bodies are posited equal, the velocities are likewise equal. Therefore their momenta are as the weights (for since the weights of bodies are as their masses, and the quantities of motion of two bodies driven with equal velocity are as their masses, they will also be as their weights). Wherefore the momentum of the one that is greater in weight will exceed the momentum of the other; and, the equilibrium being removed, it will preponderate. The third part too is clear: since the distance of one body is greater than the distance of the other, the velocity of the former will likewise be greater than the velocity of the latter.

The bodies will therefore stand in equilibrium. From these principles is taken the rationale of weighing instruments, or Statical ones: the chief of them are held to be the Balance and the Steelyard.

## ON THE BALANCE

> POM . MR s

364

The balance, or scales, is the best-known instrument of Statics, by which the unknown weight of a given body is explored by taking another of known gravity.

Several parts are distinguished in it. The first is the beam AC (Fig. XXX.), namely a rigid rod divided into two parts AB and CB, equal both in length and in weight, which are called the arms. The second is the handle DB, to which the beam is so fitted, by means of a small axle passed through the center of motion B and through the holes of the handle, that it can move freely about the holes of the handle as about a center. The third is the tongue x, which is fixed immovably at right angles to the middle point of the beam: it is also called the trutina, examen, or argumentum of the balance, because it shows either the parallelism of the beam with the horizontal plane or its inclination. The fourth are the pans E and F, which, hung from the extreme parts of the beam, receive the weights.

365 For this whole Statical organ to be exact, it is necessary, first, that not only the arms but also the threads from which the pans are suspended be equal in weight. Secondly, it is required that the pans too be of equal weight. Thirdly, that the friction upon the beam be, as far as can be done, slight and almost none.

Hence, to lessen the friction, the axle inserted in the tongue is made cylindrical, and the hole in the tongue round, so that the contact may turn out smaller. Indeed, if the axle ends in an edge on the side where it touches the tongue, the motion of the beam will be quicker. Moreover, the following belong in general to the perfection of the balance. Let the arms be longer; for an inequality of the weights, which in shorter arms is sometimes scarcely discerned by sense, betrays itself very easily in longer ones. Let the tongue likewise be made longer, for a not dissimilar reason.

The pans are better suspended from little metal chains than from threads, inasmuch as the temper of the air sometimes acts upon threads in various ways.

366 As regards the more excellent use, that balance is to be preferred to the others whose center of motion is above the straight line from whose extremities the bodies to be weighed hang: whence, other things being equal, all require that the center of gravity of the beam be placed a little below the center of motion. The use of the balance is very well known, so that there is no need to mention anything about it. A defect is brought into the balance chiefly by the inequality of the arms; for, their inequality being posited, the bodies which, placed on the pans, are in equilibrium will be not of the same but of unequal weight, as

BD, is divided into parts equal among themselves, ab, bd, de, etc., each of which equals the distance of the point D from the point A, or the length of the shorter arm. These parts are divided again into other smaller parts, equal among themselves, for determining minute quantities. The pan, or hook, is hung from the extremity of the shorter arm, so that the body to be weighed can be placed on it or suspended from it. The counterpoise N is movable hither and thither, and is therefore called the runner of the steelyard.

368 For this instrument to be exact it is required that the shorter arm, together with the hook, equal the weight of the longer arm when the counterpoise is removed: or, if that is not done, that the longer arm be divided into proportional parts, a division that is found by trial. Steelyards have this advantage over the balance, that the weight even of large bodies can be explored by means of them with a single weight, and that a fairly small one; although in this the scales excel, that in them we can discern even small particles of an ounce, and more conveniently, and in our regions we usually do so; not so with steelyards. The weight of a given body is examined with this instrument by the following law:

the body M, whose weight is being explored, being hung on, the counterpoise N is set at that place of the longer arm at which it obtains equilibrium with the body to be weighed; equilibrium being now established, the hung body has the same ratio to the counterpoise that, reciprocally, the distance of the counterpoise from the center of motion has to the distance of the hung body from the same, or to the shorter arm: namely, if the counterpoise N is of one pound, and its distance Dm is to the distance DA as 4 to 1, the body M will be of four pounds.

370 Moreover, several defects can creep into the steelyard; for if the shorter arm, taken with the hook or pan, does not keep equilibrium with the other arm when the counterpoise is removed; likewise if the parts into which the longer arm is divided are unequal, or lack the due measure, the steelyard will always be deceitful: indeed, since it can deceive those who use it on other heads as well, and it is not so easy to detect the deceit, the distinguished Wolff says (p) it is better that it be banished from common life.

## DISSERTATION III

> ( p) Elem. Mechan. $. 778,

MECHANICS, or

The doctrine of Machines.

echanics, or the Machinal science, hands down the principles and laws by 371

M              which a power, of itself unequal to sustaining and moving a body, can be

rendered fit by the aid of certain machines either to sustain it or even to move it. Whence a mechanical machine is the name for that through which a power applied to it is rendered fit for sustaining or moving a body, neither of which it could accomplish. One machine is called simple, another compound. The former does not coalesce out of several, each of which would separately suffice to produce the effect: the latter arises out of other simple ones fitted to each other by a fixed law.

372 In this place there now comes to be set down the single principle of the

Machinal science, a general one indeed, by which alone it has pleased us to embrace the several principles that others have established here.

374 For let the force of the power be = p, and the weight to be moved = P, the velocity of the power = C, and the velocity of the weight = c. If the velocity of the power has a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight to the force of the power, it will be C : c > P : p; and therefore the product, or momentum, of the power, pC, will be greater than the momentum of the resisting weight, Pc. The heavy body will therefore be moved by the power. Since, further, the product pC turns out the greater the more the ratio C : c exceeds the ratio P : p, it follows that a huge body can be moved, by means of a machine, the more easily even by a slight power, the greater the ratio of the velocity with which the power is endowed to the velocity of the weight is than the ratio that holds reciprocally between the weight and the force of the power.

This being established, let us weigh the machines for a while, so far as is necessary for the purpose of Physics.

The lever, the first machine of Mechanics, is an oblong stake consisting of solid material, which is conveniently employed for moving huge weights more easily. Three things are distinguished in it, namely: the moving power, or momentum; the resistance, or weight to be sustained or moved; and finally the fixed point on which the lever rests, immovable: this is called in Latin fulcrum, by the Greeks hypomochlion, by Vitruvius pressio. But since these three points can be disposed in the lever in a threefold manner, a threefold kind is therefore usually distinguished.

376 The first is when the fulcrum holds the middle place between the power and the weight, such as the lever AB (Fig. XXXII.), where the fulcrum C is intermediate between the power B and the weight A. The second kind is when the fulcrum C (Fig. XXXIII.) is found at one extremity, the power A at the other extremity, and the weight B holds the middle. The third is had when the power

A (Fig. XXXIV.) occupies the middle between the fulcrum B and the weight C.

The lever of the first kind they call heterodromous; of the second, homodromous; that of the third kind they refer to the homodromous.

The same holds in the lever of the second kind; for by as much as the distance AC exceeds the distance BC, by so much more efficaciously will the power overcome the resistance of the weight. In the third kind of lever there is only this advantage, that the moving power can move a lighter weight with a greater velocity: which is not without its utility when a saving of time is sought.

## ON THE WHEEL AND AXLE

> 378 A in peritrocbio , fecunda Mechanicae machina, eft inf-

378

The wheel and axle, the second machine of Mechanics, is an instrument suited to lifting weights, in which the cylinder hi (Fig. XXXV.), which they call the axle, sustained on either side by the props k, l, has placed around it a drum, me, which they call the peritrochium: in its circumference are fixed round rods, ac, bd, which are called spokes, or scytalae, by which the power applied turns the peritrochium with the axle, and lifts the weight by means of a rope wound round it. Elsewhere the name peritrochium is given to that circular plane itself, in place of which the scytalae are substituted. If the scytalae are joined to an axle having a horizontal position, it is called a Windlass; but if the axle is set up perpendicularly, it is named a

Capstan. The use of windlasses is very great in mines. The capstan has this advantage, that several men together can be applied to each of the scytalae without hindering one another.

379 This machine is referred to the lever of the first kind; indeed, in reality it is a perpetual lever. For the hypomochlion is in the middle of the axle, namely at the point m, or f; indeed, points of this kind are rightly conceived through the whole axle: the moving power placed at a or b has the distance am, or bm, from the fixed point: the resistance is constituted at the point e of the surface of the axle itself, and is distant from the fixed point f only by the semidiameter of the axle, ef.

Whence, by as much as the distance am exceeds the distance ef, by so much more easily does the power at a overcome the resistance at e: and therefore, the greater the scytala is to be, the more the forces of the power increase. And from this same principle are deduced the force and efficiency of wheels whose motion is driven by treading, or by the inflow of water, likewise of the sails that are turned round by the wind in mills, and of other instruments of that kind.

The pulley, the third machine of Mechanics, is an instrument consisting of one or several little wheels revolving about their axles, which are fixed somewhere, by which, with a rope wound round them, which is called the ductarius, weights are drawn in. If only one little wheel is employed, it is called a simple pulley, and monospastos; if it is composed of two, three, four or more, it is called, according to their number, dispastos, trispastos, tetraspastos or polyspastos.

381 A simple pulley revolving about an immovable axle does not increase the forces of the moving power; for as much as the weight D ascends (Fig. XXXVI.), so much does A descend, and so the motions both of the weight and of the power are equal. Wherefore its whole advantage lies in this, that the direction of the power is changed, while, namely, by the aid of the pulley the power is moved downward which would otherwise have to be moved upward for the weight to be raised.

Moreover, in the descent of the power, the forces grow from the very weight of the moving body. Finally, the rope rolled round the wheel is less worn by friction.

382 It is plain, moreover, that the pulley BC is a perpetual heterodromous lever; for the fixed axle L, about which the little wheel revolves, is like a fulcrum, around which the power and the weight, which behave just as if they were applied to the extremities of the diameter CB, are moved together. If the simple pulley (Fig.

XXXVII.) is movable, since A, the extremity of the diameter AaD corresponding to the immovable point F, is the fulcrum on which the rope rests by means of the pulley, the power is placed at the other extremity of the diameter, D, and the weight, finally, in the middle, a; and so, since a pulley so arranged is a lever of the second kind, and the distance of the power from the fulcrum is to the distance of the weight from the same, namely DA to Aa, as 2 to 1, it is clear (from the preceding Chapter) that there will be equilibrium if the power is to the weight as 1 : 2. But the weight will be moved by the power if the latter is to it in a greater ratio than subduple: for supposing it is as 4 : 6, since the distance DA is double the distance

Aa, and then since the power moves twice as fast as the weight (by Princip. I of

Stat.), the velocity of the power will therefore have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself to the force of the power, namely 2 :

1 > 6 : 4, and so the weight will then be moved by the aid of the movable pulley (by the Princip. of Mechan.). The former pulley is called monospastos of the first kind; this other, monospastos of the second kind.

383 In the Dispastos, one little wheel of which is immovable and the other movable (Fig. XXXVIII.), the power P moves twice as fast as the weight M; for the lower little wheel cannot ascend from a to D unless the power P descends through a space = Da + bx, that is, through double the space covered by the weight.

Wherefore, since all increase of the moving power is to be derived from the movable little wheels, and this force grows by as much as its velocity exceeds the velocity of the weight, for that reason in the trispastos (Fig. XXXIX.) the power is tripled, since indeed the little wheel MN cannot be raised from d to b unless the power P, in descending, covers a space triple the height db, that is: unless three segments of the rope equal to the height db are drawn in. Thus in the tetraspastos the power is quadrupled, in the polyspastos it is multiplied many times over.

> De Prancratio.

384 Whence by means of the polyspastos a huge weight will be lifted with a slight power employed, if the ratio of that power to the weight is greater than the ratio of unity to the number of little wheels constituting the polyspastos. Wherefore, given the value of the power = 10, and the number of little wheels likewise = 6 (Fig. XL.), the product will express the value of the weight to be sustained by the power applied to this machine, = 60; and this weight will be carried upward if a little greater force of the power is added. Specifically, the part AB of the polyspastos is the upper pulley, and the part CD the lower pulley; each is named rechamus in Vitruvius.

The Pancratium, the fourth machine of Mechanics, is a complex of several toothed wheels associated by a certain artifice and under such a law that the teeth of one are inserted into the little teeth of another wheel revolving about its own axis, whereby it comes about that, when one is moved about its little axle, all the others are set in motion. This machine is named Glossocomum by Pappus (q), and, on the same witness, it was either invented or explained by Hero of Alexandria, for which reason it is commonly called Hero’s Glossocomum. Its form and construction are various: it will be enough to have sketched one, from which it may appear how greatly the forces are increased by a composition of wheels of this kind (r).

386 Let there be (Fig. XLI.) a Pancratium composed of four axles with toothed wheels. Let the larger wheels have, as to diameter, the ratio to the smaller of 10 : 1, and let the ratio of the number of teeth be the same. Let the handle AB, or radius, to which the power is applied, be ten times longer than the radius of the little wheel C; the velocity of the power will be to the velocity of the wheel C as 10 : 1. On the second axle the greater wheel D, furnished with ten times more teeth than the little wheel C, is turned once while C meanwhile revolves ten times. To the same axle is joined a little wheel E, equal to the former

Let the teeth in the wheel F likewise be ten times more numerous than the little teeth of the little wheel E, so that the latter must revolve ten times before F is borne once round its axle and carries off with it the attached wheel G. Finally the wheel H, itself too having ten times more teeth, will turn once with the axle IH and the cylinder K, which is contained by the same diameter as the wheel C, and which, revolving about the axle IH, lifts the weight by means of a rope.

387 This series and proportion of revolutions being posited, the velocity of the power A will be to the velocity of the little wheel C as 10000 : 1000; the velocity of the latter to the velocity of the little wheel E as 1000 : 100; that of this one to the velocity of G as 100 : 10; finally the velocity of G to the velocity of the cylinder, and of the weight L, as 10 : 1. Wherefore this proportion holds (ex aequo ordinata): the velocity of the power A is to the velocity of the weight L as 10000 : 1. And hence, by the aid of this machine, a force able to lift one pound is rendered fit for lifting 10000

An inclined plane is a plane surface forming unequal angles with the horizontal plane on which it stands. It is counted among the Mechanical machines on this account, that huge weights are either sustained or lifted on it more easily. Wherefore the laws by which the forces of moving bodies are increased by the aid of this plane come to be weighed a little; but before this let it be noted that the weight with which a body placed on an inclined plane strives to descend, and which must be overcome, is called the respective weight; but the whole weight of a body resting on no prop, the absolute weight.
