615 I say: Sound as it is regarded in the sonorous body, or primitive, consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body; [p. 195] but as it is in the medium through which it is transmitted, and hence derivative sound, it is placed chiefly in a tremulous motion of the air, which arises from the tremor and quivering of sounding bodies and is propagated all the way to the organ of hearing. The first part is demonstrated. Only those bodies are sonorous which, when struck or vibrated, take on a tremor, and hence which consist of elastic parts fit for performing very swift vibrations; but by that very fact primitive sound consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body: therefore. The major is established, since we have found by experiments that those bodies which are more elastic, and hence fitter for tremulous motion, are also more sonorous. Thus, because tin is stiffer than lead, silver more than gold, steel than iron, for that reason the one is more sonorous than the other; and it is commonly known that bodies consisting of excessively flexible parts are destitute of sound. Moreover: we know that bells, by the mere contact of a hand applied while they are sounding, give back a diminished sound, because the tremulous motion is in some part impeded.

> (u) Effai de Phyfique. L (x) Memoir de l* Academ. 1409.

616 The second part is proved: namely, that bodies are not sonorous through a tremor, or vibrations, that are total, but through particular ones, that is, through a tremulous motion of small parts; which the distinguished men Perrault (u), Carré (x) and de La Hire (y) discovered, whereas formerly bodies were thought to be sonorous through total vibrations. The thing is proved by common experiments. I shall use only two. If a musical string is struck rather vehemently with a bow greased with tallow, even though total vibrations are bound to occur, it gives no sound; but if a bow made rough with pitch or resin is drawn over the same string, a sound is clearly perceived: but no other reason can be given for this than that the bow coated with resin is roughened and as it were obtains little teeth, with which it rubs and agitates the smallest parts of the string, which the bow made slippery with tallow cannot graze: therefore. Secondly: if the ends of a pair of flexible, elastic fire tongs, pressed together by the fingers, are suddenly released, either no sound is heard or a moderate one, although the arms of the tongs are set into a vibratory motion by their elasticity; yet they sound clearly if they are struck with a hard body: therefore the tremulous motion of small parts produces primitive sound.

617 The 3rd part is proved: by derivative motion we understand that which is apt to strike the organ of hearing: but such is the tremulous motion of the medium, and chiefly of the aerial particles: therefore. The major is established: for since the sensation of sound does not arise in us unless the organ of hearing is changed by the sounding body, and it cannot be changed by it immediately, since it is not immediately touched by it, for that reason it must be changed through an interposed medium. But that this medium

619 The nature of sound having been examined, let us weigh its principal affections, as far as we may. The celerity of sound, or its diffusion through a certain space in a determinate time, is rightly reckoned among its principal affections. Various learned men have tried to observe it carefully, as can be seen in Musschenbroek (a). At length, according to the more celebrated observations, it was fixed at 180 French perches in the interval of one second; but because there was still controversy about this very result, a more exact inquiry into this matter was for that reason entrusted by the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris, in the year 1738, to the most distinguished men de Thury, Maraldi and de La Caille. These, then, chose for their operations a line 14636 perches, or toises, long, and found, first:

> (2) Legoas de Phyfique Tom. 5. Lec. 1 1. Exp. 4. (a) Comment. Acad. del Cimento P. 5. p. 115. (5) Memoir. del Acadm. 1758. 57^ 7

620 That sound, in the space of 1 second, both by day and by night, in rainy as in clear weather, covers 173 perches or toises, as we have said elsewhere. 2: that a wind blowing along the same line which the sound runs through either retards or accelerates it in proportion to its own celerity, that is: a contrary wind retards the sound, a following wind furthers it. 3: that the celerity of sound is always constituted by such a law that it runs through equal spaces in equal times. 4: that the intensity of sound, or its force, changes nothing in its celerity; for although a more vehement sound is diffused farther than a weaker one, the latter nevertheless runs through 173 perches in 1 second just as the other does (b).

621 The reason of which seems to be this: that since the impression, e.g., from a cannon, is stronger, the nearest aerial particles, by approaching the neighboring ones more on account of the greater force, do indeed cover a greater space; yet in order to restore themselves to their places again, they must have just as much space once more: but the particles of air less impelled by a pistol, just as they make less space in going forward on account of the smaller force, so in going back they run through less. From these things it now follows:

622 The knowledge of the uniform celerity with which sound is carried is very useful for determining the distances of places where geometrical operations cannot be applied: namely, for measuring straits of the seas, mouths of rivers, the distance of a siege trench from a bulwark, etc. That is, if between the discharge of a cannon or of a musket and the hearing of the sound the seconds are counted, then, since each corresponds to a distance of 173 perches, and these are multiplied by the number of seconds, the distance of the place in which the cannon was discharged will be had (understanding the distance along the straight line along which the sound is diffused); thus, if 10 seconds elapse between the fire seen and the sound perceived, the distance will be 1730 perches. Moreover, it will also be possible to measure the celerity of the wind; for since a following wind furthers the sound, if from the celerity increased by the wind you subtract the 173 perches corresponding to each second, the remainder will show the celerity of the wind.

623 Reflection is a singular affection of sound. That is, sound, no otherwise than any other motion, changes its direction when it strikes an obstacle, and according to the general law of motion is so reflected that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. But nothing is more admirable in the reflection of sound than the resonance which is called Echo, and which takes place when the air, variously agitated by the sounding body and falling on an opposite body, is thrown back with exactly the same modification, so that this repercussion presents to the ears almost the same sound as the direct sonorous rays produce. But not every reflected sound, sent back from an obstacle into the ear, brings it about that an Echo is formed: certain conditions, namely, must be present.

> Ííoni reflexi, ut melius corpus fonans €xaudiatur. . - 6:5

624 And first, indeed, it is required that the distance of the hearer from the obstacle from which the sound returns be such that the organ of hearing is perfectly changed beforehand by the direct sound before the reflected sound reaches it: the reason of which is that, if the time which intervenes between the impact of the direct sound and that of the reflected sound is not distinct, only one motion and change of the organ will be excited by both sounds, or at least the subsequent one will follow the prior with such haste that they can by no means be discriminated; and hence also only one sound will be perceived by us. This coincidence of the direct sound and the reflected sound nevertheless makes the sounding body heard better.

625 It is required, secondly, not only that there be a reflection of the voice and of the sounding body from a due distance, but also that the reflection be of such a kind that by its force the voice leaps back from certain as it were vaulted passages, windings and cavernous grottoes, so that the sonorous vibrations, collected through obstacles of this kind, reach the ear after the prior ones, which first set the air in motion, have already ceased: the reason of which again is that, if any reflection whatsoever, and every one at all, sufficed for this resonance, an Echo would always exist; but it is established by experience that a repercussion occurs only when the direct voice is carried into obstacles bristling with various passages, ducts and windings. Obj. 1: The sound of a trumpet is heard from more than a hundred paces, although the motion of the air stirred by the trumpet is scarcely perceived from two paces: therefore sound is diffused as far as the motion of the air cannot reach. I reply by denying the conseq., and I say: when a trumpet sounds, the tremor of the air reaches the same distance to which its sound extends; but this motion of the air, since it is only tremulous and composed of very minute vibrations, is altogether imperceptible to the sense of touch, for on account of its tenuity it does not suffice to change that sense; it is perceived, however, by the sensorium of hearing, on account of the exquisite texture, proportioned to this, which it has, by reason of which it is affected by such slight percussions.

627 But that the tremor of the air runs out to the same distance which the sound reaches is plain from experience; for when a cannon is fired, windows, especially glass ones, even a thousand or two thousand paces distant, tremble, and they do not tremble before the sound of the explosion is heard; and since such a tremor can only come from air impelling them, it becomes evident that the tremor of the air is inseparable from sound and reaches the same distance with it.

> 616 O* 1: Tubae fonus ex plufquam centum pafsibus audis c) Ia Phonurgia.

628 Obj. 2: If, inside a glass phial hermetically sealed, a little bell is struck by some artifice, the sound is perceived; but this would by no means happen if sound consisted in a vibratory motion of the air: for the air enclosed within the phial cannot pass through the glass so as to drive the external air all the way to the ear: therefore. I reply that whenever any sound is excited, not only the air but also the other bodies are stirred with a certain tremulous motion: for we frequently experience that, when the thicker strings of a musical instrument sound and the larger pipes of a pneumatic organ sing, the tables, the seats, nay even the very floor on which the said instruments stand, tremble. What wonder, then, if, in the case of the objection, when the air enclosed in the phial vibrates, the glass itself is stirred with a similar tremor, as experience testifies? For if the phial is gripped by the hand, a deaf, as it were, and very dull sound is heard, namely because the vibrations of the glass are in part prevented by the applied hand.

Proof of the major: the air cannot be set in motion at the same time by different motions together; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear. I reply by denying the proposition. For the tremulous motion of the air also consists of its own small motions; hence, when the alternating percussions of different bodies are communicated to the same organ, the air can be stirred by different motions in the same sensible time; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear, and consequently different sounds can be perceived in the same sensible time.

630 You have an example in standing water: if you throw little stones into different parts of it at the same time, you will surely see the whole of it ruffled into swelling ripples in the manner of a circle, which, continually spreading themselves out, intersect one another without any disturbance whatever. Likewise, therefore, in our case the vibrations excited by different sounding bodies run all the way to the ear without any disturbance, and affect it in different ways, whence it comes about that different sounds are perceived at the same time.

631 Obj. 4. If sound consisted in the aforesaid vibrations, we could not measure the distance of a sounding body by hearing: therefore. I reply: since the vibrations in the air are formed in the manner of a circle, and the air is rippled in waves in every direction, at the center of which circle the sounding body stands, hence the farther vibrations of this kind recede from the center, the greater the circumferences they make, and consequently a smaller portion of them, or a smaller arc, affects the more remote air than the nearer; hence the particles of air that strike are fewer, and at the same time less united; they therefore impress a smaller affection on the sense the farther one stands from the sounding body; and by means of this greater or smaller affection the distance of the sounding object is perceived.

632 Obj. finally: according to the more probable opinion, a low sound consists in slower vibrations, a high one in swifter vibrations; but the vibrations of the drum of the ear must be isochronous, or of the same duration, as are the vibrations of the same string equally stretched: therefore the same sound would always be heard as to low or high, which is contrary to experience, especially since the same body, keeping the same tension, cannot be set now into slower, now into swifter vibrations. Reply: by denying the supposition, namely that the drum of the ear always keeps the same tension. For the drum of the ear performs for hearing nearly the same office that the crystalline lens performs for sight.

633 For just as the crystalline lens receives the rays of light in such a way that by the force of its convexity it projects them onto the base of the retina with due distinctness, and to accomplish this changes its convexity to greater or smaller according to the different falling-in and different incidence of the rays: so also the drum of the ear is so constituted that, according to the different falling-in of the vibrating air, it now increases its tension, now diminishes it; so that, just as the crystalline lens increases or diminishes its convexity by

636 I say first: light as it is regarded in a luminous body, or primitive light, is rightly made to consist in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of that body. Proof: primitive light is rightly made to consist in that [p. 201] which is always joined with light itself in a body, and on which light so depends that, when it is posited in bodies, light is at once had in them and they are made luminous, whereas when it is taken away light straightway perishes; but always joined with light is a most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the body, so that there is no luminous body in which a motion of this kind is not detected; and as soon as the subtler parts of bodies are driven into agitated motion, light is emitted by them, but it is extinguished as soon as the agitated parts are brought back to rest: therefore primitive light consists in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of a body. The minor is demonstrated part by part most plainly.

637 And as to the first part, namely that all luminous bodies are endowed with such a motion, it is altogether most certain. For in flame and in burning coals a vehement motion of the parts is visible; likewise that putrefying bodies, putrid fish, wood corrupted by rot, which emit light, are agitated by an intestine motion of the parts is manifest from what has been said elsewhere, since fermentation and putrefaction cannot be explained without motion and agitation of the parts. The other part too is clear, namely that bodies emit light as soon as their subtler particles are set in motion.

638 “Do not all bodies (says the most distinguished Newton (e)) which abound with terrestrial parts, and especially with sulphureous ones, emit light as often as those parts are sufficiently agitated, whether this be done by heat, or by friction, or by percussion, or by putrefying, or by some vital motion, or by any other cause whatever? As sea water, the back of a cat stroked obliquely with the hand in a dark place, wood, flesh and fish while they putrefy, the vapors from putrid waters which are commonly called ignes fatui, glowworms and the eyes of certain animals by a certain vital motion, the Bononian phosphorus agitated by the rays of light, and certain liquors mixed with one another whose particles come together with an impetus, as oil of vitriol distilled from an equal weight of niter, and then mixed with a double portion of oil of cloves or of aniseed?”

639 But there are countless things that make this truth manifest, and the consideration of electrical phenomena demonstrates it to evidence. The last part is shown quite easily: for no one is unaware that, when the motion of the parts ceases, light is not spread from bodies; that flame is extinguished when the inflamed body is compressed; that light in burning bodies, for example in coals and in red-hot iron, vanishes when they are plunged into water, by which the agitation of the parts is stopped.

640 I say second: derivative light, or lumen, is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line. Proof, part by part. And first, that light is a corporeal substance is made

(e) Opticks, query 9. [p. 202] evident from this, that it shares in the affections of a body: for, first, while it passes from one medium into another, it is refracted. Second: falling upon an opaque surface, it is reflected toward the opposite side. Third: propagated light can be gathered and, as it were, condensed into one point, if it is received by a concave mirror or a convex lens, in the point which they call the focus, in which it produces a heat so intense that it sets on fire, after a few minutes, any combustible bodies placed in that spot, melts and dissolves metals and all fusible things, and turns into glass those which are least liable to liquefaction and abound in salt, as may be seen in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (f), where a great many things are related of the concave mirror which, from its inventor D. Tschirnhaus, is called the Tschirnhausian. (g)

641 Fourth: light strikes the organ of sight, and by its abundance or vehemence (just as an excessive crash offends the ear) it disturbs it, nay hurts it greatly; but all these things manifestly prove a corporeal, or impenetrable, substance: therefore. And indeed, as the distinguished Gassendi argues very well (h), just as a ball driven against a wall rebounds from it, because, since it is a body, it cannot pass through a place occupied by a body, so a ray of light driven against a body is struck back by it, because that body occupies the place with its bulk; for it is a constant rule that natural effects of the same kind have the same causes, as we have said [§. 22.]. Next, that it is a most subtle substance is evident from this, that it enters the pores of glass most easily. What of the fact that the structure of the tiniest animalcules demonstrates the tenuity of light? For if the animalcules themselves, as we have already said [§. 164.], are of such tenuity, if their eyes and the pupils of them are of so slight a bulk, how much smaller must the matter of light be, so that it may glide into the eyes and the pupil and easily permeate these organs?

(g) But since the gathering of the rays, and hence the powers of mirrors, increased by their aid, depend on their concave figure, therefore any material whatever is suitable for a burning mirror, provided it can be polished exactly. Hence, on Wolff’s testimony, the celebrated Dresden craftsman Gärtner constructed great burning mirrors of wood, which were said to surpass the Tschirnhausian ones in effectiveness. Indeed Zahn [in Wolff, Elem. Catoptr. §. 223.] relates that a mirror was made by Neumann by which metals were rendered fluid, out of rather hard paper with straw glued onto it. Nevertheless, the texture of the material from which mirrors are prepared must be so constituted that it sends back the rays of light and does not absorb them, as happens in black bodies. For that reason the distinguished Boyle, by means of a mirror which he made in the form of a burning glass out of black marble, could not burn wood set in the focus, even though the sun had fallen upon the mirror for quite a long time, as Musschenbroek relates [Essai de Physique §. 975.].

642 That the motion of those corpuscles is very swift is proved, first, from the very swift diffusion of light. Second, it is demonstrated from that astonishing force of the burning mirror of which we have spoken [§. 640.]: for since a force of this kind is that very force by which those corpuscles are moved, and this arises from the product of the mass into the celerity [§. 275.], the mass of each of those corpuscles, being most slight, as indeed it is, cannot give them a force as great as we have seen it to be unless they are moved with the greatest celerity; and so it is necessary that they be moved with the greatest celerity. Finally, we have it ascertained by experiment that this motion is rectilinear: a luminous ray let in through a very small hole into a dark chamber is always propagated in a straight line, and falls upon the point opposite the little hole along a straight line: therefore light is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line.

643 I say 3: the propagation of light, or derivative light, or lumen, is not rightly explained by a fiery outflow emanating from luminous bodies. This is against the distinguished Gassendi and Newton. Proof: if it were so, a medium once lit up would remain illuminated even when the luminous body was taken away. For the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium itself, even though the luminous body from which they were emitted is no longer present to it; but it is false that the medium remains illuminated when the luminous body by which it is lit up is taken away: therefore. Next, the light spread by a candle in a small room, or by the sun through the air, ought to become the more intense the longer the body is present there; for since the luminous body emits new corpuscles of light at every moment, it is necessary that in the same part of the medium through which the light is diffused the corpuscles always become more abundant, and therefore the light more intense; yet each of these conflicts with experience.

644 Each of these reasons is strengthened by the comparison that the distinguished Gassendi uses to explain his opinion about light: for he says that light is produced just as odors are, namely by the emission of slender corpuscles; but it is certain that an odor is preserved even when the body spreading the odorous molecules is taken away; it is likewise certain that an odor is made continually more intense and more lively in the same part of the medium the longer the presence of the bodies from which the odorous corpuscles emanate lasts: therefore light is not rightly placed in a substantial effluvium of the luminous body.

645 The Newtonians say that the medium, once lit up, does not remain illuminated when the luminous body is taken away: because, although the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium through which they have been diffused, they do need it in order not to cease being moved in it, and therefore in order to show the medium itself lit up to us.

646 But against this, argues the most distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: for no projected body needs the presence of the projector in order to persevere in the motion that it received from it; but it goes on being moved even if the projector

> [p. 204]

[p. 204] fails after impressing the motion on it: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light need the presence of the luminous body, lest the motion which they received from it should perish in them. Moreover, neither the corpuscles of sound nor those of odor so depend on the sounding or odorous body from which they emanate that they can be moved, and excite sensation in us, only in its presence: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light so depend on the luminous body that they should come to a halt in their motion and be rendered wholly unfit for exciting the sensation of light in us as soon as the luminous body is no longer present to us.

647 But if someone should say that the corpuscles of sound can be moved even when the sounding body from which they were emitted is absent, because their motion is perturbed and spreads through the air in every direction, whereas the corpuscles of light can be moved only when the luminous body by which they were darted forth is present, because their motion is rectilinear: against this it is urged that, just as the perturbed motion of corpuscles does not need, in order to be preserved, the presence of a body moving them in a perturbed way, so neither should the rectilinear motion of corpuscles need, lest it perish, the presence of a body vibrating them along a straight line. For the reason of each motion is altogether the same, namely the independence of the body moved from the mover, so that it retains the motion it has once received, whatever that motion may be. Nay, so far is the duration of a rectilinear motion once impressed on a body from depending on the duration of the mover, that among the laws of nature this is one: every body once set in motion is always moved along a straight line, so long as it is not compelled by some external cause to change its direction [§. 294.].

648 But hence none of those who hold for certain that the substantial effluvium of the luminous body, in which they make light consist, needs some notable interval of time in order to reach us from the sun and the other stars, can deny that it will come about that light remains in the medium through which it has been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it is produced is taken away. For it is evident on this hypothesis that light is preserved in the medium independently of the luminous body for that whole time which elapses while it travels from the luminous body itself to us. For if it is supposed that one hour is required for light to be propagated from the Sun S to the earth T (Fig. 117.), it is evident that the light diffused from S remains in the space from S to T even if, within that interval of one hour, the Sun S, which emitted that light, ceases to exist.

650 I say fourth: the propagation of light seems to be explained by a rectilinear pressure of an ethereal substance endowed with vibratory motion, a pressure proceeding from the motion of the luminous body and impelling the organ of sight.

> ^;id$ Cizal4elh uia RINIDLIall, Gb X LLLO AeILni$ a DOLI$ fRIII[EÍR!.

Proof: for the ethereal matter claims for itself the affections of a corporeal substance, and can be refracted, reflected and move the organ; and since it is most subtle, it can receive motion from the particles of the luminous body; and since it is had diffused everywhere, the propagation of motion through it is explained in the best possible way. Moreover, it is established that the organ of hearing is so affected by the tremulous motion of the air alone, entering the cavity of the ears, that the sensation of sound arises in us; but among all things there is the greatest analogy between light and sound: therefore by the vibratory motion alone of a most subtle ethereal substance, which penetrates the pupil of the eye, the organ of sight can be so altered that the sensation of light is excited in us.

I deny the proof of the antecedent: for in order to prove that light does not rebound in the way that is required for it therefore to be called a body, it is not enough to show that it is not reflected from a mirror like a ball. For neither does sound rebound like a ball when an Echo occurs, and yet those aerial particles in whose tremor [p. 206] sound consists, even according to the Peripatetics, are corporeal, and it is certain that sound is reflected because those particles are corporeal: therefore light too is reflected not metaphorically, but truly and properly, even though it does not rebound like a ball from a wall.

653 Obj. 3: the particles of light are most tenuous: therefore they cannot meet with [such resistance] that they can be reflected and refracted: for since light […] in […]: therefore refraction is said of light only metaphorically. I deny the consequence. For just as […] the tenuity of the particles of light, and […] by motion […], since among them they can […] and be reflected, since […] than they are impelled by the luminous body […]. For since those particles are corporeal, […] no one fails to see that there can be in them the texture in which the […] of bodies is placed, and on which their […] depends.

654 Obj. 4: bodies which are refracted in passing from a rare medium into a dense one recede from the perpendicular, because their motion is compounded of two, namely of the perpendicular one, which arises from gravity, and of a horizontal one impressed from without; but light is not so refracted, since it approaches the perpendicular: therefore it is not a body. I deny the consequence. For although a leaden ball, for example, is refracted in this way in passing from air into water because it is a body, it is not rightly inferred from this that light is not a body because it is not refracted in the same way as a leaden ball; but it must be said that light is not refracted toward the same side as that ball, not because the ball is a body, but because light is refracted not with a recession from, but with an approach to, the perpendicular, either for the reason already brought forward by us [§. 3…], or because it is attracted more strongly by water than by air, as the most distinguished Newton held. In order, then, to prove that the corporeality of light is not well proved by the Moderns from its refraction, the Peripatetics ought to demonstrate that only such a refraction arises from corporeality as is performed, in the passage from a rarer medium into a denser one, with a recession from the perpendicular.

655 Nor does it avail to say that light is not refracted of itself, but by reason of its subject, namely the air in which it is produced. For, first, the Peripatetics ought now to explain why illuminated air, although it is a body, is nevertheless not refracted as solid bodies are, namely with a recession from the perpendicular, while it is forced to enter water. 2. They must give the cause why air suffused with light can enter glass, while air lacking light cannot. It stands, then, that the corporeality of light is most firmly demonstrated by the Moderns against the Peripatetics from its reflection and refraction.

I distinguish the major: it is compenetrated in such a way that it truly enters and passes through the solid particles of that body, I deny the major; inasmuch as it enters its pores and runs freely through them, I grant the major, and I deny the consequence: for the pores with which a diaphanous body abounds are set in a straight line and communicate with one another, so that light is diffused through them in such a way that it passes through the body itself and runs freely beyond it. The whole body, moreover, seems to be occupied by light, that is, there seems to be no part at all in it which is not suffused with light, because the pores of that body are not only innumerable, but also so close to one another that we ourselves can discern no interval whatever between them. And just as […] it does not follow that glass is compenetrated with water, so must it be said of light […] illuminating the glass.

657 Inst.: those parts of the glass which exist between the pores are either opaque or diaphanous. Not the first, because then the whole glass would be opaque, since the pores are not glass but empty spaces, which are nothing. But if those parts are diaphanous, they are then receptive of light: therefore light is received not only in the pores of the glass, but also in the very body of the glass. I reply that those parts are opaque, and I deny that it will therefore come about that the whole glass is opaque. For although the pores are nothing but empty spaces, yet if they are so disposed as to be set in a straight line and to communicate with one another, they constitute a diaphanous body, although they do not constitute the light which falls into it, but make the free passage of the rays. The Peripatetics themselves […] two bodies […]. A body, then, is porous, and is rightly called a body, although its pores are not a body but the empty spaces of a body, which are nothing: therefore by the same reason a body is rightly called diaphanous, although the pores, from whose right disposition its diaphaneity is derived, are not a body.

> M-- oc -—i dnju .- -o ew "—-- o LPS

658 Moreover, although the particles which bound the pores of a body are entirely solid and the pores are not a body, the Peripatetics do not on that account infer that the body is altogether solid: therefore by the same reason a body can be diaphanous although those particles of it are not diaphanous, but opaque. […] it is necessary that the particles be solid from whose position and mutual adhesion we call a body solid […]. A body, then, can truly be, and be called, fluid, although the particles which constitute it are solid: therefore it can also be, and be called, a diaphanous body, although the particles of which it is composed are opaque; and just as from this alone, that the component particles of a body are solid, it cannot be inferred that the whole body is solid, so from this alone, that the particles of which a body is made up are opaque, it is not rightly deduced that it is opaque.

660 You will say: the whole glass is denominated luminous, just as the whole […] is said to receive light, which is by no means affirmed of a sieve pierced with very small holes, whose parts are not diaphanous, but receive light only through the holes. But I reply very easily: the whole glass is called luminous because both its pores, through which light passes, and the very particles which bound them and […] reflect it, are of so small a magnitude that they altogether escape the senses. But in a sieve the matter stands the other way. For however many the holes may be which […] light in it, and give it passage, they are nevertheless far […], just as also the parts in it […] by which the incident rays of light are sent back to us.

Ton which it falls. Thus light is said to be reflected when it goes back from the surface of a mirror toward the opposite side. The incident ray of light is the straight line along which light is propagated in falling; the reflected ray, on the other hand, is the straight line along which it is propagated in being reflected:

so that, if light falls on the surface A B (Fig. LXV.) along the straight line a b, and rebounds along the straight line b d, the straight line a b will be the direct ray of light, and the straight line b d the reflected ray. Recall to memory what we said when we spoke of the reflection of motion.

664 A ray of light falling on the polished surface of an opaque body is reflected by this constant law, that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. For it is most evidently established that light let in through a very small hole of a darkened room, if it is received on the polished surface of a mirror, always rebounds from it in such a way that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; and this proposition is so certain that it is assumed as an axiom in Catoptrics by common consent.

It is helpful to recall what we have said of the refraction of motion. The universal principle of the refraction of the rays of light is this: Light passing obliquely from a rarer medium into a denser one, namely from air into water or glass, is refracted by approaching the perpendicular: but passing from a denser medium into a rarer one, namely from glass or water into air, it is refracted by receding from the perpendicular line.

667 Proof of the first part. Let there be a glass vessel with a flat bottom D F H E (Fig. LXVI), covered with an opaque plate very finely perforated at B. Let a ray of light A B enter the vessel itself through the hole B. It is ascertained by experience that, while the vessel is filled with air alone, the ray A B proceeds straight to b, but on the contrary goes on to a if, the position of the vessel remaining entirely the same, the vessel itself is filled with water. Therefore the ray A B approaches the perpendicular B e while it passes obliquely from air into water. As to the second part, the matter is very well known: a coin A (Fig. LXVII.) placed on the bottom of the vessel C A B is seen from the spot a if the vessel is filled with water, but cannot be seen from the same spot if the vessel itself is full of air alone. The ray A B, therefore, breaking out of the vessel full of water, turns aside from the straight path and is therefore refracted by receding from the perpendicular B E while it passes from water into air: therefore light, etc.

668 But it is worth noting that, although it is most true that light is refracted in this way while it passes obliquely from air into water or glass, and conversely from water or glass into air, it is not therefore true, as is commonly said, that light is universally refracted by approaching the perpendicular, or by receding from it, while it proceeds obliquely from one medium into another of different density; nor is it universally true that light is refracted by approaching the perpendicular whenever it passes obliquely from any rarer medium into any denser one, or on the contrary is refracted by receding from the perpendicular whenever it likewise passes obliquely from any denser medium into any rarer one: for the most ingenious ’s Gravesande observed and certainly detected the contrary (n).

That light is refracted toward the perpendicular in the passage from alum into Danzig vitriol, although the density of these bodies is entirely the same. That light is likewise refracted by approaching the perpendicular in the passage from water into spirit of turpentine, and hence from a denser medium into a rarer one. For the density of water is to the density of spirit of turpentine as 8 to 7.

671 Optics is the science of direct vision, or the Physico-Mathematical science by which we are taught by what mechanism objects which send rays of light from all their points to the eye are seen by us. Catoptrics is the science of reflected vision. The universal principle of the reflection of rays from polished surfaces is not at all different from the law which other bodies keep in reflection, namely that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. Further, surfaces of this kind, in which this regular reflection of light is detected, are called mirrors. Mirrors, moreover, are divided chiefly into plane, convex and concave: that is called plane which is bounded by a plane surface, convex that which is bounded by a convex one, concave that which is bounded by a concave one.

673 Dioptrics is the science of refracted vision, which considers chiefly the bending of luminous rays in glasses. Glasses, moreover, are usually divided into various classes, distinguished by their different figure. A plane glass is bounded by plane surfaces parallel to each other. A lens is a glass of lenticular form: one is convexo-convex, namely that which is enclosed by a double convex spherical surface; another plano-convex, which is bounded by one plane surface and the other convex.

675 Glasses, or spectacles, for the eyes are most useful to the myopic, or those who […] see distant things confusedly; for since, owing to the too convex conformation of the eye, […] they need light with diverging rays, they therefore use concave glasses, which render parallel rays diverging: on the contrary, to presbyopes, or those who see distant things more clearly and distinctly and near things confusedly, convex glasses are of great help: for the rays from […] near objects […] are fixed in their […]; for which reason they fittingly use glasses of this kind, which gather the rays, or at least promote their convergence. The distinguished Redi (o) affirms that the [invention] of these spectacles is owed to Alessandro della Spina, and […] about the year […].

> 4. ALD anl uirum

676 Further, from the combination of both kinds of glass the Telescope came forth, its author being (as seems to most) Zacharias Jansen, toward the end of the sixteenth century. It was constructed on this plan: that a convex glass should be turned toward the objects and a concave one toward the eye […]. This telescope is also called the Galilean, because […] for observing the phenomena of the heavens by Galileo. […] first perfected this instrument […]; the Astronomical telescope derived its origin from the same source, consisting of two glasses convex on both sides; but since it seemed somewhat inconvenient that […] the object […] inverted, […] added two further glasses, which should set upright what the former had inverted; and then, for viewing terrestrial objects, a telescope […] with four convex glasses […].

677 Finally, from glasses which swell out with a convex surface […], since they enlarge the images of minute objects, microscopes, or engyscopes, are constructed by the fit composition of various glasses […]. The first of those who […] this instrument is said to be, as Musschenbroek (p) [relates], Francesco Stelluti, who in the year […] published a description of the parts of the […] which he discovered with this aid. Then followed Power, Hooke, Grew,

678 James Gregory in the year 1663 invented and described a catadioptric telescope composed of lenses and mirrors. Both, however, at length, after an interval of some years, […] namely John Hadley brought them to perfection.

679 From the combination of a lens and a mirror the Polemoscope was likewise made: namely an instrument by whose aid one can view objects while looking in another direction. Its chief part is a plane mirror […] inclined, from which the image of the object is sent back toward the eye of the beholder, since he himself cannot have it along a straight line. In this way it will be possible to observe without danger the movements of the enemy, […] behind the defenses of bulwarks, […] and to […] who […], etc.

## DISSERTATION V

> -. DISERTATIO V. . .. De Qualitaübus infenfibilibus.

On insensible Qualities.

## CHAPTER I

> B CAPUT T. « De Sympathia, Antipathiz, Idiofyncrafia, E & Antiperíftafi.

On Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis.

hose qualities are called insensible, or occult, which do not themselves act 682

T           immediately on our senses, but are known from their effects and by rea‐

son; the name of occult, however, is held to be undeservedly given to them by the Modern Philosophers, who follow the right method of philosophizing and are not content with abstract words wrongly used, in which the Peripatetics delight exceedingly, namely faculty, or quality, or form, and others like them, but they inquire into the causes of things, which can be grasped not indeed with the eyes, but with the mind. Among qualities of this kind are reckoned Sympathy, Antipathy and all the others mentioned above, of which we are to treat in this place.

683 Sympathy, then, is the name for that agreement of things by which it comes about that, when one is affected, feels, is moved or suffers, the other too is affected, feels, is moved and suffers. To this likewise is referred a certain friendship, or rather fitness, between men, and a certain natural love. Antipathy, on the contrary, is the name they give to a repugnance and, as it were, a certain enmity between things, such that one rejects and turns away from the other. They speak of idiosyncrasy when we either turn away from harmless, nay salutary, things and cannot bear them, or seek and easily tolerate things harmful and otherwise adverse. Antiperistasis is defined in the

Schools as the resistance of one body against a contrary body by which it is besieged on every side, growing in strength, and the intensification of a quality on account of the contrary quality.

684 The explanation of these qualities does not seem so recondite to the Modern

685 I say first: Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis are rightly attributed to substantial outflows, and to the motion, rest, figure and situation of the parts, and to other mechanical affections; likewise to custom, to manners, to temperament, or to imagination. Proof, part by part. First, by explaining sympathetic effects most clearly from the said principles. Thus, for example, the powder from calcined vitriol which is called sympathetic, and which, when thrown into blood freshly let out of a wound, is found to stop its flow and to heal the wound, will be conceived to produce this effect in no other way than through the corpuscles of the vitriol, which, mixed with the still warm particles of the blood and set into fermentation together with them, are carried to the wound from which the blood was pressed out (just as transpiration takes place), and indeed, like wedges, entirely block up the open passages through which the blood flows forth.

686 The reason of other effects of this kind, likewise in men and animals, is given from our conclusion. Thus, that when one yawns another yawns, that when one dog barks another barks too, that when some little birds sing others are stirred to warble, comes from this, that men and animals which have a fit disposition of body are easily stirred to the things that are done by others: for when certain ideas are excited, the members of the body conspire, and are easily stirred to motions determined according to a certain idea. The force of custom also contributes much to sympathetic effects, when through it a particular disposition and aptitude is induced in bodies. Finally, the inclination of one man toward another arises above all from the agreement of manners, the congruence of temperament, and likewise from elegance in speech, body, life and manners. For these provoke and win love, and bind men as with silent chains. Antipathetic effects have, in their own way, the opposite cause. Thus the causes of aversion between men are easily detected: for in the face, manners, life, speech or actions something is always found by which the one cannot but be averse to the other. Effects of this kind in animals too are fittingly derived from the principles already established. Thus who will deny that the flight of the lamb when the wolf is present, the wolf ’s rush upon the lamb, and the clucking of hens when the kite flies past, are brought about by certain impressions?

(t) In a special dissertation on the herb mimosa. [p. 216] having, namely, first set out the anatomy of this kind of plant, having noted the reticular composition of the leaves out of fibers, utricles, small vessels and little vesicles swollen with air of various kinds, and having weighed the equilibrium of the sap-bearing vessels and of the tracheae, he illustrates the matter: namely, when a hand approaches, the air contained in the vesicles is rarefied and expanded by the warm exhalations emitted, hence the sap-bearing vessels are in some measure compressed; when these are compressed, the more abundant inflow of the sap, from which the leaves obtained their vigor and extension, is checked, whence the leaves grow pale, become flaccid and contract. When the hand is then withdrawn, it is no wonder that the vigor of the herb is restored, since, the cause of the expansion ceasing, the rarefaction of the air is overcome by the sap flowing in through the vessels.

688 The chief reason of idiosyncrasies lies in this, that, owing to a singular disposition, constitution and likeness of the organs, and above all a more tender, softer, looser or more rigid etc. constitution of the nervous fibers, certain impressions affect the mind, and according as they are either agreeable or adverse to the mind, it is affected in various ways, either calmly, or unpleasantly, or impetuously; whence there follow determinate motions of the common sensorium and of the nerves which are stretched out and distributed from there to the parts and through them. It is accordingly explained why certain men fear cats, dogs, mice, and shudder at and abominate other animals, and grow pale and tremble even at their name.

689 For if infants have been frightened and offended by things of this kind by ignorant old women (as happens very often, not without great harm to health, nay even with danger to life), since the fibers of the brain, still tender in the infant, have been too much agitated and weakened by the vehement impression, therefore, through the rest of life thereafter, when a similar material idea, or imagination, is brought back and arises anew, the impression and agitation in the weakened fibers is more vehement than is right; and in the mind an immaterial idea arises that is most disagreeable and adverse. And from the foundations stated, more or less, the reason is given of idiosyncrasies that are hereditary, adventitious, or contracted in various ways after birth, and acquired by custom.

690 Likewise, if attention is paid to the different ways in which our organs, and the animal spirits diffused through the nerves, are affected by various objects, and to the fact that these spirits, by the aid of the imagination, can be moved very swiftly through the whole body, in brutes as well as in men, it will not be difficult to explain those effects which, through the nerves of the mother, on account of a lively imagination, are propagated into the tender, and hence easily changeable, little body of the fetus.

691 Those effects which are attributed by the Peripatetics to Antiperistasis as to an occult quality can just as well be explained by mechanical affections, without that metaphorical battle of qualities: as, for instance, that underground places are colder in summer than in winter. And indeed the experiments which, for the proof of this occult quality,

> [p. 217]

[p. 217] are adduced either arise from the deception of the senses or are insufficient to establish that quality. For the same place, though equally tempered, seems to the judgment of sense now hot, now cold, according to the different constitution of the sensorium, as was explained by us in the Logic.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732

B          tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the

motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air, then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the

6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firmament with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining

Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discovered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally he

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

> «irca quem proxime movetur Mercurius, tüm Venus, deinde Tellurem cum Luna fb: circumgyrante pofted Mariem , tüm Jovem; denique Saturnum 1evolvi arbitratur: ultrà omnes Planetas vero, & quidem ad immenfíam paefié diftantiam ponit Spheram Stellarum fíxaram omni penitüs modi deítitutam. Planetis fingülis, unico Sole excepto, quem propterea é Planetarum numero expungir ; motum periodicum tribuit, nempé fub Zodiaco fecundum fignorum feriem.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

> 736 Yellui triplicem adfignat motum, videlicet: primum verrigizis circa proprium axem ab. Occafu in ortum, quo declarare volunt Cope:n cani viciísitudinem noctis & diei ; fiquidem pofito hoc. mou Sol nobis ab orta in Occafum gyrari videtur, ac tellus aliam fem. per faciem illumninandam Soli objectat: motum hunc diurnum. vocat, quód intervallo unius dici perficiatur. Alterum periodicum dicit in orbe magno circa Solem fub ecliptica, quo motu tellus per figna ita progreditur, ut Sol nobis in eo fiszno, quod tegit, efle videatur, adeoque dum terra elt in fignis borealibus, ipfe nobis in auftralibus, & contrà, verfari adpareat: ayotum hunc eznsus adpellat, qui anni unius fpatio abfolvitur.

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

704 Monkshood, by excessive heat, thins and agitates the blood with which it is mixed, and burns up the delicate substance of the viscera; water hemlock, on the other hand, by excessive cold gradually halts the particles of the blood in the finer and extreme veins, so that there it grows torpid as though congealed; then, as these approach the heart little by little with rest and cold, it renders the blood stagnant in the heart itself, whence death follows. We omit what they say of the basilisk, namely that its look is deadly, and likewise of the remora, the little fish that holds ships back, things which indeed are reckoned among old wives’ tales by critics of better note. The motions, however, which are excited in certain men by the bite of the tarantula (which is a species of spider well known in Calabria near Tarentum), we shall explain later.

705 The manner of acting of Alexipharmics consists in this: either that they blunt and break the sharp points of the poison, as oily things do; or that they restore the ordered motion of the blood, by resolving the thicker parts and rousing the weak spirits, as theriac etc. does; or by receiving the poisoned corpuscles into themselves on account of the mutual proportion of the pores and parts. Thus a wound inflicted by a Scorpion (commonly alacrán) is healed if the scorpion itself, crushed, is at once laid on the wound, since the poisonous particles left in the hand by the bite are sucked out, as by a sponge, by the homogeneous particles which are found in the crushed body of the scorpion; or, finally, antidotes have their force against some particular poison placed in a motion which is opposite to the motion of the poison itself.

706 So the most effective remedy against the bite of the tarantula is the motions and vibrations of a musical instrument; for when the blood has been condensed by the poison and the little vessels obstructed, the inflow of the animal spirits is impeded, and the nerves are consequently relaxed; but by the harmonic vibrations of the music the blood is agitated, the spirits receive vigor, these run through the fibers and nerves, and the fibers and nerves, brought to a constitution in unison with the strings or sounding instruments, receive the vibrations of the strings; hence the motion of the limbs, and finally leaping; by the exertion of leaping the agitation of the blood is increased and sweat is drawn out, whence the poison too, thinned and agitated, is gradually dissipated by transpiration; and in proportion as the poison is dissipated the sick man is better, and this recovery of health spurs him on to continue the leaping, whence it comes about that all the poison breathes out and the blood recovers its fluidity and its former course.

712 Obj. finally: such phenomena, and very many others, are explained more conveniently by the Peripatetic substantial forms than by the texture of the parts and substantial effluvia, since it is incredible that effluvia should flow unceasingly from hard and solid bodies: therefore. Dist. antec.: more conveniently and more suitably to the nature of true Physics, I deny; not so, I grant. What is included in the antecedent stands answered in several places of our Physics where we spoke of effluvia.

Moreover: no one has hitherto denied that most gems, and diamonds themselves, bodies certainly very hard, are powerful in electric force, which can by no means be understood without a substantial efflux. What more? From the regulus of antimony little vessels are made which give an emetic force to wine or beer poured into them, and they are used for this purpose for many years without any sensible diminution of their weight. So too mercury, boiled a little in water, gives it a force by which it kills worms, to omit very many other things.

714 The principal parts of this sphere, in which, as at one glance, the constitution of the universe and the variety of the motions which the chief bodies of the world require are beheld, are: I. The Axis, or diametral line, passing through the center of the sphere in such a way that the sphere turns about it; its extreme points are called the poles. II. The greater cut the whole sphere, as also the other greater circles, into two equal parts, and they are these: the Equator, the Meridian, the Horizon, the Zodiac, the two Colures. 716 The Equator, or equinoctial or equidial circle, is that in which, while the Sun is placed in it, day is equal to night. In the course of one year the Sun is in it twice: when it touches the beginning of the sign Aries, about the 20th of March, and when it enters the sign Libra, about the 23rd of September. The equator is distant from each pole of the world by a quadrant; it therefore divides the sphere into two equal parts, the Boreal and the Austral. Its use is defined in a manner by these points: I. It divides the whole world into the two hemispheres just named. II. It indicates the two equinoxes of the year, namely the vernal and the autumnal. III. It measures days and hours; for its 360 degrees pass by in the space of 24 hours, and so each 15 degrees make one hour. IV. It is the boundary from which the declinations of the Sun, the Moon and the other Stars are taken; for the declination of any star is its distance from the equator toward one or the other pole, which is measured by the arc of a circle passing through the poles of the world and the center of the Star. V. It defines the cardinal points of East and West on the horizon. VI. By its different position with respect to the horizon it brings it about that the horizon presents itself as right, oblique, or parallel.

Undé quum pun&ta haec ex diametro oppofita; dum ab alio loco in alium commeamus, quin relaté ad quemvis hominem; alia fint atque alia, patet horizontem mutari identidém , :eolque rotidem diveríos efle, quot punéta in Íphaerae iuperficie coeitará poffunt. 717 The Horizon is understood to be described from the vertical point, which in Arabic is called Zenith, and from another set on the opposite side, which is called Nadir (both are counted among the cardinal points), and it cuts the sphere into equal parts, the upper and the lower, in such a way that the plane of the circle passes through the center of the world. Hence, since these diametrically opposite points, as we travel from one place to another, nay, relatively to each man, are different and different again, it is plain that the horizon changes again and again, and that there are as many different horizons as there are points that can be thought on the surface of the sphere. And this concerns the Astronomical, or rational, horizon, so called because it is considered by Astronomers observing the motions of the Heavens, and is perceived by reason only, not by sense. For there is another horizon, sensible or physical, which everyone set in some vast plain, or in the middle of a calm sea, defines by turning his sight round. Wherefore, mathematically speaking, the sensible horizon neither actually forms a greatest circle, since it in no way extends through the center of the world, nor consequently does it separate the sphere of the Heaven into equal parts; yet it is always parallel to the rational horizon.

Ff [p. 224] the upper, which rises above the rational horizon, and the lower, which lies beneath that same horizon; the sensible horizon, on the other hand, distinguishes the part of the Heaven visible to us from the invisible. II. It determines the risings and settings of the stars. III. It designates, for each particular region, the stars that never rise or never set. IV. It defines the length of the artificial day and of the night: for that interval during which the Sun remains above the horizon is called the artificial day, as the night is taken to be this space during which it is depressed below the horizon. V. It is the boundary from which the altitude of the Stars is found: for the altitude of a star above the horizon is as great as the arc of the circle drawn through the poles of the horizon and the very center of the Star, comprehended between that center and the point of the horizon. The same holds of the depth of the Stars which they have below the horizon. VI. The Horizon, according to the different position of the sphere, makes it now right, now parallel, now oblique. This circle is not usually marked on Geographical Maps. In the armillary Sphere its office is performed by a broad and immovable rim, on which three things are inscribed: namely the degrees which the Sun runs through in the Zodiac, the old and the new Calendar, and the cardinal points of the winds.

719 The Zodiac is the circle under which the Planets are perpetually moved, and which cuts the equator at oblique angles in two opposite, equinoctial points, while in two others, likewise diametrically opposite, the solstitial, it touches the tropics: the summer tropic at the beginning of Cancer, the winter one at the beginning of Capricorn; its poles are therefore distant from the poles of the world and of the equator itself by a space of about 23 degrees and 30 minutes (c).

720 It is divided according to its latitude, which according to the Ancients comprises 12 degrees, according to the Moderns 16, nay even 20, into three circles, of which the middle and greatest is called the way of the Sun, the royal road, because the center of the Sun constantly describes this path by its periodic motion; it is likewise called the ecliptic from the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, which occur only in it or near that same line; the remaining two lesser circles, equidistant from the middle one, are called the limits of latitude. According to its longitude it is divided, in the order of the signs, into 12 equal parts, each of which comprises 30 degrees and takes its name from the neighboring sign. The signs of the Zodiac, further, are some called starry, others marked: the former are asterisms, and chiefly figures of animals composed of several stars, so that they symbolically signify the nature of the year through the months; the latter are their characters. The signs to which the characters are usually added are comprised in two verses, by the first of which the northern ones, by the other the southern ones are expressed, namely:

721 The use of the Zodiac is contained in these points: I. As the equator measures the diurnal motion, so the middle of the Zodiac, or ecliptic, measures the periodic motion of the stars, and chiefly of the sun; for the periodic motion is said to be completed when an entire revolution under the ecliptic is completed by the Stars. II. The eclipses of the Sun and Moon take place under this same circle. III. It causes the inequality of days and nights; for neither are the days equal among themselves, nor these to the nights, for the reason that the Sun is carried along in the ecliptic. IV. The constant alternation of the seasons, of which one succeeds another in turn in every yearly course, depends on the position of the ecliptic. V. The ecliptic is the boundary of the latitude of the Stars; for the latitude of a star is the arc of the circle (which is therefore called the circle of latitude, and is a greatest circle) drawn through the poles of the ecliptic and through the centers of the Stars themselves, intercepted between this center and the ecliptic itself. VI. The longitudes of the stars are numbered in it: for the arc of the ecliptic, proceeding from the beginning of Aries in consequentia, or according to the series of the signs, comprehended as far as the circle of latitude, is the longitude of the star.

722 The Meridian is the circle described from the two points of true rising and setting, or those in which, at the time of the equinox, the Sun rises and sets, which again are called cardinal, and passing through the poles both of the world and of the horizon, or the points Zenith and Nadir, and therefore cutting the horizon at right angles; when the Sun reaches it in its ascent, it makes midday. Hence all those points of the Sphere have the same meridian which are not distant from one another except along a straight line drawn from one pole of the world to the other; on the contrary, those places obtain a different one which are distant from east to west, or vice versa: so that the meridian changes while we travel from east toward west, or vice versa, but not at all when we proceed from north to south, or conversely. As many meridians, therefore, are really reckoned as there are vertical points that can be designated from east to west. Yet from one we take the beginning, which is named the first, so that from it the rest come into the count, the reckoning being made from West to East. This is fixed by some in one place, by others in another. The French had fixed it in the last of the Canary Islands, which is called the Island of Ferro, before the more recent Astronomers of that Nation established the first meridian in the Astronomical Observatory of Paris itself, as is customary today. We give the use of the meridian circle briefly.

723 I. It divides the Heaven into two hemispheres, the Eastern and the Western. II. It measures the greatest altitude of the Stars above the horizon, for a star is raised above the horizon until it reaches the Meridian; then, receding from it, it is depressed: it is said to culminate when it reaches it. III. Throughout the whole year it determines the point of midday and of midnight: for it bisects all those circles which the Sun runs through by its diurnal motion. The other offices of the meridian, known to Astronomers, we pass over: for we go through these things not as Astronomers but by the office of Physicists.

724 The Colures are two greatest circles which, while they pass through the poles of the world, divide each other there at right angles, and divide the equator, and likewise the ecliptic, into four by an equal partition. The colure of the equinoxes is drawn through those points of the Zodiac in which, when the Sun is there, the equinoxes occur, namely through the beginnings of Aries and Libra. The colure of the solstices is drawn through the solstitial points (so called because the Sun, on reaching them, seems in some manner to stand still, or to make a station, that is: for some days not to change its declination from the equator at all), namely through the beginning of Cancer and of Capricorn.

725 The use of each colure consists in these points. I. They determine the four cardinal points of the Zodiac, namely those in which, when the Sun is placed there, the turnings of the seasons are brought about: in Aries the vernal, in Capricorn the winter, in Cancer the summer, in Libra the autumnal. Hence three signs correspond to each part of the year: to spring Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. II. As the colure of the equinoxes defines in the Zodiac those two points while the Sun occupies which day is equal to night, so the colure of the solstices marks two others in that same circle, in which, when the Sun is there, now the longest day and the shortest night, now conversely the longest night and the shortest day take place. III. As the colure of the equinoxes divides the signs of the Zodiac into six northern ones: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and as many southern ones: Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces; so the other colure separates the ascending signs, which are contained from the beginning of Capricorn to the first degree of Cancer, from the descending ones, or the rest, etc.

726 The Tropics are two lesser circles in the Sphere, at which, when the Sun reaches them, it does not run out further either to the north or to the south, but turns back to the Equator. They are also usually called Solstitial, because they are drawn through the solstitial points of the Zodiac: hence one is called the tropic of Cancer, the other the tropic of Capricorn. These circles are distant from the equator 23 deg. and about 30 first minutes, from each other 47 deg., from the nearer pole 66 deg. and about 30 first minutes. Their use is distinguished as threefold. I. They bound the path of the Sun. II. They define the longest and the shortest day on an oblique horizon. III. They close the torrid zone and begin the temperate.

These circles, together with the tropics and the equator itself, are commonly called parallels, because all of them stand apart from one another by an equal interval at every point of their circuit. The use of the polar circles is: I. That the stars enclosed within the arctic circle never set for those to whom the sphere is either oblique or parallel, and those comprehended within the antarctic never rise. II. By their interposition the temperate Zones are distinguished from the frigid. All these things will be understood more clearly by inspecting some armillary sphere.

I       oblique and the parallel, according as the position of the equator with respect

to the horizon is different. The sphere is right when the equator stands perpendicularly over the horizon and cuts it at right angles, so that its poles are set in the horizon. Those who dwell under the equator are said to have this position; where, therefore, throughout the whole year the days are equal to the nights. The sphere is oblique in which the equator is inclined to the horizon obliquely, or at unequal angles. Those enjoy this whose latitude, or distance from the equator toward one or the other pole computed on the meridian of the place, does not reach 90 degrees, that is: all those who dwell between the equator and the poles; for them, therefore, the days are unequal to the nights.

729 The sphere, finally, is called parallel in which the equator keeps parallelism with the horizon. This position of the sphere is had by those whose vertex coincides with one of the poles of the world, and so whose latitude equals 90 deg., or by those who live under the poles: for those who dwell under it there is in the yearly course only one day and one night, each bounded by as great an interval of time as the Sun takes in traversing six figures of the Zodiac; for since their horizon and the equator coincide, six signs of the Zodiac stand perpetually above the horizon, and as many lie hidden below it; for that reason it is necessary that the Sun shine upon them above the horizon for as long a time as is demanded for it to run through six signs of the

Zodiac, and again lie hidden below the horizon for as great an interval of time as is required for it to be moved through as many lower signs, that is, the space of 6

months.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

> » anno 16:0 perífpe&tum eft. ,, Hactenüs ille. ( Fig LXX. oculis fubjicit Syftema Copernicanum ) ,

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

> (e) Praele&t. Theolog. Tom. 1. Praelect. 1, de Opificio mundi P?g. 130 edit. Venet, Ann, 1742.

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. Ptolemaic and the Tychonic. We show this first in general. For the hypothesis of Copernicus is not opposed to Physics and Astronomy as the Ptolemaic system is. For who could understand, in the latter, how the primum mobile carries away all the lower spheres from east to west, while these nevertheless enjoy that motion in such a way that, by a contrary reckoning, they at the same time advance daily from west to east according to the series of the signs under the Zodiac? For if the surfaces by which these spheres touch one another, namely the convex surface of the lower and the concave of the upper, are smooth, it will come about that the upper imparts no motion to the lower sphere, and so the former can revolve without carrying the latter along with it; but if they are made rough, so that their projecting parts fit into one another, it is clearly evident that one and the same motion will be effected both of the upper and of the lower spheres, as Gassendi rightly argues (f).

739 The phenomena clearly show that the Ptolemaic system agrees very little with Astronomical observations. For it has been found that Mercury and Venus are seen by us from the earth now at the sides of the Sun, now above it. But in this hypothesis they ought always to appear below the Sun and nearer to us. Not to speak of the awkward position of the fixed stars, since they are all set fixed in one surface, whereas it is manifest among Astronomers that they are located in different planes, some more remote than others.

740 Second: the Copernican hypothesis is more orderly, and weaves together the position and disposition of the celestial bodies in a neater series; for in it none of the primary Planets cuts the orbit (g) of another, as in the system of Tycho; then the revolutions of all the Planets are performed about the same center, namely the Sun, contrary to what happens in the Tychonic. Moreover, the hypothesis of Copernicus, by attributing motion to the earth while meanwhile the Sun and the fixed stars stand in their places, explains the phenomena of the Heaven much more simply and from fewer principles than
