742 The diurnal motion, indeed, by which the earth itself is turned from west to east, brings it about that the Sun, the Planets themselves and the fixed Stars seem to us to revolve from east to west; hence the alternation of day and night follows; for, as all who know the nature of motion are forced to admit, since all things which appear to us to be moved in place are perceived in this way because either they themselves really change their place, or the spectator proceeds in the opposite direction while those bodies are unmoved, according to that line of Virgil (i):

But it will be enough to have hinted at these things.

744 The Tychonians frame their chief argument against the Copernican hypothesis from the Sacred Scriptures. They contend, namely, that the doctrine of Copernicus is opposed to their words, inasmuch as these manifestly teach that the Sun moves, but that the earth stands still. Thus Genesis 19: The sun was risen upon the earth. Psalm 92: He hath established the world which shall not be moved. Ecclesiastes ch. 1: But the earth standeth for ever. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place; and Josue ch. 10 (when the Leader of the Jews commanded that the Sun should not move over against Gabaon): So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down the space of one day. Isaias ch. 38: And the sun returned ten lines by the degrees by which it was gone down. And from these very many conclude that the Copernican system, which asserts the motion of the earth and the rest of the Sun, seems to be opposed to the authority of the Holy Scriptures.

(i) Aeneid, bk. III, v. 72. [p. 232] and according to appearance. They answer that Divine Scripture tempers itself to the capacity of the common people. The reason they give for asserting this is that “God (as the distinguished Muratori says (k)), speaking through his Scriptures, did not have this aim, to feed men’s vain curiosity about things not necessary to know, about the elements of the world and about bodies, but to hand down things truly useful for attaining eternal happiness. For He does not speak in the learned words of human wisdom, but lowers Himself to the use of those expressions which, although they are recognized as less accurate and as improper when weighed in the balance of human wisdom, yet set forth some useful and salutary truth more conveniently to an unlearned people.” For the rest, they profess that they do not wish to depart from the common ways of speaking, and that they will speak in accommodation to what appears by the testimony of the senses: The Sun rises; it is raised to the point of midday; it declines toward the West, etc.

746 The distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry too, after adducing the testimonies of Sacred Letters cited above, rises up thus against the adversary of the Copernican hypothesis (l): “Do you wield the censor’s rod on account of those few little words of Scripture? Why not rather, if you are a Theologian, until the Church condemns the ingenious System, bend the words of Scripture cited to a convenient sense? So that those words which are paraded in favor of the immobile stability of the earth may be understood only of firmness, consistency and duration, in no way excluding local motion: for Divine Wisdom is also said to have established the Heavens, or the sky above, Prov. 8, though motion according to Ptolemy’s System is in no way at odds with that firmness of the heavens: while those which are brought forward from Sacred Letters in favor of the mobility of the Sun were said not according to the truth of the thing, but according to the opinion of the common people and the common manner of speaking, so that the Sacred Writers might accommodate themselves to the understanding of an unlearned people: which we have made manifest by so many other examples; and in this very one which is especially objected, about Josue, it is most certain, namely that it was said according to the opinion of the common people, if the whole narration of the deed is attended to more diligently. Move not, O sun, says Josue, toward Gabaon: and yet, since the earth is a small mass in comparison with the Sun, and Gabaon on that same globe of the earth is as a most minute point, what, I ask, is the Sun commanded, that it should not move toward Gabaon? Could the huge globe of the Sun so correspond to this point as either to move or to stand still over against it? Josue therefore alluded to the common judgment of the eyes, for to our eyes the Sun appears as a disk to be measured by two palms at most, running over a small space of the sky.

common people: that that place of the heavens seems to them the middle which is equally distant from the East and the West. The narration is finally closed with these words: there was not before nor after so long a day. Has then no longer day ever shone in the whole world? But it is well ascertained by those who travel through the regions situated under either Pole that the Sun shines longer there and that longer days occur: nay, it is most certain that this very thing is proved by a demonstrative and most evident reasoning by those skilled in Astronomical Science. The narration, therefore, was accommodated to the Jewish people, to whom the effects of the Sun in the polar regions were unknown.

## APPENDIX

What is to be thought of the influence of the Stars?

ublicly debated is the question whether the stars concur in producing the 750

P        effects observed on the earth, or, as it is commonly put, whether they influ‐

ence sublunary things. The Sun chiefly, and the Moon, seem to some to share a communion of effluvia with our earth: an argument which they extend from these two Stars to the rest; nor are they content to say that the stars act on sublunary things through heat and light, but they think that various other influences

> [p. 234]

Gg 2 [p. 234] are exerted upon the earth, while they attribute different specific properties to the Stars: that the Moon, being exceedingly moist, excites the humors on the earth; that Saturn is cold; Mars dry and hot, etc.; so that, accordingly, the rising of some brings on rain, that of others induces drought, etc. It is not our pleasure to pursue these and more things of the kind any further: we shall set forth our view of the influence of the Stars in brief. Wherefore the conclusion follows.

> 2134. ELEM. REC. PHILOSOPH. P. IV.

751 Apart from the action of light we acknowledge no other influence of the stars upon the earth: except, however, the Sun, which by its heat, sensible enough, warms our earth, and also the Moon, which, if not by heat or cold, yet certainly by its weight upon the atmosphere beneath it, can press upon our globe variously according to its varying position. For, in the first place, certain substantial effluvia, moist, dry, etc., cannot be transmitted from the stars to the earth; for what cause can be adduced by which such effluvia should be propelled through the longest spaces beyond the atmosphere of their star, which extends only some miles? Certainly about terrestrial effluvia all agree that they by no means run out beyond the atmosphere into the region of the Moon: then, even if effluvia were thrust out, what can be imagined that would direct them to our earth rather than to some other space and celestial body? Finally, if the Moon, in which our adversaries place the greatest force, scattered its effluvia spherically, then, since these diverge from one another the more, the further they recede from the lunar body, and at so great a distance as the Moon has from the earth can and must be spread very far apart, those effects which are attributed to the influence of the moon can by no means be produced by so stingy and meager a dew of effluvia.

752 It is shown, secondly. The action of light can be the cause of all the effects; for light consists in the rectilinear pressure of the ethereal substance, propagated all the way to us. Therefore a different motion of the smallest particles can be excited, namely a vehement, varied and perturbed one; and once this motion is posited, one effect follows, and when it ceases, again another, without any need to have recourse, in order to explain the moisture of the nights, to I know not what outflowings of the Moon. Wherefore, when we see the whole of nature cherished and propagated, plants growing up, grain turning yellow, fruits ripening, in a word, generations, alterations and augmentations promoted; when we experience the seasons of the year recurring with a fixed regulation, and more particular changes of the air, often very diverse, taking place according to the concurrence of other causes, it is necessary that we attribute these things to the action of the Sun; but to the Sun acting in no other way than by its light and the heat consequent upon it.

Philosopher, both because it is reproved by the Sacred Scriptures, condemned by the Councils of Braga and Toledo, censured by the Fathers, and forbidden by the authority of the Supreme Pontiffs and by the canon and civil laws, and because it is hissed off with laughter by all the wise. Certainly that division of the

Heaven into 12 houses, on which the horoscope is founded, or the figure of the celestial configuration that exists at the moment of birth, is a fiction. Moreover, neither do the same fates befall all who are born under the same star, as is plain from the example of the twins Esau and Jacob, who had the most different propensity and fortune; nor do those who experience similar fates enjoy the same horoscope, as is manifest: since many perish together by shipwreck, fire, plague, or battle, although they were brought into the light at the most different times. Not to mention that the whole supposition of this art, taken from the septenary number of the planets and from the situation of the celestial houses, is false. The first is shown by the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn, indeed even by the single one of Venus; the second, because the constellations to which they gave the name of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, in whose order they hold that their

12 houses are found in the Heaven, have long since already receded 30 degrees from their original place. But there is no leisure to dwell on trifles.

Aeroscopic astrology, or that which foretells storms and changes of the air from the stars, is to be rejected by the Philosopher: for this art is confirmed neither by any reason nor by experience; for soothsayers of this kind posit certain properties in the planets: Saturn cold and dry, Venus a hot and moist planet, etc., which suppositions are not philosophical conjectures but fabulous ones; for why should one be hot, another moist, when all are opaque masses not much unlike our earth? By experience they cannot establish their art; [p. 236] for this rests on frequently repeated observation, whereas the astrologers neither have nor can have an observation in which, from a similar position of the stars, a similar event has followed in sublunary things: since it is certain from the astronomers that the same aspect of the same stars does not return within many millions of years; and even if such a position had returned, it would have been unknown, as regards all the stars, to those unskilled men, since until the past century they were ignorant of the secondary planets.

756 Nor do predictions that sometimes come true do anything for a presumption of truth; for who is there, says Cicero, who, hurling darts all day long, does not sometimes hit the mark? Besides the fact that the far more numerous false ones carry very great weight toward detracting from the astrologers’ credit, there are innumerable examples of this. Thus in the year 1524, on account of great conjunctions of the planets in Aquarius, entire and certain deluges were predicted, yet the year was most serene; in the year 1586, winds and storms on account of conjunctions of all the planets, although the whole year was passed in calm. Certainly the astrologers themselves do not agree among themselves in their predictions: hence a certain Frenchman bought himself so many calendars that for each single day he could choose one conformable to the heavens, whereby it came about that he said his calendar was conformable to the heavens the whole year round; and although these prophecies are sometimes inserted in calendars, it is by no means proved that this is done by the counsel of the wise, or that credence is given by them to these follies, since one will hardly find in the whole world a learned astronomer who does not indignantly reject this simplicity, unworthy of a learned man, as Amort says. stones, which are consumed by fire in a few hours; and when this happens, it ought to seem no wonder at all if the moisture of the air reduces these stones, just as it does lime, to powder. Similarly, he continues, it is falsely thought that the bones of animals are full of marrow while the Moon waxes and empty while it wanes; for when he had observed this for more than 25 years, he always found some bones full of marrow and others empty, both while the Moon was waxing and while it was waning.

> DISSERTATIO II. —^De Terra elementari. e /^— A CAPUT L

759 Wherefore another cause is to be assigned: it is most likely that the bones of certain animals are empty of marrow either because the animals have lacked nourishment or because they have been worn out by labor. Falsely too, and wholly against experience, has it been believed that the Moon, according to her various phases, fills out or thins lobsters, oysters, etc. If the bodies of fish sometimes seem diminished, this happens either from a lack of nourishment, or because they are too much agitated, the waves being stirred up by a storm, or even by their own exertion; which will seem most likely to those who know that the fish caught in the Strait of Calais, where the water is most agitated, are generally less full than those caught near

> De Natura "Terrae.

Boulogne, where the sea rests somewhat more tranquil. Finally, the other effects are to be attributed not to a moist influence of the Moon, but to the constitution of the atmosphere present at the time, filled, namely, either with excessive moisture or with other noxious effluvia.

difficulty by the force of fire, and its particles cannot be blown off into the air, they must be coarser; and since, united together, they make a consistent and fixed mass and shut off the passage of light, they are in all likelihood of an irregular figure, such as to be variously entangled with one another and to form winding passages. Finally, since the earth is held to be, as it were, the basis and foundation of the other miscible bodies, and since the hardness, fixity, solidity, and gravity of bodies is derived in great part from the earth, it is fitting that its particles be not only coarser and more entangled with one another, but also less apt for motion.

> "propterea maxime propria illorum corpufculorum videatur, quae ad aridum, iners, fixumque conflituendum corpus, funt à natura deítinata. De hoc veró nos nihil certi conftituimus.

44.]. Gassendi, with the Epicureans, would have it made up, like the other firm and dry bodies, of little rings and hooked atoms mutually adhering to one another. Fr. Regnault asserts that the particles of earth are branching, such as do not transmit light and make a consistent mass. The distinguished da Brescia says that we cannot divine with certainty of what figure the primitive corpuscles of earth are. It is probable, he then adds, that the primitive particles are affected with a cubic figure: since this, as Plato says, possesses the firmest and safest bases, and therefore seems most proper to those corpuscles which are destined by nature to constitute a dry, inert, and fixed body. On this, however, we determine nothing certain.

We here contemplate the Earth as a mundane body, which is usually called the orb, or the terraqueous globe. The Earth, then, is a mundane body compacted of earth and water, with a fiery fluid interspersed here and there, into a vast mass, surrounded on every side by air, the common habitation of men and of brutes. Under the name of earth there comes here first of all the heap of solid and coarser bodies of various kinds: sand, clay, fat earths of diverse colors, stones, salts, etc.: a heap which is found in the Earth, [p. 239] as no one, unless he were ignorant both of history and of narratives, would deny. By water is understood that fluid and moist substance which God, Best and Greatest, in the first creation separated from the solid and dry, and gathered into the sea, which occupies a great part of the terrestrial surface.

764 That fire is diffused through the interior parts of the earth is plain, both from the fact that it is contained in mixed bodies, and from hot springs, the heat of mines, various exhalations, and fire-vomiting mountains. That the body of the Earth is compacted into a vast mass, no one is unaware; and it has its compaction and firmness from the cause of gravity, by which, namely, its parts are compressed and driven together on every side. But this is more difficult to resolve: into what figure this mass has been compacted: whether, namely, it holds a spherical one? Or a spheroidal one; and this, whether depressed at the poles and raised at the equator, or, on the contrary, rising at the poles and sinking at the equator.

765 Physicists endeavor to demonstrate that the Earth is spherical as regards sense, and physically. First, from the very eclipses of the Moon; for she suffers an eclipse because she enters the shadow of the Earth, and divides it just as if she were a plane parallel to the base of that shadow: since, namely, the Moon revolves around the Earth. But the shadow of the earth in all the lunar eclipses observed hitherto through so many centuries has always appeared round: therefore. Secondly, because all appearances, celestial as well as terrestrial, are explained most aptly and without error under a spherical figure of the Earth, as is plain in artificial globes and spheres. Thirdly, because those who travel see the summits of mountains and the tops of towers sooner than their bases, and that equally in every direction. We have said that the Earth is round in the physical sense, not the mathematical. Very high mountains in no way hinder its figure from being spherical as regards sense, for the earth, as Seneca says, is to the mountains as a huge ball to a hair. Nor does the flatness of the plains stand in the way, when the earth seems to us to stretch out into a plane: for this comes partly from its magnitude, partly from the visible horizon, which, relative to the whole globe, is a very small part and has no sensible curvature.

For besides the fact that the arguments set out above establish a round figure for the Earth in the physical sense, it is certain that neither of these opinions is greatly opposed to the physical and sensible roundness of the Earth.

768 Nor does the argument for the first opinion, taken from the daily motion of the Earth, prove anything; from this revolution the patrons of this hypothesis think it follows that the parts, by a greater centrifugal force under the equator than toward the poles, recede farther from the axis of the Earth, and so are more elevated under the equator than under the poles, and form the spheroidal mass of the Earth. It does not, I say, prove anything: for, granting the motion of the Earth about its axis, it does not evidently follow that the parts about the equator swell out and are compressed toward the poles: for the mass of the Earth is not soft but firmly compacted, nor does it seem conformable to experience that a sphere revolved about its axis should be changed into a spheroid compressed at the poles of the revolution, with whatever speed it be turned.

769 As regards the situation of the Earth, the common opinion is that it is placed in the very center of the universe, at least as regards sense. For although, by the Copernican hypothesis, the Sun is set in the center of the universe and the Earth is turned in the great orb around the Sun, yet in the judgment of the astronomers the semidiameter of the great orb, if it is compared with the semidiameter of the starry heaven, as it were vanishes, and brings it about that the Earth is distant from the center of the universe by no sensible interval.

770 The reasons, moreover, that establish this situation of the Earth are these. The first, because at either equinox the time during which the Sun stays above the horizon exactly equals the time during which it stays below the horizon. The second, because to us who exist on the surface of the Earth, whatever region at last we may inhabit, the stars always appear of the same magnitude, whether at their rising, or at their setting, or in the middle of the heaven, provided there are absent vapors, mists, and exhalations, which impede the sight and change the figure of bodies. The third, because in whatever part of the earth, setting aside the hindrances of mountains and valleys, we always see half of the heaven: thus of the 12 signs of the Zodiac, 6 are perpetually seen above the horizon, and of stars diametrically opposite, such as are, more or less, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion, when one rises on the eastern horizon, the other sets on the western.

## CHAPTER III

> De nonnullis corporibus terreftribus, ac primum de petrificationibus.

On Certain Terrestrial Bodies, and First on Petrifications.

cannot fail to make mention of a certain kind of terrestrial bodies, 772

I       namely of shells, oysters, and other testaceous bodies, which occur

among the strata of certain mountains. On their origin the opinion of physicists is threefold. Woodward derives this phenomenon from the universal deluge, namely: when all the lands were covered by the waters, then indeed rocks, marbles, metals, all bodies were divided into minute particles and molecules; thus divided, they were carried confusedly hither and thither by that force of the waters, but toward the end these bodies, immersed in the water, were precipitated according to the laws of gravity: hence it came about that those marine testaceous shells, being somewhat heavier, sought the part that belongs to rocks, stones, and the like, among which they are found even today for this very reason. The second hypothesis, which Leibniz recently defended, asserts that the sea was once in all those places in which shells and oysters are found, but that the sea itself has at present receded from those places, leaving the bodies there.

773 The third holds, with Lazzaro Moro, that testaceous bodies are found among the strata of mountains because the mountains themselves, together with those bodies, were once cast up from the bottom of the sea by the action of subterranean fire. It is not my pleasure at present to sift and weigh these hypotheses, which demand a fuller discussion. It will be enough to hint at this one thing: that there is not one and the same cause and origin, universally, of the oysters and testaceous bodies of this kind found in mountains and in more prominent places. It does not seem, indeed, to stray from likelihood that those marine spoils which the investigators of Nature find here and there on the surfaces of mountains, or at no great depth,

774 But those which are not rarely discovered in deeper caverns were, I think, deposited there by earthquakes, often violent ones: for in this way, the earth being shaken, the mountains burst asunder, and swallowed up, the spoils of animals could be buried together, and in the course of a long time be converted into stones, that is, be petrified. But if they are of the kind of marine spoils, these were carried there, together with a part of the sea, through subterranean passages made and hollowed out in these motions of the earth, where the water, having dried away in the length of time, and having been diffused into the strata of the earth or driven off into vapors, deposited spoils of this kind.

shepherd, who is said to have first discovered it on Mount Ida, when the iron tip of his staff adhered to a stone of this kind, which is now called a magnet. It is a stone not unlike iron, showing a blackish color, heavy, pregnant with iron; since indeed, when subjected to fire, it exudes steel, and moreover it is dug out of iron mines. Its force, which is called magnetic and is still wrapped in many difficulties, is reduced chiefly to three heads: to its direction, to the attraction of a magnet or of iron, and to the communication of its virtue. The directive force consists in this, that a magnet suspended in the air sets itself toward the meridian of the place and turns its southern pole toward the northern pole of the Earth, as also happens in the magnetic needle. However, this direction toward the pole is not constant everywhere; for now by more, now by fewer degrees, according to the diversity of regions, more or less, now hither now thither (that is, now toward the east, [p. 243] now toward the west) the nautical needles decline; indeed, after a notable time they sometimes change their direction in the same place; and this affection is called declination.

777 To this also pertains another affection of the same, which is called inclination, various indeed, but constant, by virtue of which a magnet, or a magnetic needle freely suspended in equilibrium, preponderates toward one side and is inclined, by this law: that the inclination is more or less notable according as the tract of the earth is more remote from or nearer to the equator; for under it a perfect equilibrium is had. The attractive force is that by which a magnet draws to itself either another magnet or iron; with this difference, however, that a magnet snatches iron to itself by either of its sides, but draws a magnet to itself by one side and repels it by the other. Finally, the force communicative of itself is that by which it imbues steel or iron with the same virtue in which it is itself strong: namely, the directive and the attractive. These things set out, we inquire into the cause of these phenomena: in which altogether obscure matter we shall lay down whatever may have an appearance of likelihood and may in some fashion expound the said effects to the understanding. Before we carry this out, a preliminary hypothesis is laid down.

779 This is explained, 1: because iron implements acquire a magnetic force from mere contact and application to the earth: especially if they have stood erect upon the earth for a rather long time. So too iron rods which have remained a long time, especially in the line of the meridian plane, acquire a conversive force toward the pole. Secondly, because magnetic needles suspended by a thread are inclined toward the globe of the earth just as they are observed to be inclined toward a magnet.

From the magnetism of the terraqueous globe it is concluded that certain effluvia, having gone out from one pole of the Earth, travel around the Earth toward its other pole, and there, entering into it again, go out through the other pole of the world; and thus a perpetual circulation of effluvia of this kind is set up in the Earth, not otherwise than a perpetual circulation of subterranean water, together with the terrestrial surface, is said to be carried on from pole to pole: although the cause by which it comes about that the fluid bursting forth from the bowels of the earth is borne from one pole toward the other still escapes the industry and intelligence of physicists, and must be deduced elsewhere, at the proper time, from mechanical principles. Moreover, these effluvia are indeed communicated also to other bodies existing in this globe, but chiefly to those which are most earthy, such as the magnet and iron, in which an apt disposition of the particles and pores offers itself both for receiving and for emitting them.

Then the very disposition of the particles of the magnet can prove this, since they are inclined more to one side than to the other, and are so disposed that they can afford ingress through one side but not, in turn, egress; that such a disposition of the parts can come about is plain from this, that while the magnet was being formed in its mine, the magnetic matter, crossing the earth from one pole to the other along lines parallel to the axis and returning in a perpetual circuit, could fit the passages of the magnet in such a way as to press down their interior little hairs toward that side to which it was carried.

783 The distinguished Helvétius holds, with Mr. Du Fay, that the pores of magnets are furnished within with little hairs, and that these are so laid down and bent that their points incline toward the north poles of the magnets. Those little hairs, therefore, do not delay the motion of the magnetic matter from the pole of ingress, that is, the one which the effluvia enter, to the pole of egress, that is, the one through which they burst out, since they are bent toward that side; but they resist the return of the same matter through the same passages, since they are inclined toward the opposite side with the greatest difficulty, or not at all. These things laid down, let the conclusion be:

The directive force of the magnet is, namely, that by which the magnet turns itself toward each pole of the world. But this is fittingly traced [p. 245] to the effluxes set forth in the said manner; for these, moving thereafter through the same passages of the magnet which they had made for themselves in the mine, accordingly set the magnet, by the rule of their own motion, along lines parallel to the axis of the earth, as is gathered from what was said a little before. Indeed, since it is plain that no body can perpetually incline toward its due point except by the contact of another body driven toward the same point, as Helvétius rightly says, it is evident that there are fluids spread closely around the Earth which are driven, in the direction of their motion, from the southern pole toward the northern.

785 Certainly this is shown manifestly also from the fact that if an iron needle, not yet imbued with magnetic force, is placed on a pivot in a nautical box, it will be seen in equilibrium, parallel to the horizon; but when the needle has been rubbed on a magnet and has obtained the directive force, then in northern places the part of the needle directed toward the north is depressed somewhat below the horizon, so that a little ball of wax must be added to the southern point of the needle to restore the equilibrium. At the Equator, or at an equal distance from either pole, the needle is not depressed at all. Once the Equator is crossed toward the south, the northern part of the point is raised and the southern is depressed. All of which certainly confirm, not in vain, the efflux and the influx, and the circulation, of the effluvia around the surface of the Earth.

Hypothesis. For it is certain that the parts of the terrestrial globe are very heterogeneous, and that various veins of iron occur here and there; indeed, in the same place not only the mountains, but also the rocks and the other parts lying hid under the earth or the sea, are now more copiously endowed with magnetic veins, now, whether because a certain tract has been shaken by a motion of the earth and the situation of its parts changed, or by excavations, or in some other way, are sparsely interspersed with veins of this kind. What of the fact that in the bowels of the lands magnets in some places lie hidden deep under the earth, and elsewhere cling in the summits, the bowels, and the roots of mountains; that the said veins of iron are frequently altered, diminished, and twisted, either by earthquakes, or by subterranean fires, or by floods of subterranean waters, or by diggers; and indeed that the air itself and the corpuscles diffused in it perhaps drive the magnetic effluvia somewhat out of their straight motion?

787 Therefore from these causes a varied declination of the same needle and magnet can occur even in the same place, so that in places not far distant from each other it is very notable, and in one it inclines toward the East, in another toward the West. In confirmation of this there serves the experiment reported by

Kircher and Jansonius: namely, that at Naples, after the notable conflagration of

Mount Vesuvius, a notable change of the magnetic declination was continually observed.

The phenomenon of inclination is also explained: for, magnetic effluvia being supposed to burst forth from the earth, it is no wonder that the needle inclines toward the terrestrial globe along that part along which the stronger and more copious effluvia flow out, namely in the northern parts along one of its parts, in the southern along the other, and this the more, the nearer the regions are to the north or to the south pole. Nor is it any wonder that the needle under the Equator, where, namely, neither effluvia prevail and the place stands off from the poles by an equal interval, keeps a perfect equilibrium, free of all inclination.

From these principles it is illustrated why the magnet, outside the mine, on the surface of the Earth, has a situation contrary to the situation which it held in the mine; for if the magnetic outflows are conceived to enter through the southern pole of the earth, they must also enter the southern pole of the magnet turned toward the same part of the earth while it is still in the mine: but since the effluvia flowing from south to north along lines parallel to the axis in the interior of the earth return on its surface from the northern pole to the southern, the magnet, drawn out of the earth, must be disposed in a contrary situation for receiving those outflows, and its southern pole must be turned toward the northern pole of the Earth, whence the effluvia are supposed to burst out.

The attractive force of the magnet is derived not from the impulse of air coming in behind, but from the motion of the atmosphere surrounding the magnet, in all likelihood by the same mechanical manner of acting as the approach of homogeneous bodies. The first part is plain. In a vacuum both the attraction of iron to the magnet and its adhesion take place: indeed, iron is seized more quickly by the magnet when the receiver has been exhausted.

Therefore the attractive force cannot be traced to the action of the air. Since into the place of the air there succeeds a stronger body (namely, the effluvia excluding the air).

791 The second part is demonstrated. To explain the attractive force of the magnet it is necessary that a reason be given why poles of the same name, whether one southern and the other southern, or two northern, repel each other [p. 247] not only in the magnet but also in the magnetic needle; then why poles not of the same name, namely one southern and the other northern, approach each other; and finally why iron is snatched by a magnet from either side. But these things are conveniently explained by the force of the magnetic atmosphere. For if, as we laid down above [§. 781 ff.], the internal configuration of magnets and the structure of their pores is such that the smallest molecules, laid down and bent like little hairs, incline with their tips toward one pole of the magnetic body, e.g. the northern, it will come about, this contexture of the parts being supposed, that the fluid running into the southern pole can freely pervade it and be carried flowingly over the surface of the little hairs, no force being brought upon them; whereas the parts of the subtler fluid that have slipped into the northern pole will bring force upon the tips which occupy and line the paths of the little hairs. Wherefore, if one magnet is placed toward another in such a way that the northern pole of the former faces the southern pole of the latter, then, since the atmospheric fluid of the one is driven in the direction which the inflection of the little hairs has in the other, the most subtle parts of the fluid will pass along the very surface of the little hairs with no force and impression, or the least, made upon them.

Atqui hsec commode explicantur per vim atmolphaerae maguetie cae. 792 But when those poles of the magnets are joined from which the subtler torrent of atmosphere bursts forth, then indeed the molecules of this fluid flowing out of the pole of the one will be unable to enter the pores of the like pole in the other magnet, since the points of the little hairs are stretched out and so resist: hence, force being brought upon these paths, they will strive to repel the magnet into which they rush. But if those poles of the magnets into each of which the surrounding fluid breaks in are placed not far from each other, then, besides the fact that the directions of the magnetic fluid oppose each other, repulsion must follow from this, that the twin atmospheres do not coalesce into one in such a way that all the other fluid interposed is removed and so an approach follows; and although an entrance lies open to the effluvia through each of these poles, yet because each is supposed to be endowed with such a habit of pores that only the magnetic fluid can enter through them, the commingling of the atmospheres and their conjunction, in a manner, into one vortex (other heterogeneous fluids being excluded) is for that reason impeded: hence it will come about that the magnets do not approach each other, but are repelled by the opposite directions of the effluvia on either side. The same is to be thought of the magnetic needle.

794 The assertion is confirmed by an exposition of the phenomena; and first a reason is given why, besides iron or steel, no other bodies are drawn by the magnet: namely, because such is the disposition of the pores in iron, and the configuration of its parts, as in a body homogeneous with the magnet, that the effluvia penetrate it more easily than the other bodies: hence, while the torrent of effluvia crosses the pores of the iron in greater abundance, the resistance in the intermediate space is diminished, and, this being removed, these bodies are joined by the forces of the pressing fluid.

795 From this likewise the reason is drawn why a magnet, if it is clothed with steel or iron, or, as they say, armed, with well-polished steel plates placed around it, attracts far more strongly and holds fast what it has attracted: for the effluvia seem to flow more easily through steel than through air, and therefore a more abundant supply of them then bursts into the iron that is to be attracted, which before wandered more freely around the sides of the magnet and were less collected. 797 I say thirdly: The magnetic force communicated to iron or steel is to be derived from magnetic outflows. For magnetic force is communicated to iron or steel when these bodies are rubbed on, or applied to, the pole of a magnet or of its armature; and it consists in this, that the iron or steel directs itself toward the poles of the world and attracts other iron. But this force without doubt proceeds from magnetic outflows; for while a nautical needle is rubbed on the pole of a magnet or of its armature, those outflows rush into the needle and incline its little fibers, or hairs, to one side, according as the iron has been drawn along the magnet, so that they form for themselves two poles in the iron or the needle, one of ingress and the other of egress, not otherwise than they are in the magnet itself; which gains likelihood from the fact that these pores are interchanged by drawing the magnet in the contrary direction: therefore.

798 That this can come about by the help of effluvia is fittingly shown; first of all from the fact that the little fibers of iron are softer and more flexible than those of the magnet, as the diversity of their texture suggests. Then this very thing is explained by the analogy of mercury entering into a rod of gold; for it is understood just as easily that the mineral effluvium of the magnet enters into iron and confers magnetism on it, as that the effluvium of mercury enters into gold and whitens it. What of the fact that, just as the mercury imbibed by gold is separated from it by fire, so the magnetic force is said to be removed from magnetic iron by fire?

Certainly for no other reason is the nautical box of no use in the places nearest the pole than because the magnetic outflows, bursting from the pole almost perpendicularly, direct the needle itself no more to one side than to another; which the Dutch report that they experienced on their voyage.

> I: 2 . DI$S4

800 Nor is a similar gyration around the magnet itself fictitious; for if we ascribe an atmosphere to all other bodies, we should surely deny it preposterously to the magnet. However, the effluvia are driven to perpetual motion by a most subtle universal fluid; but by what mechanism this is accomplished remains to be taught; and toward this circuit around the magnet they are, as it were, determined by the very disposition of the pores and parts in the magnet, which are apter for receiving them than any other bodies whatever, and indeed on one side better accommodated for letting them in, on the other for emitting them. Both points are suggested and expounded by the analogy of the juices in plants, which insinuate themselves through fibers and do not return through the same, and by their perennial circulation through little canals. Many more things about the magnet are handed down by Kircher, Gaspar Schott, Lana Terzi, Wolff,

Musschenbroek, and many others.

he nature of water is made by Gassendi, with the Epicureans, to consist 801

Tin smooth and round particles, which are slippery and separated by frequent little voids. Others claim that the atoms of water are cubic, because water can scarcely be compressed. Descartes thinks they are oblong and rounded.

> * aquae atomos eíÍe praetendunt, eoquod aqua vix. comprimi po'sit. Carteftus oblongas effe, & téretes exiítimat.

802 I say: Water is more probably a substance consisting of parts that are oblong, rounded, flexible, slippery, voluble, little entangled with one another, and oval, that is, endowed with an egg-shaped figure.

> 8o2 Dico: Aqua verofimilius eft lubftantia partibus oblongis; teretibus, fexilibus, lubricis, voluoilibus, fioi minus implexis, ac-que ovalibus, five ovata figurá donatis, con(tins,

803 For, this nature of water being supposed, the phenomena and all the properties belonging to water can be fittingly accounted for. Thus fluidity is deduced from slipperiness and volubility; from which likewise is derived the force of dissolving bodies that cohere more loosely. The force of moistening flows from flexibility and from the oblong and rounded figure; for thus the particles easily insinuate themselves into the little pores of bodies, roll around the more prominent parts on their surface, and adhere to them. The force of washing off dirt is also understood from these things; and this washing is done more conveniently when the body to be washed is prepared with a viscous matter, such as soap: for since dirt is generally fatty, it adheres more easily to the viscous matter, and then the water purges away the dirt together with the viscous matter.

> $03 Etenim hac pofità naturá aquae, phaenomena, omneíque pro« . prietates; aquae competentes expediri congrue poffunt. Sic fluidiras — deducitur ex lubricitate, & volubilitates ex qua pariter vis fole vendi corpora lax:us cohaerentia derivatur, Vis humectandi ex fle»

804 The force of lubricating and of flowing off depends on smoothness and on the rounded figure, on account of which water runs off easily from polished and clean bodies, such as glass, or from fatty ones, as happens with the feathers of birds. Quick and swift evaporation is derived from particles little entangled. Gravity, from density, etc.; from which also arises its aptitude for passing into ice, beyond other liquors which are composed of finer particles: hence too it is that water is rarefied in a wonderful manner, but can scarcely be compressed, since its parts, touching one another immediately and rolled over one another, cannot be joined more closely. Finally, the lack of odor as well as of taste in water proceeds from its flexibility and volubility; for flexible and voluble particles, or molecules, run over the organ of taste and of smell with a gentle motion, and do not strike its papillae and fibrils with any edge. The reason of the other properties too will easily be deduced from that structure and conformation of the parts.

In order to constitute the nature of water, insofar as it is a fluid substance, it is first of all required, as is clear (from what was said on fluidity), that its parts be divided and dissociated from one another and touch one another in few planes. The distinguished Helvétius judges that an oval figure of the aqueous molecules agrees better with all the effects which they produce; for these, he says, “will not touch one another except along the smallest surfaces, and accordingly they can be carried flowingly by the least force; and yet they will congeal into ice, because the interstices placed between them are smaller than those which would be given if the parts of water enjoyed a spherical figure. Moreover, the parts of water endowed with this figure can accomplish the dissolution of bodies more easily, because their extremities are finer than their middle part.

The origin of springs and rivers is what we chiefly weigh here, and on it there is a twofold opinion. Of the Moderns, some trace their origin from the sea, others from rains and melted snows. The first teach that the waters of the sea are carried through subterranean passages into the mountains and the other places in which the sources of springs are found, and that, having deposited in them their saltness and bitterness, they then leap forth through hidden passages and fissures. The latter contend that the part of the waters which falls down in rains and is drunk in by the earth penetrates through the fissures and chinks of rocks and of mountains, is received and collected in certain cavities of them and in reservoirs, from which the waters then flow down little by little through certain narrow outlets and give origin to springs, from which rivers are derived. What is to be thought in this controversy our conclusion establishes.

807 Springs and rivers arise not from the sea, by a hidden route penetrating the earth and thence welling out, as if by a road made for it, but from rains, melted snows, and vapors. The first part is proved. If springs arose from the sea, the sea waters would have to deposit their saltness and bitterness, and to ascend, as it were of their own accord, to that height above the mountains at which [p. 252] we observe springs welling forth. But neither seems capable of being maintained; for in this way the sea water would lose its saltness and bitterness insofar as it deposited, or left behind, its salty and bitter particles in those windings which the adversaries posit; but this cannot happen: for one of two things must follow: either that at length, in the course of time, those ways and passages are obstructed by the adhering salt, or this other, that the salt is scraped off and carried away by the water coming upon it, and so the waters burst forth from the springs filled with a more potent salt, or with a greater quantity of it.

> $08 Alterüm 'conciliari/ nequit cnm principiis Hydroftaticis: ex his enim certum habemus , aquam in tubis communicantibus, cu. jufícumque demum figurae, & perimetri, non tueri acquilibrium, nifi eandem in iis altitudinem obüuverit, hoc eft: fuperficiem in utroque tubo lineae horizontali. phyficé. parallelim conftituerit. 808 The other cannot be reconciled with the principles of Hydrostatics: for from these we hold it as certain that water in communicating tubes, of whatever figure and perimeter at last, does not keep equilibrium unless it has obtained the same height in them, that is, has set its surface in each tube physically parallel to a horizontal line. But the places of very many springs are higher than the surface of the sea. Therefore the sea water cannot ascend to the height from which springs well forth.

809 The second part is proved: Springs and rivers are had when vapors, rains, and melted snows are given; when these are taken away, they perish; when these are increased or diminished, they are increased or diminished. For it is proved by constant experience that those regions abound in springs in which it often rains and snows; whereas very few rivers are interspersed in those in which rain is rare; none in those on which no rain and snow ever falls. Then it has been found by experience that when rains last rather long the springs swell, and even after the rains have ceased the rivers still remain higher; that in dry weather springs are diminished, and in a long drought they disappear entirely.

> E MES H

810 Thus the distinguished Mariotte attests that in the year 1681, which had been very dry in France, the waters of very many springs were dried up: and he confesses that he learned by his own experience and observation that after a long drought, when the rains came on, the less deep wells received water and rose first, the deeper ones more slowly: an evident indication that a moderate rain, sufficient for replenishing the first, does not suffice for the second.

812 He relates, moreover, that on the island of St. Helena, often at night on the summit of a mountain exceeding the surface of the sea by 2400 feet, he experienced so great a condensation of vapors even in clear weather that within not many minutes it had so wetted the optical glasses that they had to be wiped, and were otherwise little fit for astronomical observations. The paper, too, on which he was writing was so quickly wetted by the falling dew that the ink was diluted by the dew: whence one may understand how great a quantity of vapors is condensed on the very lofty summits of mountains.

813 Wherefore, if we join the condensed vapors with rains and melted snows, there will be water enough to feed all springs. Besides, diggers testify from their own experience that huge reservoirs of rain and snow waters are spread out beneath the earth: of such hydrophylacia Kircher enumerates four altogether memorable: one, the chief of Asia, in the Kingdom of the Mogul; another, of Europe, under the Rhaetian Alps; the third in Africa, under the Mountains of the Moon; the fourth, among the American ones, between Peru and the Kingdom of Chile. Nor does that text of Ecclesiastes, ch. 1, stand in the way: all the rivers run into the sea . . . unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return. For it suffices that the sea waters are condensed into vapors and resolved into rain or snow for it to be truly affirmed that the rivers go out from the sea.

814 Of waters there are diverse species and properties, according to that saying of Pliny: waters are such as the earth through which they pass, understanding not only earth strictly so called, but also juices, and minerals, and in general all subterranean things from which the water flowing through can take up something. Hence the origin of hot springs, of thermal baths, and of other healthful waters. From similar causes some waters and springs are metal-bearing; and very many rivers furnish gold to the washers of their sand, while, having flowed past veins and channels teeming with gold, they carry down very minute particles.

817 That the molecules of air are subtle and minute appears from this, that they readily insinuate themselves into the pores of bodies, which is chiefly noticed by those who attempt experiments by means of the air pump. That they cohere loosely, and hence that air is porous, is taught by its fluidity; then by its impurity, since it in some manner saturates itself with the particles of other bodies, which it receives into its pores, and on account of which it very often shows itself malignant to the animal body. Its flexibility together with rigidity is evident from its elasticity, in which it is constantly and very greatly powerful: hence Descartes conjectured that air is a very rare body, like soft little feathers; Guglielmini thinks it is an aggregate of spirals twisted spherically and filled with ether, which can penetrate into their cavity only through the narrow openings of the convolutions.

818 That the aërial fluid is different from vapors and terrestrial exhalations, and hence that air consists of particles of its own proper kind, [p. 255] is evident above all from this, that it is established that vapors and exhalations ascend, but that they cannot be raised unless they are thrust out by a heavier body; so that accordingly around the globe of the Earth some other body, distinct from vapors and exhalations, which is air, must necessarily be admitted. Moreover, it is ascertained that air enclosed in a metal vessel, and even very strongly compressed, persists unchanged, which is not at all true of vapors. Finally, its elasticity is proportional to its density, and it occupies spaces which are reciprocally proportional to the compressing weights, which does not belong to vapors and exhalations.

And as regards this last, it is certain that compressed air exerts it in any directions whatever; for in whatever place a vessel full of compressed air is pierced, the air will burst out continuously; and it bursts out inasmuch as it strives to dilate itself in every direction. It is further to be observed that the spring of compressed air equals the force by which it is compressed; for it is compressed until the force by which it resists the pressure has become equal to the compressing force: for then, on account of the equilibrium, the compression is ended; and therefore the elastic force of the lower air equals the weight of the upper air in the atmosphere.

Earth, is called the atmosphere of the Earth; about its height there is no agreement among Philosophers. Nollet, having weighed all the trials that have been made by means of the barometer, says that the height of the terrestrial atmosphere cannot be less than 6 French leagues, nor can it exceed 15 or 20 leagues, and hence that the height of the atmosphere lies between these measures.

821 The ancient Philosophers divided the whole air into three spheres, or regions; the first and supreme they called that which is nearest to the lunar orbit, filled with no exhalations at all, or with very subtle ones; the lowest was held to be that which, girding the terraqueous globe most closely, is occupied by thicker and heavier exhalations: whence it is denser than the rest and more misty, and moreover now hot, now cold, according as it is regarded by the Sun now directly, now obliquely: the middle is that which is conceived as situated between the two. Hence it is deduced:

823 Next, the Sun excites winds by rarefying vapors with its heat; similarly while, by its action, the snows with which the summits of mountains are covered melt; for then the released particles press on the air and propel it toward that very region which lies beneath the Sun, since, being rarer, it resists their dilatation less; hence at the approach of spring north winds are very frequent, and south winds at the approach of autumn, because, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Cancer, the snows lying on the northern mountains begin to melt; but on the contrary, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Capricorn, the snows lying on the southern mountains are dissolved: to which is referred another cause of the winds as well, namely the admixture of the exhalations which are rather copiously scattered in the atmosphere, and the effervescence arising thence.

824 Finally, winds can have their origin in the bowels of the earth, and burst forth from them no otherwise than from the bottom of the sea; the more probable causes of these subterranean winds are subterranean fires, copious exhalations, etc. As regards the velocity of the winds, it is various. Musschenbroek says that it is gathered from Derham’s observations that the most violent winds were driven with such rapidity that they covered 66 English feet in a second, and 45 miles in the space of an hour; and, by the same witness, they had such great force that they tore apart a stone statue 12 feet high, 5 wide and 2 thick.

825 Diverse are their properties and qualities, which arise from the diverse vapors and exhalations which the winds carry down with them, and meet in their course, and snatch away with them; so that the north wind is cold, because it carries down with it a great quantity of nitrous and cold particles; the south winds tepid and humid, because they bring hot exhalations from the torrid Zone, or from the parts nearer to it, and at the same time humid vapors from the Mediterranean Sea.

826 The diversity of the winds is manifold: besides the winds, too, which are divided variously by reason of the various quarters from which they blow, there is besides another variety, relative to the time of blowing; similarly some winds are called provincial, which prevail in certain particular places or provinces; others have their diversity from their force and swiftness, or on the contrary from a gentle breath; the former are called stormy, the latter gentle; whose names and condition there is no leisure to pursue.

body is plain from this, that it communicates fluidity to other bodies, as to metals, and in others also preserves their fluidity, and brings itself back to equilibrium, as we observe in a room, where the heat is at length evenly diffused. That the molecules of fire are most subtle and most hard we gather from this, that it pervades all bodies, however compact, whereas the other fluids, even supremely volatile ones, can be kept in glasses or other vessels; then from this, that, as a universal solvent, it so tears apart and dissolves almost all bodies that by no industry of ours can they be restored to their former state; whence it is proven that the greatest mobility is in fire: it is necessary too that, to effect the motions of rarefaction, dissolution, combustion, etc., the quantity of motion in fire be very great.

Fire does not consist in sulphurous and nitrous particles agitated by the subtle matter, as the Cartesians suppose; for, to pass over many things, this is plain from this, that in the focus of a burning mirror, where the fire is so great that the imperfect metals at least turn in a short time into glass, nothing of sulphur or nitre is found; nor may one take refuge in air impregnated with these corpuscles, since the same thing happens in an exhausted receiver; nor let an escape be sought in the metals, since no sulphur is extracted by the chemists from gold, flint or diamond.

830 The colors of flame arise from its diverse matter: the blue around the base, from an oily humor not yet well concocted and dissipated; for the purer the flame is, and the greater the quantity of little fires it contains, the whiter it is; in the middle, many earthy particles mixed with the fire produce the red color, for if a small plate is thrust into the middle of the flame, it is stained with much soot, not so at the base and the tip. That the tip of the flame whitens is owing to the purified matter of the flame: besides, a kind of down appears, as it were, round the flame, which seems to be nothing else but an attenuated humor, not well kindled, and hence mixed partly with the air, partly with the fire, no otherwise than, e.g., a drop of wine mixed with water disperses itself, as it were, into certain filaments. No one hitherto (that I have seen) has treated of fire better than Boerhaave, so often and never sufficiently praised, in the Elementa Chemiae. Consult him, if you want more.

eteor means the same as appearing on high; whence the things that 831

Mare called by the Greeks meteora, or more precisely metarsia, are commonly called in Latin sublimia [lofty things]. They are conveniently divided into three kinds, or classes. The first contains the aërial or aqueous ones, in which, namely, air or water predominates. The second embraces the fiery ones, in which most subtle and spirituous exhalations prevail. The third class are the luminous or emphatic meteors, in which either solely, or at least for the greater part, light and splendor fall under consideration. A meteor, universally, is said to be an imperfect mixture consisting of certain attenuated (or, as the Chemists speak, sublimated) exhalations, and formed in the upper air. Of each we shall touch on a few things, and we shall show this general definition and nature of a meteor in each one singly.

832 A cloud is an aggregate of vapors suspended on high. It arises from vapors which at the beginning are so tenuous that they are not sensible, but which then, by the accession of some particles to others, constitute larger molecules by mutual conjunction; and these, adhering to others, form a very vast cloud, so that a cloud is accordingly to be called an aggregate of minute little bubbles in which aqueous vapors consist. Mist differs from a cloud only in its degree of density and in place; for each arises from little bubbles of humid [p. 259] exhalations agglomerated together in great quantity: they differ, however, in this, that the little bubbles constituting a cloud are far wider, and hence lighter with respect to the air, than those which make a mist, so that they lie, as it were, upon them: mist is changed into clouds by the very fact that the lower air thrusts out the bubbles, rarefied and therefore made lighter and dissipated: hence it is plain why, as the Sun approaches the meridian, mists for the most part pass into clouds.

833 Rain arises from the broken little bubbles of the clouds, which are broken from several causes: namely, either on account of the excessive heat of the Sun, by which they are very greatly dilated; or if they collide with one another by the force of contrary winds; or if they are pressed against the sides of mountains; or, finally, if they are too much constricted by an intense cold of the air. The evening damp is a certain humor, like a most subtle and insensible rain, falling from on high as night comes on; and it arises from most tenuous aqueous little bubbles, which, carried on high, are broken and turn into insensible drops as soon as the air, after sunset, is seized by some cold: hence there is none in wintertime, but only in summer, and chiefly in spring and autumn, when, moreover, no wind is blowing. And when the sky is stormy and rainy, and in winter too, those thicker droplets are dissipated by the winds, or are not dilated by rarefaction into such minute ones.

834 The morning dew differs only in respect of time: for it falls a little before the rising of the Sun, because the air is then more humid, and hence those exhalations which remained over in the air concrete; wherefore the opinion of those is less true who think that dew is nothing else than the sweat of plants, continually breathing out from the orifice of their little vessels and congealed by the force of cold; for although we do not deny this transpiration, yet something else must be affirmed of dew, since it is established that linen and woolen cloths and other bodies, glass likewise, which transmit nothing of a sweat of this kind, are sensibly wetted if they are exposed to the open air at the time when the dew is falling. Hoarfrost is nothing other than dew frozen by a sharper cold; it scorches and sucks out the tenderer crops and leaves, such as the buds of vines, indeed not seldom the vines themselves; for the nutritive juice, which, thrust out from the earth, is diffused into all the fibers of the plant, is condensed by the cold of the hoarfrost: hence the texture of the little fibers is constricted and changed.

835 Hail is rain congealed by the very cold region of the air: it is made when thin flakes of vapors, liquefied by warm air into very small drops and already tending downward, meet another, cold air, and are at once coagulated and hardened by it, new coats, as it were, being thereupon added on account of the vapors which they touch in falling. Hence it is plain why it does not hail in winter: for then the clouds are too near the Earth for very many of those very minute droplets, into which the first ones turn, to be able to come together into one before they are seized by the cold; likewise why, the higher the cloud from whose resolution the hail is formed, the larger the grains of hail are.

836 Snow is produced if the little bubbles of a humid exhalation, while turning into rain, [p. 260] are frozen by cold; for the flakes of snow are nothing else than most tenuous droplets of water, which, seized by cold, are united first among themselves like threads, when they become entangled with one another in diverse ways in their descent. The figure of snow is sometimes regular, sometimes irregular; often, if it is examined with a microscope, it shows a hexagonal star, at times a lily, and not seldom a rose; which figures seem to depend on the diverse exhalations frozen together. From these things it is easily understood what honeydew, manna, and the hair of Venus, or virgin threads, which appear like spiders’ threads over hedges and grasses, are, and whence they draw their origin.

837 The fiery meteors are, first, the flash; second, thunder; third, lightning, of which enough has been said in the Electrology; fourth, Helen and Pollux, which are fires that appear to those sailing, in the lowest region of the air, and are formed from spirituous fumes, which the sea, agitated by storms, transpires, carried up little by little, gathered together and kindled. If one appeared, it was called Helen; when two were seen, Castor and Pollux. Fifth: falling and shooting stars are certain fiery globules kindled in the upper air, and so moved through it that at times they appear to us to proceed straight, at other times to glide headlong from the sky. Sixth: the licking fire, and the foolish fire, is a fat exhalation sweating out from the flesh of men or of bodies, and from fattier matter, which is kindled by compression or friction, and clings to horses or men without harm.

838 The foolish fire is a certain marshy exhalation from putrefied plants, corpses and other oily dissolved bodies, prepared by the daily heat of the Sun, which, upon the onset of friction or fermentation, is kindled, shines, and, as it were, burns. They are called foolish fires because not only do they run hither and thither by no certain law, in the manner of a foolish man, but also because they follow those who flee them, and in turn flee those who follow them; whence they are feared by simple folk, who do not understand, namely, that this happens for the reason that he who pursues the fire, both by the motion of his body and by his breath, drives the air before him, and with it the foolish fire; while he who flees from the fire draws the air after him, and with the air the foolish fire, while he yields the place left by his body to be filled by the air.

839 Seventh: nearly the same is the account of the phenomena of the aforesaid meteors, which are distinguished among themselves only by their diverse figure; for if a marshy or bituminous exhalation, gathered together with nitrous spirits and suddenly kindled in the upper air by means of fermentation, friction or compression, presents the appearance of a fiery globe, and has about it hanging flakes, as it were, and is borne with a leaping motion, it is called the Leaping Goat; if it is oblong and parallel to the horizon, the Beam; if it swells in its middle, the Dragon; if it is round and flat, the Shield; if smooth and cylindrical, the Column; if it ends in a point, the Pyramid; if it is widely dispersed and shows, as it were, kindled straws, it is named the Stubble. Eighth: the Aurora Borealis, or northern light, is

[p. 261] that glow which in the nighttime at times appears to us in the northern quarter of the sky in such a way that the sky itself seems, as it were, to burn in that part. The history of this phenomenon is extensive; since it is found everywhere among the Moderns, for brevity’s sake I adduce only what is necessary.

840 In the first place, it has its seat in the atmosphere of the Earth, like the other fiery meteors, and is produced in it; for this light has at times been seen below the clouds, as Mayer testifies: then, if it extended beyond the atmosphere, it would be very high, and hence would be seen even from places near the equator, which, however, is contrary to experience, especially since it often happens that it is seen in one place and is not observed in another a few miles distant. Wherefore we think that this light, like the remaining fiery meteors, comes from an exhalation and vapor carried on high from the earth, or from the matter of lightning and of flashes not yet well ripened, so to speak, and not yet prepared for the effects of lightning and of flashes.

841 The luminous or Emphatic meteors are: first, the Rainbow, which is a many-colored arc formed in a dewy cloud by the refraction and reflection of the Sun opposite; whence it either brings down or naturally indicates rain, but without a great flood of waters; for clouds too heavily laden are not fit for reflecting and thus refracting the rays of the Sun. The more conspicuous colors of the rainbow are: red or crimson, yellow, green, blue, and finally purple or violet; and these in the primary rainbow hold the order mentioned and are more vivid; but in the secondary the reverse, so that in its outermost part the purple shines, then the blue, etc.; which are also seen weaker and more diluted.

842 That rainbow, moreover, is called primary which reaches the eye after two refractions of the rays and one reflection, and is seen at an angle of about 42 degrees; and the secondary, that which falls into the eye after two refractions and as many reflections, at an angle of about 52 degrees. It is to be noticed that the rainbow is not seen unless the sight is between the Sun and the dewy cloud; so when you sprinkle water from your mouth toward the light let in through windows, and stand between the Sun and the drops, you behold a rainbow, of which you also have other analogies in little leaping fountains, in spiders’ webs, on the neck of a dove, in flowers or grasses sprinkled with dew about sunrise and viewed in the due situation and place.

844 If the Halo is condensed ever larger and larger, it presages rain, because the clouds gradually concrete into a shower; if it is dissipated on many sides, or even on one side, it indicates winds arising either from several quarters or from one; if it vanishes wholly, it foretells fair weather, for then the clouds are dissipated by the force of heat. Third: the Parhelion and Paraselene are luminous meteors standing beside the Sun or the Moon and showing the images of those stars; for as often as a cloud apt to be resolved very soon into waters, diaphanous, too, toward the Sun, but terminated on the other side like a mirror, runs up to the Sun, not below it toward the earth, nor directly opposite, but at the sides and obliquely, either toward the north or toward the south, so often the Sun impresses its own image upon it, which, reflected thence to our eyes, represents the Sun to us in the cloud, so that the ignorant judge that twin Suns are shining. Moreover, it can happen that the image of the Sun, impressed in like manner on one cloud, induces again another image on a second cloud, and this again on another; the same is to be thought, proportionally, of the Moon.

> / CAPUT. POSTREMUM. . . Quid de Plantis dicendum fit.

845 Fourth: Rods are formed in the air when a straight tract of clouds shows diverse colors, for the same cause for which these are formed in the rainbow or the crown. Fifth: we call it a Chasm, a Gap, or a Pit, when on a clear night exhalations carried upward, denser in the middle and rarer in the remaining part, are placed between the light of the stars and our eye; for if they are many, they show a chasm; if fewer, a gap; if extended lengthwise, a pit or lake; since on account of the density in the middle they are less illuminated, and everything dark, although equally near and placed in the same surface, always seems more remote and more depressed, while what is bright seems nearer and more elevated. Let it suffice to have said this, in compendium, on a most copious matter.

What is to be said of Plants.

lants, by which name every kind of growth that bursts forth from the 846

P        earth is understood, are organic bodies consisting of a varied apparatus

> . animata. Adparatüm mirabilem organicorum horum corporum perqut. / B fivé [p. 263]  me 2M — [

of organic parts most wisely co-ordinated and joined together, adhering to the earth by their roots, and animated by the influx of a suitable juice going round and returning in a circuit. The wonderful apparatus of these organic bodies was investigated [p. 263] and explained by Malpighi the Italian and Grew the Englishman. Life, in a manner, and its actions are accomplished in plants by the continual motion, returning in a circuit, of the vital fluid through solid organs most wisely disposed; which motion the agitation, impulse and pressure of the ether and the air bring about, the elastic force mediating at the same time; so that on that account they are rightly called Hydraulic-Pneumatic machines; and that these may be understood more deeply, I subjoin a very brief Anatomy of them.

> ELEM. PHYSICES. EETI fivére,& explicuere Ma/pighius 1talus,& Grevius Anglus, Vita qucdin-

847 Of the parts of plants, some are fluid, others solid. The fluid part is that humor or juice which, like the blood in man, is diffused through the solid parts of the plant. This juice, and the true and genuine nourishment of plants, they say most probably to be saline, earthy and oily parts, which, prepared in the aqueous juice, attenuated, worked up, and distributed with this juice, as with a vehicle, into the whole structure of the plants, are carried round, so that the single parts can receive what is suitable for nourishing and increasing their substance. The solid parts constitute their organic body, and are: the trunk, roots, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits. The trunk, which in trees is called the bole and stock, in flowers and herbs the stalk, scape and thyrsus, in wheat and the like the straw or haulm, is, as it were, the body of the plant, which, bursting forth from the earth, rises above it and unfolds itself into branches, fronds, etc. The root is that part of the plant which, placed wholly below the earth and adhering to it, draws its nourishment for the plant. The branches, just as the limbs from the body of an animal, so burst forth from the body, or trunk, of the plant, for the most part without order, sometimes in an elegant order, and spread themselves in every direction; being of altogether the same nature as the trunk from which they arise, and furnished like it with bark, they contain pith in the middle, and are composed of the same little vessels, namely fibers, utricles and tracheae. The leaves embrace chiefly two parts: namely, the petiole, by which the leaf is attached to the plant, and the very body of the leaf.

848 The flowers are, as it were, the first offspring of the plant; in them four parts are distinguished, namely: the calyx, which is the base and support of the flower; the petals, which rise above the calyx, propagated from the dilated stalk, and consist of woody tubes, or fibers, of tracheae too, and at the same time of a manifold order of utricles; the stamens burst forth from the lowest part of the flower, various in number and figure: they consist of a filament and an attached capsule, which is made up of woody tubes, tracheae and utricles placed lengthwise: the style, finally, is that part of the flower which, occupying its center, hides and cherishes the seed of the plant in its cavity. The fruit is the last work of plants, to the producing and perfecting of which all the remaining parts are destined; it consists, moreover, of an envelope and the seed; the former differs according to the specific difference of the fruits, and is manifold, and of diverse consistency and firmness in diverse fruits; the seed pertains to the origin of plants: of which briefly.

Ll [p. 264] the first, or outermost of all, is harder than the rest; when it is removed, two little skins are met, of which the exterior is thick and almost cartilaginous, the interior very subtle, so that in a dried seed it can scarcely be separated from the exterior.

> " ^ x s -"Qorolanum. "5 5

After these integuments, which are called secundines, two or even more lobes come into view, enclosed in a certain thin and pellucid membrane, which is fourth in order; and they embrace, in a kind of little ditch, as it were, hollowed out on either side in the lobes, the germ of the future plant; which is nothing else than the whole plant itself that is to arise from the seed, complete in all its parts, namely trunk, or stalk, roots, branches, etc., so that the seminal plantlet lying hidden in the germ does not differ from the adult except in the size of its parts.

850 The rising from the seed, further, is accomplished in this way: when the seed is committed to suitable earth, the fibers of its membranes are gently loosened by the heat of the earth and of the Sun, and their passages are dilated; whence it comes about that the humor in which the earth abounds gradually enters them, is variously strained in them, ferments, and is made apt for nutrition: the nutritive juice, strained in the membranes, enters the substance of the lobes, where it is mixed with the specific juice of the plantlet, ferments, and takes on new parts; this juice, prepared in due manner in the lobes, enters the most subtle pores of the radicle of the germ itself and insinuates itself into its little fibers; and the radicle, nourished and increased by this juice, bursts forth outward, spreads out its hair, and by means of those filaments is inserted into the earth; the root being sufficiently increased, a more lively portion of the nutritive liquor passes into the remaining part of the germ, and, irradiating and impelling its parts, communicates motion to them; hence are evolved and unfolded the parts of the future plant, which lie hidden in the germ, rolled up and folded together among themselves; then by degrees these same parts are increased and come into view in their order: so that from this first evolution of the seed the remaining growth of the plant is easily understood.

There are therefore no plants that are not generated from seed. Certainly the peculiar disposition of plants, the collocation of their parts in wonderful order and distinction, the little veins, utricles and tracheae, for producing flowers and fruits of the same species, make it manifest that plants are not born from a fortuitous concourse of the elements, or from putrid matter. This very thing is shown by an experiment of Malpighi, who had enclosed earth dug out of a rather deep pit in a vessel in such a way as to cover its upper part with very delicate cloths, so that entrance into the vessel lay open to the air and the rain, but not to other very minute corpuscles carried through the air; and so he exposed it to the rays of the Sun. He found that after a very long time no herb, or sign of a plant, appeared; so that on that account he inferred that, since no seed had either lain hidden before in the earth [p. 265] dug out from deeper down, or could have fallen into the vessel through the air, plants have their genesis from seed.

852 As regards the nutrition and growth of plants, it is accomplished by the admission, elaboration and purification of a suitable juice, and by its continual circulation through the organs of the plant; for the roots draw in moisture; this, once received, ascends through the woody tubes of the plant, because it is urged upward unceasingly by the alternate dilatation and constriction of the tracheae which are interspersed among the woody tubes; and from these it is dispersed into the other parts. That the nutritive juice circulates is shown, first of all, because only in this way does it seem that the nutrition of plants can be accomplished; since indeed this cannot take place unless that which is useful, and is suitable nourishment for the plant, is separated from the useless, and this is thrust back again to those parts, so that it may be rendered fit for nutrition through a new purification and elaboration; and then it is plain from experience; for Malpighi, when the bark had been cut round in a circle and a ring-shaped portion torn away, found that the edge of the upper bark swelled notably and also increased, but that the lower obtained no increase, but only put forth buds in their season. And let these things, which have been excerpted from Fr. Klaus, suffice to have been said, so that we may put the finishing hand to the Physics, both General and Particular.

853 But if to anyone perhaps some of the things which I have brought forward in these Elements of the Newer Philosophy should seem briefer than was fitting, I would wish him to consider that I have written for Young Men alone. Many large volumes of learned men, far fuller ones, are available for the convenience of others. Nor yet would I think on that account that I have failed in my office, since I judged it more useful to make plain whatever could cause trouble to beginners, and with these Elements rather to help the American Youth than to burden them with a greater mass of disputations. For Philosophy is to be acquired both by meditation and by experiments, and it has nothing of great advantage placed in prolixity.
